title: Constraint-Aware Test-Time Scoring for LLM and VLM Candidate Selection
summary: When an LLM or VLM produces several candidate answers, picking the best one usually relies on the model's own confidence, a learned judge model, or a domain check. Each has a known weakness: an answer can be fluent but insecure, mathematically plausible but physically infeasible, or rated highly by a judge while quietly breaking a task requirement. We propose a scoring framework that combines a small set of hard checks every answer must pass with a wider set of softer checks whose scores are blended into one number per candidate. This adaptive scoring framework consists of three components: a drafting model that produces the candidates, a configuring model that selects and weights the checks for each task, and scoring models that rate properties no grounded tool can compute. We apply our proposed method to four tasks: writing code that is both correct and secure (CWEval), generating robot manipulation plans (LIBERO with added safety variants), passing competitive-programming hidden tests (LiveCodeBench), and answering questions from retrieved documents (HotpotQA). An ablation study isolates the contribution of each component and finds that the largest gains come from combining hard checks with candidate comparison: on tasks where the first sampled answer is often broken or unsafe, this pairing lifts joint correctness-and-safety by up to +0.21 (retrieval-augmented QA) and code-generation safety by up to +0.28 (CWEval), with the size of the gain tracking how weak the first sample is, falling to near zero or slightly negative where it is already strong. The per-task layer that selects and weights the softer checks adds no measurable value over simpler alternatives. This builds a unified scoring framework, together with an ablation that identifies the grounded hard checks, not the soft-factor configuration, as the source of the gain.

Introduction LLMs and VLMs are increasingly deployed in scenarios where wrong outputs carry real consequences: code that runs against production systems, plans that drive physical hardware, factual claims that inform decisions. The failure modes that matter are not surface errors but confident outputs that look right and act wrong. To solve this, there are commonly two recipes. The first is to ground the output against something other than the model: compilers and unit tests for code, symbolic planners and collision checks for robot plans, retrieval and entailment for factual claims. These are reliable where they apply, but each is narrow. A compiler verifies that code is well-formed, not that it solves the problem. A kinematic check verifies that a trajectory is realisable, not that it achieves the goal. The reliable part of a grounded check is what its formalism expresses, and the formalism never expresses everything that can go wrong. The second is to ask another model. Best-of- with a learned verifier, process reward models, and LLM-as-judge frameworks all take this shape cobbe2021gsm8k,lightman2024lets,zheng2023judging ; recent work scales by ensembling model-based verifiers lifshitz2025multiagent,llmasfuser2025 . This generalises across tasks, but the verifier shares the original model's weaknesses. Errors decorrelate partially, not fully: miscalibrated confidence llmasfuser2025 , agreement that reflects shared rather than independent reasoning entanglement2026 , bias toward outputs from the same model family judgemultilingual2025 . Neither recipe is sufficient alone. kambhampati2024llmmodulo argues that LLMs cannot reliably plan or self-verify but can be productive inside systems that integrate them with grounded checks; the position has held up across robotics ahn2022saycan,huang2022inner,liang2023codeaspolicies,song2023progprompt,grigorev2025verifyllm,spca2026 , code generation, and structured reasoning. What is missing is a principled way to combine the two when each contributes partial coverage. Recent work combines grounded and model-emitted checks in pipelines for RL training verif2025,t3rl2026 , but at test-time selection existing systems typically commit to one validator type: SayCan ahn2022saycan multiplies an LLM utility with one learned affordance value; RoVer rover2025 applies a single learned PRM; TPVQA tpvqa2023 validates against a symbolic planner; RoboMonkey robomonkey2025 selects with one VLM. A practitioner with both a kinematic check and a VLM scorer has no off-the-shelf machinery for combining them, and the literature has not carefully ablated which pieces of such a combination actually contribute. We introduce a scoring framework for this gap. Unlike verification, which asks whether a single output satisfies a goal property (e.g.\ obstacle avoidance, reachability), scoring asks which of several candidate outputs to pick. The candidates need not include a correct one, and the framework does not certify that the chosen output is correct; it only ranks the candidates by how well they meet the available checks. For a task class, the architect fixes a backbone of universal grounded checks any acceptable output must satisfy. For a specific task, a configuring model selects optional checks and weights for softer factors. The configuring model is kept distinct from the model producing candidates, so it cannot tilt the scoring rule toward the candidates it would itself have produced; the same conceptual gap that produces a faulty plan does not also produce a configuration that fails to look for the fault. The checks produce outputs of different types (pass/fail flags, continuous margins, judge scores), and we normalise them to a common scale before combining log-linearly, with hard vetoes (a check whose failure removes the candidate from the pool regardless of other scores) for backbone failures and soft penalties for safety-critical violations. We evaluate our strategy on four domains spanning binary and continuous outcomes: robot manipulation on LIBERO with SafeLIBERO augmentations, joint correctness-and-security code generation on CWEval, contamination-controlled code generation on LiveCodeBench, and retrieval-augmented QA on HotpotQA. We make four contributions: We build a unified test-time scoring framework that handles checks of mixed type (pass/fail, continuous, probabilistic) under one rule, with hard vetoes for the strict checks and soft penalties for the graded ones; the same scoring core runs unchanged across the four domains above despite their very different output spaces and check types. We present a component-level ablation that disentangles which parts of the pipeline improve selection and which do not. We uncover a fundamental obstacle to per-task configuration of the soft factors: a dedicated model that chooses and weights them performs no better than three simpler alternatives (uniform weights, letting the generator weight them itself, or a learned linear combiner fit to the same features), and when a single grounded factor dominates the pool, simply selecting the candidate that maximises that one factor does better still. We identify the mechanism behind this negative result: soft-factor scores cluster too tightly among the survivors of the hard checks for re-weighting to change the top pick. The framework is intended as a universal scaffold that applies across the domains we consider (code generation, robot manipulation planning, retrieval-augmented QA) and is portable to others where similar checks exist. Its significance is therefore broader than any one of the four benchmarks. For robotics, it offers a principled way to let a non-negotiable physical check (reachability, collision, a keep-away margin around a fragile object or a person) override a VLM's opinion about a plan, so that a planner built from off-the-shelf components can be made safer without retraining the models involved. For software engineering, the same structure turns a collection of existing tools (compilers, test runners, static analysers, security judges) into a single selection rule, and the verdict it produces can be fed back to the generator as a structured repair signal. For retrieval-augmented systems, it gives a way to enforce that answers cite documents that exist before a judge is asked to rate them. Beyond these applications, the ablation tells practitioners building any selection pipeline where to invest effort (in eliciting reliable hard checks) and where not to (in tuning how soft factors are blended). Related Work Test-time verification of LLM outputs A substantial line of work scales test-time compute by sampling multiple candidates and selecting with a verifier. Best-of- cobbe2021gsm8k picks the highest-scoring under a learned reward model. Verifiers have evolved from discriminative reward models to process reward models lightman2024lets,uesato2022solving , generative verifiers zhang2024generative , and thinking verifiers that produce verification rationales thinkprm2025,rewardingprogress2025 ; surveys catalogue the design space verificationsurvey2025 . More recent work derives continuous verifier scores from scoring-token logits and scales verification by decomposing the criteria a judge is asked to check kwok2026verifier , scores candidates jointly rather than one at a time kim2026multiseq , and studies best-of- when only partial, per-claim verification is available zhang2026boe . Large-scale audits of LLM judges find that high agreement and consistency coexist with severe position and format sensitivity norman2026reliability,dev2026harness , which is one reason we confine model-emitted scores to the soft-factor pool. The closest related line of work is multi-verifier ensembling. Multi-Agent Verification lifshitz2025multiagent combines aspect verifiers each prompted to check a different property; LLM-as-a-Fuser llmasfuser2025 ensembles model judgements to reduce overconfidence. Both beat a single verifier, though the verifiers they combine are all model-based and share failure modes entanglement2026 . A second wave combines grounded and model-emitted verification directly at training time: VerIF verif2025 pairs rule-based code verification with LLM verification when training instruction-following models, T RL t3rl2026 uses code-execution evidence to upweight verified rollouts during test-time reinforcement learning updates, and Reasoning Arena zhou2026arena applies a rule verifier first and falls back to LLM-judge tournaments only where the verifier gives no signal. AutoPyVerifier pezeshkpour2026autopy learns a minimal set of executable checks whose conjunction approximates a target objective, and finds that the checks it retains are predominantly structural and grounded, which is consistent with our finding that the grounded factors carry the signal. Our framework adopts the same hybrid grounded-plus-model structure but treats the two sources differently: grounded checks can sit in the hard backbone and override soft factors entirely, while model-emitted checks are confined to the soft-factor pool. The test-time selection setting, that structural separation, and the ablation of which pieces contribute are what distinguish our work. A closely related finding from a different domain is that equal-weighted multi-dimensional rubrics underperform their best individual dimensions when dimensions differ in predictive validity criterionvalidity2026 . The mechanism (a strong dimension diluted by weak ones in a fixed-weight combiner) is structurally the same as one we report on LiveCodeBench. A separate line of work is the LLM-modulo framework kambhampati2024llmmodulo : LLMs cannot reliably self-verify but can be productive inside systems with external symbolic verifiers. We extend it by treating the integration as a scoring problem rather than an iterative refinement loop, allowing checks of mixed types, and formalising how heterogeneous scores combine. Grounded verification of LLM-generated plans in robotics Grounding LLM outputs against the physical world has been central to LLM-based planners since their first wave. SayCan ahn2022say

title: Why Does Sensor Depth Fail Learned Manipulation Policies? Finding the Failure Mode with ACT
summary: Learned manipulation policies, from task-specific imitation policies to vision-language-action (VLA) models, rely primarily on RGB images. While some studies report gains from sensor depth, others avoid depth cameras because of measurement noise. Depth cameras introduce both noise and missing depth values (holes), whose relative effects remain unclear. In this study, we calibrate a sensor model using a real wrist-mounted stereo camera and separately evaluate noise and holes on RGB-D imitation policies with three visual encoders in simulation. We found that complete depth improves success by approximately ten percentage points, and most of this gain persists even at twenty times the camera's noise level. In contrast, holes covering about one-sixth of the wrist image eliminate the detectable benefit of depth. The validity mask strongly influences depth reliance: marking a small fraction of pixels as invalid reduces reliance, while filling holes and marking them valid restores most of the benefit. Policies trained on clean depth also lose performance when holes appear only at deployment, sometimes falling below RGB-only performance. These findings suggest that depth cameras for learned policies should therefore be judged by depth coverage more than measurement precision.

Perception for grasping and manipulation; RGB-D perception; deep learning for visual perception; imitation learning. Introduction sec:intro ision -language-action (VLA) models have emerged as a prominent approach to robot manipulation and are pretrained on large-scale images and texts datasets, which gives them a strong sense of what objects are and what an instruction asks for rt2,openvla,pizero . However, robotic manipulation is also a geometric problem, and a robot must know about the position of an object relative to its gripper to grasp or place it precisely. While an RGB image provides indirect cues about the pose and relative distance of a three-dimensional geometry, a depth sensor can directly measure distances in metric units. As a result, VLA models and task-specific manipulation policies are increasingly incorporating depth maps or point clouds as additional inputs. However, existing studies differ on whether depth information should be acquired directly from sensors or inferred through learning-based policies. Studies such as 3D Diffusion Policy~ ze2024dp3 , RISE~ wang2024rise , iDP3~ ze2024idp3 , FP3~ yang2025fp3 , 3D Diffuser Actor~ ke2024dda , Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) and Vision Language Action (VLA) policies~ pointact2025,chen2026pointact etc. incorporates depth maps or point clouds through direct sensor measurements and report improved performance. In contrast, several other studies seek to eliminate the need for depth sensors during deployment by estimating or predicting depth from images, thereby distilling geometric information into the policy, or add 3D supervision during training for inferring depth depthvla2025,qdepthvla2025,peafowl2026,di22024,augvla2026,g3vla2026,spatialforcing2025,evodepth2026,stereopolicy2026 . A common motivation for these approaches is the susceptibility of depth sensors to measurement noise and missing depth information~ evodepth2026,stereopolicy2026,qdepthvla2025,peafowl2026,spatialforcing2025 . One possible explanation for these differing findings is that ``sensor quality'' encompasses two distinct limitations: measurement noise and missing depth values (holes). Measurement noise affects the accuracy of valid depth measurements, whereas holes occur when the sensor fails to return a depth value. A camera or sensor can be very precise where it provides a measured value, and at the same time, may leave a large part of the image without any depth information (holes). Consequently, a sensor may provide accurate measurements while exhibiting substantial missing data. Previous studies have extensively characterized measurement accuracy of depth and associated noise~ servi2021realsense,servi2024realsense,ahn2019d435 ,however, the impact of missing depth or holes on robotic manipulation remains less understood. We therefore ask three questions: (1) Does complete depth information improve manipulation performance? (2) How do measurement noise and missing depth values (holes) independently affect this benefit? (3) What causes the performance degradation, and how can it be mitigated? To address these questions, we characterize the distance-dependent noise and missing-depth rate of a real wrist-mounted stereo camera on a teleoperated robot. Using noise-free depth rendered in simulation, we independently introduce measurement noise and missing values at the measured levels and under scaled perturbations. We evaluate Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) policies~ zhao2023act using three visual encoders: ResNet-18 trained from scratch, DINOv2~ oquab2024dinov2 with 2D pretraining, and ~ moge2 with geometric pretraining. We quantify the contribution of depth using two metrics: benefit, defined as the improvement in task success relative to an RGB-only policy with the same encoder, and reliance, defined as the reduction in success when depth input is removed at deployment. All policy evaluations are conducted in simulation using ACT, without training VLA models. Fig.~ fig:teaser summarizes the key findings. Complete depth information improves manipulation performance, and most of this benefit persists even when measurement noise increases to 20 times the measured level. In contrast, depth holes eliminate the benefit by causing policies to disregard depth information. This behavior is driven by the validity mask, which distinguishes missing depth from measured depth values. By filling the holes and marking them as valid restores most of the benefit. Moreover, policies trained on complete depth can perform worse than RGB-only policies when depth holes are introduced at deployment. These trends are consistent across all three visual encoders. This paper makes four contributions: (1) a controlled evaluation of depth noise and holes, with a sensor model fitted to a real wrist camera; (2) provide evidence that the holes, not noise, remove the benefit of sensor depth for the studied policies; (3) provide evidence that validity masks cause policies to disregard incomplete depth information; and (4) provide practical guidance for depth sensor selection and preprocessing, along with a metric (reliance) to quantify whether a trained policy uses depth information. Study Design sec:design To isolate the effects of individual depth input qualities, experiments need to be designed such that one property varies at a time while holding all others constant. Since measurement noise and missing depth values cannot be independently controlled on a physical camera, we render ground-truth depth in the ManiSkill3 simulator~ maniskill3 and introduce controlled degradations using a model calibrated to real camera measurements. The experimental setup consists of a 7 degrees-of-freedom Franka Emika Panda robotic arm equipped with a wrist-mounted camera and a third-person camera. We employ a factorial design across depth conditions and visual encoders, maintaining identical policy architectures, demonstrations, action spaces, evaluation episodes, and training schedules across all configurations. Sensor Model Fitted to a Real Wrist Camera sec:sensor We recorded teleoperated episodes at ~Hz on a Franka Emika Panda driven by a GELLO leader arm~ wu2024gello (Fig.~ fig:design a). The episodes cover task families, such as pick-and-place, stacking, pushing and drawer opening. The wrist camera is an Intel RealSense D405, a short-range stereo camera with an 18\,mm baseline and a rated range of 7--50\,cm. The third-person camera is a RealSense D435. To quantify depth measurement noise, we select a fixed ,cm patch on the table and record its depth measurements across successive video frames. For each frame, a best-fit plane is estimated from the valid 3D points within the patch, and the noise level is defined as the root-mean-square distance of these points from the fitted plane. The depth hole rate is defined as the fraction of pixels in each frame without valid depth measurements (Fig.~ fig:design c). For the wrist camera, the hole rate ranges from in the nearest distance to in the farthest, reaching a maximum of at intermediate distances. The rate also depends on surface characteristics, as stereo matching relies on visual texture and can fail on reflective or transparent surfaces. Using the calibrated sensor model, we independently introduce depth noise and missing values into the simulated depth maps. Measurement noise is modeled as zero-mean Gaussian noise applied independently to each pixel, with the standard deviation determined by its depth. This model excludes systematic bias, spatial noise correlation, and artifacts near depth discontinuities, such as flying pixels. title: FOCI: Trajectory Optimization on Gaussian Splats for Gaussian Robots
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has recently gained popularity as a faster alternative to Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) in 3D reconstruction and view synthesis methods. Leveraging the spatial information encoded in 3DGS, this work proposes FOCI (Field Overlap Collision Integral), an algorithm that is able to optimize trajectories directly on the Gaussians themselves. FOCI leverages a novel and interpretable collision formulation for 3DGS using the notion of the overlap integral between Gaussians. The formulation presented applies to different robot morphologies (e.g., fixed and mobile base manipulators, legged robots, UAVs) and handles both static and dynamic Gaussian-Splat environments. Contrary to other approaches, which represent the robot with conservative bounding boxes that underestimate the traversability of the environment, we propose to represent the environment and the robot as Gaussian Splats. This not only has desirable computational properties, but also allows for orientation-aware planning, allowing the robot to pass through very tight and narrow spaces. We extensively test our algorithm in both synthetic and real Gaussian Splats, showcasing that collision-free trajectories for legged, aerial and manipulator robots can be computed in seconds, even with hundreds of thousands of Gaussians making up the environment. The code is available at https://github.com/leggedrobotics/foci

Supplementary Material : \\ Code: : \\ Code: INTRODUCTION Trajectory planning is integral to autonomous mobile robotics to ensure guided and safe operation. However, in order to make an informed decision, these planning algorithms heavily depend on the underlying environment representations. Popular representations include occupancy grids, signed distance fields, 3D Meshes, and point clouds. Recently, ~ Mildenhall2020 have been proposed as a novel neural representation of the environment. However, they suffer from having slow inference speeds because new views have to be created using a computationally expensive ray-casting procedure. More recently, ~ Kerbl2023 has been proposed as a promising alternative to . Instead of using a neural network to represent the radiance field, it is defined explicitly by a set of 3D Gaussian ellipsoids. Because of this, new views can be efficiently generated by projecting these ellipsoids into the view plane. Given the advantages that offers when compared with , the natural question is how a robot can leverage this Gaussian representation for navigation. In this paper, we propose an algorithm that enables a robot to perform trajectory optimization directly on the 3D Gaussians. Although some steps have been taken in this direction~ Chen2024,lei2025gaussnav,goel2025distance, marticorena2025remosplat , the huge number of Gaussians a scene can have, together with the specific formulation of an explicit collision measure, makes this problem especially hard. To overcome these challenges, we propose FOCI, a trajectory optimization algorithm that leverages the overlap integral -- the spatial integral over the multiplication of two functions -- as a proxy measure for the collision between two Gaussians. By representing both the robot and the environment with 3D Gaussians, evaluating the full-body collision between them reduces to a sum of normal distribution evaluations. Furthermore, the resulting expression is fully differentiable, yielding expressive gradients in the optimization step. This work extends , and its contributions are summarized as follows: 1pt 0pt 2pt A novel collision measure between Gaussian Splats based on the overlap integral between Gaussians. A GPU implementation of the trajectory optimization. An evaluation of the proposed algorithm on the ANYmal legged robot in simulation and the real world . In particular, the new contributions of this version with respect to are: ) 1pt 0pt Background and Related Work Radiance Fields Radiance Fields are widely used in visual computing to represent 3D scenes and perform novel view synthesis. The preliminary form is a ~ Mildenhall2020 , which provides a neural mapping from position in space and a viewing angle to visual density and color along a ray. As an alternative, ~ Kerbl2023 produces similar quality reconstruction with an explicit basis at far faster speeds. creates a series of 3D Gaussian ellipsoids with colors and Spherical Harmonics~ fridovich2022plenoxels to encode view-dependent effects. Instead of ray casting each Gaussian, the ellipsoids are splatted~ 964490 onto the viewing plane for rasterization levels of speed. Trajectory Optimization Standard Methods Trajectory planning generates a path for a robot that is collision-free with the surrounding environment and further minimizes a performance metric such as execution time or control efforts. Depending on the formulation, trajectory optimization also includes optimizing control inputs to follow the trajectory. Similar to other works~ Chen2024,lei2025gaussnav,jin2024gs , we assume robust low-level control that can track reasonably smooth state trajectories, so we omit the control inputs in our optimization formulation. Graph-based methods such as A*~ astar , and sampling-based methods such as RRT*~ karaman2011anytime are straight-forward to implement and produce a series of collision-free waypoints. Trajectories produced by graph-based methods are often good initial guesses for other approaches. Unlike graph- or sampling-based methods, spline-based methods optimize a continuous trajectory instead of a series of waypoints. Collision avoidance is ensured by either constraining the convex hull of this spline to a predetermined safety corridor or by ensuring no collision at discretized points along the spline. Zhou~et~al.~ Zhou2020 obtain an obstacle gradient to push spline trajectories out of obstacles to achieve collision-free trajectories while Gao et al.~ gao2016,Gao2019 construct a safe flight corridor around an RRT* path through a point cloud and optimize a spline trajectory inside the corridor to ensure safety. Radiance Field Methods There are numerous trajectory optimizing algorithms designed to work on standard scene representations such as meshes or point clouds, and now -- with the recent emergence of Radiance Fields -- are being used to tackle the problem. Planning directly on Radiance Fields can be favorable as they are often trained from monocular images, and the extensive reconstruction allows for their use in multiple downstream tasks from planning and SLAM to teleoperation. Pantic~et~al.~ Pantic2022 propose a method to obtain an directly from a by inserting an additional head into the neural network to output the encoded distance. Adamkiewicz et al.~ adamkiewicz2022vision directly use the opacity output by the as a collision measure at a set of points of the robot body. Starting from an A*-initial guess, a joint cost function consisting of a control effort and opacity term at the control points is minimized. In CATNIPS~ Chen2023 , a probabilistic approach is used and shows that a is equivalent to a Poisson Point Process, which allows for direct quantification of the collision probability. Using this property, they formulate a chance constraint trajectory optimization. Due to its novelty, few papers have been published on trajectory optimization for Gaussian Splats. In GaussNav~ lei2025gaussnav , Lei et al. reduce the Gaussian Splat to a point cloud of its means, which is voxelized and then projected to a two-dimensional cost map where trajectories are planned. This produces quick results but does not fully leverage the explicit 3D nature of . Splat-Nav~ Chen2024 additionally takes the covariances of the Gaussians into account and computes a polyhedral safety corridor around an A* initial guess. The free space is determined by calculating the distance between the robot ellipsoid and the confidence intervals of the environment Gaussians. Inside this safety corridor, a spline trajectory is optimized to produce a safe path. The GS-Planner~ jin2024gs constrains the position along the trajectory to be outside of the confidence interval of the joint Gaussian of the ellipsoid and robot radius. Unlike Splat-Nav~ Chen2024 , which uses a safety corridor as an intermediate representation, this constraint is directly imposed on the spline. Goel and Tabib~ goel2025distance propose a method to derive an and collision probability of a Gaussian Surface Model (GSM) for an ellipsoidal robot with a fixed orientation, which can then be used to plan trajectories. While these works present considerable steps towards planning, they consider only ellipsoidal robots with a fixed orientation. However, in real-world settings~ dong2024efficient, Funk2023 , optimizing orientation is crucial to navigating through narrow passageways. By leveraging a detailed whole-body overlap model, we propose a solution to this shortcoming. Table~ tab:comparison provides an overview of how our algorithm compares to related work. Method Our methodology can be split into three parts: 1) trajectory representation to create an initial spline, 2) collision measure and 3) optimization loop. . Trajectory Representation We employ cubic B-splines for the optimization to generate fully differentiable and smooth trajectories in dimensions. With B-splines, every point along the trajectory can be expressed as a weighted sum of the control points of the trajectory. Since we are using unclamped uniform cubic B-splines, each spline segment is parameterized by control points, resulting in individual segments. The progress along the trajectory is usually parameterized by a progress variable , which can (but is not required to) be equal to the system time . Using knots , the spline is parameterized on . Since each individual spline segment is parameterized between , we define with to index the corresponding segment. title: RoboARC: Physical Puzzles for Robotic Manipulation under Spatial Constraints
summary: Many hard manipulation tasks come down to a spatial constraint that only a few motions satisfy, such as passing a part through a gap barely wider than itself or separating two interlocked parts. These motions depend on the exact geometry of each scene, so demonstrations and skills recorded elsewhere rarely transfer. We therefore ask: when manipulation hinges on spatial constraints, can robots reason out the right motions? We introduce RoboARC, a benchmark of 90 tasks in six constraint types over rigid and soft materials, on three robots in MuJoCo. Every task is a frozen scene with a physics-based grader and a verified reference solution that replays bit-identically. Each task comes in a Privileged regime, with the full simulator state and resets, and a Standard regime with real-sensor inputs (camera images and proprioception) and a single attempt without resets. We evaluate seven coding agents and four VLA policies, none trained on these tasks. The strongest agent, GPT-6 Astra in Codex, solves 86% of the tasks in the Privileged regime and 43% in the Standard regime, and the four VLA policies, run zero-shot, solve none of their 18 one-arm puzzles. On 15 puzzles that GPT-6 Astra solved in the Privileged regime and failed in the Standard regime, object poses add 4 points and part geometry 13, but both together add 36, from 24% to 60%. Only 7% of the coding agents' failed runs pass more than half of a task, and 53% of the failed runs in the Standard regime are stuck on a single step. Frontier coding agents already reason out the right motions for many of these tasks once they know where the parts are and what shape they have. From their own sensors, in a single attempt, the strongest solves fewer than half of the tasks. The website can be found at https://roboarc.embodied-first-exam.ai

Untangling a cable, threading a rope through a fixture or sliding a board into a frame~ grannen2020untangling,seita2021deformableravens,lee2021ikea succeeds only along the few motions that a spatial constraint leaves open: a gap barely wider than the part, two parts that interlock, or a rope that must not pass through itself. Which motions remain is set by the exact geometry of the scene and changes from scene to scene. Policies learned from demonstrations, as in vision-language-action (VLA) models~ zitkovich2023rt2,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0 , and programs composed from known skills~ liang2023codeaspolicies,huang2023voxposer succeed when the right motion resembles one seen before, such as a grasp, a push or a placement. Coding agents built on models that reason well in symbolic domains, from abstract puzzles~ chollet2019measure to computer use~ xie2024osworld,terminalbench , already control robots through code~ fu2026capx and could work out a motion for the scene at hand. This raises the question: When manipulation hinges on spatial constraints, can robots reason out the right motions? Existing benchmarks do not address this question. Manipulation benchmarks draw their difficulty from the number of steps and the variety of objects~ james2020rlbench,mees2022calvin,liu2023libero,nasiriany2024robocasa,li2024behavior1k,tao2024maniskill3 , rarely from the geometry a motion must clear ( ). Reasoning benchmarks pose puzzles in text, images or abstract environments~ chollet2019measure,mindtopo,chain2026 , where no motion has to satisfy a contact. Motion planning has long used physical puzzles such as the alpha puzzle as tests for planners that are given the exact geometry~ amato1998alphapuzzle,zhang2020disentangle . poses them to complete systems and grades the motion the robot executes. To answer this question, we introduce , a benchmark of physical puzzles under spatial constraints ( ), built on three principles. , difficulty comes from spatial constraints. Like ARC~ chollet2019measure , each task is easy to state, but its solution is specific to its geometry, and the agent is given no demonstration of it. Unlike ARC, the answer is a motion. has tasks, from puzzle families and IKEA scenes, in six constraint types: interlocking, narrow passage, assembly, untangling, threading and shape control ( ). They span rigid and soft materials and three robots in MuJoCo~ todorov2012mujoco . , each task comes in two regimes. A policy can fail because it cannot see the constraint, because it cannot reason through it, or because it cannot carry out the motion. Each task therefore comes in two regimes that share the scene, the physics and the grader ( ). The regime gives the simulator itself, with its full state and resets. The regime gives real-sensor inputs, calibrated cameras and proprioception, and one live episode. RoboARC sec:roboarc A task is a frozen simulated scene, a robot, a goal stated in words and a grader that checks the simulated state. A policy of any class must reach the goal within a wall-clock budget (about \,h per task, ). Problem formulation sec:formulation We cast each task as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP)~ kaelbling1998pomdp . A state is the full configuration of the scene: the robot's joints, the poses of rigid parts, the shape of deformable ones, and their contacts. An action is a chunk of joint or end-effector targets, and the transition is the physics simulation, deterministic from the frozen start state . The grader defines a goal set (a ring free of its post, a rope without crossings) and a failure set , possibly empty (a forbidden contact, a part dropped). A policy chooses from the task instruction and its history , with observations , and succeeds if where is the last step the wall-clock budget allows. What makes the tasks hard is the shape of the feasible set: the state trajectories that reach without touching form a thin tube around one path through a millimetre clearance, an interlock or a knot, so a plan made from slightly wrong geometry falls outside it. The two regimes share and and differ in what the policy can access. In the regime the policy observes the state itself, , and may reset to , so it can try and check motions in the simulator before it delivers one. In the regime it observes camera images, proprioception and the camera calibration, and must infer from them within a single episode. Task suite sec:suite Constraint types. We organize the tasks by the spatial constraint that decides success and by material ( ). The rigid types are interlocking (separating or joining hooked or keyed parts), narrow passage (guiding a held part through millimetre clearances) and assembly (fitting parts together, up to IKEA furniture). The soft types are untangling (untying knots, freeing rings caught on cords), threading (passing a rope or fibers through holes or a ring in a given order) and shape control (unfolding, flattening or folding a blanket). Success is defined by the final state, often by its topology, and the same rope is threaded in one family and untied in another. r 0.47 Six constraint types over rigid and soft materials, on three robots. title: Best-of-$N$ Test-Time Steering Can Lead to Reward Hacking in Vision-Language-Action Models
comment: 17 pages, 11 figures, to be presented at 1st Workshop on Physical World AI at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown promise for general-purpose robotic manipulation, but adapting to changing environmental conditions still remains challenging. Recent test-time steering methods have shown promise in enabling adaptive VLA policies by utilizing additional computation during deployment. In this paper, we consider best-of-$N$ test-time steering for VLA models, where multiple action candidates are sampled from a fixed policy and a verifier is used to select the best one during deployment. We show that increasing $N$ does not always improve performance when the verifier is inaccurate, and can favor candidates whose scores exploit prediction errors, a form of reward hacking. We study this effect on 60 LIBERO-Safety task-level cases using a $π_{0.5}$ policy, with ten repetitions per case. We introduce controlled errors in a MuJoCo trajectory verifier and show that as $N$ increases, selected candidate rewards diverge from the accurate verifier rewards, leading to reward hacking. We also show that verifier calibration and softmax-based candidate selection can mitigate reward hacking in some settings.
full_text: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown promise for general-purpose robotic manipulation, but adapting to changing environmental conditions still remains challenging. Recent test-time steering methods have shown promise in enabling adaptive VLA policies by utilizing additional computation during deployment. In this paper, we consider best-of- test-time steering for VLA models, where multiple action candidates are sampled from a fixed policy and a verifier is used to select the best one during deployment. We show that increasing does not always improve performance when the verifier is inaccurate, and can favor candidates whose scores exploit prediction errors, a form of reward hacking. We study this effect on 60 LIBERO-Safety task-level cases using a policy, with ten repetitions per case. We introduce controlled errors in a MuJoCo trajectory verifier and show that as increases, selected candidate rewards diverge from the accurate verifier rewards, leading to reward hacking. We also show that verifier calibration and softmax-based candidate selection can mitigate reward hacking in some settings. Introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models map visual observations and language instructions to robot actions and have shown broad manipulation capabilities brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,pi2025pi05 . However, their performance can deteriorate when deployment conditions differ from those seen during training fei2025liberoplus . There are two ways to improve the generalization capabilities of VLAs. The first is to collect additional demonstrations and retrain or fine-tune the policy; however, this can be computationally expensive lu2025vla, kim2025fine . Another widely used and less computationally expensive approach is test-time steering, where additional computation during execution is used to steer the VLA actions nakamoto2024vgps,dai2025rover or select the best one from a few sampled candidates kwok2025robomonkey,zhang2026veritas . Recent test-time steering methods such as RoboMonkey and VERITAS have shown promising results with best-of- (BoN) test-time steering, which samples multiple action candidates and uses a verifier to select the best one for execution kwok2025robomonkey,zhang2026veritas . However, its benefit depends on the verifier's ability to rank those candidates. In practice, perception errors, inaccurate predictions of physical motion, or an imperfect scoring rule can cause a poor action to receive a high score. This problem has been identified in large language models (LLMs), where a reward model or verifier is used to pick the best of several sampled responses. gao2023overoptimization showed that when best-of- selection uses an imperfect reward model, the true quality of the selected response first improves and then drops as grows. Similar effects have been shown when selecting solutions to math problems with a learned verifier~ cobbe2021training and when selecting code with unit tests~ stroebl2026limits , where wrong answers that pass the check limit the benefit of more samples. Recent work explains this pattern in theory and shows that it is expected for best-of- selection when is large~ huang2025bestofn, khalaf2025inference , and terms it inference-time reward hacking. These works also suggest ways to mitigate this effect, such as down-weighting candidates with uncertain scores~ huang2025bestofn or using softmax-based selection instead of always taking the top-scoring candidate~ khalaf2025inference,wang2026slop . Similar effects have recently been reported in robotics literature. luo2026critichack showed that optimizing robot policies against a learned visual critic can increase failures in which the robot acts on the wrong object, because the critic scores some of these failures above real successes. bakshi2026goodhart showed that sampling-based planning with rewards learned from human preferences can reduce the true task return by up to 76 , and that best-of- selection with such a reward can perform worse than taking a single action. A recent survey of verifiers for robot policies notes that how far a policy can be optimized against a verifier before its score stops tracking the task is still largely unexplored~ wan2026nofreechecker . These studies use learned scores and focus on task success. In contrast, we use a MuJoCo simulator whose errors we control, and a proxy reward function. We measure both safety violations and task completion. This raises the central question of our study: when the verifier is imperfect, does additional search still improve robot behavior, or can it reduce task performance and safety? We study this question on the LIBERO-Safety benchmark~ cui2026liberosafety , which requires robots to complete manipulation tasks while following constraints on how objects are grasped and avoiding contact with nearby obstacles and simulated human hands. In these tasks, task progress and safety can conflict: an action can move an object toward its goal while violating a safety constraint. We keep the VLA policy and the execution environment fixed, and add controlled errors only inside the verifier, either by adding noise to the predicted object positions or by changing the simulated dynamics. For each selected action, we compare the proxy score from the perturbed verifier with its clean score from the unperturbed simulator. We find that best-of- steering of VLA policies is prone to inference-time reward hacking: as increases, the gap between predicted and clean reward grows, and for some tasks the gains in safe completion seen at small are lost while violations increase. Best-of-N steering with an imperfect verifier At replanning step , the VLA samples candidate action chunks from , given the current observation and language instruction . A verifier scores each candidate using a predictor to estimate the trajectory that would produce over a short horizon, and from this trajectory computes a safety score and a task-progress score (Section~ sec:scores ). The scores are combined, and the best candidate is selected using: where and set the relative weight of safety and task progress. We use in the main experiments. The selected chunk is executed for five control steps before replanning. To measure how good the selected action actually is, we score it again with the unperturbed MuJoCo simulator. We call this score the clean reward . It uses the same short-horizon scoring rule as . A perfect verifier is one that selects candidates using directly. We define where is the expected proxy reward assigned by the verifier to the selected candidate, and is the expected clean reward assigned to that same candidate by the unperturbed simulator. The expectation is taken over evaluation tasks, replanning steps, and candidate samples. We say that reward hacking is shown when the gap between proxy and clean reward grows, and the increase in is not matched by clean reward or closed-loop outcomes. The clearest case is when, for two candidate counts , proxy reward increases while clean reward does not: and . For example, in Figure fig:opening A, the proxy reward keeps rising as increases from 5 to 50, while the clean reward of the same actions falls. Safety and task scores sec:scores The verifier scores each candidate from its predicted rollout of control steps. Let be the number of constraint violations in the predicted rollout, counted over all steps and all constraints. The safety score is A candidate with no predicted violations scores , and each violation gives a score of . Task score. The proxy task score is computed from the same predicted rollout. Each task is specified by a list of goal conditions, such as putting the apple on the plate, and the score measures progress toward the first condition that is not yet satisfied. Its dense scoring part rewards moving the gripper toward the target object and grasping it, and, once the object is held, lifting it and moving it toward its goal location. We add the simulator's sparse reward summed over the rollout, , and a success bonus that equals if the predicted rollout completes the task: where dividing by scales the score to a range similar to that of . We evaluate pi2025pi05 using the LIBERO-Safety-finetuned checkpoint released with the benchmark cui2026liberosafety . We evaluate 60 task-level cases from four task suites: affordance-aware grasping, human-robot interaction, tabletop obstacle avoidance, and hand-object avoidance. Each suite contains five task instructions evaluated at three levels of difficulty (L0-L2), giving 15 tasks per suite. Episodes run for at most 200 control steps. At each replanning step, the policy samples action chunks from its current observation. Episode comparisons use ten policy-sampling repetitions per case, condition, and . Imperfect verifier details. We compare an unperturbed predictor against three imperfect predictors. Output noise adds independent Gaussian noise with standard deviation ~m to predicted object , , and coordinates. Under-responsive and over-responsive dynamics make the robotic arm respond more weakly or strongly to the same commands. These settings modify actuator strength, damping, friction, armature, gripper strength, and object mass in the MuJoCo simulator. The simulator state is restored before execution, so the errors affect only candidate scoring. Episode metrics. Task completion means that the benchmark's full task goal was reached, regardless of safety. A violation means that at least one benchmark constraint was violated. Safe task completion requires both task completion and no violation in the evaluated episode. We report pointwise 90 Wilson intervals. Mean predicted reward curves show means over replanning decisions without confidence intervals. title: Model Predictive Control of a Multirotor UAV with a Cable-Suspended Payload: A Comparison of Shifted and Transformer-Based Warm Starts
summary:
This study investigates model predictive control (MPC) of a multirotor drone (unmanned aerial vehicle, UAV) carrying a cable-suspended payload, comparing conventional shifted initialization with Transformer-based warm starting of a sequential convex programming (SCP) optimizer. The controller uses a coupled mechanical model with an elastic cable and a double-pendulum representation of the suspended load. Its formulation includes move-blocked control inputs, finite-difference sensitivities, constrained quadratic subproblems, and input-feasibility projection. A Transformer trained on expert SCP solutions predicts an initial control sequence, which is subsequently refined by the same optimizer used for the conventional methods. Numerical experiments compare zero, shifted, and Transformer initialization under identical controller settings. For independently solved MPC problems, Transformer initialization reduces computation time relative to zero initialization. In sequential closed-loop simulations, however, shifting the preceding optimized control sequence provides the lowest computation time, while all three methods produce similar tracking behavior. These findings emphasize the importance of comparing learned warm starts with conventional initialization methods that reuse previous MPC solutions. The measured optimization times exceed the control sampling period; consequently, real-time implementation is not demonstrated.
  Keywords: Model predictive control; sequential convex programming; Transformer; warm start; cable-suspended payload; multirotor drone.
full_text: Multirotor drones carrying cable-suspended payloads require coordinated regulation of vehicle motion and suspended-load oscillations while respecting rotor constraints and cable dynamics. In this study, the drone is modeled as a multirotor unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV). This study develops a physics-based model predictive control (MPC) framework for a multirotor with an elastic cable and a reduced double-pendulum representation of its suspended load, and compares two approaches to initializing its sequential convex programming (SCP) optimizer: conventional receding-horizon shifting and Transformer-based sequence prediction. The controller combines numerical propagation of a coupled mechanical model with move-blocked control decisions, finite-difference sensitivities, constrained quadratic subproblems, and feasibility projection of the initial control sequence. Expert SCP solutions are used to train the Transformer, and the learned and shifted initializations are evaluated using the same prediction model, constraints, and solver settings. Mechanical consistency checks, data-generation and feasibility studies, tests of independently solved MPC problems, and sequential closed-loop experiments establish a common basis for the comparison. Although Transformer initialization improves computational performance relative to zero initialization in the tests of independently solved MPC problems, the shifted solution is more efficient in the sequential closed-loop benchmark and achieves comparable tracking behavior. The results show that learned sequence accuracy and downstream optimizer efficiency are distinct properties, and that previous-solution shifting is an essential baseline when assessing learning-assisted MPC. The measured optimization times remain above the nominal control sampling period, so the study does not demonstrate real-time deployment. Keywords: model predictive control; sequential convex programming; UAV; suspended payload; Transformer; warm start; move blocking. set \\ & Transformer decision predictor \\ & Inference, projection and SCP runtime (s) \\ Introduction Multirotor unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) carrying suspended loads are coupled mechanical systems: changes in rotor thrust and vehicle attitude affect the payload trajectory, while cable deflection, extension, and payload swing feed back into the forces acting on the vehicle. A controller intended for constrained tracking must therefore represent the relevant coupled dynamics without making repeated online prediction prohibitively expensive. This balance between mechanical fidelity and computational effort motivates the present comparison of model predictive control (MPC) initialization strategies. The suspended-load literature offers different levels of mechanical detail. Goodarzi, Lee, and Lee goodarzi2014 derive a coordinate-free quadrotor--payload formulation with a flexible cable represented by serially connected links and develop a geometric stabilization controller with stability analysis. Tolba and Shirinzadeh tolba2025 instead consider a fifteen-degree-of-freedom multirotor and rigid-body payload model that includes elastic cable behavior, slackening and tightening, shifted centers of gravity, arbitrary attachment locations, and double-pendulum motion; they investigate an output-weighted linear-quadratic regulator. These studies establish the importance of cable and payload dynamics, but neither is an evaluation of Transformer initialization for a common predictive optimizer. Our control-oriented model has eleven generalized coordinates, including vehicle translation and attitude, an extensible suspension segment, and two swing-direction pairs. It does not reproduce all the effects represented in the more detailed models, and the reported results must be interpreted within that modeling scope. Predictive control provides a framework for handling tracking objectives and explicit constraints rawlings,dingyang2024,borrelli2017 . For quadrotors, Ru and Subbarao ru2017 formulate constrained trajectory-tracking MPC using a state-dependent-coefficient representation and sequential quadratic programming. Rohr et al. rohr2021 develop and flight-test predictive velocity control for a tiltwing UAV using an identified aerodynamic model; their use of preceding solutions as optimization references should be distinguished from using a shifted solution as the initial iterate. These works illustrate the importance of selecting a control-oriented prediction model and a practical numerical optimization procedure, but do not directly establish the performance of the coupled suspended-payload controller considered here. Computational cost remains a central issue in receding-horizon control. Wang and Boyd wangboyd demonstrate that exploiting quadratic-program structure can substantially accelerate online MPC. Move blocking reduces the number of independent control decisions, but Cagienard et al. cagienard also show why blocking choices cannot be assumed to preserve stability and constraint-satisfaction guarantees. Diehl, Bock, and Schl\"oder diehl develop a real-time iteration scheme for approximate online optimization, providing a complementary example of trading iterative solution accuracy against the time available between control updates. In the present sequential convex programming (SCP) implementation, the numerical workload also includes repeated integration of the coupled mechanical model to construct finite-difference sensitivities and evaluate trial steps. Faster quadratic-program solutions alone therefore need not imply faster control updates. Learning-based models address different parts of this computational problem. Gu, Primatesta, and Rizzo gu2024 investigate physics-informed neural modeling of quadrotor dynamics, highlighting model accuracy and physical consistency; their network serves a different purpose from the initialization predictor studied here. Davoudi et al. davoudi2020 likewise illustrate the influence of aerodynamic and wind-model fidelity on quadrotor flight simulation. Our Transformer does not replace the mechanical prediction model or estimate the wind field. It predicts an initial control-decision sequence for subsequent physics-based SCP optimization. Transformer-assisted trajectory optimization provides the immediate methodological motivation. Celestini et al. celestini use sequence modeling to generate initial guesses or target plans for constrained trajectory optimization and report improvements in convergence and runtime in their evaluated settings. Such benefits cannot be presumed for a different plant, solver, and prediction horizon. In particular, a shifted previous solution is an inexpensive and informative baseline in receding-horizon control, and learned inference and feasibility projection add their own computational costs. We therefore compare three initializations of the same move-blocked SCP controller: zero deviations from hover, a shifted and reblocked previous solution, and a Transformer-generated candidate. The shifted and Transformer-generated initial control sequences are adjusted, when necessary, to satisfy the imposed input constraints before optimization. Zero initialization already satisfies these constraints. The reported experiments assess both isolated optimization behavior and matched closed-loop episodes, including measured initialization-and-optimization time, solver iterations, and physical tracking outcomes. The principal contribution is a controlled numerical comparison of zero, shifted, and Transformer-based initialization strategies within a common SCP-MPC framework for a coupled UAV--cable--payload system. The study evaluates their effects on computational effort, optimization iterations, and closed-loop response under identical modeling and control constraints. The results establish the relative performance of these initialization strategies for the investigated numerical scenarios, without implying formal closed-loop stability or real-time flight readiness. title: FreshVLA: Frequency-Regularized Time Scale Hierarchical Latent Actions for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Learning reusable latent actions from action-free videos offers an effective route to improving Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies. However, reconstruction-oriented latent actions do not necessarily benefit policy learning: as they may encode task-irrelevant static appearance with scene identity, or entangle slowly varying task progress with fine-grained execution dynamics in limited discrete code. We propose FreshVLA, a VLA framework built on a frequency-guided, dynamics-sensitive learning paradigm for acquiring temporally hierarchical continuous latent actions. FreshVLA uses a high-pass prior to guide visual transition encoding toward dynamical regions, thereby reducing reliance on static appearance cues. It further organizes latent actions into coarse-grained task progress and fine-grained execution dynamics through cross-timescale sampling and frequency-domain regularization, enhancing their capacity to represent long-horizon behaviors. During policy training, we freeze the pretrained latent action encoder and transfer its representations to robot control through joint flow-matching of latent and robot actions. FreshVLA achieves 98.2% average success on LIBERO and 98.0% on LIBERO-Long, exceeding GR00T-N1.6 on the latter by 3.6%. It also reaches an average sequence length of 4.52 on CALVIN and strong overall success rate of 80.4% in the zero-shot LIBERO-PLUS evaluation. Furthermore, FreshVLA exhibits greater robustness to visual perturbations and a more distinct division of roles between two branches in modeling low- and high-frequency motion, respectively. In 35-step action regression, it achieves a 51.3-percentage-point higher relative error reduction than its hierarchical discrete counterpart. Real-world experiments demonstrate that FreshVLA improves the average success rate over $π_{0.5}$ by 7.5%. The FreshVLA project page is available at https://freshvla.github.io/.
full_text: Introduction Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models aim to translate language-conditioned visual understanding into executable robot behavior. Recent systems have advanced this paradigm through larger multimodal backbones, broader robot datasets, and more expressive action decoders~ brohan2023rt2,ghosh2024octo,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0 . Nevertheless, a fundamental interface challenge remains: policies must transform visual intent into temporally coherent control behavior. This requires representing the visual transitions that should occur in a scene, including which object should move, how contact relationships evolve, and how local execution supports longer-horizon task progress. Latent Action Models (LAMs) provide a natural means of learning such representations. By predicting or reconstructing observation transitions, LAMs infer latent actions from adjacent frames or observation sequences~ ye2025lapa,liang2025clam,bu2025univla . These variables can provide supervision for policy pretraining while reducing the need to directly align raw action spaces across embodiments. However, reconstruction objectives do not guarantee that latent actions capture controllable and task-relevant changes. They may instead encode background layouts, static appearance, or other cues that help predict future observations but are only weakly related to control~ bu2025laof,cai2025spaceMotion,bu2026whatMatters . ~ lipman2023flowMatching,li2026rotvla . With 2B parameters, FreshVLA achieves an average success rate of 98.2 on LIBERO, reaches 98.0 on LIBERO-Long, and attains an average sequence length of 4.52 on CALVIN. These results exceed those of GR00T-N1.6~ nvidia2025grootn16 by 1.2 and 3.6 percentage points on the two LIBERO metrics, respectively, and by 0.28 subtasks on CALVIN, highlighting its strength in long-horizon manipulation. In zero-shot LIBERO-PLUS evaluation, it achieves 80.4 macro-average success and outperforms OpenVLA-OFT~ kim2025openvlaOft across all seven perturbation categories, reaching 88.9 , 97.0 , and 97.1 under language, lighting, and background shifts, respectively. Representation analyses further show that FreshVLA’s latent actions are more robust to visual perturbations and exhibit complementary frequency preferences across temporal scales. On the 35-step action-regression probe, FreshVLA achieves a relative error reduction 51.3-percentage-points higher than that of its hierarchical discrete counterpart. Across four real-world tasks, FreshVLA improves mean success by 7.5 percentage points over , suggesting more reliable object interaction and long-horizon execution. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce a temporally hierarchical continuous latent action representation that organizes visual transitions into substage-scale components capturing long-horizon task progress and execution-scale residuals preserving local dynamics. We propose FreshVLA, which learns this representation using a temporal high-pass visual prior and frequency-domain regularization. A frozen latent action encoder then provides targets for VLA policy training through joint flow matching over latent and robot actions. FreshVLA achieves strong results on LIBERO and CALVIN and generalizes well to perturbations in zero-shot LIBERO-PLUS evaluations. Additional experiments and real-world deployments further demonstrate its effectiveness on long-horizon manipulation tasks. 8pt plus 2pt minus 2pt Related Work Vision--Language--Action Models Vision--Language--Action (VLA) models map multimodal context---including visual observations, language instructions, and available proprioceptive states---to executable robot control. RT-1 and RT-2 established scalable language-conditioned robot-policy learning~ brohan2023rt1,brohan2023rt2 . Subsequent generalist policies scale this paradigm by integrating heterogeneous robot data or pretrained multimodal backbones with specialized action generators~ oneill2024openx,ghosh2024octo,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,nvidia2025grootn1 . Despite their improved generality, these policies are trained to predict robot actions whose coordinates and control conventions remain embodiment dependent~ oneill2024openx,bu2025univla . At the level of labeled action representation, FAST applies DCT-based compression for efficient tokenization of high-frequency action chunks~ pertsch2025fast , whereas MINT decomposes action chunks in frequency space into coarse intent and fine execution~ huang2026mint . title: $\mathrm{M}^{2}$-WAM: Efficient Hierarchical Memory Across Modalities and Timescales for World-Action Models
summary: Long-horizon robotic manipulation requires historical context, yet retaining extensive visual histories incurs growing storage and retrieval costs, while aggressive compression risks losing fine-grained information needed for subsequent decisions. Moreover, executed action histories capture intermediate behaviors that sparse visual observations may miss. Preserving this complementary context efficiently calls for modality-specific memory mechanisms that balance recent detail with long-term retention. To this end, we introduce $\mathrm{M}^{2}$-WAM, a world-action model equipped with hierarchical visual and interaction memories. $\mathrm{M}^{2}$-WAM preserves recent visual observations in dense short-term memory while consolidating entries evicted from this window into fixed-size associative long-term memory through gated delta updates. Within the same short- and long-term hierarchy, interaction memory encodes executed action prefixes into compact temporal representations, complementing visual observations with behavioral context. These complementary memories are integrated into world-action modeling through layer-wise retrieval, enabling memory-augmented action generation with a bounded online memory footprint independent of episode length. On the memory-dependent simulation benchmarks MIKASA-Robo and RMBench, $\mathrm{M}^{2}$-WAM achieves +53.2% and +61.2% absolute improvements in average success rates over Fast-WAM, respectively. These gains extend to real-world manipulation, where $\mathrm{M}^{2}$-WAM achieves a +29.3% absolute improvement over LingBot-VA in average success across three tasks. These results suggest that $\mathrm{M}^{2}$-WAM offers a promising approach to efficient memory-augmented world-action modeling.

Introduction sec:intro Long-horizon robotic manipulation often requires reasoning beyond the current observation zheng2025tracevla,xiao2026avavla,lin2026hifvla . For example, in a shell game task, a robot must track a target object as it is occluded and moved beneath visually identical cups, relying on historical observations to identify its location cherepanov2026memory,guo2026chameleon . Such tasks are inherently non-Markovian with respect to instantaneous observations, requiring policies to reason over past observations and interactions kaelbling1998pomdp . Recent world-action models (WAMs) have demonstrated promising capabilities by jointly modeling visual dynamics and robot actions ye2026worldactionmodelszeroshot,lingbot-va2026,yuan2026fastwam . However, many WAMs still rely on current observations or limited contexts, making it difficult to exploit information from earlier stages of execution. Historical context must support ongoing decisions while preserving information from earlier task stages. Recent observations provide spatial detail, whereas earlier observations may contain cues that remain relevant after they leave view. As shown in Figure~ fig:overview (a,b), a memoryless WAM lacks access to earlier observations, whereas retaining full visual history incurs storage and retrieval costs that grow with episode length. A sliding window preserves recent detail but discards older observations wang2026nativemem,yang2026eventvla . Alternatively, compact or recurrent memories reduce storage costs, but compression can limit access to fine-grained historical information yang2026memorywam,zhao2026dram . We argue for allocating memory capacity across timescales: retaining recent observations explicitly and consolidating older entries into a compact, persistent state. This design preserves recent detail without compressing all observations and extends historical coverage beyond a fixed window, drawing inspiration from short- and long-term memory atkinson1968human and complementary learning systems mcClelland1995why . However, retaining history across timescales is only part of the challenge: memory must also capture complementary information from observations and executed actions. Visual observations describe scene configurations and changes, but may omit behavior between sampled frames. Denser sampling increases visual encoding and storage costs for the same duration. Executed action prefixes complement these observations by recording the intervening actions, providing compact, temporally denser behavioral context zhou2026action,zhao2026remember,pala2026membodied . This motivates modality-aware memory that preserves both scene observations and executed actions. We therefore adopt visual and interaction memories that preserve spatial details and temporal action patterns, respectively, within a common short- and long-term hierarchy. Building on these considerations, we propose M -WAM , which augments a mixture-of-transformers (MoT) architecture with complementary visual and interaction memories across timescales, as illustrated in Figure~ fig:overview (c). The visual memory preserves an initial observation anchor and recent observations as dense spatial key-value (KV) representations, while consolidating older information into fixed-size, layer-wise associative states through gated delta updates yang2025gated,hatamizadeh2026gated . To accommodate robot image sequences, we apply temporal decay once per observation according to elapsed time, rather than repeatedly across its spatial tokens. We further replace channel-wise erasure with a scalar erase gate per token and head to improve numerical stability. In parallel, the interaction memory encodes executed action prefixes into compact temporal representations and maintains a shared associative state. These memories are integrated into world-action modeling through layer-wise, query-conditioned retrieval. By combining bounded short-term memories with fixed-size associative states, M -WAM enables persistent history conditioning with online memory storage and retrieval costs independent of episode length. Our main contributions are as follows: 1) We propose M -WAM, a world-action model equipped with modality-specialized hierarchical memory that jointly preserves visual observations and executed interactions across short and long timescales. 2) We develop modality-specific memory representations and associative consolidation mechanisms, together with complementary retrieval pathways that incorporate historical information into world-action computation with bounded online memory and retrieval costs. 3) We conduct extensive experiments on MIKASA-Robo cherepanov2026memory , RMBench chen2026rmbench , RoboTwin~2.0 chen2025robotwin , and three real-world tasks, complemented by ablation studies and qualitative and quantitative analyses. Results demonstrate improved performance on memory-dependent tasks with bounded online memory and retrieval costs, supporting the effectiveness and efficiency of our method. Related Work sec:related_work World-Action Models Recent robot policies learn compact state representations liu2026stamo , couple visual prediction with policy learning tian2025seer,hu2025vpp,cheang2024gr2generativevideolanguageactionmodel , or plan with predicted future states du2023learning,zhao2025cotvla,zhang2026foreact,huang2026pointworld . World-action models connect visual dynamics prediction with action generation through unified generative models or coupled video–action architectures zhu2025uwm,cen2025WorldVLA,bi2025motusunifiedlatentaction,kim2025cosmospolicy . DreamZero and LingBot-VA demonstrate the potential of video-based world modeling for generalizable robot control ye2026worldactionmodelszeroshot,lingbot-va2026 . Recent studies further investigate video-action coupling and its role in policy learning and task transfer ma2026dit4dit,wang2026patchwam,cen2026worldbridgebridgingvideoaction,OneWM . Inference efficiency is also a practical concern for robot policies zhang2025molevla . Fast-WAM retains video co-training but skips future prediction at test time, whereas Faster-WAM preserves future conditioning through selective video-action interactions yuan2026fastwam,zhao2026faster . Building on Fast-WAM, we investigate how visual and executed-action histories can support action generation under a bounded online memory budget. Memory-Augmented Robotic Policies Memory-augmented robotic policies address partial observability through explicit memory banks, compressed visual histories, and selective retrieval yin2026simplememvla,wang2026nativemem,gao2026gatedmemorypolicy,cen2026worldbridgebridgingvideoaction,li2026trmvla,wang2026dual . MemoryVLA maintains perceptual and cognitive memory streams, retrieving historical context with current tokens and consolidating redundant entries shi2025memoryvla . MemoryVLA++ combines this memory with imagined future latents to condition action generation shi2026memoryvla++ . BridgeVLA++ pairs temporal memory of historical keyframes with spatial memory of the initial scene geometry, supporting task-progress reasoning and localization under occlusion li2026bridgevlaplus . MemoryWAM combines recent observations, anchor frames, and historical gist tokens yang2026memorywam , whereas HiMem-WAM stores compact task states at predicted skill boundaries sun2026himemwam . To retain history without accumulating tokens, recurrent approaches maintain fixed-size associative states using gated delta updates yang2025gated,hatamizadeh2026gated . DRAM jointly incorporates tokens within each observation zhao2026dram , while MemBodied combines action summaries with their observed visual consequences pala2026membodied . The latter also highlights the relevance of behavioral history, explored through joint visual-action representations in AEM and executed-action memory in ActMem-VLA zhou2026action,zhao2026remember . M -WAM organizes visual observations and executed action prefixes into separate pathways, each combining explicit short-term storage with associative long-term consolidation. Dense visual KV features and compact temporal action representations are retained and retrieved through modality-specific structures, while entries evicted from each short-term window update its corresponding fixed-size associative state. Method sec:method Problem Formulation and Architecture We consider long-horizon robotic manipulation under partial observability, where action generation may depend on information beyond the current observation. At each replanning step , the robot receives an observation , comprising multi-view images and proprioceptive state, and a task instruction . Given a bounded memory bank representing past observations and executed actions, the policy predicts an action chunk : Here, is the prediction horizon and is the action dimension. The online memory satisfies , where is a fixed budget independent of episode length. As illustrated in Figure~ fig:architecture , M -WAM builds on Fast-WAM's MoT backbone, comprising a video Diffusion Transformer (DiT) peebles2023dit and an action DiT. During inference, the video DiT encodes the current observation into layer-wise visual KV representations that condition iterative action denoising in the action DiT, without generating future video. We augment this architecture with complementary visual and interaction memories, each combining bounded short-term memory (STM) with fixed-size associative long-term memory (LTM). title: RoboJackVR: Turning Robot Tasks into VR Games for Scalable Demonstration Collection
summary: Scaling robot demonstration datasets requires collection systems that accommodate more participants and diverse tasks, yet teleoperation barriers and task-adaptation effort limit this expansion. We present RoboJackVR, a standalone virtual reality (VR) game in which players manipulate simulated robots to execute combat skills and contribute demonstrations. MuJoCo simulation and demonstration recording run locally on the headset, removing the need for an external PC or simulation server during collection. Tutorials, skill selection, combat consequences, and character progression organize repeated task attempts within a continuing game. Task contracts declare assets, controls, resets, success criteria, and recording semantics; separate game configurations specify guidance, attempt groups, skill effects, and course placement. Shared bindings connect these declarations to task execution, outcome handling, and recording, allowing tasks to reuse the game flow while retaining their control and success semantics. Batch tools package supported resources and generate configurations, with manual adaptation and review for new interfaces and unsupported predicates. We instantiate the approach with SO101-Nexus-derived and LIBERO tasks. On the 66 LIBERO-90 tasks covered by the collected data, ACT policies trained solely on VR demonstrations retain approximately 91% of the full-standard simulation-demonstration baseline's success rate on held-out initial states, averaged over four training seeds. These results support the utility of play-collected VR demonstrations for policy learning in this setting.
