On the 66 LIBERO-90 tasks covered by the collected data, ACT policies trained solely on VR demonstrations retain approximately 91 of the full-standard simulation-demonstration baseline's success rate on held-out initial states, averaged over four training seeds. These results support the utility of play-collected VR demonstrations for policy learning in this setting. : Human-to-Robot Learning, Virtual Reality, Demonstration Collection, Gamification, Imitation Learning Introduction sec:introduction Scaling robot demonstration collection requires broader participation and more task coverage, but teleoperation barriers and the effort of adapting new tasks limit both~ robocrowd2024,iris2025 . DROID illustrates the value of diverse demonstrations alongside the hardware, labor, and coordination needed to obtain them~ droid2024 . Extended reality (XR) interfaces to simulation may still depend on an external simulation host~ iris2025 ; running task execution on the headset removes this additional computing requirement from the participant's collection setup. Accessible interfaces and reusable task infrastructure address parts of this challenge; games provide a way to organize repeated contributions within an activity that players can understand and choose to continue. We ask: How can existing robot task collections become VR game content through a reusable gameplay and collection workflow, and can demonstrations collected during play support robot learning? Our central idea gives each task two connected roles: an operation challenge that players choose and master, and a demonstration unit with explicit controls, success criteria, and recording semantics. The design must connect task execution to game consequences while preserving the information needed to interpret the data. We present RoboJackVR, a VR adventure game built around robot manipulation. Players select skills according to the battle state, operate simulated robots, and progress through subsequent challenges. Opening a drawer, for example, executes an attack skill: the task outcome changes the battle state and produces a demonstration record. Task contracts declare execution and recording interfaces; separate game configurations specify guidance, attempt groups, skill effects, and course placement. Shared bindings connect them to instruction, control, feedback, progression, and recording (Figure~ fig:framework ). New tasks can extend the same game while retaining their task-specific control and success semantics. The paper focuses on expanding playable task coverage, instantiated with SO101-Nexus-derived~ so101nexus and LIBERO tasks~ libero2023 . Concrete bindings identify reusable components and the configuration or implementation that remains task-specific. A policy-learning study on LIBERO-90 using Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT)~ zhao2023act compares full and reduced standard-data budgets, VR-only training, and joint training on VR and reduced standard data. Standard demonstrations here are LIBERO's public simulation data, not physical-robot recordings. The study connects on-headset demonstration collection, trajectory conversion, and downstream policy training within a common experimental pipeline. Our contributions are: A reusable task-to-game interface that preserves declared task controls and success conditions while connecting robot-task execution to shared guidance, combat feedback, progression, and demonstration recording. A standalone VR game that runs MuJoCo simulation and demonstration recording on consumer Quest headsets, with default combat configurations for 130 LIBERO and four SO101 tasks. A pipeline that converts VR records into the standard LIBERO demonstration format, and a LIBERO-90 ACT study comparing standard-data budgets, VR-only training, and joint VR and standard-data training. RoboTurk combines smartphone teleoperation with cloud infrastructure, and early VR work identified gaming communities as potential contributors~ roboturk2018,crowdvr2018 . DART combines augmented reality (AR) teleoperation and cloud simulation; COBALT adds concurrent collection and contributor training~ dart2024,cobalt2026 . RoboCrowd studies public participation and incentives, including crowd-data pretraining followed by expert-data fine-tuning~ robocrowd2024 . These approaches motivate connecting access, contributor experience, and downstream data use. RoboJackVR organizes repeated task attempts within a continuing VR game. In robot learning, Play-LMP learns from unsegmented teleoperated play, and MimicPlay combines human-hand play videos with limited robot demonstrations~ playlmp2020,mimicplay2023 . Our focus is explicit game rules for interaction with existing robot tasks. The closest precedents connect game content to downstream learning. RoboCade embeds games in remote real-robot teleoperation and co-trains on support tasks sharing manipulation skills with target tasks~ robocade2025 . Project Kitchen collects bare-hand VR cooking interactions, extracts contact points and sub-goals, and transfers affordance supervision to policies trained with limited robot data~ projectkitchen2026 . Other VR robot games study motion and workspace coverage, while CrowdHRI uses multiplayer mixed reality to collect interaction data~ vrrobotgames2026,crowdhri2025 . RoboJackVR uses existing task collections as content for a complete adventure game: task operations execute selectable combat skills, and outcomes connect to progression and later choices. title: PROVE: Predict-to-Specify and Observe-to-Verify for Human-Aligned Evaluation of Mobile Manipulation
summary: Judging open-world robot manipulation is hard because layouts, articulated fixtures, and valid goal configurations vary widely. On RoboCasa365, simulator predicates agree with human judgments on only 69.09\% of rollouts, and a frontier VLM judge on 86.12\%. We present \textbf{PROVE} (Predict-to-Specify, Observe-to-Verify), which first specifies what success should look like and then checks the outcome. PROVE refines success conditions from the instruction, the initial scene, a target-object reference image, and a generated goal image. The goal image only sharpens the conditions and never serves as evidence. On 6,500 human-annotated rollouts over 65 atomic actions, PROVE reaches \textbf{96.83\%} agreement. Applied to open-source policies, it reports far lower success than native checks and changes their ranking. To reduce evaluation overhead in policy learning, we distill PROVE into \textbf{PROVE-Lite}, a 4B evaluator that needs no reference images. In one forward pass, PROVE-Lite predicts the outcome and the terminal state of each task condition. It reaches \textbf{91.20\%} agreement while running about 38$\times$ faster than PROVE. Mapped to a severity-aware reward, its diagnoses improve PPO post-training over both simulator and binary rewards.
full_text: Judging open-world robot manipulation is hard because layouts, articulated fixtures, and valid goal configurations vary widely. On RoboCasa365, simulator predicates agree with human judgments on only 69.09 of rollouts, and a frontier VLM judge on 86.12 . We present PROVE (Predict-to-Specify, Observe-to-Verify), which first specifies what success should look like and then checks the outcome. PROVE refines success conditions from the instruction, the initial scene, a target-object reference image, and a generated goal image. The goal image only sharpens the conditions and never serves as evidence. On 6,500 human-annotated rollouts over 65 atomic actions, PROVE reaches 96.83 agreement. Applied to open-source policies, it reports far lower success than native checks and changes their ranking. To reduce evaluation overhead in policy learning, we distill PROVE into PROVE-Lite, a 4B evaluator that needs no reference images. In one forward pass, PROVE-Lite predicts the outcome and the terminal state of each task condition. It reaches 91.20 agreement while running about 38 faster than PROVE. Mapped to a severity-aware reward, its diagnoses improve PPO post-training over both simulator and binary rewards. Project page: . Introduction sec:intro Mobile manipulation benchmarks decompose household tasks into atomic actions such as grasping, placing, closing doors, and turning knobs. Judging these actions reliably matters for benchmark credibility robocasa2024,robocasa365_2026,zhou2025autoeval and for policy improvement zang2025rlinfvla . In open-world scenes, this is harder than it looks. Layouts and articulated fixtures vary across kitchens, and one instruction often admits several valid goal configurations. An evaluator should tell whether the robot succeeded and which physical conditions remain unmet. Ideally, this diagnosis should also help improve the policy. Existing evaluators fall short. Simulation benchmarks check fixed predicates over privileged object states. These states are unavailable on physical robots, and the predicates cannot anticipate every valid outcome. On RoboCasa365 robocasa365_2026 , they agree with human judgments on only 69.09 of rollouts. They err in both directions, accepting failures and rejecting successes, and never explain why ( ). VLM judges du2023successvqa,sermanet2024robovqa avoid privileged state, but instruction-and-terminal-only judging omits the initial scene context. Prompted with the instruction alone, they turn plausible yet irrelevant expectations into requirements. For example, they may demand closing a cabinet door that was already open. Such a judge reaches 82.52 agreement with our 8B backbone and 86.12 with a frontier model, GPT-6.1 Sol~ openai2026gpt61sol . Human judges do better because they separate two questions. What should success look like in this scene, and did it actually happen? They first set the standard from the task, the scene, and the expected outcome, and only then consult the evidence. VLMs understand instructions, objects, and spatial relations qwen3vl2025 . Image-editing models can predict the intended post-action configuration brooks2023instructpix2pix,black2024susie . Generated images, however, contain artifacts and implausible contact. They tell us about the goal but are unreliable as a reference for matching. We therefore let predictions specify and observations verify. The goal image only sharpens the success conditions. The terminal observations alone decide whether those conditions hold, so the outcome never shapes its own standard. Following this principle, we build PROVE, an evaluation harness that mirrors the human process ( ). One frozen MLLM refines success conditions in three stages. It starts from the instruction alone (M1) and adds the initial scene and target object (M2). The last stage adds a generated goal image (M3). On 6,500 human-annotated rollouts over 65 atomic actions, this progressive grounding raises agreement to 96.83 . Ablations confirm that the goal image helps only as specification, and that the gain transfers across backbones. Applied to four open-source policies, PROVE reports far lower success than native checks and reorders them. When the two disagree, blind human review sides with PROVE in 95.42 of cases. PROVE suits offline evaluation, where each rollout is judged once. Policy training is different: thousands of rollouts must be judged on the fly. There, PROVE's multi-stage inference and reference assets become too costly. We therefore distill hinton2015distilling it into PROVE-Lite, an evaluator that needs no reference images ( ). In a single forward pass, PROVE-Lite predicts the outcome and the terminal state of each task condition. Trained only on PROVE's pseudo-labels, it reaches 91.20 agreement while running about 38 faster. We validate PROVE-Lite where it is meant to be used: as the reward in policy post-training. Its diagnoses describe how far each condition is from its target. They can therefore grade failures instead of treating them alike. A narrow door gap, for instance, is penalized less than a wide-open door. We map each diagnosed state to a fixed severity. The resulting terminal reward gives failed rollouts bounded partial credit while keeping binary success dominant. In controlled PPO schulman2017ppo post-training, it beats simulator rewards by 4.58 points and binary PROVE-Lite rewards by 2.00 points. Our contributions are three-fold: Predict-to-Specify, Observe-to-Verify evaluation. PROVE grounds success conditions in the task, the scene, and a generated goal image. It verifies them against real observations only. Reference-free evaluation for policy learning. PROVE-Lite is distilled from PROVE without manual labels. Beyond the outcome, it diagnoses the terminal state of each task condition in one forward pass. Diagnosis-guided terminal reward. The reward grades failed rollouts by the physical severity of their unmet conditions. It outperforms simulator and binary rewards in PPO post-training. Related Work sec:related Evaluating Robot Manipulation Simulation benchmarks including RoboCasa~ robocasa2024,robocasa365_2026 , RLBench~ james2020rlbench , and LIBERO~ liu2023libero use simulator-state checks. BEHAVIOR~ srivastava2022behavior,li2023behavior1k formalizes initial and goal conditions with predicates. For physical robots, AutoEval~ zhou2025autoeval learns success classifiers. Following the broader model-as-judge paradigm~ zheng2023judging , SuccessVQA~ du2023successvqa and RoboVQA~ sermanet2024robovqa formulate judgments as visual questions. RoboJev~ chen2026robojev adapts the JEV-27B-VL judge~ autotrust2026jev27bvl with LoRA and reads success from two calibrated tokens in one forward pass. Eval-Actions~ liu2026evalactions pairs policy rollouts, failures included, with teleoperation data to grade execution quality. PROVE grounds evaluation criteria in scene-specific visual context and fixes them before inspecting terminal evidence. Generated Goals in Robot Learning SuSIE~ black2024susie and UniPi~ du2023unipi generate goal images or video plans for control; Gen2Act~ bharadhwaj2024gen2act conditions robot policies on generated human videos. VoxPoser~ huang2023voxposer grounds language-derived affordances and constraints in 3D value maps for planning. PROVE uses a generated goal to refine evaluation criteria instead. Since generated images can contain artifacts and cannot enumerate all valid outcomes, we retain textual conditions and withhold the generated image during verification. Rewards from Foundation Models VLM rewards use image--text similarity~ rocamonde2024vlmrm,baumli2023vlmrewards , video--language matching~ sontakke2023roboclip , and preference feedback~ wang2024rlvlmf ; Eureka~ ma2024eureka instead uses an LLM to write reward code. LIV~ ma2023liv jointly learns representations and value-based rewards. GVL~ ma2025gvl , Robometer~ liang2026robometer , and ProcVLM~ procvlm2026 estimate progress using in-context reasoning, trajectory comparisons, and procedural structure, respectively. Closest to our terminal grading, RoboReward~ lee2026roboreward already scores partial and near-complete outcomes under an end-of-episode rubric. Our distinction is condition-level terminal diagnosis with a fixed class-to-severity mapping, learned from a teacher that separates criterion specification from verification. Robot Failure Explanation REFLECT~ liu2023reflect summarizes execution experience for failure explanation and correction. AHA~ duan2025aha provides failure feedback for planning and reward refinement; Guardian~ pacaud2026guardian uses structured reasoning to detect manipulation failures. PROVE-Lite restricts diagnosis to terminal evidence: it predicts a closed set of per-condition physical states mapped directly to reward severity, without inferring an unobserved execution history. Evidence-Grounded Action Evaluation sec:method Evaluation Formulation sec:method_formulation Simulator predicates robocasa2024,robocasa365_2026 cannot capture the diverse layouts, articulated fixtures, and multiple valid goal configurations of open-world manipulation. Human judges instead combine task understanding, scene context, expected outcomes, and visual evidence. We abstract this process into three steps: (1) task and scene grounding, which establishes the intended physical outcomes in the current environment; (2) goal anticipation, which predicts the expected post-action configuration; and (3) evidence-grounded verification and diagnosis, which checks each condition against actual observations and identifies the primary deficiency when execution fails. We instantiate this formulation on the 65 atomic mobile manipulation actions in RoboCasa365 robocasa365_2026 , where each evaluation instance corresponds to one rollout specified by a natural-language instruction . Our MLLM-based evaluation framework, PROVE, strictly decouples goal specification from outcome verification. Before inspecting the terminal observation , PROVE first states the required physical postconditions from and progressively refines them using context that describes the goal rather than the execution outcome: the initial scene , a target-object reference , and a predicted goal image ( ). Only after locking in these criteria does PROVE examine to output a binary decision alongside a primary failure reason , ensuring that the actual outcome never shapes the standard by which it is judged ( ). Progressive Condition Grounding sec:method_teacher Across condition grounding and outcome verification, PROVE uses a single frozen MLLM qwen3vl2025 instantiated with role-specific prompts: for initial condition generation, and for scene- and goal-guided refinement, and for terminal verification and failure diagnosis. Task instructions specify the intended action but often leave scene-dependent completion criteria implicit. For example, an instruction to place an object inside a cabinet does not fully specify the target region, acceptable spatial tolerance, or required support condition. The expected physical outcomes must therefore be grounded in the actual scene before execution can be evaluated. We progressively refine textual verification conditions through three stages ( b). Instruction-derived semantic conditions establish the initial specification (M1). Scene context and object references resolve ambiguities in that specification (M2). Finally, a predicted goal image provides additional guidance about the intended post-action configuration (M3). The resulting conditions form the explicit criteria for subsequent verification. Instruction-Derived Semantic Conditions (M1) The first stage establishes task-level expectations using semantic and physical priors. Given the task instruction , the MLLM derives a set of concise physical postconditions: Without scene context, M1 relies on generic language priors and may turn plausible but task-irrelevant expectations into required postconditions. title: VersionGS: Compact and Motion-Robust Dynamic Gaussian Splatting via Versioned Gaussians
comment: 16 pages, 6 figures, 12 tables, including supplementary material
summary: Recent dynamic Gaussian splatting methods encode temporal change, either as smooth functions of time or as constrained updates between frames. We observe that their reconstruction quality degrades significantly under fast motion. In challenging dance sequences, their PSNR drops by 1.1-4.0 dB on high-motion frames compared to low-motion frames. To overcome this limitation, we propose VersionGS, a method that directly encodes per-frame Gaussian states and uses motion estimation only to guide reconstruction. Within each group of frames, unchanged Gaussians keep their current versions in a shared dictionary, while modified Gaussians are appended as new versions. To maximize version reuse, we introduce selective sequential construction, which refines the Gaussians selected by optical flow, photograph differences or rendering errors and leaves the others unchanged. The dictionary is then pruned, fine-tuned with simulated quantization and encoded as images. Adjusting the pruning ratio trades off storage and quality without rebuilding the dictionary. On the fast dance sequences of DanceNet3D, VersionGS improves foreground PSNR by 2.7 dB over the best baseline, and its PSNR decreases by less than 0.3 dB on the highest-motion frames. On N3DV and Technicolor, it requires 6.0x and 5.7x less storage than TAD-GS, the strongest baseline overall, while achieving even higher PSNR. Finally, playback is fast and requires no motion model or neural network, only a 3DGS rasterizer.

Introduction sec:intro Free-viewpoint video allows viewers to explore captured dynamic events from novel viewpoints. Reconstructing such scenes requires capturing fast motion, deforming clothing, and objects entering or leaving the view, while keeping the representation compact for streaming and lightweight to decode on everyday devices. While 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl3Dgaussians enables real-time rendering of static scenes, and recent image-based formats bring compressed static Gaussian scenes to web and mobile viewers~ morgenstern2024compact,playcanvas2025sog , extending 3DGS to dynamic scenes requires an effective representation of how the Gaussians change over time. Existing methods model temporal changes in two primary ways. One group models the change of each Gaussian as a smooth function of time, through deformation fields over a canonical set~ Wu_2024_CVPR,yang2024deformable,huang2024scgs,ke2026streamstgs , time-conditioned Gaussians~ yang2023gs4d,Li_STG_2024_CVPR,sandu2026tadgs or keyframe trajectories~ lee2024ex4dgs . Frame-to-frame methods instead update the Gaussians of the previous frame with per-frame transformations~ sun20243dgstream,gao2024hicom,Hu_2025_CVPR , quantized residuals~ girish2024queen or sparse control-point motion~ zhang2025dfcgs . = -1 However, both groups lose quality as the magnitude of the motion increases. On fast dance sequences~ wei2026dancenet3d , these methods suffer a 1.1--4.0\,dB PSNR drop on the frames with the highest motion compared to those with the least ( ). In temporally shared Gaussian representations, fast motion must be modeled either by persistent Gaussians that explain all timestamps or by transient Gaussians with short temporal lifespans, and neither works well. Optimizing a persistent Gaussian frame by frame under large inter-frame displacements degrades other frames~ kim2026implicit , whereas transient Gaussians with short lifespans are rarely sampled for densification, leaving dynamic regions under-reconstructed or blurry~ sandu2026tadgs . Meanwhile, frame-to-frame methods' position gradients are computed only within a limited local neighborhood and become inaccurate when objects move outside it, so Gaussians fade or are incorrectly recolored~ trackersplat and large inter-frame motion is underestimated~ lee2026morgs . =-1 To avoid these problems, we propose VersionGS, which stores the Gaussian states of each frame rather than modeling their change. Within each group of frames (GOP), Gaussians that do not change are reused, a Gaussian that changes is stored again as a new version, and all versions form a dictionary shared by the frames of the GOP ( ). A changing Gaussian never has to explain all timestamps, and faster motion increases storage rather than degrading quality. =-1 We build this dictionary offline, frame by frame, with selective sequential construction. Multi-view optical flow~ kroeger2016dis identifies moving Gaussians and translates them to follow large motion. These and additionally selected Gaussians are further refined to recover residual error, while newly appearing content is captured by spawning validated new Gaussians ( ). All remaining Gaussians keep their exact prior versions, since refining them as well would slightly perturb static primitives and spawn redundant versions, which multiplies the storage without improving quality. For efficient transmission, we adapt static 3DGS compression~ morgenstern2024compact,morgenstern2026kissgs to each GOP dictionary: we prune versions by their contribution across frames, fine-tune them with simulated quantization and encode attributes into 2D images. Varying the ratio of kept versions adjusts the storage without rebuilding the dictionary. At playback, each GOP is decoded once, and each frame gathers its active versions via a binary mask for a standard 3DGS rasterizer, completely bypassing motion models or neural networks. Our contributions are as follows: 0pt 0pt Per-frame states over motion models. VersionGS encodes explicit per-frame Gaussian states in a shared dictionary, reusing static Gaussians exactly while appending modified ones as new versions, so fast motion trades off storage rather than visual quality. Compact by construction. Selective sequential construction updates only Gaussians with clear evidence of change, cutting storage by up to 9.6 over full-frame refinement, while GOP-level pruning and image-based encoding enable flexible rate adjustment without rebuilding. Motion-robust quality at low bitrate. VersionGS improves foreground PSNR on DanceNet3D by 2.7\,dB over the strongest baseline with under 0.3\,dB degradation on the fastest frames, reduces storage by 6.0 on N3DV~ li2022n3dv and 5.7 on Technicolor~ sabater2017technicolor over TAD-GS at higher PSNR, and renders using only a standard 3DGS rasterizer. Related Work sec:related Temporal Gaussian representations. Building on 3DGS~ kerbl3Dgaussians , deformation-based methods transform canonical Gaussians with HexPlane features and a small decoder~ Wu_2024_CVPR , a time conditioned MLP~ yang2024deformable or sparse control points~ huang2024scgs . Space-time methods make primitives functions of time, as in native 4D Gaussians conditioned on time~ yang2023gs4d , Spacetime Gaussians with temporal opacity and polynomial motion~ Li_STG_2024_CVPR , and TAD-GS~ sandu2026tadgs with temporal visibility and offset warping. Trajectory methods store poses per frame under a rigidity prior~ luiten2024dynamic or interpolate them between keyframes~ lee2024ex4dgs . Temporal Gaussian Hierarchy~ xu2024tgh shares Gaussians across segments where content changes little. SPIN-4DGS~ kim2026implicit predicts attributes from spatiotemporal positions to handle large displacements. Sequential reconstruction. Streaming methods sequentially adapt Gaussians inherited from the previous frame. 3DGStream~ sun20243dgstream predicts translations and rotations with a hash-grid cache and adds Gaussians for new content. HiCoM~ gao2024hicom , ReCon-GS~ recongs2025 and MoRGS~ lee2026morgs model the motion hierarchically or with flow supervision, and QUEEN~ girish2024queen learns residuals of all attributes with gated, selective updates. Population control from static reconstruction, by splitting, cloning and pruning~ kerbl3Dgaussians or by MCMC relocation under a budget~ kheradmand2024mcmc , covers content these updates cannot. Like QUEEN and PackUV~ rai2026packuv , which freezes static Gaussians identified by optical flow and fits attributes in UV atlases, we update only selected Gaussians, but we store each changed Gaussian as an unrestricted new version rather than as a residual. Static Gaussian compression. Static methods combine compaction, which removes Gaussians~ fan2024lightgaussian,fang2024minisplatting,kheradmand2024mcmc , encoding, which lowers the bits per Gaussian by vector quantization~ navaneet2024compgs,lee2024compact,niedermayr2024compressed or learned context models~ lu2024scaffold,chen2024hac,chen2025hacpp,fcgs2025 , and adaptation of the parameters to the codec~ bagdasarian2025zip,morgenstern2026kissgs . Learned coders reach high compression ratios, but their networks must run at decoding. Image-based layouts~ morgenstern2024compact,morgenstern2026kissgs instead sort the Gaussians into smooth attribute images for standard image codecs, so that decoding reduces to image decompression, and web viewers such as SuperSplat already use them~ playcanvas2025sog . Layered models add progressive streaming~ shi2025lapisgs . We build on the image-based layout. Dynamic Gaussian compression. Dynamic methods predict each frame from the previous one, code a temporal parameterization, or code frames jointly. Prediction-based methods, namely 4DGC~ Hu_2025_CVPR with its progressive extension~ zheng20254dgcpro , D-FCGS~ zhang2025dfcgs and a binary transformation cache~ tang2025compressing , reach low rates, but their quality depends on how well the motion model predicts the next frame, and their decoders run networks. Parameterization-based methods compress keyframe trajectories~ lee2025rd4dgs , or code canonical attributes as images and temporal features as video~ ke2026streamstgs,wang2024v3 . title: RegHarness: Regulating What Code-as-Policy Agents Keep from Steps to Skills
summary: Code-as-Policy agents generate, execute, and revise robot programs, but often lack explicit mechanisms to govern what persists across executions: which actions are retained within a trial and which code modifications carry over to subsequent runs. This leaves two critical aspects of agent behavior insufficiently controlled: step-level execution and cross-run adaptation. We present RegHarness, a two-level harness that governs both forms of persistence for the RATs agent team, without relying on a vision-language-action (VLA) policy or demonstrations. Within each trial, run-time governance evaluates each proposed step from a reset scene, replaying the committed steps, while a fixed-rule controller commits the step only when both RATs' verifier and a task-long LLM auditor approve it. Between runs, a coding agent uses logged failures to develop and test revisions to skills, primitives, and rules, which remain disabled by default until explicitly enabled by the authors. Using a single low-cost model across all run-time roles, RegHarness achieves an 87.8% success rate (158/180) on paired LIBERO-PRO trials, compared with 39.4% for RATs, and a 72.0% success rate on MolmoSpaces trials. A $2\times2$ ablation study of RegHarness's two levels shows that its skill refinement alone increases RATs' successful trials from 71 to 135, whereas run-time governance alone achieves 105 and RATs' native stepwise reset-and-replay mode achieves only 46. These findings suggest that, for Code-as-Policy agents operating with low-cost models, task success depends not only on how generated programs are executed, but also on the quality of the reusable skills they invoke and how those skills evolve across runs.

Introduction sec:intro Consider the task in : pick the black bowl on top of a cabinet and place it on a plate. ~ zhang2026rats , a Code-as-Policy~ liang2022cap agent team that we run with a low-cost language model, makes six attempts at this ~ zhou2025liberopro task, each a program for the whole plan. Its static checker rejects one program before it runs, and none of the five that run lifts the bowl: the first leaves it on the cabinet, the last two knock it onto the table. Over the 180 paired trials, solves 39.4 (71/180) within six attempts but only 13 on the first. In its published loop, judges each step only after the whole program has run; a retry, though prompted to keep what worked, is a complete program run again from the reset scene, so a passed step can change and must pass again. All 692 retries are complete programs, and 86 (493/574) of those that follow a diagnosed failure change code outside the failed step (criteria in the supplementary material). Nor does a clean verdict mean the work is done: in 117 of the 670 failed executions, the verifier flags no failed step. What these agents lack is a rule for what to keep: which executed steps stay committed within a trial, and which code changes carry over to the next run. Testing one step at a time does not supply it by itself: the released code already contains a stepwise mode, off by default and not described in its paper, that resets the scene and replays the passed steps before every try, but it commits a step on the verifier's pass alone and, once a step's tries run out, commits the step unverified so that the plan can go on. A reset protects a retried step from what the failed test left behind, but it also erases what that test revealed; a trial therefore needs a memory that outlives the reset, and a commit rule that never keeps an unverified step instead of letting the coder's next program decide which code survives. title: FailPoint-X: A Policy-Matched, Failure-Anchored Benchmark for Offline VLA Post-Training from Human Takeovers
comment: 34 pages (8-page main paper, references, and 24-page supplementary material), 9 figures, 20 tables. Zirui Li and Yujie Yan contributed equally. Project page: https://lzrbit.github.io/FailPoint_X/ ; Code: https://github.com/yujieyan81/failpoint-x
summary: Human takeovers offer corrective supervision for vision-language-action (VLA) policies, but their contribution to offline post-training must be separated from that of continued optimization. We introduce FailPoint-X, a benchmark for offline VLA post-training with human takeovers. To represent uncertainty in failure onset, an annotator marks an interval for each failure, and training takeovers start at seeded frames sampled within it. From one fixed $π_{0.5}$ checkpoint, which also initializes post-training, we assemble 629 natural failures across 10 LIBERO-X task families at up to five difficulty levels. All 2,823 takeover attempts are logged; 2,400 are accepted recoveries, of which 2,320 are used for post-training. Evaluation restarts every method from the fixed midpoints of 384 held-out failure intervals. Under matched actor-update counts, we compare behavior cloning of recoveries, value-based offline learning on recoveries and failed rollouts, and continued training on existing demonstrations. Within 1,200 steps on the 240 L1-L3 held-out failures, cloning improves recovery by 29.4 percentage points (pp) over the demonstration-only control; the value-based learner does not establish a further gain (1.5 pp). In exploratory evaluation from L1-L5 nominal starts at the same horizon, cloning loses 30.0 pp of success relative to the base policy; mixing in demonstrations reduces the loss to 16.5 pp, a reduction that shrinks under a stricter, pre-specified horizon. Restorable failure states and a shared evaluator let all methods be compared from identical starts.

Introduction sec:intro Vision-language-action (VLA) policies map visual observations and language instructions to robot control actions. Embodied agents more broadly must decide and act reliably under partial observation, from judging whether a target is present to searching unseen environments for it~ lewis2026safevantage,ji2026sornav,cai2026intentnav . Reliable manipulation, however, requires handling states induced by the robot's own errors, including missed grasps, misplaced objects, and interrupted task progress. At such states, a human takeover can supply corrective actions that restore progress toward the original goal. Offline post-training seeks to make such recovery autonomous, learning from human corrections or from the robot's own mixed-quality deployment experience~ ren2026mixedquality ; we study it on human recoveries recorded at a fixed policy's own failures. Training uses failed policy executions and human takeovers from their intermediate states; the resulting policy must autonomously complete the original task from held-out failure states of the same task configurations. The contribution of takeover data is difficult to isolate from overall task success alone. From a nominal start, a higher success rate may reflect either avoiding an error or recovering from one. Moreover, post-training adds optimization steps, so comparing a post-trained policy directly with the base policy conflates the effect of new data with that of continued optimization. LIBERO-RECOVER~ liu2026liberorecover reports recovery gains from fine-tuning on recoveries mixed with demonstrations, without a demonstration-only control matched in training recipe and optimizer steps. RePO-VLA~ liufu2026repovla includes a matched-budget ablation of value conditioning on the real-robot Fold Towel task and evaluates recovery under injected perturbations, and SimPT~ wang2026simpt compares post-training methods at matched policy-update counts on held-out environment seeds; neither reports recovery from the base policy's own held-out failures against a matched demonstration-only control. We therefore ask two questions about using recovery data for offline post-training. Q1: At matched actor updates, does training on human recoveries improve failure recovery more than continued training on existing demonstrations? Beyond the successful corrections, the preceding failed executions provide an additional negative training signal. Q2: Does value-based post-training on both recoveries and failed rollouts improve upon behavior cloning of recoveries alone? Collecting recovery data also requires deciding when to intervene. Selecting a single frame, whether by a model or a human, commits data collection to a single temporal judgment, yet perceived event boundaries depend on physical changes, interpreted goals, and temporal granularity~ kurby2008segmentation . We therefore let an annotator bracket the failure onset with an interval and start training takeovers from seeded frames sampled within it. We introduce , a policy-matched benchmark for offline VLA post-training with human takeovers: one checkpoint both generates the failures and initializes post-training ( , Table~ tab:related ). Because simulation can restore exactly the same recorded physical state across policies, the benchmark's failure-anchored protocol ( ) restarts every evaluated policy (arm) from the interval midpoints of the same held-out failures and, separately, from nominal starts to measure retained task performance. The unchanged base policy ( ) provides a reference. continues training on existing demonstrations for as many actor updates as the takeover-trained arms: clones accepted recoveries, adds failed training rollouts and a learned critic, and mixes recoveries with demonstrations. Q1 and Q2, paired over task families, are confirmatory on the held-out L1--L3 failures of all families; , the L4--L5 failures, and nominal starts are exploratory. Our collection pipeline ( , ) supplies recovery supervision from restorable failure states and logs its human cost. From rollouts of a fixed ~ black2025pi05 checkpoint, we assemble natural failures across ~ wang2026liberox task families at up to difficulty levels, split by seed into training and held-out sets. Takeovers are protocol-timed: the protocol, not the operator, draws seeded start frames per training failure, and unsuccessful attempts are retried at the same frame. We retain all attempts, including accepted recoveries, of which are used for post-training. In exploratory evaluations from L1--L5 nominal starts at the same horizon, loses pp of nominal success relative to the base policy; mixing in demonstrations reduces this loss to pp but lowers recovery ( b). This smaller loss depends on the evaluation horizon: under the stricter, pre-specified horizon ( : mean demonstration length), and change nominal success by similar amounts ( and ~pp; ). Thus, takeover data improve recovery in this study, while nominal-task evaluation reveals an accompanying retention loss. Related Work sec:related Learning from human interventions. Human interventions supervise the states a learner actually visits, which independently collected demonstrations may cover poorly. DAgger aggregates expert labels at learner-visited states~ ross2011dagger , and HG-DAgger lets the human decide when to intervene and return autonomy, yielding contiguous corrective segments~ kelly2019hgdagger . Sirius weights original demonstrations, autonomous rollouts, human interventions, and pre-intervention segments within an iterative deployment-and-training loop~ liu2023sirius . Extending human corrections to VLA reinforcement learning, ConRFT combines offline initialization on demonstrations with online intervention-guided learning~ chen2025conrft . instead fixes one round of protocol-timed human recoveries from a single base policy's failures and compares ways to use them for offline post-training. Offline learning from corrections and failures. While corrective trajectories supply direct action targets for imitation, autonomous rollouts additionally carry information about action outcomes. Prior work learns from such data with both imitation and value-based objectives: Sirius evaluates behavior cloning (BC) and Implicit Q-Learning (IQL) on deployment logs~ liu2023sirius , and RECAP integrates demonstrations, autonomous experience, and human corrections via value estimation and advantage-conditioned policy training~ pi2025pistar06 . Focusing on failure recovery, RePO-VLA imitates corrective suffixes and adds progress-aligned value supervision to learn from successful, failed, and corrective trajectories; it includes a non-value control on the same data and budget and an offline RECAP baseline matched in training steps and recovery-data budget~ liufu2026repovla . Similarly, SimPT benchmarks HG-DAgger, RECAP, and preference-based objectives on fixed datasets of policy rollouts and simulated expert corrections generated from per-task parent policies, matching policy-training steps and evaluating from held-out initial states~ wang2026simpt . We compare such objectives under controlled data and evaluation conditions. Our value-based arm adapts the advantage weighting of IQL~ kostrikov2022iql to the VLA's flow-matching objective; contrasting it with recovery-only behavior cloning evaluates the coupled choice of data composition and learning objective. title: $\widetilde{\varepsilon}$: Does Initial Noise Induce Directional Bias in Vision-Language-Action Models?
summary: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) have widely adopted diffusion-based action generation for continuous robot motions, enabling fine-grained control across diverse tasks. However, recent studies have shown that their performance is highly sensitive to initial noise, with resulting action errors that make recovery difficult during execution. Existing approaches search for favorable noise initializations to improve performance, yet the action expert itself remains sensitive to noise. In this work, we reveal that initial noise induces a consistent directional bias in action space that closely aligns with the noise's temporal mean. We thus introduce a simple yet effective framework that improves robustness to initial noise through interventions during both training and inference. During training, we enforce consistent action predictions from antithetic noise pairs $(ε, -ε)$ and, at inference, remove the noise's temporal mean. Our method substantially reduces action deviation and improves task performance across simulation benchmarks. In real-robot experiments, our method increases the average task success rate of $π_{0.5}$ from 40% to 68%, with more stable and consistent execution.

Introduction sec:intro Recent advances in diffusion models~ ho2020denoising,song2020denoising,rombach2022high,lipman2022flow have enabled vision-language-action models (VLAs) to generate continuous action sequences for smooth robot control~ chi2025diffusion,black2024pi,pmlr-v305-black25a,bjorck2025gr00t . As a result, VLAs can perform an increasingly broad range of tasks, from simple pick-and-place operations to long-horizon manipulation~ kim2024openvla,kim2025fine,cen2025worldvla,bu2025univla,zheng2026x,shukor2025smolvla,wen2025dexvla,team2025gemini . However, recent studies identify initial noise as a key factor contributing to inconsistent task performance~ patil2026you,yang2025steering . Since a single inaccurate motion can significantly alter the next observation and trigger cascading failures, robustness to initial noise is crucial for consistent manipulation. Also, recovery can be particularly difficult when such errors change the physical state of objects, as illustrated in~ ~(a), where a cube falls during stacking. Therefore, improving robustness to initial noise is essential for reliable real-world deployment of VLAs. Prior works have explored two main approaches to address initial noise sensitivity in diffusion-based policies. One research direction is to improve manipulation performance by searching for favorable initial noise or evaluating multiple generated action candidates~ patil2026you,wagenmaker2025steering,kwok2025robomonkey,yang2025steering . Another line of work learns the noise distribution or modifies the noise-to-action mapping during training~ dai2026should,zhong2026noise,liu2025sample . However, both approaches often require additional computation during inference or training for task-specific adaptation. Furthermore, they do not fully explain the systematic changes that initial noise induces in action space, and the resulting policies remain sensitive to noise initialization. To address this limitation, we analyze how initial noise affects action generation. We find that it inherently induces directional deviations in generated actions, which we refer to as directional bias. We empirically reveal that the same noise sample produces similarly directed deviations despite different observations and language instructions, while antithetic noise pairs tend to induce biases in opposite directions. These observations suggest that the initial noise is a primary driver of directional bias. Further analysis reveals that this direction closely aligns with the temporal mean of the initial noise. By assuming the action distribution as Gaussian, we theoretically show that the directional bias remains aligned with the initial noise’s temporal mean. These findings motivate a method that reduces directional bias for more stable action generation across noise initializations. Guided by these insights, we propose intuitive solutions that address directional bias at both training and inference time. Specifically, during training, we enforce consistency between action predictions obtained from antithetic noise pairs to reduce the effect of initial noise. This encourages the action expert to generate more consistent actions across different noise initializations. At inference, we directly subtract the temporal mean from each sample and use it to initialize the action generation (see ~(b)). Through comprehensive evaluations, we confirm that reductions in noise sensitivity are generally accompanied by improved task performance, supporting the importance of addressing the directional bias. These gains are achieved through simple corrections that can be readily applied to a variety of VLA models. The improvements also extend to real-robot execution, where our method increases the average task success rate of \( _ 0.5 \) from 40 to 68 , while improving motion stability. Related Work sec:2_rel_work Improving Diffusion-Based Robot Policies -time intervention. During the denoising process, various intervention methods can be applied to improve the stability of generated actions. These approaches can be broadly categorized into three groups based on where the intervention occurs: initial noise selection, intermediate denoising guidance, and final action selection. (a) Initial Noise Selection. Favorable noise initializations steer a frozen policy toward desirable actions~ simsir2026lagrangian, ho2026start, tang2026improving . DSRL~ wagenmaker2025steering uses reinforcement learning to learn a policy that selects initial noise, while Golden Ticket~ patil2026you searches for a high-performing noise vector reusable across observations. (b) Intermediate Denoising Guidance. Guidance redirects intermediate samples toward task objectives~ yang2026guided, sirigiri2026bayesfp, park2026acg, zhou2026test, du2026dynaguide . VLS~ liu2026vls uses a vision-language model (VLM) to generate rewards that reflect spatial and semantic requirements, while Hume~ song2025hume evaluates partially denoised candidates and completes selected proposals through cascaded denoising. (c) Final Action Selection. Candidate evaluation selects among sampled actions using value estimates, verification, or distributional criteria~ nakamoto2024steering, kwok2025robomonkey, jang2026verifier, nguyen2026self, zhao2026action, xu2026vgas . KeyStone~ dai2026geometry selects the medoid of the dominant cluster, while TACO~ yang2025steering uses a pseudo-counting module to select actions. However, such interventions often introduce additional preparation or inference costs due to noise search or repeated candidate evaluation. -time source and policy design. Another line of work improves diffusion-based robot policies by redesigning their action generation framework. ResVLA~ zhong2026noise anchors generation to predicted motion intent through a residual diffusion bridge, while WarmPrior~ kang2026warmprior constructs a temporal source prior from previous action predictions. Relevant methods incorporate sources conditioned on the state~ dai2026should , learned motion priors~ machado2026flowing , or stochastic dynamics conditioned on observations~ liu2025sample . Also, GeCO~ zhang2026generative uses convergence to guide adaptive refinement, while BehaviorVLA~ hu2026abstraction improves policy representations by modeling long-horizon behavior. However, these approaches may be sensitive to errors in predicted priors and require changes to existing model architectures or generation processes. Does Initial Noise Induce Directional Bias? title: Integration of Vision-Language-Action Control for Autonomous Forklift Unloading with Limited Real-World Data
summary: Forklifts play a critical role in warehousing and distribution, but existing automation systems remain limited in handling complex tasks that require sequential decision-making. Recently, vision--language--action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising approach for multi-step decision-making by directly generating control actions from visual observations and language prompts. Although VLA-based control has been extensively researched for manipulators, to the best of our knowledge, its application to forklifts remains unexplored. Therefore, this study demonstrates the integration of VLA control for an autonomous forklift unloading task with limited real-world data. Moreover, training VLA models typically requires large-scale datasets. As there is currently no public dataset for forklift operations, we use a VLA model pretrained primarily on robotic manipulator data and construct a training dataset via simulation, which can be scaled up at low cost. We then adapt the pretrained VLA model to forklift control using 9.38 h of simulation data and 0.8 h of real-world demonstrations, with the latter accounting for approximately 8% of the collected forklift data by duration. The integrated system was validated through 72 real-world trials across four model variants. The results show that the proposed system can accomplish an unloading task even with limited real-world data.
full_text: Forklifts play a critical role in warehousing and distribution, but existing automation systems remain limited in handling complex tasks that require sequential decision-making. Recently, vision--language--action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising approach for multi-step decision-making by directly generating control actions from visual observations and language prompts. Although VLA-based control has been extensively researched for manipulators, to the best of our knowledge, its application to forklifts remains unexplored. Therefore, this study demonstrates the integration of VLA control for an autonomous forklift unloading task with limited real-world data. Moreover, training VLA models typically requires large-scale datasets. As there is currently no public dataset for forklift operations, we use a VLA model pretrained primarily on robotic manipulator data and construct a training dataset via simulation, which can be scaled up at low cost. We then adapt the pretrained VLA model to forklift control using 9.38 h of simulation data and 0.8 h of real-world demonstrations, with the latter accounting for approximately 8 of the collected forklift data by duration. The integrated system was validated through 72 real-world trials across four model variants. The results show that the proposed system can accomplish an unloading task even with limited real-world data. Introduction sec:intro Forklifts are among the most widely used industrial vehicles in warehousing and distribution. In the context of rapidly expanding global logistics, forklifts are indispensable material-handling equipment, and their automation has become increasingly important. Forklift automation has already been implemented in restricted environments, using system designs broadly similar to those reported by Walter et al.~ walter_Pallet_Manipulation and Teller et al.~ teller_Voice . However, these approaches rely heavily on accurate state estimation using multiple sensors and hard-coded logic tailored to constrained spaces ~ hadwiger2026partial . In real-world deployments, where forklifts operate under diverse and changing conditions, hard-coding decisions for all possible situations is prohibitively costly to engineer and maintain. This motivates the need for an alternative approach to conventional systems that depend heavily on human-engineered design. Recently, with the rapid progress of vision--language models (VLMs), there is a growing interest in vision--language--action (VLA) models that extend VLMs to directly output actions Yin_GPT,rt1,rt2, kawaharazuka . VLA models address decision-making scenarios that are challenging for conventional approaches, enabling automation in long-horizon and complex tasks~ kim2024openvla,openX, black2024pi_0, bjorck2025gr00t . This capability can reduce reliance on hard-coded logic, which is inflexible and costly to maintain as operating conditions vary. Applying VLA models can potentially automate decision-making in complex forklift operations. However, most VLA research has focused on manipulators, and forklift-specific studies remain limited. In this study, we integrate a VLA model into a forklift unloading system and automate the unloading sequence by directly generating actions from language and visual observations (Fig.~ fig:zu1 ). Our integrated system can handle task goals in natural language and generate action sequences while jointly predicting the current task phase, eliminating the need to manually enter numeric targets or implementing extensive hard-coded logic. Moreover, training VLA models requires large-scale datasets. However, to the best of our knowledge, no public dataset currently exists for forklift operations. Therefore, we employed a VLA model pretrained primarily on robotic manipulator data and constructed a simulation dataset so that the embodiment gap between manipulators and forklifts could be bridged without large-scale real-world forklift data. We performed real-world evaluation of our approach on a 1/14-scale forklift platform by conducting 72 trials, including baseline comparisons. Although full-scale forklifts are the intended target, the 1/14-scale platform enables safer, real-world iterations during early-stage learning-based development. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first real-world integration study of VLA-based end-to-end action generation for a forklift unloading task. The main contributions are as follows: We integrate a VLA model into a forklift unloading system, enabling phase inference and action generation from onboard sensor observations while supporting low-latency execution. We present a cross-embodiment adaptation recipe that combines simulation-based mid-training with post-training on 0.8 h of real-world forklift demonstrations. We evaluate the proposed integrated system through 72 real-world trials across four model variants and demonstrate that it can accomplish the unloading task even with limited real-world data. Section~ sec:work reviews related work, Sections~ sec:system -- sec:data describe the integrated system, Section~ sec:demo reports real-world experiments, and Sections~ sec:lim and sec:con discuss limitations and conclusions. Related work sec:work Recent forklift studies have combined advanced sensing technologies with deep learning to improve the robustness of environmental perception for autonomous forklift operation~ Iinuma_2020jrm,huemer2025adapt, shokki_sii . Nguyen et al.~ nguyen2025lang2lift used Florence-2~ Xiao_florence , a VLM, for pallet detection and target selection of forklifts. While these studies improve perception robustness and reduce part of reliance on hard-coded logic, the transition from perception to task execution still requires manual system design. Reinforcement-learning (RL)-based action generation has also been studied for forklift tasks~ hadwiger2026partial, oishi . RL learns actions in a human-like manner, allowing the system to rely only on onboard sensors such as cameras and velocity. However, RL-based studies primarily focused on short-horizon skills, such as pallet approach. Applying RL to the entire unloading task is difficult owing to the increased complexity of reward design for long-horizon behaviors with multiple conditional branches. Considering these challenges, this study introduces recent VLA techniques to forklift control, thereby aiming to reduce hand-coded logic and reward design while retaining a minimal onboard sensing setup comparable to prior RL-based studies. VLA models are commonly developed by first acquiring visual understanding and decision-making capabilities from large-scale non-robot web data, then transferring these capabilities to robot control using large-scale robot datasets, and finally fine-tuning the model on data from the target robot~ kawaharazuka . The first two stages require large amounts of data, and collecting real-world robot data is costly and time-consuming. Existing robot datasets are biased toward robot arms~ rt1,openX and autonomous driving~ cardata ; therefore, directly applying existing VLA models to industrial machinery, such as forklifts, is challenging. Recent advances in simulation have enabled automatic generation of high-quality robot data, and sim-to-real transfer has been demonstrated in some robotic tasks~ Orbit_isaac,oishi . Although simulation data can be less diverse than real-world data and cannot cover all real-world conditions, it can provide useful supervision for transferring action generation to a new embodiment. Based on this observation, we use digital-twin-generated data to adapt a VLA model pretrained on web and robot-arm data to forklift action generation, and then fine-tune it with a small amount of real-world data. VLA models have also been developed for robot navigation~ cheng2025navila . Because forklift unloading requires accurate pallet alignment, pickup, and placement in addition to navigation, we use ~ pmlr-v305-black25a , which is pretrained on robotic manipulation data. Additionally, simulation-based data generation automatically provides most of the subtask labels. We demonstrate that this training recipe enables a VLA policy to perform a complex forklift unloading task even when large-scale forklift operation data are unavailable. Moreover, the simulation environment and the 1/14-scale forklift platform are based on Oishi et al.~ oishi . Recent VLA studies have proposed techniques for long-horizon control and real-time deployment. For tasks consisting of multiple subtasks, methods that jointly learn task progress or semantic states with action generation have been explored~ pmlr-v305-black25a,bjorck2025gr00t . We integrate a simplified version of the semantic prediction approach of Black et al.~ pmlr-v305-black25a by jointly training subtask prediction with action generation. In addition, because VLA inference is often slower than the control cycle of industrial machinery, asynchronous action chunking has been proposed to perform inference while previously predicted actions are being executed~ black2024pi_0,black2026real . Our system implements a simplified version of this idea for real-time execution on a physical forklift platform. System overview sec:system The proposed integration combines an online VLA-based forklift control system with an offline adaptation pipeline, as shown in Fig.~ fig:system . As a target task, we address pallet unloading from a wing truck using a 1/14-scale forklift platform for safe and repeatable evaluation. Task setting sec:task The unloading task consists of subtasks, including picking up the pallet, backing out, searching the right side for the target color while backing out, and placing the pallet at the specified color location. Fig.~ fig:subtask illustrates the subtasks that compose the primary task. The forklift starts approximately 0.15 m in front of the pallet. The operator only provides the prompt; all other operations are executed autonomously. Hardware platform sec:hardware We used the 1/14-scale forklift platform introduced by Oishi et al.~ oishi (Fig.~ fig:hard ). Most hardware and sensing specifications follow those reported by Oishi et al.; therefore, we describe only the components and any deviation relevant to this study. This platform is a counterbalance-type forklift, which is the most common forklift configuration, with rear-wheel steering and front-wheel drive. The visual data were captured using two pinhole cameras mounted on the left and right sides of the forklift. For the determination of the vehicle speed and yaw rate, we used a motion-capture system owing to the ease of implementation. In a full-scale forklift, these speeds are typically available directly from the vehicle. Fork height was measured using a rotary encoder mounted near the top of the fork assembly, which estimated the lift height based on the amount of chain winding. For actions, the throttle command was specified in the range 0--100 , the steering command was defined as the servo motor angle, and the fork-height command specified the target height. The forklift was equipped with a Raspberry Pi 4, which communicates with the inference PC via robot operating system (ROS)~ ROS to exchange action commands and sensor observations. Integrated architecture sec:integ Fig.~ fig:system shows the overall architecture of the proposed system. The offline pipeline first trains a VLA policy on web-scale vision--language data and large-scale robot manipulation data, and then adapts it to forklift control. Simulator-generated forklift data serves as a mid-training stage that bridges the embodiment gap between robot manipulators and the forklift, while a short post-training stage on a small amount of real-world data specializes the policy to the target platform and its operating environment. The use of robot manipulation data is also motivated by its structural similarity to forklift operation. Our pallet unloading task is essentially a pick-and-place problem: the forklift

title: X-World: Transferring Video Priors to Cross-Embodiment Robot Control
summary: Language-instructed manipulation requires robust closedloop policies, yet action-labeled robot trajectories are costly and limited in coverage. Human and robot videos provide complementary spatiotemporal priors for crossembodiment control. We propose X-World, which adapts pretrained video diffusion to variable views. A Q-Former compresses hidden states into tokens for a shared flowmatching expert that predicts action chunks. Datasetspecific projections map native states and actions. We adapt the backbone on large-scale robot and human videos, freeze it for action-only pretraining of the Q-Former and action expert, then post-train on the target platform. At inference, X-World responds at 20 Hz and overlaps updates with execution via asynchronous real-time chunking. X-World performs strongly on LIBERO and under zero-shot shifts on LIBERO-Plus. On hardware, it averages 81.7% success across six bimanual tasks on the side-mounted dual-arm UR5e, one of three real-robot configurations presented.

Introduction sec:intro Language-instructed robotic manipulation~ brohan2022rt,brohan2023rt requires policies that translate high-level instructions into robust low-level actions under diverse contacts, partial observability, and long horizons. Recent vision-language-action (VLA) policies~ brohan2022rt,brohan2023rt,kim2024openvla,team2024octo,bjorck2025gr00t,black2024pi0,pi05 rely on large collections of action-labeled trajectories that are costly to obtain and often limited in task, embodiment, and viewpoint coverage. Internet-scale videos of humans and robots capture spatiotemporal patterns such as motion and contact. How can video world priors improve closed-loop manipulation across embodiments with limited action supervision? Prior work~ ye2024latent,du2023learning,hu2024video suggests that pretrained video diffusion models can aid action generation. Many methods assume a single view or a fixed camera layout, making them harder to deploy on robots with different numbers of cameras. Multi-view adaptations~ liao2025genie can shift the backbone away from its pretrained behavior and weaken transfer. Across robot embodiments, datasets~ o2024open,bu2025agibot,wu2025robocoin,jiang2025galaxea,wu2024robomind define states and actions in different coordinate frames, units, and control conventions. Directly pooling these action targets in one space can produce incompatible supervision and destabilize learning. Iterative sampling and large backbones can hinder real-time control by increasing latency. To address these limitations, we propose , which (i) adapts a pretrained video diffusion backbone (LTX-Video~ hacohen2024ltx ) to variable-view robot observations via view embeddings and a zero-initialized cross-view attention module, (ii) distills diffusion hidden states into a compact token sequence via a Q-Former as a world-prior interface for action generation, (iii) trains a shared action expert across embodiments and, following X-VLA~ xvla , uses dataset-specific projections to encode states and actions and decode predictions into native actions, and (iv) supports continuous control via asynchronous real-time chunking that decouples inference updates from action execution to avoid waiting latency. We train in three steps to separate learning a transferable video world prior from learning control. First, we adapt the pretrained video diffusion backbone on large-scale robot~ o2024open,bu2025agibot,wu2025robocoin,jiang2025galaxea,wu2024robomind and human videos~ grauman2022ego4d,zhao2025humanoid to acquire a strong spatiotemporal prior. Then, we freeze the video diffusion backbone and optimize the Q-Former and action expert with the action-only objective for knowledge isolation, so action gradients do not perturb the learned prior. Finally, we post-train on target-platform data to adapt the policy for benchmark or real-world deployment. We evaluate on LIBERO~ liu2023libero and test the same checkpoint under zero-shot distribution shifts on LIBERO-Plus~ fei2025liberoplus . The policy performs well on both benchmarks, with its largest gains over OpenVLA-OFT~ OFT on LIBERO-Plus occurring under robot, language, and layout perturbations. On real hardware, we evaluate on six bimanual tasks on the side-mounted dual-arm UR5e. Figure~ fig:teaser shows task examples from all three configurations, including textile handling on the shared-frame dual-arm UR5e and interaction with a household appliance on the Unitree G1. Our contributions are threefold. (i) We upgrade a pretrained video diffusion backbone to variable-view robot videos via view embeddings and a zero-initialized cross-view attention module. (ii) We distill diffusion hidden states into a token sequence via a Q-Former and train a shared flow-matching action expert across embodiments, with dataset-specific projections for native state and action spaces. (iii) We train in three stages by adapting the video diffusion backbone on large-scale videos and learning action generation with the backbone kept frozen for knowledge isolation, and deploy with asynchronous real-time chunking for low-latency control. Related work sec:related -action models. Video-action models bridge visual dynamics and control by leveraging world priors inherited from video foundation models for action generation. Recent advancements in this domain~ hu2024video,liao2025genie,li2026causal have demonstrated capabilities comparable to vision-language-action (VLA) policies across a broad spectrum of tasks. Furthermore, in evaluations targeting generalization and zero-shot task completion, these models have been reported to match or even surpass VLA policies in specific settings~ ye2026world . Early frameworks~ du2023learning,du2023video,wen2024vidman typically adopt a two-stage design, where they first generate future observations as explicit video rollouts and subsequently employ inverse dynamics to map predicted state transitions back to actions. While this pipeline renders the world rollout explicit, prediction errors can propagate to the downstream control module, and the decoupled architecture often increases engineering complexity for closed-loop deployment. To mitigate these issues, recent works extract internal generative features, such as denoising hidden states or latent representations, to serve as world priors for action generation. Certain methods~ hu2024video,yang2025covar compress these features into compact tokens for cross-attention with an action expert, whereas others~ bi2025motus,liao2025genie,ye2026world,li2026causal,pai2025mimic jointly model video and action sequences using mixture-of-transformers architectures. In parallel, Cosmos Policy~ kim2026cosmos represents actions as image-like tokens and reuses video generators to synthesize action sequences directly, offering an alternative that avoids a separate action expert. In contrast, adapts a pretrained video diffusion backbone to variable-view robot videos and bypasses explicit video rollouts by compressing its per-layer denoising hidden states into a token sequence via a layer-aligned Q-Former, while following a three-phase training pipeline to better preserve the video model priors. -embodiment training. The emergence of robotic foundation models has been significantly propelled by scaling training across expansive datasets from diverse platforms~ o2024open . However, naive aggregation of trajectories from disparate embodiments often yields diminishing returns, primarily due to inherent discrepancies in action interfaces and observation spaces. A burgeoning line of work~ doshi2024scaling,wang2024scaling,zheng2025universal,xvla addresses these heterogeneities by introducing alignment layers or adapters that project dataset-specific signals into a canonical representation. Beyond action-state mismatches, observation heterogeneity arising from varied camera extrinsics and robot morphologies poses additional challenges. For instance, VLA-LPAF~ bian2025vla alleviates viewpoint-induced shifts via representation-level feature alignment, while other strategies operate at the data level through novel-view synthesis~ chen2024rovi or embodiment inpainting~ chen2024mirage,chen2024rovi,ji2025oxe . Distinctively, capitalizes on large-scale video pretraining to internalize world dynamics across diverse observations, while concurrently bridging heterogeneous action interfaces via modular adapters to facilitate unified policy learning. Method sec:method Overview subsec:method-setup We study language-instructed closed-loop manipulation where, at time step , the policy takes variable-view RGB observations , a language instruction , and proprioceptive state , and outputs a short action chunk in the embodiment's native action space. In Sec.~ subsec:method-arch , we introduce , which seamlessly adapts a pretrained video diffusion model to robot observations and leverages its world prior to scale action learning on heterogeneous VLA datasets. In Sec.~ subsec:method-training , we describe a three-stage training pipeline that learns the video world prior from videos and transfers it to action generation. Finally, in Sec.~ subsec:method-inference , we present asynchronous real-time chunking for low-latency closed-loop control. Figure~ fig:pipeline shows the full pipeline. Model architecture subsec:method-arch consists of three modules: (i) a variable-view video diffusion backbone that encodes spatiotemporal world representations, (ii) a Q-Former that distills them into a compact token sequence serving as a world prior, and (iii) a shared action expert that attends to this world prior to generate action chunks, with dataset-specific modules aligning state and action interfaces across datasets. images/video-generation.pdf Future-video predictions. We show predictions at frames 8, 16, and 24. These examples demonstrate that the model supports future-video generation from various views. images/video-generation-real-world.pdf Future-video predictions on real-world teleoperation. For each of two tasks, we show the observed frame and predictions at frames 8, 16, and 24, illustrating how the model anticipates plausible task progression. diffusion backbone. We start from a pretrained LTX-Video diffusion backbone~ hacohen2024ltx and adapt it to variable-view robot observations. Given an instruction and a single variable-view history frame at time , the backbone is trained to predict a future clip over a video-adaptation horizon of , distinct from the executable action chunk used for closed-loop control. Its video VAE downsamples by spatially and temporally, reducing token count for efficient training and inference. Robot setups vary in camera count and viewpoint. Genie-Envisioner~ liao2025genie extends LTX-Video to three views by replacing pretrained self-attention with cross-view attention, concatenating tokens across views before attention and splitting them afterward. However, this modification changes the backbone function at initialization and can shift it away from the pretrained distribution. Moreover, Genie-Envisioner is trained on the three-view AgiBotWorld dataset~ bu2025agibot , constraining downstream policies to a three-view observation format. To preserve the pretrained computation at initialization, we retain per-view self-attention and add cross-view attention as a zero-initialized residual branch (illustrated in the appendix). We also add a view embedding to encode view identity without assuming a fixed semantic ordering, and we randomize view order during training to improve robustness to heterogeneous camera setups. Each training sample uses three view slots. For samples with one or two views, we fill the remaining slots by replicating an existing view and apply independent diffusion noise to each replica, avoiding padding. title: SEEK: Self-Evolution through Execution Knowledge for Agentic Robot Manipulation
summary: General-purpose multimodal foundation models enable robots to adapt during deployment from observations and execution feedback, without task-specific demonstrations or training. However, the robot retains what it learns only in the model's working context. Once the task ends, it loses this execution knowledge, such as how to carry a bowl between two grippers. On the next attempt at the task, the robot may take just as long and repeat the same mistakes. To avoid this repetition, robots must retain execution knowledge across attempts. Yet replaying past actions is insufficient, because their effects depend on the current conditions.
