Introduction Recent advances in robot learning have been driven by scaling demonstration data and model capacity, producing policies with broader task coverage and stronger generalization~ rt12023,rtx2024,rt22023,octo2024,openvla2024,gr00tn12025 . Yet these capabilities remain bounded by the distributions represented in the training data~ rt12023,openvla2024,rax2026 . Extending these policies to new embodiments, tasks, or conditions beyond this coverage typically requires additional data collection, training, or fine-tuning~ droid2024,octo2024,openvla2024,geminirobotics2025,pistar062026 . As a result, capability growth remains closely coupled to pre-collected demonstrations and the imitation distribution they define~ rtx2024,rax2026 . General-purpose multimodal models offer another route to robot adaptation through reasoning during deployment~ saycan2022,codeaspolicies2023,voxposer2023,rekep2024 . By combining current visual observations with task instructions and execution feedback, these models can guide the robot’s actions and adjust its behavior as execution unfolds~ innermonologue2022,voxposer2023,roboicl2026 . Through this interaction, the robot acquires execution knowledge: the effects its actions produce under given conditions and the procedures that prove effective. For example, it may find that a thin coin remains on the table when pinched at its center but lifts when pinched at its rim. However, the robot retains this knowledge only within the model’s working context. Once the task ends, the knowledge is lost. On its next attempt, the robot may again pinch the coin at its center before rediscovering the rim, taking just as long as before. Avoiding this repetition requires retaining execution knowledge across attempts. Yet simply replaying past actions is insufficient. The same action can yield different effects under different conditions. The robot therefore needs reusable procedures that determine each action from the current scene. Existing and concurrent approaches have begun to retain such procedures as skills and programs~ voyager2023,lrll2024,embodiedevo2026,robofoundry2026,rax2026 . However, retaining a procedure does not ensure that it will handle conditions beyond those encountered in earlier attempts. When a procedure encounters such conditions, measured action effects provide evidence for deciding how to revise it. This evidence should include actions from failed attempts. Procedures and measured action effects therefore need to be retained together, so that a procedure can act without the model where it applies and be revised from this evidence where it does not. Existing methods that keep action-level evidence still leave each action to the model or a learned policy~ lexp2026,robodoctor2026,robofoundry2026 , while programs that act without the model are frozen once developed~ etm2026 . To this end, we introduce , a framework for agentic robot manipulation that enables self-evolution through execution knowledge while keeping the underlying model fixed. retains this knowledge in two coupled forms. At the procedure level, a Self-Evolving Programmatic Policy (SEPP) encodes observation, action generation, verification, task progression, and recovery as executable procedures. During execution, these procedures use current observations to determine actions. At the action level, a Persistent Action-Effect Bank (PAEB) records the measured effect of each executed action with its execution context, including actions from failed attempts. Drawing on these records, the fixed model makes decisions or revises a procedure, and each revision retains references to its supporting evidence. Together, the two components form a continual self-improvement loop: execution supplies evidence for policy revision, and revised procedures carry the resulting capability into subsequent attempts. Once a retained procedure applies to the current scene, it can generate actions without another model request, so successive attempts reuse previously acquired behavior instead of repeating model deliberation. We evaluate on RoboDojo~ robodojo2026 , a simulation benchmark of 42 dual-arm manipulation tasks. To isolate the contribution of retained knowledge, we compare the same system with and without it on scenes unseen during self-evolution; both conditions allow adaptation within an attempt. Across the 42 tasks, knowledge retained over ten attempts more than doubles task performance. Compared with GPT-6.2 Astra acting directly on 34 of these tasks, with the same model raises the task score from 49.6 to 80.1 after five attempts and uses 77.6 fewer model requests. We further measure the fraction of executed steps generated by retained procedures, and ablate PAEB and SEPP to separate the contributions of action-level evidence reuse and procedure-level policy evolution. Finally, on a smaller set of tasks, we replace the underlying model and run on a real robot; in both settings, again improves task performance. Related Work Foundation Models for Robot Control. Foundation models support robot control through learned action policies~ rt22023,openvla2024 and agents that reason during execution~ saycan2022,innermonologue2022 . General-purpose multimodal models can also act as the policy directly, deciding each action from observations and execution feedback without task-specific demonstrations or training~ roboprobe2026 . The execution knowledge such an agent gains is held only in the model's working context and is lost once the task ends. Reusable Programs for Robot Manipulation. Executable programs preserve control logic as reusable procedures. Code as Policies and ProgPrompt express robot behavior as programs that compose available perception and action interfaces~ codeaspolicies2023,progprompt2022 . PyRUA-Lean extends these interfaces with Python cells that perform local checks, retries, and selective observation without additional model requests~ pyrua2026 . These cells build on a primitive library that its authors wrote for the benchmark's dual-arm station and on operating notes, including how strictly the benchmark judges a final scene. Its programs are written anew in each attempt, which therefore starts from what the authors supplied rather than from what earlier attempts revealed. A retained program that acts without the model removes repeated deliberation for behavior already resolved, and one that also remains revisable during execution can be corrected as soon as it meets a condition that earlier attempts did not cover. COAP retains its programs. Coding agents develop a shared library for perception, state tracking, and control through offline refinement from execution traces, then freeze the code for execution without the model~ etm2026 . This refinement uses state information that a robot acting from its own observations does not have. The agents compare the measured object state against simulator ground truth, and the perception code takes the object shapes published with the benchmark as constants. Once frozen, the code can no longer be revised when it meets a condition that development did not cover, such as an object below a fixed size threshold, and each new task requires further offline development. Voyager, PhysicalRSI, and RoboFoundry keep their skills revisable from execution~ voyager2023,physicalrsi2026,robofoundry2026 , but the model remains in the loop; in RoboFoundry it is called at every step. Retained Experience for Robot Manipulation. Interaction history, lessons, and execution evidence preserve what prior actions have revealed. Reflexion and ExpeL retain reflections and extracted insights, while DROC distills language corrections into reusable knowledge~ reflexion2023,expel2024,droc2024 . RoboICL conditions the model on a task demonstration and keeps observations, actions, and execution receipts only within an attempt~ roboicl2026 . LEXP and RoboDoctor carry lessons and execution records across attempts together with their supporting evidence~ lexp2026,robodoctor2026 , but as context for the model. Neither retains an executable procedure, so each action is still decided by the model or by the learned policy it supervises. EmbodiedEvo brings procedural and diagnostic knowledge together by distilling physical feedback into reusable code Skills and Lessons during exploration in a separate scene~ embodiedevo2026 . Only these distilled artifacts reach the test scene, where they are read-only. The interaction records behind them are not carried over, and the coding agent still writes each program that calls the Skills. HexaShell develops its tools on the task itself. After each development attempt, an optimizer agent reads the attempt's log and adds or repairs task-specific tools, which are then frozen~ hexashell2026 . As with EmbodiedEvo, what carries forward is the distilled tools and notes rather than the records, and the acting agent still issues every command that calls a tool. couples persistent action-effect evidence with revisable executable procedures, both acquired from the robot's own attempts, allowing observed effects to directly support procedure revision and subsequent execution. Where a retained procedure applies, it generates actions without a model request; where it meets a condition it does not cover, the fixed model revises it within the attempt. Table~ tab:execution_knowledge compares these capabilities. title: Beyond the Happy Path: Generalizing Robot World Models from Simulated Failures
summary: Robot world models are increasingly used to evaluate and plan policies, yet robot training data are dominated by successful demonstrations. Off the happy path, when a grasp is misaligned or mistimed and the object is pushed, tilted, or slips, their predictions break down. Across five pretrained action-conditioned models, object-motion error is at most 10.4% lower than that of a static baseline that copies the first frame, and two models are worse than this baseline. We present WorldReforge, which teaches world models what happens when manipulation goes wrong. We construct the Reforge dataset of 62k simulated trajectories by perturbing reference grasps in position, orientation, and closure timing, recording each resulting push, slip, or failed pickup with ground-truth object pose, contact, and surface points. WorldReforge turns this ground truth into two training signals without additional inference cost. Interaction Alignment focuses reconstruction on the small object and contact regions that a global loss underweights, and Surface Correspondence trains backbone features to follow the same physical surface points across frames. On Cosmos3 Nano, WorldReforge reduces object trajectory error by 28.2% overall and by 35.0% on unseen objects, and it lowers the error in predicting how two actions' outcomes diverge by 43.3%. Although trained only in simulation, it also improves reconstruction on DROID and on real failure videos. Controlled data studies show that failed contact and successful holding teach complementary physics: failed contact teaches how objects respond, and holding teaches how a grasped state persists. Our code, data, and models are available at aim-uofa.github.io/WorldReforge/.

Introduction sec:intro Action-conditioned world models increasingly replace real-world rollouts for policy evaluation, data generation, and planning~ worldarena,worldoracle,ewmbench,dreamdojo . Their value depends on predicting how different actions produce different outcomes. Manipulation is where this requirement is hardest to meet. A grasp shifted by a centimeter or closed too early does not simply fail. The object is pushed, tilted, or slips from the fingers. Yet their robot training data are dominated by successful demonstrations~ openx,droid , so this branch of physics is rarely observed. We find that this happy-path bias is severe. On our simulated evaluation, five pretrained models from three families~ cosmos3,dreamdojo,lingbot achieve object-motion error at most 10.4 lower than a static baseline that copies the first frame, and two are worse ( ). Their predictions keep objects near the initial pose even when the recorded object is pushed or rotated ( ). Such predictions risk overrating the policies being evaluated~ curewm,fact . Recent work fine-tunes on failures obtained by perturbing or executing actions~ curewm,hfwm,fact,dreamtrue . These methods keep the original generative objective~ curewm , supervise outcomes through progress or reward signals~ fact,hfwm , or learn failure dynamics without ground-truth failure videos~ hfwm . Two limitations remain. First, contact dynamics occupy a small fraction of each frame, so a global reconstruction loss gives them little weight. Second, outcome-level signals indicate whether an interaction failed, not how the object moved. Simulation provides what real robot logs lack: failures can be produced at controlled offsets and timings, safely and at scale, each with exact object pose, contact, and surface geometry. We present , a post-training framework that exploits this ground truth ( ). The dataset contains 62k simulated trajectories over 96 objects, generated by perturbing successful reference grasps in translation, rotation, and closure timing. Trajectories link execution variations to observed outcomes, including contact formation and loss, pushing, tilting, slipping, and whether a grasp is established and maintained. These labels support controlled training compositions. Reforge-Real provides 300 real failure trajectories for evaluation. adds two objectives to the generative loss. Interaction Alignment (IA) reconstructs object and contact regions with a dedicated, area-normalized signal. Surface Correspondence (SC) requires intermediate backbone features to locate the same physical surface points across frames, supervised by simulator-projected trajectories. Neither adds inference-time parameters. Post-training on alone reduces object error by about a quarter for Cosmos3 Nano and LingBot-VA, and IA and SC further lower or match every motion error across all three model families. On Cosmos3 Nano, reduces object ADE by 28.2 overall and by 35.0 on objects unseen during post-training, and it predicts the divergence between two actions' outcomes with 43.3 lower error. Trained only in simulation, it improves PSNR by 1.04\,dB on DROID and 0.68\,dB on real failure videos. Controlled data studies reveal a division of labor. Adding failures in which the gripper closes without securing the object reduces object error on such contacts by 18.0 , while successful holding remains the best teacher for keeping a grasped object stable. Feature alignment complements training: REPA aligns denoising features with pretrained visual representations~ repa , VideoREPA aligns spatiotemporal token relations~ videorepa , and PhysisForcing aligns feature trajectories and semantic relations~ physisforcing . ABot-PhysWorld uses decoupled discriminative feedback for preference optimization~ abotphysworld . WorldReforge uses physical ground truth for local reconstruction and surface correspondence. Forecasting research motivates careful metric comparisons~ hyndman2006 , and TAP-Vid provides point-tracking protocols~ tapvid . RAFT estimates optical flow~ raft ; PIPs tracks individual points through occlusion~ pips ; TAPIR refines point trajectories~ tapir ; and CoTracker jointly models tracks, with CoTracker3 scaling supervision through pseudo-labeling~ cotracker,cotracker3,sam2tap . VBench and VideoScore assess video quality across multiple dimensions~ vbench,videoscore . EWMBench evaluates scene, motion, and semantic quality~ ewmbench , while WorldArena connects perception to data generation, policy evaluation, and planning~ worldarena . Framewise appearance alone does not establish action-dependent physical accuracy. We separately evaluate object motion, gripper motion, and video quality, alongside paired-action response differences. Method sec:method Action-Conditioned World Model An action-conditioned world model (AC-WM) predicts future observations from visual context and a robot action sequence~ visualforesight,sv2p,unisim . For physical interaction, the prediction must resolve how contact location, object pose, and gripper state affect the environment's response. We study future RGB prediction conditioned on an initial image and the recorded end-effector poses and gripper states. Given an initial observation and robot states , the action adapter of backbone maps adjacent states to action conditions . The resulting conditional distribution over future frames is The adapter preserves each backbone's action representation within a common prediction task: modeling the visual response to the recorded robot execution. The Reforge dataset sec:data Scale and Hierarchical Structure sec:data_distribution The Reforge dataset integrates diverse interaction experience with synchronized physical ground truth. In simulation, we construct successful reference executions using RoboLab~ robolab and cuRobo~ curobo , then perturb end-effector translation, rotation, and gripper closure timing. The resulting successful and failed interactions are recorded with synchronized RGB video, robot motion, and physical states, linking execution conditions to observed responses. summarizes this hierarchy. The dataset comprises 62,425 trajectories across 106 object assets. Its simulated component contains 62,125 trajectories from 96 assets, including 13,577 failure-related trajectories. Reforge-Real contributes 300 real-world failure trajectories across 10 objects, while Reforge-Eval denotes the simulated evaluation component. Inputs distinguish physical context---object attributes, initial poses, and scene configurations---from execution variations. In the simulated component, execution labels describe end-effector translation (51,964 trajectories), rotation (5,720), and gripper closure timing (4,356), relating robot actions to the conditions under which objects respond. Outputs separate time-aligned contact and object-motion events from grasp outcomes. Event labels record contact formation and loss, object translation, rotation, tilt, and post-grasp slip. Outcome labels indicate whether a grasp is established and maintained. Coexisting events are retained to distinguish transient object responses from sustained holding.

title: Targeted Adaptation of World-Action Models via Interaction and Motion Heads
summary: World-Action Models (WAMs) are a promising new paradigm of robot manipulation policies that jointly generate future video and actions. Successful manipulation requires both identifying where to interact and modeling how the robot and objects move. Yet standard adaptation methods, such as full fine-tuning and LoRA, do not explicitly select parameters aligned with these manipulation-specific capabilities. Motivated by this challenge, we discover two functionally specialized families of attention heads: Next-Interaction Heads, which localize upcoming grasp-and-release targets, and Motion Heads, which track movement across frames. Furthermore, we introduce HeadLight, a parameter-efficient refinement method that jointly adapts Next-Interaction Heads and Motion Heads. On RoboTwin tasks unseen during fine-tuning, HeadLight achieves 62.28% success, compared with 57.89% for full fine-tuning and 58.66% for LoRA, while updating only 1.1% of parameters. Inference-time ablations further validate the functional importance of these heads: ablating Motion Heads reduces manipulation success from 57.89% to 0.94%, while ablating Next-Interaction Heads lowers it to 40.61%, both substantially more than ablating equally many random heads. Finally, we show that our approach is effective across multiple WAM architectures and real-robot manipulation settings.

Introduction Robot manipulation has been explored through various policy architectures~ chi2023diffusion,zitkovich2023rt2,black2025pi0 , with World-Action Models (WAMs) emerging as a promising approach that generates both future video and actions~ ye2026dreamzero, zhou2026zerowam, kim2026cosmospolicy . Research in motor control and task-and-motion planning describes manipulation in terms of discrete contact events and continuous motion~ flanagan2006control, garrett2021tamp . These aspects translate into two complementary capabilities that WAMs need: anticipating where the next grasp or release should occur, and representing the continuous motion of the robot and manipulated objects across frames. Current WAMs implicitly rely on large-scale video pretraining~ wan2025wan to acquire these capabilities. Such pretraining allows them to generate visually plausible videos, yet visual plausibility alone does not ensure that the manipulation capabilities are actually learned~ motamed2026physicsiq,qiu2026agra . In practice, WAMs may fail to identify the correct interaction targets, and their generated actions may not accurately follow the motion in their predicted videos. These failures are especially pronounced when generalizing to unseen tasks. Although full fine-tuning and LoRA~ hu2022lora can adapt WAMs, neither method explicitly selects parameters based on their roles in interaction targeting and motion. As a result, optimizing the prediction loss may encourage the model to fit visual details, such as appearance and texture, without necessarily improving interaction targeting and motion modeling. This raises two natural questions: Can we identify the model components associated with interaction targeting and motion? If so, can we selectively refine them to strengthen these capabilities rather than merely fitting visual details? Previous work has shown that robot policies can be improved by adapting a small set of internal components, either through steering sparse features at inference~ zhou2026steeract or by fine-tuning attention heads selected from demonstrations of a specific task~ mitra2026robotsteering . In both cases, the identified components are selected separately for each task. We instead ask whether some heads support more fundamental capabilities shared across manipulation tasks, namely interaction targeting and motion. To answer this, we investigate attention heads in pretrained WAMs and identify two families associated with these capabilities: Next-Interaction Heads and Motion Heads. We identify the former by analyzing attention to upcoming interaction locations, and the latter by measuring the agreement between cross-frame attention and optical flow. Ablating Motion Heads reduces manipulation success from 57.89 to just 0.94 , while ablating Next-Interaction Heads reduces it to 40.61 , with both causing substantially larger declines than ablating equally many random heads. These experiments also reveal distinct failure modes: ablating Next-Interaction Heads often causes the robot to miss its intended targets, while ablating Motion Heads disrupts the motion in predicted videos. These results suggest that WAMs rely on a small number of specialized attention heads to localize interaction targets and to model motion. Building on these findings, we introduce , a parameter-efficient refinement method that uses these two head families to guide complementary adaptation pathways. We selectively fine-tune Next-Interaction Heads to improve target localization and use Motion Heads to guide the adaptation of action prediction, helping generated actions follow the predicted motion. By combining these two pathways, our method aims to improve both interaction targeting and motion execution without updating the entire model. We evaluate on RoboTwin~ chen2025robotwin tasks unseen during fine-tuning. On Zero-WAM, our method achieves 62.3 success, compared to 57.9 for full fine-tuning and 58.7 for LoRA, while updating only 1.1 of parameters. Using either adaptation pathway alone does not achieve the same improvement, supporting the importance of their combination. We further demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on LingBot-VA~ li2026causalwam , which uses a different WAM architecture. Finally, we validate in real-robot manipulation using a Franka robot. To summarize, our main contributions are threefold: (i) We identify Next-Interaction Heads and Motion Heads in pretrained WAMs and validate their distinct roles in interaction targeting and motion through attention analysis and controlled ablations. (ii) We introduce , which combines two complementary adaptation pathways guided by these heads to improve interaction targeting and motion execution while updating only a small subset of model parameters. (iii) We demonstrate improvements over standard adaptation methods on unseen manipulation tasks, with effectiveness across WAM architectures and in real-robot manipulation. Together, these findings suggest that the functional structure of WAMs can guide which parameters to adapt, improving generalization to unseen tasks. Related Work sec:related World-action models. World-action models jointly model future visual observations and robot actions for manipulation~ guo2024pad,kim2026cosmospolicy,li2025uva,li2026causalwam,wu2024gr1,ye2026dreamzero,zhu2025uwm . Among these, Zero-WAM conditions its predictions on human demonstration videos to specify unseen tasks~ zhou2026zerowam . While these models focus on learning to predict video and actions, we investigate the functional structure of their attention heads and how it can guide parameter selection for adaptation. Functional specialization of attention heads. Prior studies have revealed functional specialization in language transformers, where attention heads capture linguistic relations~ voita2019specialized,clark2019bert and task representations during in-context learning~ todd2024function . Similar properties have been explored in video diffusion models: DiTFlow extracts patch correspondences from cross-frame attention for motion transfer~ pondaven2025ditflow , while HALO identifies motion- and structure-sensitive heads, validates attention-derived displacements against optical flow, and leverages them for training-free motion transfer~ jung2026halo . In embodied models, EWAM further reveals a layer-wise progression from semantic information to visual foresight and action~ wang2026ewam . Building on these observations, we identify Next-Interaction Heads and Motion Heads in WAMs and examine their functional importance for closed-loop manipulation through controlled ablations. Head selection, steering, and adaptation. Existing approaches adapt pretrained models through parameter updates or activation interventions. LoRA~ hu2022lora constrains the rank of parameter updates without explicitly specifying which heads to adapt. For robot policies, activation steering modifies behavior through interventions on feedforward activations~ haon2025vlasteering , while SteerAct~ zhou2026steeract selects a sparse feature from successful and failed rollouts and modulates its activation during execution. Other approaches focus on attention heads: Sparse Attention Vectors~ mitra2025savs use few-shot examples to select attention-head activations for vision-language classification without fine-tuning, while Robotic Steering~ mitra2026robotsteering ranks heads using nearest-neighbor action regression on task demonstrations and selectively fine-tunes them with LoRA. In contrast to task-specific head selection, HeadLight selects heads based on manipulation functions shared across tasks: selective reliance on upcoming interaction targets and alignment of cross-frame attention with optical flow. The HeadLight Method sec:method We investigate whether functional specialization exists within pretrained WAMs and can guide parameter selection, aiming to strengthen interaction targeting and motion execution rather than fitting task-irrelevant visual details. First, given a frozen WAM, we identify two functionally specialized families of video attention heads, Next-Interaction Heads and Motion Heads, by scoring each head on how much it depends on the upcoming interaction target and how well its attention follows the motion of the scene ( ). Second, we introduce , which uses these identified heads to establish two complementary, parameter-efficient adaptation targets: Next-Interaction Heads for localizing the upcoming interaction target, and Motion Heads for action execution ( ). Preliminaries: Joint Attention in WAMs sec:prelim A WAM jointly generates future videos and actions via a transformer~ vaswani2017attention operating on both video and action tokens. At layer and head index , we denote the attention head processing video tokens as a video head and its counterpart for action tokens as an action head . The two modalities interact through joint attention~ liang2025mot : at every layer, each action head attends to video tokens by querying the keys and values from its corresponding video head . This one-to-one correspondence allows us to select target action heads through their paired video heads. Identifying Manipulation-Relevant Heads sec:discovery Given a frozen WAM, we evaluate all video heads over manipulation episodes along two axes corresponding to discrete contact events and continuous trajectories: (i) selective reliance on the upcoming interaction target, and (ii) cross-frame alignment with scene motion. As a manipulation task progresses, the task-relevant spatial target shifts dynamically from the object to be grasped to its intended release location. A true Next-Interaction Head should selectively track this upcoming contact region rather than merely attending to visually salient objects or static background features. title: Keep or Roll Back? Out-of-Loop Judges for Self-Improving VLA and End-to-End Embodied Policies
summary: Self-improvement is now a practical recipe for embodied policies: a policy collects experience, is retrained, and is kept when a judge rates it higher. However, the judge is usually trained or chosen inside the same loop, so its evidence is not independent of the policy. We introduce SealedLoop, an evaluation framework that adds a sealed judge: an evaluator outside the loop that the improver cannot see or optimize against. A new policy is kept only when a sequential test on the sealed judge confirms the gain, with a bounded probability of keeping a worse one. Running the same loop under each judge, we separate two sources of a false gain, which we call judge error (the loop's judge is wrong on its own data) and transfer gap (a real gain there does not carry over to unseen conditions). We evaluate on LIBERO manipulation, NAVSIM driving, and a full-scale real vehicle. In manipulation, a success classifier accepted 65 of 196 failures in one generation. In driving, policies that gain on the loop's own frames lose in an unseen city, so even an exact in-loop judge would keep 8/15 of them. When the sealed test decides, a driving loop built to improve ends with a better policy than under its own critic (0.674 against 0.649 PDMS, from 0.638), and on driving pairs with known sealed gain the test accepted 11 of 12 real gains and none of 59 losses. In a real-world field experiment on a published improvement step, the reinforced version drove further into a curve than the version it started from in all 6 blind pairs, though neither completed it. These results show that evidence from inside the loop, however accurate, is not enough to decide whether a policy has improved. SealedLoop offers a foundation for trustworthy self-improvement of embodied policies, in which progress is judged by evidence the improving system cannot influence.

Introduction sec:intro Self-improvement is now a practical recipe for embodied policies: a policy rolls out, a judge labels its episodes, the policy is fine-tuned on what was judged good, and the cycle repeats. Robot policies improve this way through reinforcement-learning fine-tuning and deployment experience~ ax2509_09674,ax2510_25889,ax2410_21845,ax2502_05450,recap2025,ax2509_15937,ax2606_10305 , and driving planners through self-play and reinforcement learning against a simulator's score~ ax2502_03349,ax2606_19641,ax2506_08052 . Every round ends with the same decision: is the new policy better, and should it replace the old one? Run without a human, the cycle is a bounded form of recursive self-improvement~ ax2607_07663,axcs_0309048,ax2410_04444,ax2608_24735 , and it is only as reliable as this decision. In most loops, however, the judge that supplies the training signal or selects the training episodes also provides the evidence for this decision. The evidence is therefore not independent of the policy it evaluates. In language-model self-improvement, the loops that run reliably without a human are those whose judge the optimizer cannot influence, such as a code executor or a test suite~ ax2505_22954,ax2506_13131,ax2505_03335 , whereas loops with a learned judge stop improving within a few rounds~ ax2412_02674,ax2507_00075 . Embodied loops face the same problem. The gain a loop reports can disagree with an independent evaluation for two reasons. First, the judge may mismeasure performance on the conditions it observes. Learned judges carry measurement error even before a policy is optimized against them: the best of 22 general robot reward models differs from human-verified progress labels by 0.67 points on a five-point scale on average~ ax2601_00675 . Optimization then widens the error. A policy trained on a learned reward overshoots the true objective~ gao2022overopt,ax2505_18126,ax2606_21090,ax2606_14629 , and progress rewards can be gamed by stopping short of the goal~ ax2512_23703 . Second, a genuine gain on those conditions may not transfer to conditions the loop has not seen. We call the first judge error and the second the transfer gap. shows one case of each. In manipulation, a success classifier accepts failed placements that look like successes (a). In driving, gains on the loop's own evaluation frames turn into losses in an unseen city (b). A more accurate judge reduces judge error. The transfer gap can only be seen with evidence from outside the loop. But physical evaluation is slow and cannot be replayed, so embodied loops rarely collect such evidence. A wrong decision does not stay in its round, because each kept policy collects the data for the next one. In driving, trajectory refinement guided by a learned critic peaks after two to three iterations~ ax2508_09158 . Seeing such effects requires following a loop generation by generation and counting the cases where the policy exploits its judge. Among the embodied loops we surveyed, a per-generation curve with a quantified case of such exploitation has not yet been reported ( ). How the two sources affect successive acceptance decisions has not been measured. Measuring it requires an evaluator the improver cannot influence and an acceptance rule with a controlled error rate. Both exist elsewhere: sealed evaluation and anytime-valid acceptance for software agents~ seal2026,ax2608_12841,ax2607_00871 , and sequential tests for comparing robot policies~ ax2603_13616 . We bring them to embodied self-improvement, where the judge is learned from the loop's own data and sealed conditions differ from those the loop sees. We propose , an evaluation framework that adds a sealed judge to the loop ( ). A sealed judge is an evaluator outside the loop whose data, parameters and schedule are hidden from the improver. It runs beside the loop, and a new policy is kept only when an anytime-valid sequential test~ waudbysmith2024betting on it certifies the gain. The sealed conditions are fixed before the improver runs and drawn independently of it. The probability that the test keeps a worse policy therefore does not exceed a level set in advance, whatever the improver does. The test is also sequential, so each decision comes with the amount of evaluation it used. Running the same loop twice, once with its own judge deciding and once with the sealed judge deciding, shows what the choice of the deciding judge changes. Both judges score every generation in either run. The difference between the gain the loop reports and the sealed gain, the judge gap, can therefore be measured in every generation. The true score on the loop's own data separates it into judge error and transfer gap. We apply to two simulated loops, LIBERO manipulation and NAVSIM driving, and to a full-scale real vehicle. In manipulation the judge gap is judge error: in one generation the success classifier accepted failures of the policy it trained, and of generations report a gain where the sealed judge finds a loss ( a). In driving a transfer gap appears in every generation, and of report a gain with a sealed loss ( b). Policies started from the released checkpoint gain on the loop's own evaluation frames and lose in an unseen city, so even an exact in-loop judge, one with no error on the loop's own data, would keep of them. The sealed test still accepts real improvements: on driving pairs whose sealed gain is known, it accepted of real gains and none of losses. In a driving loop built to improve, it certified all first-step gains ( to PDMS), of which the loop's learned critic accepted . In a real-world field experiment, the reinforced version of ReCogDrive~ ax2506_08052 , whose gain is measured in simulation, drove further into a left curve in all blind pairs, but neither completed it ( c). Our contributions are: We propose , an evaluation framework for embodied self-improvement loops. A judge sealed from the improver, rather than the judge the loop trains with, decides each update through a sequential test, and running the loop under both judges separates a false gain into judge error and transfer gap. We show that evidence from inside the loop is not enough to approve an update. On LIBERO and NAVSIM, in-loop judges keep policies that are not better, and even an exact in-loop judge would keep of the driving policies that lose in an unseen city. We test a published improvement step on a full-scale real vehicle with a sealed judge. In a blind, paired field experiment, the direction of its simulator gain holds on the road: the reinforced version goes further into a curve in all pairs, though neither version completes it. Related Work sec:related Self-improvement loops run without a human when the optimizer cannot influence their judge, as with agents judged by an executor or a test suite~ ax2505_22954,ax2510_21614,ax2504_15228,ax2505_03335,ax2203_14465,ax2603_25681,ax2607_07663 . Loops that update weights under a learned judge plateau within a few rounds~ ax2401_10020,ax2412_02674,ax2507_00075 : judges favor outputs like their own~ ax2410_21819 , and learned rewards are over-optimized~ gao2022overopt,ax2505_18126 . For software agents, the judge has been moved out of the loop by hidden-rollout harnesses~ seal2026 , test windows scored once~ ax2608_12841 , error-controlled verifiers~ ax2512_03109,ax2607_00871 and pre-registered analyses~ ax2606_31511 . In embodied loops the judge is learned from the loop's own data and the sealed conditions differ from those the loop sees, so a reported gain can fail through judge error or a transfer gap; measures both, where a sealed evaluation alone gives only their sum. Anytime-valid inference~ ramdas2023gametheoretic,waudbysmith2024betting has been used to compare robot policies~ ax2603_13616,ax2405_05439 , evaluate language models with fewer samples~ ax2606_20820 and tell a drifting judge from a drifting system~ ax2606_15474 . We use it as the loop's acceptance rule, bounding the probability of keeping a worse policy. Reinforcement-learning fine-tuning of vision-language-action models is judged by the simulator~ ax2509_09674,ax2510_25889,ax2505_17016 . On hardware, the judge is a human, a reward classifier trained in the loop~ ax2410_21845,ax2502_05450,ax2412_09858,recap2025,ax2606_10305 , a vision-language critic~ ax2509_15937 , a synthetic verifier~ ax2606_19980 or a world model~ ax2505_12705,ax2511_09515,ax2602_12063,ax2602_11075 . Such judges carry measurement error before any optimization~ ax2601_00675,ax2511_20325 , and exploitation has so far been described qualitatively~ ax2512_23703,ax2606_10305 . Driving planners trained against rule scores~ ax2502_03349,ax2502_14706,ax2606_19641,ax2506_08052,ax2512_07745,ax2509_17940 report single runs, and learned-critic refinement peaks or saturates within a few iterations~ ax2508_09158,ax2604_27366 . Across the surveyed loops, a per-generation curve with a quantified case of exploitation has not yet been reported ( ). Transfer is a further open problem: open-loop and closed-loop metrics disagree~ ax2312_03031,navsim2024,ax2506_04218 , a benchmark gain can reverse when only the executor changes~ ax2609_34440 , and driving models lose 22.8 of their success rate under distribution shift~ ax2604_08535 , while reinforcement-learning fine-tuning leaves visual robustness unchanged~ ax2505_19789 . Simulated evaluation must be calibrated against hardware~ ax2405_05941,ax2510_04354 . Physical evidence is rare: one study compares two policies over about 200\,km in three runs~ ax2606_19836 . Building on these loops, we measure judge error and the transfer gap generation by generation on two embodiments, and compare both versions of a published improvement step in blind pairs on a full-scale vehicle. title: QK-Bench: Benchmarking Quantitative Kinematic Understanding for Dynamic Spatial Intelligence
summary: Spatial intelligence concerns both scene structure and its temporal evolution. Yet a semantically correct description can conceal a quantitative error: recognizing that objects are approaching does not determine their closing speed or whether they will meet. Such errors are critical in collision avoidance, trajectory tracking, and reactive grasping, where actions depend on motion magnitude, timing, and relative geometry. We study quantitative kinematic understanding in multimodal large language models (MLLMs): resolving motion magnitude, rate, reference-frame dependence, and future spatial evolution from visual evidence. We introduce the Quantitative Kinematics Benchmark (QK-Bench), comprising 2,341 multiple-choice QA pairs from 379 videos and 17 tasks spanning Object-Centric Kinematics, Camera Ego-Motion Kinematics, and Multi-Object Kinematic Relations. Hidden geometric and temporal signals support trajectory construction and filtering, while fixed kinematic rules map physical quantities to verifiable answers, including categorical labels. Trajectory and question validation ensure target reliability and sufficient visual support in the sampled frames. All models receive a unified monocular RGB input. Evaluations of proprietary, open-source, and spatial MLLMs reveal substantial limitations: the strongest model achieves only 41.2\% overall accuracy, and spatial MLLMs show no consistent advantage. These findings indicate that current advances in spatial intelligence do not reliably transfer to quantitative kinematic understanding.
full_text: Spatial intelligence concerns both scene structure and its temporal evolution. Yet a semantically correct description can conceal a quantitative error: recognizing that objects are approaching does not determine their closing speed or whether they will meet. Such errors are critical in collision avoidance, trajectory tracking, and reactive grasping, where actions depend on motion magnitude, timing, and relative geometry. We study quantitative kinematic understanding in multimodal large language models (MLLMs): resolving motion magnitude, rate, reference-frame dependence, and future spatial evolution from visual evidence. We introduce the Quantitative Kinematics Benchmark (QK-Bench), comprising 2,341 multiple-choice QA pairs from 379 videos and 17 tasks spanning Object-Centric Kinematics, Camera Ego-Motion Kinematics, and Multi-Object Kinematic Relations. Hidden geometric and temporal signals support trajectory construction and filtering, while fixed kinematic rules map physical quantities to verifiable answers, including categorical labels. Trajectory and question validation ensure target reliability and sufficient visual support in the sampled frames. All models receive a unified monocular RGB input. Evaluations of proprietary, open-source, and spatial MLLMs reveal substantial limitations: the strongest model achieves only 41.2 overall accuracy, and spatial MLLMs show no consistent advantage. These findings indicate that current advances in spatial intelligence do not reliably transfer to quantitative kinematic understanding. Introduction Spatial intelligence enables multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to perceive and reason about the geometric and relational structure of the physical world~ spatial457,3dsrbench,vsibench,spatialbench . In dynamic environments, object motion, camera ego-motion, and multi-object interactions continually change that structure. A system may describe motion correctly while using incorrect quantities to decide when or where to act. In autonomous driving, recognizing an approaching vehicle does not establish its closing speed; underestimating this speed can make the time available for avoidance appear longer than it is. Manipulator trajectory tracking requires estimating target motion relative to the robot, whereas reactive grasping depends on the target position at the intended contact time. Errors in these estimates can cause tracking deviations or failed grasps of moving object. For robotic and embodied systems, the quantities omitted by a qualitative description can therefore determine whether an action is timely and spatially appropriate. These applications motivate evaluating the motion information on which downstream prediction, planning, and control depend. Recent benchmarks have extended spatial intelligence from static scenes to dynamic settings~ stibench,vlm4d,dsibench,spatial4dbench by assessing motion, viewpoint changes, and evolving spatial relations. This progress raises a further evaluation requirement: distinguishing motions that share a correct qualitative description but differ in quantitative properties and future outcomes. Two scenes may both show objects ``approaching'' yet differ in the time of closest approach; two trajectories may both be ``turning'' yet differ substantially in turning angle. A model can recognize either pattern correctly yet still misjudge these quantities. The distinction concerns the precision of spatial understanding, beyond the recognition of change alone. We term this capability quantitative kinematic understanding. It extends spatial understanding from where entities are and how they change to how much and how fast they change, in which reference frame, and what spatial configuration follows from current motion. This spans individual object motion, camera ego-motion, camera--object relative dynamics, inter-object kinematic relations, and short-term prediction. Reliable evaluation requires constructing kinematic ground truth with consistent geometry and accurate timing. The resulting targets must distinguish motions that share a qualitative description but differ in magnitude, rate, or future outcome. Even categorical answers must be derived from measured quantities through fixed decision rules, so that selecting a plausible motion label alone is insufficient. Figure~ semantic illustrates why reference frames matter for quantitative kinematic understanding. Similar leftward image changes arise from object motion in Clip A but primarily from camera ego-motion in Clip B. A model may correctly recognize this leftward change yet misjudge how far or how fast the object moves by attributing camera-induced changes to the object. Accurate quantitative judgments therefore require accounting for camera ego-motion and measuring change in the reference frame specified by the question. We introduce the Quantitative Kinematics Benchmark (QK-Bench) to evaluate this capability. It comprises 2,341 question--answer pairs from 379 videos, organized into 17 tasks spanning Object-Centric Kinematics, Camera Ego-Motion Kinematics, and Multi-Object Kinematic Relations. The two-stage pipeline uses hidden geometric and temporal signals to construct trajectories, compute physical quantities, and derive answers through fixed task-specific rules. Each target can therefore be traced to its source evidence and derivation. Trajectory filtering and question validation ensure both label reliability and the visual evidence needed to answer each question. QK-Bench uses monocular RGB video as a common evaluation interface, consistent with existing spatial-intelligence benchmarks and applicable to heterogeneous MLLMs. Models receive RGB observations, corresponding timestamps, and natural-language questions. Geometric signals remain hidden during evaluation, enabling verifiable target construction while testing what models can infer from a shared visual input. As shown in Fig.~ radar , evaluations of proprietary, open-source, and spatial MLLMs reveal substantial limitations. The strongest model achieves 41.2 overall accuracy, and the strongest open-source model achieves 39.1 . Spatial MLLMs do not exhibit a consistent advantage in quantitative motion, camera--object relative dynamics, or future relational reasoning. These findings indicate that current advances in spatial intelligence do not yet translate reliably into quantitative kinematic understanding. Our contributions are as follows: We formulate quantitative kinematic understanding as an evaluation objective for dynamic spatial intelligence: resolving motion magnitude, rate, reference-frame dependence, and future outcomes that qualitative descriptions leave unspecified. We introduce QK-Bench, with 17 tasks spanning object motion, camera ego-motion, and multi-object relations. Its two-stage construction pipeline connects hidden geometric and temporal evidence to quantitative targets through trajectory validation and fixed kinematic rules. We evaluate proprietary, open-source, and spatial MLLMs, finding a best overall accuracy of 41.2 and no consistent advantage for spatial MLLMs. The results identify quantitative kinematic understanding as a remaining limitation of current spatial intelligence. Related Work Dynamic Spatial Intelligence Benchmarks Recent MLLM benchmarks have extended spatial intelligence from static scenes to temporally evolving environments. STI-Bench~ stibench evaluates object pose, displacement, motion estimation, and prediction, while DSI-Bench~ dsibench studies the coupled effects of camera self-motion and object motion. OmniSpatial~ omnispatial , VLM4D~ vlm4d , Dyn-Bench~ thinkingindynamics , and Spatial4D-Bench~ spatial4dbench further broaden dynamic spatial evaluation through viewpoint changes, object tracking, multi-object interactions, and temporal scene evolution. More recently, DSR-Bench~ tencent constructs dynamic spatial questions from geometric and motion cues, while 4DP-QA~ 4dpqa explicitly addresses the entanglement of camera and object motion. Prior work already includes motion estimation and prediction, with some benchmarks explicitly assessing numerical quantities. QK-Bench makes quantitative kinematic understanding the organizing objective of evaluation across object motion, camera ego-motion, and multi-object interactions. The required distinctions concern by how much a configuration changes, how fast it changes, relative to which reference frame, and what spatial relation follows from the current motion. These requirements concern the information needed to determine an answer, rather than its numerical or categorical format. For example, a turning category defined by fixed angular thresholds encodes a quantitative distinction even when the answer is expressed in words. QK-Bench uses such physically defined targets to assess whether models resolve differences in motion and future outcomes that qualitative descriptions can leave unspecified. Table~ comparison separates dynamic scope from the quantities and predictions evaluated. The three task families organize this assessment; the central requirement is that answers resolve specified quantitative distinctions within each family. Quantitative Kinematics and Motion Estimation Quantitative physical understanding has also received increasing attention in multimodal evaluation. QuantiPhy~ quantiphy evaluates numerical physical properties such as object size, velocity, and acceleration, showing that semantically plausible visual interpretations can remain quantitatively inaccurate. QK-Bench shares this concern with quantitative correctness and studies it within dynamic spatial intelligence. Its focus is how motion quantities determine the evolution of spatial configurations: individual object motion, reference-dependent camera--object dynamics, inter-object relations, and future spatial interactions. Numerical estimation and relational prediction are therefore evaluated as connected aspects of quantitative kinematic understanding. Quantitative estimation of motion and geometry is fundamental to perception in robotics and autonomous systems. MonST3R~ monst3r and MegaSaM~ megasam recover dynamic scene geometry and camera motion from monocular videos, while SpatialTrackerV2~ spatialtrackerv2 jointly models geometry, camera ego-motion, and object motion for world-space tracking. Recent 4D reconstruction methods such as Any4D~ any4d further recover metric geometry, camera poses, and dense 3D motion. Their explicit estimates provide geometric and temporal information for downstream localization, forecasting, planning, and interaction. QK-Bench examines whether MLLMs can infer quantitative kinematic information from visual observations and use it to answer questions about motion and its spatial consequences. Such estimators could serve as reference baselines on compatible task subsets, provided that their outputs and sensing assumptions are matched to the benchmark's target definitions. Models and Data for Dynamic Spatial Intelligence Progress in dynamic spatial intelligence has also been driven by specialized models, targeted supervision, and richer data resources. 4D-RGPT~ 4drgpt introduces region-aware representations for dynamic scene understanding, while EgoDynamic4D~ egodynamic4d provides egocentric RGB-D observations, camera poses, and temporally consistent 4D annotations. MLLM-4D~ mllm4d improves the understanding of object motion, camera ego-motion, and camera--object relations through targeted data construction and post-training. Large-scale resources such as SpatialVID~ spatialvid and OmniWorld~ omniworld further provide diverse dynamic videos and geometric annotations for learning dynamic spatial representations. These developments motivate a direct test of whether representations learned for spatial understanding support quantitatively correct judgments of motion, relative dynamics, and future interactions. title: Aegis-VLA: Reliability-Gated Action Refinement via a Trajectory World Model for Dynamic Object Manipulation
summary: Dynamic object manipulation requires maintaining spatial and temporal alignment with targets that continue to move during inference and execution. Although future prediction can inform action correction, an accurate forecast does not establish whether modifying an existing action would be beneficial. We present Aegis-VLA, a world-model-guided vision-language-action (VLA) framework that generates predictive action corrections and separately determines whether and how strongly to apply them. A Trajectory World Model combines kinematic extrapolation with learned residual dynamics to predict object motion and estimate positional uncertainty. Discrepancy-Guided Action Refinement uses differences between history-only and base-action-conditioned end-effector forecasts to propose bounded arm corrections. A Reliability Gate learns when to admit corrections based on demonstration-relative improvements over base actions, and regulates their application during inference using predictive uncertainty and anticipated object--end-effector proximity. Rejected corrections preserve the corresponding base actions. Aegis-VLA introduces only approximately 2.45M trainable parameters. On the simulated Dynamic Object Manipulation (DOM) benchmark, Aegis-VLA achieves 56.72\% success over 1,800 evaluation trials, exceeding our reproduced DynamicVLA baseline of 45.44\% by 11.28 percentage points.
full_text: Dynamic object manipulation requires maintaining spatial and temporal alignment with targets that continue to move during inference and execution. Although future prediction can inform action correction, an accurate forecast does not establish whether modifying an existing action would be beneficial. We present Aegis-VLA, a world-model-guided vision-language-action (VLA) framework that generates predictive action corrections and separately determines whether and how strongly to apply them. A Trajectory World Model combines kinematic extrapolation with learned residual dynamics to predict object motion and estimate positional uncertainty. Discrepancy-Guided Action Refinement uses differences between history-only and base-action-conditioned end-effector forecasts to propose bounded arm corrections. A Reliability Gate learns when to admit corrections based on demonstration-relative improvements over base actions, and regulates their application during inference using predictive uncertainty and anticipated object--end-effector proximity. Rejected corrections preserve the corresponding base actions. Aegis-VLA introduces only approximately 2.45M trainable parameters. On the simulated Dynamic Object Manipulation (DOM) benchmark, Aegis-VLA achieves 56.72 success over 1,800 evaluation trials, exceeding our reproduced DynamicVLA baseline of 45.44 by 11.28 percentage points. Introduction sec:introduction Manipulating a moving object requires the robot and target to meet at the right place and time~ dbctfp,gem,dynamicvla . A grasp that is geometrically appropriate at planning time can become ineffective before contact if the object continues moving. The same observed position can demand different actions depending on whether the target is approaching, receding, or changing direction. Partial visibility obscures motion, while perception, inference, and physical execution introduce delays during which the scene evolves. Dynamic manipulation therefore requires maintaining spatial and temporal alignment between robot actions and target motion. Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) and generalist robot policies provide increasingly capable foundations for language-conditioned manipulation~ rt2,openvla,pizero . Recent methods further incorporate motion history~ tracevla , improve inference efficiency~ smolvla , and coordinate action generation with execution~ chunk,vlash . Temporal observations, continuous inference, and temporally aligned action streaming enable VLA policies to account for aspects of target motion and execution timing~ dynamicvla . We therefore ask how predictive evidence can justify modifying a base action that may already be appropriate. World models offer information about how a scene may evolve beyond the latest observation. Video and representation prediction can support policy learning and planning~ gr1,vpp,worldvla , while recent approaches explicitly incorporate target motion or predicted future observations into dynamic manipulation~ puma,dynamicwam,ahead . World-model-based approaches also evaluate or revise action proposals~ dreamtrajectory,dynawm . However, predicting target motion alone does not establish whether applying a proposed correction would improve execution compared with leaving the base action unchanged. As illustrated in Fig.~ left (a), target motion can invalidate an anticipated contact during execution. A forward adjustment may improve alignment when the base action trails the target. If the base action already compensates for that motion, however, an additional adjustment may worsen alignment even with an accurate forecast. An apparently useful correction may also depend on an unreliable forecast. Useful refinement must therefore assess whether a proposed correction improves on the base action and whether the motion forecast is sufficiently reliable to justify the correction. Residual learning provides a way to adapt an existing controller or policy~ residualrl,policydecorator , including observation-conditioned per-step action correction~ a2c2 and uncertainty-guided corrective exploration~ uncertaintyresidual . However, freezing backbone weights does not by itself preserve task performance once residuals alter the executed actions. Aegis-VLA builds on this residual formulation by separating correction generation from admission through the three coordinated modules in Fig.~ overview . Our contributions are summarized below: Trajectory World Model. We combine kinematic extrapolation, learned residual dynamics, and positional uncertainty estimation to provide shared motion context for action refinement and predictive evidence for regulating corrections under uncertain target motion. Discrepancy-Guided Action Refinement. We generate bounded arm corrections from position and orientation discrepancies between history-only and base-action-conditioned end-effector forecasts, linking each proposal to the base action it modifies. Reliability Gate. We separate correction proposal from adoption by learning admission from demonstration-relative improvement of each candidate over its base action, while uncertainty and proximity regulate application at inference. Aegis-VLA introduces only approximately 2.45M trainable parameters. On the simulated Dynamic Object Manipulation (DOM) benchmark~ dynamicvla , Aegis-VLA achieves 56.72 success over 1,800 evaluation trials, exceeding our reproduced DynamicVLA baseline of 45.44 by 11.28 percentage points. Ablations demonstrate that structured refinement already improves the backbone, while learned admission and reliability regulation further improve on an independently trained ungated alternative. Related Work sec:related_work Dynamic Manipulation and Responsive Execution Vision-language-action (VLA) models and generalist robot policies provide reusable foundations for manipulation~ rt2,openvla,octo,pizero,pizerofive , leveraging temporally coherent action sequences~ act,diffusionpolicy and efficient action generation~ openvlaoft,smolvla . Dynamic manipulation additionally requires motion-aware perception and control~ dbctfp,gem,tracevla,contextvla together with responsive execution~ chunk,rtvla,vlash . DynamicVLA~ dynamicvla combines temporal observations, continuous inference, and temporally aligned action streaming. title: SplatWAM: Splatting World Action Models for Real-Time 3D Imagination
summary: World models typically predict future observations in pixel or latent space, limiting their ability to directly represent true 3D scene evolution. We present SplatWAM (Splatting World Action Model), a generative world model that learns action-conditioned dynamics directly over compact 3D Gaussian primitives. A tokenizer SplatWAM-T first encodes a variable number of unposed views into a fixed budget of Gaussian tokens. A dynamics model SplatWAM-D then predicts future Gaussian states in a single forward pass per action, using log-Euclidean covariance coordinates and differentiable rendering supervision to facilitate learning in an explicit 3D space. Each predicted state can be rasterized from arbitrary viewpoints, enforcing a shared 3D representation across views by construction. On OGBench Scene, SplatWAM renders novel views 12x faster than video world models (~80 FPS on an RTX 5090) with up to 2.0 dB higher PSNR. We further introduce SplatWAM-P, a lightweight flow-matching policy head jointly trained with the dynamics model. Across 8 task suites, model-free Gaussian-token policies outperform pixel-based counterparts by up to 24.8 percentage points. SplatWAM-P improves over Latent Particle World Model (LPWM) by 12 percentage points and matches HIQL without a learned value function. On LIBERO, our ~1B model outperforms WorldVLA (~7B) and the robot-pretrained OpenVLA (~7B), while matching OpenVLA-OFT when both are trained without large-scale robot pretraining. Code and checkpoints will be released.

Code and checkpoints will be released. Introduction sec:intro Video generation models have become the dominant route to world modeling~ genie,unisim,cosmos . However, these models are pixel-first and may produce geometrically impossible predictions ( sec:exp_sim , Fig.~ fig:counterfactual ). To obtain an explorable world state for downstream planning or control, a second stage of feed-forward splatting~ pixelsplat,splatt3r or per-scene lifting~ 3dgs is required. Even recent 3D-aware variants inject geometry only as conditioning, , a rendered point-cloud cache~ gen3c or a latent spatial memory~ mirage . The output remains video, and every new viewpoint requires another sampling pass, often with multi-billion-parameter models trained on thousands of GPUs~ cosmos . This view dependence also affects control, as pixel-based policies degrade under camera shifts~ knowcamera,mvdemos . Multi-view supervision~ mvmwm and geometric pretraining~ geo3drep reduce this sensitivity, but use the extra views and geometry only to train the representation, not as the state the model predicts. Because the state is never geometrically grounded, consistency has to be learned rather than enforced, even when several views are predicted jointly~ ctrlworld . Without a shared 3D state, independently generated views may disagree in geometry, occlusion, and parallax, with inconsistencies compounding over long rollouts. Camera-controllable video diffusion~ cameractrl,gen3c takes viewpoint as input, but fixes the camera trajectory before generation. Latent world models~ dreamerv3,tdmpc2,vjepa2,lewm avoid pixel generation but do not directly expose a 3D state, requiring additional decoding to support novel-view rendering, and therefore do not explicitly enforce geometric consistency. At the other end of the spectrum, the 4D Gaussian splatting lineage~ 4dgs,yang4dgs,deformable3dgs keeps an explicit rasterizable state and models motion directly, but it is a per-scene optimization that densifies to many primitives. With no generative prior, these methods primarily reconstruct observed motion rather than predict controllable future scene states. Feed-forward splatting~ pixelsplat,noposplat avoids per-scene optimization but yields a static snapshot. These existing approaches either learn dynamics in compressed latent spaces or rely on per-scene reconstruction. We instead propose SplatWAM, an action-conditioned world model that directly predicts compact 3D Gaussian states from a feed-forward representation of unposed RGB views. The resulting states can be rasterized from arbitrary viewpoints without a learned latent decoder (Fig.~ fig:teaser ). We evaluate on two robot manipulation benchmarks: OGBench~ ogbench for goal-conditioned and LIBERO~ libero for language-conditioned behavior cloning. Our contributions are as follows: A compact, geometry-grounded 3D state. SplatWAM- maps a variable number of unposed context views to a fixed budget of Gaussian tokens. As policy inputs, these tokens outperform pixels by up to 24.8 percentage points. Direct generative dynamics in Gaussian space. SplatWAM- learns action-conditioned transitions directly over compact Gaussian states, without a separate learned latent compression or decoding stage. Gaussian-specific covariance parameterization and differentiable rendering supervision support prediction in this 3D space. It rolls out at 80 FPS on a single RTX 5090, and any predicted state can be rendered from any viewpoint. Joint prediction and control with a shared world-model backbone. SplatWAM- adds agent tokens and a flow-matching action head to SplatWAM- , jointly optimizing prediction and control. It outperforms LPWM~ lpwm , matches HIQL~ hiql on OGBench Scene, and is competitive with pretrained vision-language-action models (VLAs) on LIBERO without robot pretraining. Related work sec:related World models Pixel-space world models predict future frames autoregressively over VQ tokens~ ivideogpt or by adapting a video diffusion prior~ ctrlworld . Latent world models such as LPWM~ lpwm model stochastic particle dynamics over discovered object keypoints, which supports goal-conditioned control but does not encode geometry and cannot be rendered from new viewpoints. Driving world models~ occworld,copilot4d predict 3D occupancy or LiDAR scenes but are not photorealistically renderable. Gaussian World Model (GWM)~ gwm reconstructs per-pixel Gaussians feed-forward, but their large number of primitives forces it to downsample and compress them into a latent in which the dynamics are learned. As a result, its predictions degrade sharply once rasterized (Fig.~ fig:rollout b). PointWorld~ pointworld scales action-conditioned 3D prediction to in-the-wild scenes but regresses deterministic per-point flow, and MRO-GWM~ mrogwm likewise regresses rigid per-object SE(3) motion, relying on object masks and posed RGB-D. Prior world models thus cannot render their state from new viewpoints, must decode it first, or regress motion deterministically. SplatWAM instead predicts Gaussian parameters directly and generatively, so its state is rendered without a decoder, can be inspected from any viewpoint, and is supervised by dense differentiable rendering without the need for masks and poses. World action models World action models~ dreamzero predict future states and actions in a single model. Unified World Models~ uwm couple video and action diffusion, and WorldVLA~ worldvla unifies a VLA and an image world model in one autoregressive model. Video Prediction Policy~ vpp conditions an inverse-dynamics policy on the future representations of a fine-tuned video diffusion model. Among 3D-aware models, ManiGaussian~ manigaussian,manigaussianpp and GAF~ gaf predict per-Gaussian motion for a single step, as auxiliary supervision for the policy or to infer actions. GaussianDream~ gaussiandream plugs into a pretrained VLA whose future head is conditioned on a horizon embedding rather than on actions and discards its decoders at deployment. 4DGS-WAM~ 4dgswam maintains a renderable 4D state whose dynamics factorize into independently transformed objects over a static background. The closest approach to SplatWAM is the structured 4D latent predictive model~ structured4d , which flow-matches a sparse voxel latent, then decodes it to Gaussians for rendering and to points for control, but requires posed multiview RGB-D. Unlike these methods, SplatWAM predicts multi-step generative dynamics directly over Gaussian states inferred from unposed RGB, which also serve as policy inputs. For any camera , a differentiable rasterizer renders the image . SplatWAM has three learned components (Fig.~ fig:arch ). A feed-forward tokenizer, trained with a novel-view-synthesis objective, lifts the context views into an explicit Gaussian scene state, Each is a partial observation of the scene, with as the observation model. A single estimate provides only a snapshot of the scene, offering no explicit temporal context for inferring its dynamics. Hence, SplatWAM- and SplatWAM- condition on a history of past states. SplatWAM- then predicts future states from this history and the actions, following the controllable world model formulation of Hou ~ wmsurvey , where is the rollout horizon, transitions to , and produces the Gaussian-state trajectory . SplatWAM- generates this trajectory autoregressively, sampling and appending it to the history before the next step. Since the rasterizer is deterministic, all stochasticity resides in . Finally, a goal-conditioned policy acts on the Gaussian state directly, where the goal is either a goal state ( tokenized from goal images) or a language instruction, and the policy outputs a chunk of actions. Latent 3D world models~ gwm,structured4d decode to Gaussians only for rendering. SplatWAM has no decoder: encodes, predicts, renders, and reads the same Gaussians, enabling direct image-space supervision ( sec:gaussiandyn ). title: Ask to Land: Learning a Mask-Conditioned Open-Vocabulary Landing Policy via Differentiable Physics
summary: Existing drone landing systems, whether model-based or learning-based, typically rely on predefined visual markers (e.g., ArUco tags) or are trained for specific platform categories, and often assume structured target motion. Recent open-vocabulary studies enable text-prompted target selection, but integrating this capability with learned closed-loop landing control remains underexplored. To this end, we present \textit{Ask to Land}, a mask-conditioned framework that enables a quadrotor to land on various platforms described by a user in natural language, including randomly moving platforms. The core of our approach is the integration of a frozen state-of-the-art open-vocabulary perception frontend (YOLO-World with MobileSAM) and a control policy learned by differentiable physics. By providing real-time, task-agnostic semantic segmentation masks as policy inputs, our framework enables the drone to land on prompt-selected targets without target-specific fine-tuning while continuously tracking dynamic target motion during descent. The frozen frontend processes the prompt, while the policy receives the mask without text embeddings or category labels. To efficiently optimize the control policy, we leverage differentiable physics learning via Backpropagation-Through-Time (BPTT), and employ a carefully designed reward that enforces visual alignment with the landing target and altitude-adaptive descent speed, together with stable control. Real-world deployments validate that our approach achieves landings on diverse user-specified objects, including static and moving platforms.

Recent open-vocabulary studies enable text-prompted target selection, but integrating this capability with learned closed-loop landing control remains underexplored. The core of our approach is the integration of a frozen state-of-the-art open-vocabulary perception frontend (YOLO-World with MobileSAM) and a control policy learned by differentiable physics. The frozen frontend processes the prompt, while the policy receives the mask without text embeddings or category labels.
