Real-world deployments validate that our approach achieves landings on diverse user-specified objects, including static and moving platforms. Autonomous landing, open-vocabulary policy, differentiable physics learning. Introduction Imagine a rescue drone deployed in a disaster zone. Its mission is to land safely on a moving pickup truck or a distinctly colored supply box. The drone does not know the exact appearance of the target beforehand, and the target's position changes unpredictably. Landing in such unstructured scenarios requires the drone to recognize user-specified targets on the fly and continuously adjust its descent speed to match unknown target motions. Current autonomous landing systems struggle with these real-world conditions. Classical model-based methods often require predefined visual markers (like ArUco tags) or exact geometric priors of the landing pad ghommam2017moving,ibvs_moving_target_2016,falanga2017moving,keipour2022visual . Learning-based methods typically train the drone for specific object categories landing2010,21iros_landing,iros18_moving,ladosz2024autonomous,landing2025 . Recent open-vocabulary systems enable prompt-based landing-target selection, but do not learn a closed-loop policy that maps the selected target representation directly to low-level commands throughout the complete landing process bong2023dovesei,bong2023peace,bong2024blabberseg,cai2025llmland . Furthermore, existing dynamic landing systems often assume the target moves along a known path iros18_moving,ladosz2024autonomous , and this assumption frequently fails when a platform changes its trajectory randomly. To address these challenges, we propose Ask to Land, a mask-conditioned framework designed to enable robust autonomous drone landing on diverse, user-specified platforms, including dynamic platforms that move along random trajectories. First, to overcome the limitations of predefined platform categories and achieve prompt-based target selection and controller transfer, we incorporate the semantic segmentation mask as the policy input. During real-world deployment, we leverage a frozen open-vocabulary detector, YOLO-World yolo-world , in conjunction with a lightweight segmentation module, MobileSAM mobile_sam . Guided by natural language prompts, this frontend generates real-time, task-agnostic semantic masks of the desired landing surface. By conditioning the control policy on these semantic representations rather than platform-specific labels or geometric priors, the learned policy can be applied to user-specified platforms of varying shapes, sizes, and categories, without requiring target-specific fine-tuning. Beyond open-vocabulary perception, we tackle the dynamic landing problem with a differentiable composite reward that first enforces persistent semantic visual alignment with the moving target, and then jointly encourages planar tracking and altitude-adaptive descent speed. In addition, we employ domain randomization and curriculum learning during training. We randomize platform geometry and appearance, ground-plane motion with varying low speeds, as well as the initial positions of both the platform and the drone. The curriculum gradually increases task difficulty, starting from static platforms and progressing toward dynamic tasks with random trajectories and speeds. Finally, to improve training efficiency, we optimize the policy with Backpropagation-Through-Time (BPTT) through fully differentiable quadrotor dynamics, exploiting analytic gradients through the dynamics for faster convergence. Our main contributions are: We introduce a mask-conditioned open-vocabulary landing system that integrates prompt-based target selection with a landing policy trained via differentiable physics through a binary-mask interface. The policy maps the mask directly to control commands without receiving language embeddings or category labels. We design an appropriate differentiable reward function that couples persistent visual alignment with altitude-adaptive descent, enabling stable tracking of platforms with random trajectories and varying speeds. We validate our system on a real quadrotor using prompt-selected static and moving platforms. The system achieves accurate and stable landings across diverse targets while adapting its descent behavior throughout the approach. Related Works Autonomous drone landing typically assumes either fixed platforms or constrained target motion. Traditional model-based approaches, such as visual servoing, rely on pre-defined visual markers or geometric priors~ ibvs_moving_target_2016,falanga2017moving,ghommam2017moving,keipour2022visual . Learning-based methods can reduce manual design but are still evaluated on fixed platform categories or dedicated landing targets~ landing2010,21iros_landing,iros18_moving,ladosz2024autonomous,landing2025 . For moving targets, prior work often assumes predefined trajectories or structured motion patterns~ iros18_moving,ladosz2024autonomous . Recent RL work achieves fast random landing but still relies on a specific marker~ shin2026uncertain_motion . In contrast, our setting considers prompt-selected landing targets and random trajectories with randomly varying speeds during descent. Open-vocabulary perception has recently become feasible through Vision-Language Models and foundation models such as SAM~ clip,sam . Previous works in robotic manipulation and navigation leverage language-conditioned visual representations to achieve zero-shot semantic generalization~ voxposer,lmnav,rt2 . Specifically, DOVESEI uses prompted segmentation with reactive visual servoing~ bong2023dovesei , PEACE refines segmentation prompts~ bong2023peace , BlabberSeg enables efficient onboard aerial segmentation~ bong2024blabberseg , and LLM-Land combines language reasoning with MPC~ cai2025llmland . Drawing inspiration from these methods, we combine YOLO-World and MobileSAM as a lightweight semantic frontend to enable flexible recognition and segmentation of prompt-selected landing targets. Our distinction lies in learning a mask-to-action closed-loop policy by backpropagating through a differentiable model of the full quadrotor dynamics, and in evaluating the controller over the complete landing process on prompt-selected static objects and randomly moving platforms. Differentiable physics learning offers an efficient route for optimizing control policies by propagating analytic gradients through physical dynamics loco1,loco2,shac . In quadrotor research, it has shown strong sample efficiency in tasks such as swarm obstacle avoidance yuang_nmi , vision-based stabilization diff2 , and optical flow-based agile flight hu . Nevertheless, these works primarily focus on aggressive flight, rather than stable grounded landing tasks for static and moving targets. Building on these advances, we use differentiable physics learning to learn a mask-conditioned landing policy that couples target tracking and altitude-adaptive descent in a unified framework. Methodology The overall architecture of our Ask to Land system is illustrated in Fig.~ fig:system . In the following subsections, we detail the core components of our methodology: the real-time open-vocabulary perception frontend, the problem formulation via differentiable physics learning, and the training details. Real-time Open-Vocabulary Perception For prompt-based target selection, we use a perception frontend that leverages the synergy between open-vocabulary object detection and promptable semantic segmentation. Unlike conventional closed-set visual pipelines that rely on predefined category labels, our approach formulates target identification as a language-conditioned perception task. By conditioning the detection module on arbitrary linguistic descriptions (e.g., ``book'' or ``black chair''), the system can instantly adapt to diverse platform semantics and geometries without task-specific fine-tuning. As shown in Fig.~ fig:semantic_mask_pipeline , the perception pipeline operates sequentially through three primary stages: Text-Conditioned Target Proposal: Given a streaming monocular RGB image and a user-specified text prompt, the open-vocabulary detector, YOLO-World yolo-world , generates a set of candidate bounding boxes. To ensure robust target acquisition during dynamic flight, we employ a relaxed confidence threshold to maximize recall, followed by a spatial-confidence heuristic that isolates the optimal target bounding box exhibiting the highest probability score and minimal spatial deviation from the image principal point. Prompt-Driven Mask Generation: The selected bounding box is subsequently utilized as a spatial prior for MobileSAM mobile_sam . By extracting geometric prompts from the bounding box, MobileSAM selectively attends to the specified Region of Interest (RoI), yielding a high-fidelity, instance-level binary segmentation mask. This cascaded coupling effectively isolates the landing target while filtering out unstructured background clutter. Semantic State Representation: To satisfy the dimensional constraints of the control policy and minimize computational latency, the high-resolution binary mask is downsampled via bilinear interpolation and subsequently binarized to formulate a compact semantic observation matrix . This task-agnostic representation intrinsically decouples the control policy from the visual appearance of the platform, thereby supporting transfer across the mask geometries, apparent scales, and visibility conditions represented during evaluation. title: End-to-End Image-Goal Navigation for Agile Quadrotors via Recurrent State Distillation
summary: Image-goal navigation asks a robot to reach the viewpoint of a target photograph without a map or goal pose. In three dimensions, this requires not only recognizing the goal but also estimating 3D displacement and generating continuous control actions to approach and settle at the target view. This is difficult because the same visual difference between current and goal image can require very different actions depending on the robot's velocity, yet monocular images alone reveal neither metric scale nor body motion. As a result, existing image-goal policies are limited to planar action spaces and rely on a state estimator for flight control. Policies that map directly from images to low-level control commands have been demonstrated for agile flight, but not toward goal images in unseen environments. We present the first image-goal navigation policy that directly commands thrust and angular rates for agile quadrotor flight in unseen 3D environments, without relying on state estimation (e.g., SLAM, VO, or SfM) or a separate velocity controller. We train a recurrent vision-based policy through a four-stage pipeline that combines geometric and motion supervision with privileged-teacher distillation and end-to-end reinforcement learning fine-tuning. On 1000 held-out flights in unseen environments, the policy achieves an 82.3% success rate with a mean terminal position error of 0.10m across successful flights. Deployed zero-shot on a real quadrotor, the policy reaches an 84% success rate over 25 trials in an unseen indoor environment.

Introduction sec:intro Human pilots navigate quadrotors through unfamiliar environments using only an onboard camera stream, without explicitly estimating the vehicle's position, velocity, or attitude~ geles2024pixels . We investigate whether autonomous flight can similarly rely on visual feedback alone: given a goal photograph, a quadrotor must reach the viewpoint from which it was taken as quickly as possible ( ). The photograph specifies a destination without requiring a map or a metric goal pose. We study how to achieve this with a policy that maps visual observations and last applied actions directly to low-level control commands, without explicit state estimation such as Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM), Visual Odometry (VO), or Structure from Motion (SfM)~ slam-handbook . Extracting the information needed for flight control from onboard frames and policy's past actions is challenging. Reaching a goal viewpoint requires translating in three dimensions, aligning the camera, and braking to hover at the destination. The appropriate control command depends not only on the displacement to the goal but also on the vehicle's current motion. However, velocity cannot be directly inferred from a single frame, and monocular observations leave metric scale ambiguous. To address these limitations, we use a recurrent policy that integrates visual information over time, allowing it to implicitly infer the vehicle's motion wang2019recurrent . The previous control command provides additional information about the vehicle dynamics, helping reduce metric scale ambiguity~ ludhiyani2019multirotor . Tilting the vehicle also changes its thrust direction and camera view together. A visual policy must account for these coupled changes over time. Recent work, such as SIGN~ yan2025sign , has explored aerial image-goal navigation. While the authors demonstrate image-goal navigation on quadrotors, including real-world flight, the method outputs planar velocity commands, relying on a separate state-estimation-based controller for flight stabilization. In parallel, vision-based policies have demonstrated agile flight by directly commanding low-level control inputs, without explicit state estimation~ geles2024pixels,heeg2025learning . Combining image-goal navigation with such direct flight control remains an open challenge, particularly when requiring three-dimensional motion, precise settling at the goal, and generalization to unseen real-world environments. We address this problem through a four-stage training pipeline ( ). First, a state-based teacher learns to fly using privileged goal-relative pose and motion information. We then train a visual representation from sequences of onboard images and a goal photograph, using geometric and motion supervision together with alignment to the teacher's latent representation. During the next stage, the student is trained through imitation learning using the teacher from the first stage. Finally, reinforcement learning fine-tunes the student policy in closed loop. At deployment, the policy receives only the current image, the goal photograph, and its previous command, with no access to position, velocity, attitude, or IMU measurements. Contributions. (1) To our knowledge, we present the first image-goal flight policy that directly commands low-level control inputs in unfamiliar environments without explicit state estimation. (2) We introduce a four-stage training procedure that combines geometric and motion supervision, latent representation alignment, imitation learning, and reinforcement learning to learn a vision-based flight policy. (3) We evaluate the policy on 1000 held-out flights in 100 unseen environments, achieving an 82.3 success rate with a mean terminal position error of 0.10\, across successful flights, and demonstrate zero-shot transfer to a real quadrotor with an 84 success rate over 25 trials in an unseen indoor environment. Related Work sec:related Aerial image-goal navigation. SIGN~ yan2025sign and Omni-IGN~ yan2026omniign demonstrate aerial image-goal navigation with planar velocity commands and dedicated flight-control loops. Their deployed systems use visual-inertial and LiDAR-inertial odometry, respectively, for low-level control. Both address goal discovery and collision avoidance, with Omni-IGN extending perception to four fisheye views. UA-NWM~ zhu2026uanwm uses a latent world model to score candidate trajectories and plan waypoints, while DreamNav~ li2026dreamnav refines relative-motion predictions by generating candidate observations. Our setting instead focuses on reaching and settling at covisible goal viewpoints under quadrotor dynamics, including altitude changes. The policy directly commands collective thrust and body rates from visual observations and previous commands, without explicit vehicle-state inputs or a separate velocity controller. Image-goal representations. Image-goal navigation has been extensively studied in simulated embodied environments~ zhu2017target,yadav2023ovrlv2,li2025regnav . FGPrompt~ sun2023fgprompt emphasizes fine-grained goal conditioning, while Monaci~ ~ monaci2025matter analyze visual fusion strategies and relate navigation performance to the relative geometry recoverable from learned representations. DEBiT~ bono2024debit pretrains a binocular transformer through cross-view completion and relative-pose and visibility supervision, then integrates its features into a recurrent navigation policy. We similarly use current--goal cross-attention, but pretrain the recurrent representation on ordered flight sequences with geometric and motion supervision. Complementary approaches such as AnyImageNav~ deng2026anyimagenav combine exploration with explicit geometric registration of the goal image using depth and pose observations. Our deployed policy instead uses the learned representation directly for flight control. Visual servoing and relative-pose estimation. Classical image-based visual servoing (IBVS)~ chaumette2006visual computes camera-velocity commands from image-feature errors. Learned representations can improve feature matching, as in ViT-VS~ scherl2025vitvs , which combines pretrained DINOv2 correspondences with an IBVS control law. However, avoiding explicit pose reconstruction in the visual front end does not necessarily eliminate state estimation from the complete flight-control pipeline. In the velocity-command IBVS baselines considered here, a separate controller uses vehicle-state estimates to track the commanded motion. Learned matching and relative-pose methods, including MASt3R~ leroy2024mast3r and Reloc3r~ dong2025reloc3r , provide geometric estimates that can likewise support modular navigation systems. Our objective is instead to perform image-goal flight without explicit vehicle-state estimation or an intermediate velocity-control loop. The recurrent policy maps visual observations and previous commands directly to collective thrust and body rates, learning to account for the coupling between vehicle attitude, translation, and camera motion. Privileged learning for visual control. Teacher--student learning transfers privileged training information to deployable visuomotor policies~ chen2019lbc,kaufmann2020acrobatics,loquercio2021wild . Xing~ ~ xing2024bootstrapping combine state-based teacher training, visual imitation learning, and reinforcement learning fine-tuning for agile flight. We adopt this progression and introduce a separate visual representation-learning stage before action imitation. Our latent alignment is related to RMA~ kumar2021rma , which predicts privileged environment and dynamics embeddings from observation--action histories, and perceptive locomotion methods that learn recurrent representations with privileged supervision~ miki2022learning . Here, the visual representation is supervised by goal-relative pose and body motion and aligned with the teacher's latent space to support reuse of its actor. Vision-based low-level flight control. Geles~ ~ geles2024pixels demonstrate agile flight without explicit state estimation using gate-based visual representations, while Dream to Fly~ romero2026dream learns flight control from pixels through model-based reinforcement learning. Heeg~ ~ heeg2025learning study differentiable training of quadrotor controllers from visual features. Gaussian-splatting environments also support visuomotor policy learning through differentiable dynamics~ chen2025gradnav or imitation of an MPC expert~ low2024sousvide , with GRaD-Nav++~ chen2025gradnavpp introducing language conditioning. Our work addresses image-goal-conditioned flight: the target viewpoint is specified by a photograph, and the policy must reach and settle at that viewpoint in unseen environments. Training does not require gradients through the simulator. 8pt plus 2pt minus 4pt 8pt plus 2pt minus 4pt Method sec:method illustrates the four stages of our training pipeline and their main components. Task Definition The objective is to fly a quadrotor quickly and precisely from an initial stationary pose to a goal viewpoint. The goal is specified by an RGB image , captured at a viewpoint with partial visual overlap with the initial observation and zero roll and pitch. At each time step , the policy receives the current image , the goal image , and the previous normalized control command . The policy is recurrent, with hidden state , and outputs The normalized action is mapped to collective thrust per unit mass and three body angular rates. Notably, the policy receives no explicit state estimates such as position, velocity, or attitude. title: CoTacWAM: Joint Modeling of Vision and Touch for Robotic Manipulation
summary: We present CoTacWAM, a world-action model that learns shared contact semantics between wrist vision and touch, achieving the best observed performance in our nominal manipulation and missing-input evaluations. The two modalities observe the same local interaction through different signals: wrist images reveal nearby geometry, while touch records physical contact. Our approach connects their common contact meaning while preserving the evidence unique to each modality, giving the policy a joint description of interaction across available input combinations. This representation supports predictive action learning alongside head-view scene context and conditions corrections after an independent detector confirms a failed attempt. Experiments across four real-world tasks demonstrate improved manipulation performance over the evaluated baselines, robustness to missing local observations, and further gains from autonomous retries.
full_text: We present CoTacWAM, a world-action model that learns shared contact semantics between wrist vision and touch, achieving the best observed performance in our nominal manipulation and missing-input evaluations. The two modalities observe the same local interaction through different signals: wrist images reveal nearby geometry, while touch records physical contact. Our approach connects their common contact meaning while preserving the evidence unique to each modality, giving the policy a joint description of interaction across available input combinations. This representation supports predictive action learning alongside head-view scene context and conditions corrections after an independent detector confirms a failed attempt. Experiments across four real-world tasks demonstrate improved manipulation performance over the evaluated baselines, robustness to missing local observations, and further gains from autonomous retries. Introduction sec:intro Learning-based manipulation models increasingly translate visual observations and instructions into useful robot behavior~ brohan2023rt1,zitkovich2023rt2 . Generalist policies extend this capability through diverse robot demonstrations~ octo2024 and pretrained vision--language knowledge~ kim2025openvla,black2025pi0,intelligence2025pi05 . World-action models further connect action learning with prediction of future sensory changes~ yuan2026fastwam . For contact-rich manipulation, useful motion depends on understanding the physical interaction it produces. Wrist vision and touch offer two observations of this interaction: an image shows the gripper closing around an object, while tactile measurements reveal the resulting contact. Their signals differ, but both carry evidence about a common event. Learning what these observations share could help a policy relate visible local changes to physical contact. Recent policies integrate heterogeneous tactile sensors~ yuan2026ftp1 and exploit visual--tactile relationships through cross-modal fusion and prediction~ heng2025vitacformer,zhang2026restacvla . Visuotactile world-action models further connect future sensory prediction with control~ tian2026vtwam,neoteai2026n0twam . However, making both streams useful to a policy does not by itself specify a common physical interpretation of their signals. We therefore ask: how can wrist vision and touch express common contact meaning, and how can this shared understanding support control? Wrist images contribute local geometry, while touch provides direct physical measurements. A useful joint representation should therefore connect their common meaning while retaining the evidence unique to each modality. With complete observations, both kinds of information can inform control; with an input missing, the remaining evidence should still support the contact concepts it can reveal. We introduce CoTacWAM, which organizes wrist vision and touch around shared physical concepts: whether pad--object contact occurs and its coarse strength. Alongside this common description, the representation preserves the sensory detail needed for manipulation. By learning this description from paired observations and varying their availability, we form a joint representation that can be read through the same interface across input combinations. Wrist vision enters through a lightweight trainable interface, while a separate head-view pathway supplies scene context. We use the learned joint representation to describe current interaction and supervise its future evolution during predictive action learning. When an attempt fails, an independent detector provides a failure event; the policy combines this context with updated joint observations to generate a correction and resume execution. We evaluate this approach on four real-world tasks spanning insertion, surface interaction, liquid handling, and fragile-object manipulation. CoTacWAM achieves 71.3 mean success without retries, compared with 35.0 for the strongest baseline. Representation analyses show that contact semantics are readable from both modalities through a shared head, while the joint representation retains physical interaction detail. Without wrist vision, the complete system retains 70 and 75 success on wiping and tofu grasping, where all three tactile baselines achieve 0 . Autonomous retries further improve insertion and wiping success. Our contributions are threefold: A joint wrist--tactile representation that establishes shared contact semantics while retaining complementary sensory evidence under varying input availability. Integration of this representation into predictive action learning and failure-conditioned correction, with head-view scene context supplied separately. Four-task robot evaluations, representation analyses, and ablations connecting task performance with semantic accessibility, information retention, and temporal learning. Related Work sec:related_work Visuotactile Representation Learning Multimodal learning provides a foundation for extracting shared representations from complementary observations~ ngiam2011multimodal . Visuotactile learning applies this idea to physical interaction, relating touch to visual observations with different spatial coverage. Early work uses external scene views for vision--touch prediction~ li2019connecting and contact-aware multimodal representations~ lee2019making . Touch and Go expands paired visual--tactile learning to human-collected interactions in natural environments~ yang2022touchgo . SSVTP collects spatially aligned local surface patches~ kerr2023ssvtp , while UniTouch aligns tactile and visual features across heterogeneous datasets~ yang2024unitouch . For policy learning, FTP-1 unifies tactile inputs across sensors~ yuan2026ftp1 , and FuSe connects heterogeneous modalities through language grounding~ jones2025fuse . ViTacFormer integrates scene and wrist views with tactile attention and forecasting~ heng2025vitacformer . These settings provide different visual contexts for contact. On robots already equipped with scene and wrist cameras, the wrist view provides local visual evidence without additional sensing hardware or a dedicated setup for aligned surface imaging. The wrist camera moves with the end effector and observes nearby hand--object geometry, while touch measures the response at the contact interface. We exploit this physical relationship to learn the contact meaning shared by wrist vision and touch, while preserving complementary sensory evidence. This local representation and the scene context from a separate head-view pathway jointly inform predictive action learning. World-Action Models for Contact-Rich Manipulation Visuomotor policies can generate action sequences directly through action chunking~ zhao2023act or diffusion~ chi2023diffusion . Sensory prediction additionally models the environmental changes associated with those actions. Visual foresight uses predicted images to plan robot motion~ finn2017foresight ; UniPi generates video plans from language~ du2023unipi , and UniSim learns interactive visual simulation for policy training~ yang2024unisim . RoboScape uses depth and keypoint-dynamics supervision to improve the physical consistency of generated manipulation videos~ shang2025roboscape . LongScape improves long-horizon video consistency through action-guided chunking and context-aware expert routing~ shang2025longscape . World-action models bring prediction into policy learning. GR-1 jointly predicts future images and actions after video generative pretraining~ wu2023gr1 , while Fast-WAM co-trains video and action prediction and omits future-video generation at inference~ yuan2026fastwam . For contact-rich manipulation, VT-WAM jointly predicts vision, tactile deformation, and actions~ tian2026vtwam , while -TWAM uses force-based tactile representations for predictive control~ neoteai2026n0twam . TacWAM incorporates mechanics-aware tactile prediction and temporal interaction history into action learning~ jin2026tacwam . These methods make the choice of sensory prediction target consequential for control. CoTacWAM focuses on how wrist vision and touch jointly describe the physical interaction used for predictive control. We learn their shared contact semantics before policy training, then use the resulting representation as both current interaction evidence and a future target. Failure Detection and Recovery Recovery requires connecting evidence of a failed attempt to an executable correction. At the task level, SayCan grounds language plans in skill affordances~ ichter2023saycan , while Inner Monologue feeds execution outcomes back into planning~ huang2023inner . REFLECT uses multisensory summaries for failure explanation and corrective planning~ liu2023reflect , while AHA learns failure detection and explanation from generated trajectories~ duan2024aha . To obtain corrective behaviors, FailSafe pairs simulated failures with recovery actions~ lin2026failsafe , and FLARE combines learned retries with reset skills selected by an online monitor~ zhao2026flare . For contact-rich manipulation, corrective actions must also account for the local interaction state following a failure. Visuotactile regrasping illustrates this connection by predicting the outcomes of candidate grasp adjustments from visual and tactile feedback~ calandra2018regrasp . We address this through shared wrist--tactile contact semantics, using the same interaction representation for nominal execution and failure-conditioned correction. An independent tactile--proprioceptive detector confirms failure, while the policy combines the failure context with continuously updated joint observations to guide adjustment. Method sec:method CoTacWAM connects wrist vision and touch through shared contact semantics, then uses this understanding of local interaction for action learning and failure-conditioned correction (Fig.~ fig:method_overview ). Overview sec:method_overview At each control step , the robot receives head and wrist images, measurements from two tactile pads, proprioceptive state, and a task instruction. Using these observations and their available history, it generates an action chunk: a sequence of arm-joint and gripper commands. The cameras provide different spatial context: the head view covers the scene, while the wrist view observes the region where the gripper interacts with objects. We retain a separate head-view pathway and introduce wrist vision through a lightweight trainable interface into a local wrist--tactile encoder. Both pathways supply evidence to action generation throughout execution. Our central question is how to connect the two local observations so that they express a common interaction state while retaining their complementary information. We first learn this joint representation, then train action generation together with prediction of its temporal evolution. When an attempt fails, the same current representation and an independently confirmed failure event condition a corrective response. Learning Shared Wrist--Tactile Semantics sec:method_representation We learn a shared semantic reference for wrist vision and touch, while preserving the complementary evidence each modality contributes (Fig.~ fig:joint_representation ). The resulting joint representation provides a consistent description of contact across different input combinations. Establishing common contact meaning. We use contact presence and coarse strength as interpretable physical concepts that both observations can describe. Let and denote the complete tactile and wrist feature vectors; superscripts T and W identify the modalities. The tactile pathway adapts the Spatially Aligned Fusion (SAF) encoder introduced in TacWAM~ jin2026tacwam . SAF fuses spatially corresponding tactile appearance and mechanical signals on each pad before combining the two pads, providing a physically supervised representation of local contact. title: WAtcher: Watching Ahead for Safe Robotic Manipulation with Efficient World-Action Models
comment: 12 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables. Project page: https://zyshan0929.github.io/WAtcher
summary: World-action models (WAMs) couple future imagination with action generation, but they execute every action chunk while ignoring the potential risk. To fill this gap, we present WAtcher, a safety-aware world-action framework in which the policy imagines the outcome of the candidate chunk before execution. For fast future preview, WAtcher builds on a compact WAM whose video expert imagines the visual outcome in only two denoising steps. In addition, we propose Safe-Guard, a lightweight module kept outside the WAM that scores each candidate chunk from its imagined outcome and triggers a bounded retreat when the risk is high. Safe-Guard is detachable and can be applied to other WAMs. To train Safe-Guard, we build an autonomous pipeline to collect hazard data from RoboTwin, LIBERO, and a real robot. Specifically, the pipeline perturbs expert demonstrations and labels each candidate chunk from the physical events recorded when it is executed, such as contacts and losses of support. Using the ~25,000 labeled windows from this pipeline, Safe-Guard reaches 92.1% balanced accuracy on a blind set, and cuts hazardous closed-loop trials on training tasks from 27.0% to 10.8% without lowering task success. On a held-out 300-question benchmark, it scores 94.2%, against 72.5% and 63.3% for zero-shot GPT-6-Astra and Claude Opus 5.5. WAtcher also reaches 90.4% and 82.4% average success on RoboTwin 2.0 and ManiSkill3, on par with or above leading WAMs, and 74.0% on five real-world tasks with Safe-Guard on, against 59.5% for $π_{0.5}$. Introduction sec:intro World-action models (WAMs) unify future forecasting and action generation in a shared generative model and have become a strong paradigm for robotic manipulation~ ye2026dreamzero,ye2026gigaworldpolicy,qiu2026vid2wam . However, mainstream WAMs execute every action chunk they generate without a check. The training demonstrations also rarely contain hazardous outcomes such as collisions, slips, or dropped objects, and the training objectives never supervise risk. Whether a chunk is hazardous depends jointly on the scene, the robot state, and the commanded motion, so the same chunk can pass safely in one layout and collide in another. Detecting risk before execution requires anticipating the outcome of each candidate, at every decision step and within the latency budget of the policy. Our key observation is that WAMs of a common design already contain the forward model that such a safety check needs. When the video and action experts share joint attention and are trained with decoupled noise levels and a video loss that reaches the action tokens~ zhu2025uwm,li2026efficientwam , the video expert can take a fixed candidate chunk as a clean condition and imagine a coarse outcome, as in the forward mode of Unified World Model (UWM)~ zhu2025uwm , so no additional world model has to be trained or used. To make this imagination fast enough for real-time use, builds on an efficient architecture~ li2026efficientwam , a compact WAM trained in this way, whose video expert, distilled from a large video generator, imagines a candidate's low-resolution outcome in only two denoising steps. This fast future preview provides a solid basis for a pre-execution risk check in practical deployment. On top of this imagination, places , a lightweight risk head, between the policy and the robot ( ). fuses the current views, the robot state, every command of the candidate, and its imagined outcome with a small Transformer, scores the action chunk, and executes low-risk chunks while replacing high-risk ones with a bounded retreat. Unlike monitors that read policy features~ gu2025safe or train a separate world model~ zheng2026contactguard,wu2025forewarn , reuses the policy's own video expert and learns from physical events recorded in executed hazards rather than from task failure~ duan2024aha,dai2025racer . Because it is trained separately and leaves the policy weights unchanged, can serve other WAMs. With Fast-WAM-Joint~ yuan2026fastwam , the variant of Fast-WAM whose video and action tokens attend to each other, ( ). To train , we build an autonomous pipeline that perturbs expert trajectories in RoboTwin~2.0~ chen2025robotwin2 , LIBERO~ liu2023libero , and on a real UR7e. The pipeline executes every candidate and labels it from recorded physical events, with an LLM agent reviewing ambiguous cases and a human verifying the real-robot labels. It constructs four hazard types: unintended contacts (e.g., collisions), losses of support (e.g., slips, failed hanging), generic motion errors, and semantic dangers (e.g., a knife moving toward a hand) that no contact threshold captures, yielding 25,000 labeled windows. Trained on this dataset, reaches balanced accuracy on a blind set of 1,352 windows, ahead of a fine-tuned 8B vision-language model (VLM; ) and a ContactGuard-style monitor ( ). It also reduces hazardous closed-loop trials in new scenes of training tasks from to , against for the ContactGuard-style monitor at the same rejection rate, without lowering task success rates. For a fair comparison with zero-shot multimodal large language models (MLLMs), we also establish a held-out 300-question benchmark that covers every hazard type in RoboTwin and LIBERO. It also includes 101 same-state pairs that differ only in the candidate. On the 300-question benchmark, our lightweight scores , against 72.5 and 63.3 for zero-shot GPT-6-Astra and Claude Opus 5.5. On simulation suites, our reaches 90.4 and 82.4 average success on RoboTwin~2.0 and ManiSkill3, on par with or above leading WAMs such as Fast-WAM~ yuan2026fastwam and LingBot-VA~ li2026lingbotva . On a UR7e robot platform, it reaches on five real-world tasks with on, against 59.5 for . For safety on the real robot, , adapted with 258 human-verified windows, reduces staged hazards from to out of 60. Our contributions are summarized as follows: [leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt,topsep=2pt] We propose an autonomous pipeline that collects and labels hazardous executions in two simulators ( , RoboTwin and LIBERO) and on a real robot, with a comprehensive 300-question benchmark and a larger-size blind set for fair evaluation. We propose , a detachable risk head that scores each action candidate from the observations, commands, and the outcome imagined by the WAM's own video expert in 32\,ms. The head can also be applied to another WAM. Based on the collected data and the , we propose , which runs a risk check before every chunk, retreats from risky ones, and reduces hazardous executions in simulation and on a UR7e robot while preserving original task success. PAD, UVA, and UWM couple video and action diffusion in one model~ guo2024pad,li2025uva,zhu2025uwm , and CoT-VLA, WorldVLA, and DreamVLA add visual forecasts to vision-language-action models~ zhao2025cotvla,cen2025worldvla,zhang2025dreamvla . Recent world-action models (WAMs) build on large pretrained video generators~ wan2025wan,nvidia2025cosmos : Genie Envisioner, VideoVLA, Video Policy, Cosmos Policy, and mimic-video turn video foundation models into policies~ liao2026genie,shen2025videovla,liang2025videopolicy,kim2026cosmospolicy,pai2026mimicvideo , and Motus, LingBot-VA, DiT4DiT, and DreamZero jointly model future video and actions~ bi2025motus,li2026lingbotva,ma2026dit4dit,ye2026dreamzero . World models can also choose among candidates: Cosmos Policy plans with predicted futures and values~ kim2026cosmospolicy , and FOREWARN verifies predicted outcomes of sampled plans with a vision-language model~ wu2025forewarn . instead scores each candidate with a head trained on executed hazards. Action-conditioned video models also evaluate policies offline~ li2025worldeval,quevedo2025worldgym,guo2025ctrlworld . The video branch dominates the cost of a WAM~ shan2026dvg . Some WAMs learn from video but act without generating it at test time~ li2025uva,yuan2026fastwam,ye2026gigaworldpolicy,collins2026tapestry,zhang2026w2a,li2026lightwam . Like ContactGuard, reads no policy features and leaves the policy unchanged. Unlike ContactGuard, it lets the policy's own video expert imagine the outcome instead of training a separate world model, covers loss of support as well as contact, and learns from hazards that our pipeline generates and labels. title: CamAct: Learning Robotic Manipulation from In-the-Wild Videos via Camera Motion
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models benefit from large, diverse datasets for robotic manipulation, yet collecting robot demonstrations remains costly. Recent work has explored egocentric videos as a source of supervision, primarily drawing on demonstrations of human-object interaction. We show that in-the-wild videos can improve robotic manipulation even when they contain no demonstrations of object manipulation. Specifically, camera motion recovered from these videos provides an additional source of motion supervision that complements robot demonstrations. Building on this finding, we introduce CamAct, which incorporates this camera-motion supervision into VLA policies alongside robot demonstrations, extending the use of human videos for manipulation learning beyond object interactions. Experiments show that incorporating this video supervision during fine-tuning improves success rates from 96.40% to 98.10% on LIBERO and from 22.96% to 29.32% on RoboCasa 365. The resulting policy also demonstrates strong results in out-of-distribution generalization on LIBERO-Plus and real-world manipulation tasks.
full_text: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models benefit from large, diverse datasets for robotic manipulation, yet collecting robot demonstrations remains costly. Recent work has explored egocentric videos as a source of supervision, primarily drawing on demonstrations of human–object interaction. We show that in-the-wild videos can improve robotic manipulation even when they contain no demonstrations of object manipulation. Specifically, camera motion recovered from these videos provides an additional source of motion supervision that complements robot demonstrations. Building on this finding, we introduce CamAct, which incorporates this camera-motion supervision into VLA policies alongside robot demonstrations, extending the use of human videos for manipulation learning beyond object interactions. Experiments show that incorporating this video supervision during fine-tuning improves success rates from 96.40 to 98.10 on LIBERO and from 22.96 to 29.32 on RoboCasa 365. The resulting policy also demonstrates strong results in out-of-distribution generalization on LIBERO-Plus and real-world manipulation tasks. Introduction sec:intro Developing manipulation policies that generalize across tasks and environments is a central goal in robotics. Vision-language-action (VLA) models unify visual perception, language understanding, and action generation within a single policy for robotic manipulation~ kim2024openvla,black2024pi0 . These models benefit from diverse training data for generalization, including robot demonstrations collected in real-world environments, as well as egocentric human videos~ bjorck2025gr00t,li2026ace . Although recent efforts have built large-scale datasets from demonstrations collected across robot embodiments~ o2024open,khazatsky2024droid , scaling robot demonstration data remains challenging due to the high cost of real-world collection and annotation, as well as embodiment-specific requirements. Egocentric human videos provide a lower-cost source of supervision for robot learning, yet existing approaches primarily focus on human--object interactions to complement robot demonstrations~ kareer2025egomimic,punamiya2025egobridge . In contrast, large language models benefit from diverse web-scale data~ bai2025qwen3, gpt, opus , motivating us to explore whether robotic manipulation can benefit from broader video sources, including egocentric videos without explicit object manipulation demonstrations (Fig.~ fig:fig1 ). Web-scale data have been widely used to train vision-language models (VLMs), with recent efforts further incorporating such data into VLA pretraining or adapting VLMs for downstream policy learning through vision-language tasks~ intelligence2025pi_,yang2026vlaser,du2026embodiedmidtrain . However, generalization in robotic manipulation requires understanding not only visual semantics but also the motion and dynamics of environments. This motivates us to explore whether the rich motion information in web videos can further benefit manipulation policy learning. CityWalker~ liu2025citywalker demonstrates that camera trajectories recovered from in-the-wild videos can provide effective motion supervision for navigation policies. Moreover, recent unified frameworks show that jointly training on navigation and manipulation trajectories can benefit both domains~ yang2024pushing,wang2026qwen,zhang2026onevla . Building on these insights, we investigate whether camera motion from in-the-wild walking videos can provide additional supervision for manipulation policies, even without explicit object interactions. As humans walk through real-world environments, egocentric cameras capture rich spatial and motion information through changing viewpoints, as wrist-mounted cameras do during robotic manipulation. Although these videos contain no explicit object interactions, their camera motion provides a potential source of supervision for learning transferable spatial and motion representations. Building on this observation, we propose CamAct, a unified VLA framework that jointly learns from robot demonstrations and camera motion in in-the-wild videos. Specifically, we recover camera trajectories offline and convert them into pseudo-actions, allowing both robot actions and camera-derived pseudo-actions to be learned through a shared VLA backbone and action head. Through this joint training, CamAct aims to improve manipulation generalization by learning from diverse real-world camera motion. We evaluate CamAct on LIBERO~ liu2023libero and RoboCasa 365~ nasiriany2026robocasa365 using StarVLA~ community2026starvla as the base model. Joint training with camera motion improves success rates from 96.40 to 98.10 on LIBERO and from 22.96 to 29.32 on RoboCasa 365. CamAct further demonstrates improved out-of-distribution generalization on LIBERO-Plus~ fei2025libero and promising performance on real-world manipulation tasks. Extensive ablations and motion distribution analyses examine how video characteristics and training configurations influence downstream performance. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We explore the potential of in-the-wild videos for robotic manipulation beyond visual-semantic learning, showing that camera motion can provide useful supervision even without explicit object interactions. We propose CamAct, a unified VLA framework that jointly learns from robot demonstrations and camera-derived pseudo-actions, demonstrating consistent improvements in manipulation performance and out-of-distribution generalization. We conduct extensive ablations and motion distribution analyses to investigate how video characteristics, data composition, and training design choices affect downstream manipulation performance. Related Work sec:related_work Vision-Language-Action Models Robot learning has progressed from task-specific imitation policies toward generalist robot policies and vision-language-action (VLA) models trained on large and diverse datasets. RT-1~ Brohan-RSS-23 demonstrated scalable transformer-based control from real-robot demonstrations, while RT-2~ brohan2023rt connected web-scale vision-language knowledge with robot action prediction. Open X-Embodiment and RT-X~ o2024open further brought together trajectories from different robot platforms and demonstrated the benefits of cross-embodiment training. Subsequent systems, including Octo, OpenVLA, , RDT-1B, and CogACT~ team2024octo,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,liu2024rdt1b,li2024cogact , as well as GR00T, Qwen-VLA, and MolmoAct2~ bjorck2025gr00t,wang2026qwen,fang2026molmoact2 , have further developed scalable policy architectures and action-generation mechanisms for generalist manipulation. Related efforts improve action representations and policy adaptation~ pertsch2025fast,kim2025oft . Alongside these developments, joint training enables VLA models to learn from heterogeneous data sources and multiple learning objectives. Lin et al.~ lin2026systematic systematically examine how data modalities and training strategies affect joint training for robotic manipulation. Recent models jointly learn from demonstrations collected across robot embodiments~ zheng2026x,team2025gemini . Beyond combining robot datasets, integrates robot action learning with vision-language tasks and high-level semantic prediction~ intelligence2025pi_ . Auxiliary tasks further extend this paradigm to visual grounding and spatial reasoning~ zawalski2025ecot,chen2025internvla,team2026ace , as well as 3D geometric supervision~ peng2026g3vla,shi2026threedthinkvla . Other approaches jointly train action prediction with future visual prediction~ wu2026foundation,cai2026internvla,li2026dypesvla or 3D spatial trajectory prediction~ kim2026pri4r,he2026elan4d . Learning Robotic Manipulation from Videos Human videos provide a scalable source of manipulation experience beyond robot-collected demonstrations. Earlier approaches use internet manipulation videos and human play to guide robot policy learning~ shaw2023videodex,wang2023mimicplay . Recent methods jointly learn from human and robot demonstrations while addressing cross-domain alignment~ kareer2025egomimic,punamiya2025egobridge , with further efforts studying the scaling and integration of egocentric supervision~ zheng2026egoscale,wu2026atomego . Camera-space action representations also facilitate human--robot transfer~ li2026ace,pan2026ironmind . Other approaches construct robot-aligned observations and action supervision through motion reconstruction, retargeting, and visual synthesis~ video,jeong2026huro,wang2026ego2robot,guo2026roboedit . VidAct~ li2026vidact reconstructs object motion to generate simulated robot demonstrations. These approaches primarily derive supervision from demonstrated object interactions, leaving motion in videos without manipulation demonstrations less explored for manipulation learning. Camera trajectories provide another form of motion supervision: CityWalker and Kuno et al. recover camera motion from walking videos for robot navigation~ liu2025citywalker,kuno2026cotraining . Within manipulation, ActiveMimic~ lin2026activemimic jointly predicts camera and wrist trajectories from manipulation videos to learn active perception and manipulation. In contrast, CamAct jointly learns from robot demonstrations and camera-derived pseudo-actions from in-the-wild walking videos that contain no manipulation demonstrations. Methodology sec:method CamAct is a unified VLA framework that jointly learns from robot demonstrations and camera motion in in-the-wild videos (Fig.~ fig:fig2 ). We recover camera trajectories offline and convert them into pseudo-actions that provide additional motion supervision for policy learning. Problem Formulation sec:formulation We consider a VLA model, where a policy predicts future actions from visual observations and a task instruction. At time step , the visual observations consist of images from the available camera views, and denotes the task instruction. The policy models a distribution over action chunks where is the prediction horizon and is the robot action dimension. We learn this policy from robot demonstrations . In addition to robot demonstrations, we use in-the-wild videos without manipulation demonstrations. Camera trajectories recovered from these videos provide pseudo-actions, yielding a dataset . Here, is the current video frame and contains the subsequent camera-motion pseudo-actions, whose construction is described in Sec.~ sec:video_data . Our goal is to improve the manipulation policy by jointly learning from robot actions in and camera-motion pseudo-actions in . Video Data Processing sec:video_data Video Data. To investigate whether camera motion can provide additional supervision for robotic manipulation, we use first-person walking videos sourced from the internet. Such videos are widely available online and capture people moving through diverse real-world environments. As the camera moves with the person, these recordings capture translations, turns, and changes in viewpoint without manipulation demonstrations. Motivated by their availability and the diversity of scenes and motions they capture, we assemble a collection totaling 44.40 hours. After filtering, 36.09 hours of valid video remain. Recovering Camera Motion. To obtain camera-motion supervision from the collected videos, we recover camera trajectories using Depth Anything~3~ lin2025depth . We address two practical issues during this process. First, the videos may contain abrupt visual transitions and sustained near-static intervals. We detect both using pixel differences between consecutive frames, partition each video into visually continuous shots, and exclude near-static footage before pose estimation. Each shot is then processed independently. Second, long shots are reconstructed over overlapping temporal windows, whose reconstructions may differ in scale, rotation, and translation. title: Escapingthe instruction blackhole of vision-language-action policies via optimal-transport wormholes
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies are trained to follow a fixed instruction, yet people change their minds while the robot acts. We identify the instruction black hole: once a VLA policy commits to a task, new instructions are absorbed and the robot completes the old task or freezes. We quantify it with a transmission ratio and an event horizon and prove it is a blind spot of static imitation, which cannot distinguish a policy that listens from a deaf one once the execution state reveals the task. We propose Wormhole, a training-free plug-in that relocates the robot instead of re-instructing it: optimal transport selects an approach-phase state of the new task, a rate-limited traversal carries the robot there, and the unmodified policy takes over. On LIBERO,Wormhole raises committed-switch success of pi to and pi0.5 from at most 1.2% to 93.1%, matching or exceeding scripted retreat-and-restart with one fifth of its action discontinuity.
full_text: Introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) policies have turned language into a universal interface for robot control. By mapping camera images and an instruction directly to short chunks of actions, models such as RT-2, OpenVLA, , and execute a wide range of manipulation tasks without task-specific controllers~ rt2,openvla,pi0,pi05 . Their training and evaluation, however, rest on a quiet assumption: the instruction is fixed for the whole episode. People do not work that way: a user who asked for the apple may, a moment later, want the banana, and a robot that shares space with people must be able to change its mind when they change theirs. We began with a simple probe. The publicly released policy fine-tuned on LIBERO~ libero,openpi was asked to put the alphabet soup in the basket; while it was reaching, we told it to fetch the salad dressing instead. Issued at control step 8, the new instruction was followed in 7 of 10 trials. Issued at step 16, with both objects still in plain view, it was followed only once. In 7 of the 10 trials, the robot put the alphabet soup in the basket as if nothing had been said. The new instruction caused no hesitation and no error; it simply vanished. We call this phenomenon the instruction black hole. Like its astrophysical namesake, it has an event horizon, a point in the execution beyond which a new instruction can no longer escape the pull of the ongoing task. The black hole is not a quirk of one checkpoint or one scene. On two LIBERO tasks that share a layout and differ only in which of two identical bowls to fetch, and follow a switch issued at the start of the episode in 80 of 80 trials, but only 2 of 80 switches issued 15 steps later, 20--40 steps before the gripper closes on the bowl. On LIBERO-Goal, follows every switch issued at the start, but only 12 of 48 switches to a different object issued 20 steps later and 1 of 48 issued after 60 steps (see Results); independent measurements report the same collapse for and OpenVLA-OFT~ switchvla . The phenomenon has three signatures: capture, in which the old task runs to completion (Fig.~ fig:teaser (a)); freezing, in which the robot stalls near the horizon; and tidal disruption, in which an escape does occur but tears the action stream apart with jerky motion. Our first research question is thus: To address , we show that the black hole reflects a lack of supervision, not of capacity. In static demonstrations, each trajectory is generated under a single instruction. Once the robot moves toward its target, the images and the arm's own motion reveal which task is being performed, and the instruction becomes redundant. We prove that in this committed region the imitation objective is exactly invariant to whether the policy reads the instruction (Proposition~ prop:blind ): a policy that listens and a policy that is deaf attain the same loss, and the documented preference of deep networks for the simplest sufficient cue~ dehaan,geirhos,shah,xing favors deafness. Hence more demonstrations of the same kind cannot close the black hole, hierarchical replanning~ saycan,yay,hirobot cannot either (the low-level policy must still listen), and amplifying the instruction at inference time can only revive a signal that is weak, not one that was never learned. This leads to our second question: To address , we turn the cause into the cure. If the state, not the instruction, decides what the policy does inside a committed region, then a robot placed inside the committed region of the new task will execute the new task, whatever it reads (Proposition~ prop:reloc ). We propose , a training-free plug-in that transduces the new instruction into such a state and carries the robot there. At the switch, samples how the old task would continue (mouth A), collects states visited by successful executions of the new instruction before their grasp (mouth B), and couples the two with optimal transport (OT)~ peyre,cuturi under the expected time to complete the new task. The coupling defines the far mouth of the wormhole, a state inside the basin of the new task; a short, rate-limited traversal brings the robot there, and the unmodified policy finishes (Fig.~ fig:teaser (b)). never asks the base policy to listen inside the black hole: the same commitment that caused the black hole now holds the robot on the new task. We evaluate the black hole and on LIBERO with and , in a switching protocol in which every comparison is a paired counterfactual from the same initial state and all choices were fixed on a development split before a single test run. The horizon is abrupt, precedes physical commitment by tens of steps, and is absent where the execution state does not yet identify the task. Without training, raises committed-switch success from 0 to 93.1 on and from 1.2 to 93.1 on (Fig.~ fig:teaser (c)) and is never captured, whereas inference-time remedies reach at most 11.2 and an action-space bridge that steers the motion without relocating the robot at most 33.1 . A scripted retreat to the initial pose followed by a restart succeeds in 83.8 ( ) and 90.0 ( ): matches it on and exceeds it on , with one fifth of its action discontinuity and without a reset pose. Finally, the switching data that the plug-in generates let a learn to listen by itself. Our contributions are: Instruction black hole. We identify the instruction black hole of VLA policies and make it measurable through the transmission ratio, the event horizon, and three behavioral signatures, together with an evaluation protocol for mid-execution switching on LIBERO. Identifiability theory. We prove that the black hole is a blind spot of static imitation (Proposition~ prop:blind ) and that the same blind spot locks a policy onto any task whose committed region it is placed in (Proposition~ prop:reloc ), which turns escape into relocation. . A training-free plug-in that transduces the instruction from language into state-space geometry: OT between the policy's sampled continuations and states of successful new-task executions selects the far mouth, and a rate-limited traversal delivers the robot into the basin of the new task, without switching demonstrations or access to the weights. Evidence, and a self-trained counterpart. Paired-counterfactual escape curves on three LIBERO suites and two backbones characterize the horizon and its failure modes, and mechanistic measurements tie it to task identifiability. On a test split evaluated once, escapes 93.1 of committed switches on both backbones, and a hand-over analysis across all methods confirms that the escape is decided by relocation. Trained on switching data from an oracle relocation teacher, a whose instruction reaches the actions only through a grounding token follows 92.1 of committed switches without any plug-in, significantly above behavior cloning trained on the same data. Large-scale imitation learning has produced generalist policies conditioned on language and vision~ gato,bcz,mandlekar,rt1,oxe,palme,vima,octo . VLA models fine-tune a vision-language backbone to emit actions, as discrete tokens in RT-2 and OpenVLA~ rt2,openvla,oft or through a flow-matching action expert in and ~ pi0,pi05,instructvla ; they predict action chunks~ act,diffusionpolicy,rdt,flowmatching , and bidirectional decoding and real-time chunking~ bid,rtc make consecutive chunks consistent, which by design favors continuing the motion under way. All assume one instruction per episode. Systems that redirect robots with language---SayCan~ saycan , Interactive Language~ interactivelang , online corrections~ sharma,cui , YAY Robot and Hi Robot~ yay,hirobot , RACER~ racer , ReKep~ rekep , and completion-aware hand-overs~ cab ---decide what the robot should do next and assume that the low-level policy will follow; the black hole violates exactly this assumption. Closest to our setting, HAMLET adds history awareness~ hamlet and SwitchVLA trains a dedicated policy on contact-phase-segmented demonstrations with rollback and advance behaviors that interpolate toward a canonical start pose~ switchvla . explains why switching fails, plugs into existing backbones, and, instead of retreating to a canonical pose, carries the robot forward to an OT-matched state in the basin of the new task. Imitation policies exploit nuisance correlates of the expert's actions (causal confusion~ dehaan ), deep networks prefer the simplest sufficient features~ geirhos,shah , generalist policies inherit such shortcuts~ xing , and compounding errors expose them at deployment~ dagger . VLA policies often disregard their instructions in static evaluation~ liberopro,liberoplus ; we show that the same mechanism has a dynamic form---language becomes redundant as execution unfolds---and prove that static imitation cannot detect it. OT provides geometry-aware correspondences between distributions~ villani,peyre,cuturi and has matched agent and expert trajectories for imitation rewards~ watchmatch ; flow matching, interpolants, rectified flows, minibatch OT couplings, and Schr\"odinger bridges~ flowmatching,interpolants,rectified,otcfm,multisample,dsb,i2sb learn paths between distributions, and SDEdit regenerates a sample under a new condition~ sdedit . Bridging the old action chunk into the new one is the natural way to apply these tools to switching, and we evaluate such an action-space bridge; instead transports between where the old task is taking the robot and where the new task is executed from, and uses the plan itself as the carrier of the instruction. title: DataForgeVLA: Fully Synthetic Manipulation Demonstrations for Vision-Language-Action Training
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures, 1 table. Dataset available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/mws-physical-ai/dataforgevla-340
summary: We present a dataset of 340 fully synthetic manipulation demonstrations generated from real seed data for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) training. The corpus contains 32,340 frames with synchronized RGB and actions across eight object categories, represented as LeRobot v2.1 episodes with H.264 video, per-frame robot states and pose-valued action labels, language task annotations, summary statistics and quality decisions. Each synthetic demonstration is produced without additional teleoperation: a LoRA-fine-tuned Cosmos-3 model generates a manipulation video, and RoboHaMeR recovers the corresponding robot trajectory from RGB. Quality screening accepted 300 of 340 episodes for policy fine-tuning. As preliminary evidence of feasibility, a pretrained GR00T N1.6 policy fine-tuned exclusively on the 300 accepted episodes reaches 16/20 (80%) real-world pick-and-place success on the Oreo-package task. A policy fine-tuned on 105 real teleoperated episodes achieved 18/20 (90%) under the same protocol. These results are based on one object and 20 trials per policy and are therefore reported as preliminary evidence rather than a general performance claim.
full_text: DataForgeVLA: Fully Synthetic Manipulation Demonstrations for Vision-Language-Action Training Sergei Kurchev Iaroslav Kolomiets Filipp Maksimov Elizaveta Semenyakina Miguel Altamirano Cabrera Artem Lykov Dzmitry Tsetserukou Kurchev et al. We present a dataset of 340 fully synthetic manipulation demonstrations generated from real seed data for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) training. The corpus contains 32,340 frames with synchronized RGB and actions across eight object categories, represented as LeRobot v2.1 episodes with H.264 video, per-frame robot states and pose-valued action labels, language task annotations, summary statistics and quality decisions. Each synthetic demonstration is produced without additional teleoperation: a LoRA-fine-tuned Cosmos-3 model generates a manipulation video, and RoboHaMeR recovers the corresponding robot trajectory from RGB. Quality screening accepted 300 of 340 episodes for policy fine-tuning. As preliminary evidence of feasibility, a pretrained GR00T~N1.6 policy fine-tuned exclusively on the 300 accepted episodes reaches 16/20 (80 ) real-world pick-and-place success on the Oreo-package task. A policy fine-tuned on 105 real teleoperated episodes achieved 18/20 (90 ) under the same protocol. These results are based on one object and 20 trials per policy and are therefore reported as preliminary evidence rather than a general performance claim. Overview of the DataForgeVLA generation pipeline. The quality gate selects clips for policy training. The public dataset also retains rejected clips and their action labels. fig:pipeline Introduction sec:intro Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies for robot manipulation improve with the diversity of the demonstrations they are trained on -- different objects, grasp poses, backgrounds, and task configurations. In practice, that diversity is bottlenecked by how the demonstrations are collected: teleoperated data collection requires human operator time, and additional objects or scene configurations can require repeated collection sessions. A LoRA-fine-tuned Cosmos-3 video model~ lora can generate robot manipulation clips from a starting frame, while RoboHaMeR can recover robot trajectories from RGB without proprioceptive logs. Together, they turn generated clips into labeled demonstrations. DataForgeVLA controls the starting scene by removing the hands and object from a real seed frame, then inserting a MuJoCo~ mujoco robot overlay and reconstructed object at sampled poses. A transfer model converts this low-fidelity composite to a photorealistic first frame before video generation and action extraction (Section~ sec:method ). The primary artifact is a documented, machine-readable corpus of synthetic RGB demonstrations paired with pose-valued action labels, together with a description of its generation and processing procedure. By generating additional manipulation demonstrations from a limited set of human-teleoperated episodes, our approach may reduce the need for repeated teleoperation across different robot and object configurations. This capability is relevant to HRI settings in which collecting demonstrations requires substantial human involvement and may entail operator fatigue and cognitive load. Our contributions are: a LeRobot v2.1 dataset containing 340 episodes and 32,340 synchronized frames for eight object-conditioned pick tasks, including video, actions, language annotations, statistics, and per-sample quality decisions; a description of a construction procedure combining controlled scene recomposition, generative video, and RGB-to-action extraction, reusing models trained on teleoperated demonstrations to create the generated demonstrations without additional teleoperation; preliminary evidence -- a 16/20 (80 ) real-world success rate for a pretrained GR00T~N1.6 policy fine-tuned exclusively on the 300 quality-screened episodes on one object -- that the extracted labels can support real-robot execution. Related Work sec:related CACTI~ cacti , GenAug~ genaug , and ROSIE~ rosie alter the appearance of objects, backgrounds, and distractors while retaining recorded action trajectories. MimicGen~ mimicgen retargets demonstrations to new object poses in simulation, which requires simulation assets and task definitions and can introduce a visual and contact-dynamics sim-to-real gap. Real2Render2Real~ real2render2real synthesizes robot trajectories from tracked object motion, while DemoGen~ demogen adapts trajectories using edited point-cloud observations. Video world models can also generate the motion itself. DreamGen~ dreamgen fine-tunes a video model on teleoperated data, generates video from an initial image, and infers pseudo-actions with an inverse-dynamics or latent-action model. Its humanoid evaluation reports real-robot generalization after teleoperation of one pick-and-place task in one environment. PhysicalAgent~ physicalagent uses generated video during execution, proposing a new motion when the robot fails. Like DreamGen, DataForgeVLA stores generated clips with recovered trajectories for policy training, with explicit control over the initial robot pose and the object's identity and pose through scene recomposition. AutodidactWAM~ autodidactwam fine-tunes a world-action model's action branch with trajectories recovered from its own videos. If a model trained this way can generate action labels that support downstream policy training, it could supply both the clip and its labels without a separate RoboHaMeR pass at generation time. Human footage offers a source of motions that were physically demonstrated. Phantom~ phantom uses hand-pose estimation and visual editing to turn human videos into robot training data. AgenticFocus~ agenticfocus retargets hand motion from first-person video to a humanoid while preserving the objects in the resulting views. Retargeted human grasps could complement the motions generated from recomposed scenes in DataForgeVLA. Our pipeline uses Cosmos-3~ cosmos3 for transfer and video generation, GR00T~N1.6~ groot for policy training, and SAM~2~ sam2 and SAM~3D~ sam3d for hand segmentation and object reconstruction. RoboHaMeR, a robot-specific adaptation of HaMeR~ hamer , recovers the trajectories directly from RGB (Section~ sec:robohamer ). Video artifacts and extraction errors can affect the resulting labels. Dataset Construction sec:method DataForgeVLA has two stages that are trained/used in sequence: first, an edge-to-RGB transfer model is trained once to make MuJoCo overlays photorealistic (Section~ sec:method-transfer ); second, that transfer model is used inside a per-scene generation loop that produces new (video, action) training pairs (Section~ sec:method-dataset ). Figure~ fig:pipeline summarizes both stages. Training an Edge-Consistent RGB Transfer Model sec:method-transfer The goal of this stage is a model that, given an edge map derived from a MuJoCo-rendered robot overlay, synthesizes a photorealistic RGB frame with correctly posed, plausible robot hands -- so that later, synthetic overlays (Section~ sec:method-dataset ) can be converted into training-quality images. Training pairs are built without manual annotation, by exploiting a calibrated camera and ground-truth robot poses recorded during ordinary data collection: From a real frame, SAM~2 provides segmentation masks for the robot's hands; those masked regions are then removed by a separate inpainting model, leaving a background plate with no robot hands. The ground-truth robot pose for that frame is rendered in MuJoCo and composited onto the inpainted plate. Because the camera is calibrated and the pose is ground truth, the rendered overlay aligns closely with where the real hands were. The composite is converted to an edge map, discarding the overlay's (synthetic, low-fidelity) texture and keeping only its geometry. The pair (edge map, original real RGB frame) is used to LoRA fine-tune the Cosmos-3 transfer model for 1,000 steps on the 105 teleoperated seed episodes, i.e., the model learns to map MuJoCo-overlay geometry back to the photorealistic appearance that originally produced it. Camera calibration and ground-truth joint configurations provide geometric alignment, making manual pose annotation unnecessary. Synthetic Scene Recomposition and Dataset Generation sec:method-dataset Given the transfer model from Section~ sec:method-transfer , each synthetic training example uses the first frame of one real teleoperated episode as a tabletop scene source and an object asset as follows: Scene emptying. SAM~2 provides segmentation masks for the robot's hands; those masked regions are then removed via a separate inpainting model, as in Section~ sec:method-transfer . SAM~3D reconstructs the Oreo asset from that frame and the seven other object assets from separate photographs. Further inpainting removes the Oreo package, leaving an empty tabletop background. Resampling. A MuJoCo robot overlay is rendered at a newly sampled pose, and the extracted 3D object asset is composited at a newly sampled position and orientation, onto the empty plate. Because the object exists as a 3D asset and the robot pose comes from MuJoCo rather than a recording, this step is not limited to combinations that were ever physically observed together. Transfer. The resampled composite is converted to an edge map and passed through the transfer model (Section~ sec:method-transfer ), producing a photorealistic first frame for the new scene configuration. Video generation. The synthesized first frame is fed to a Cosmos-3 video model (LoRA-fine-tuned for 2,500 steps on the 105 teleoperated seed episodes), conditioned on a short task instruction (e.g., ``pick up the object and place it in the center of the frame''). Cosmos-3 generates the clip at 30\,fps ( 193 frames, 6.4\,s); the raw MP4 is stored at the native 30\,fps. Action extraction. The generated clip is downsampled from 30\,fps to 15\,Hz (every other frame) before RoboHaMeR processes it; this yields 97 frames for the standard 6.4\,s clips (320 episodes) and 65 frames for the 4-second variations (20 episodes). RoboHaMeR's predictions are retargeted through the robot kinematic model and stored as per-frame absolute robot states and actions. Quality annotation. We screen each generated clip for overall consistency using the procedure in Section~ sec:VLMfilter and store the resulting decisions and scores in the accepted and rejected separate files. The output of this loop is a (video, action) pair that did not require additional teleoperation to produce. title: Rehearse in 3D, Render in 2D: Physically Consistent and Editable Robot World Models
summary: Embodied world models aim to predict future interactions that are both visually realistic and physically consistent. Yet explicit 3D motion prediction alone does not guarantee that object structure and contact relationships are preserved. Beyond motion prediction, 3D representations provide an explicit state space for imposing structural and physical constraints. Building on this insight, we introduce RehearsalWorld, an editable robot world model driven by 3D Interaction Rehearsal (3DIR). Given an initial RGB-D observation and robot actions, Interaction-Consistent Rehearsal (ICR) uses a pretrained 3D point-flow model as a motion prior. It refines the predicted trajectories through response-aware object grouping, persistent grasp memory, and contact structure refiner, preserving scene stability, object structure, and grasp attachments. Rehearsal-Aligned Video Generation (RAVG) then uses geometric projections of the rehearsal as temporal conditioning. We fine-tune a video generator on projection-video pairs to synthesize realistic interaction videos. Thanks to the decoupling of physical response from visual synthesis, RehearsalWorld also supports independent editing of material properties and camera viewpoints. Compared with PointWorld on real DROID grasping sequences, RehearsalWorld reduces gripper-relative offset by approximately 79% to 84% across deformable, articulated, and rigid objects and lowers reference motion error. For video prediction, it achieves a PSNR of 23.92 dB and an FVD of 149.
