Introduction sec:intro Embodied video world models generate action-conditioned videos of future interactions to support planning, policy evaluation, and data generation~ guo2025ctrlworld,jang2025dreamgen,agarwal2025cosmos,quevedo2025worldgym,yang2024unisim . Recent models produce visually realistic interaction videos with coherent motion. Visual realism, however, does not guarantee physical consistency: generated interactions can still contain implausible object responses~ bansal2025videophy2,motamed2025physicsiq . In robotic manipulation, object motion must also be consistent with the given actions, contact relationships, and the objects' physical properties. Recent work has introduced explicit 3D representations to better ground interaction prediction in physics. TesserAct~ zhen2025tesseract , Aether~ zhu2025aether , 4DNeX~ chen2025_4dnex , and Kinema4D~ kinema4d2026 jointly model RGB with depth or point maps to improve spatiotemporal consistency between appearance and geometry. Yet joint training alone does not ensure RGB--geometry alignment, which depends on cross-modal fusion~ chen2025_4dnex . Even well-aligned predictions can violate structural or contact constraints. Kinema4D, for example, notes that its generated environment responses can still exhibit penetration~ kinema4d2026 . Other methods learn interaction dynamics directly in 3D, using particles or point clouds to predict action-induced displacement and deformation~ huang2025particleformer,zhang2025pgnd,li2019learning,zhang2024adaptigraph . For example, the 3D flow world model PointWorld~ huang2026pointworld represents RGB-D observations and robot actions in a shared 3D point space and predicts future displacements of the initial scene points. Its pointwise predictions can capture diverse interaction responses but do not explicitly enforce structural, material, or contact constraints. On real DROID sequences, we observe background drift, excessive object stretching, and grasp slip in these predictions. In addition, the predicted flow primarily describes the motion of observed surfaces. Generating complete videos requires additional appearance modeling~ jin2026dynavid . Explicit 3D representations not only support geometric modeling and motion prediction but, more importantly, provide a state space for imposing physical constraints on object structure and interactions~ jiang2025phystwin . Prior work has explored video generation guided by physical simulation~ chen2025physgen3d,li2025wonderplay,psivg2026 . We focus instead on how to use motion priors learned from real interactions to construct more physically consistent 3D states under object-level constraints. Such states could ground both interaction prediction and visual synthesis. To this end, we introduce , an editable robot world model that uses 3D interaction rehearsal to decouple physical response modeling from video generation. During ( ) , a pretrained 3D point-flow model~ huang2026pointworld predicts future interaction trajectories from the initial RGB-D observation and robot actions. ( ) refines the predicted point displacements using , , and . This reduces background drift, excessive object stretching, and grasp slip. In ( ), we project the corrected 3D states into the target view to obtain temporal geometric conditions. We fine-tune a video generator on paired dynamic projections and recordings to synthesize realistic videos that follow the rehearsed motion and scene layout. This decoupling also enables independent editing of material properties and camera viewpoints. Material edits resimulate the interaction with different material properties while keeping the robot action fixed. Viewpoint edits reproject the same 3D interaction. Both reuse the video generator without retraining. Compared with PointWorld~ huang2026pointworld on real DROID~ khazatsky2024droid grasping sequences, reduces gripper-relative offset by about 79 --84 across deformable, articulated, and rigid objects and lowers reference motion error. On DROID and BEHAVIOR-1K~ li2022behavior1k , improves video PSNR by 4.61\,dB and reduces FVD by about 43 relative to Kinema4D~ kinema4d2026 . Our contributions are: We introduce , an editable robot world model that decouples 3D interaction rehearsal from video synthesis. We propose that refines 3D trajectories via persistent grasp memory and material-conditioned constraints, reducing slip and distortion. We evaluate 3D rehearsal on DROID and BEHAVIOR-1K and test whether gains in grasp preservation, object structure, and motion accuracy carry over to generated videos. title: Co-World Model for Human-Video-to-Robot Transfer via Co-Constructed Shared Latent Dynamics
summary: Human videos are abundant and cheap to obtain, whereas robot trajectories remain scarce and costly, making zero-shot skill transfer from a single human demonstration an appealing route to scalable robot learning. Existing methods, however, either retarget human-specific geometry or match only static visual goals, and thus stumble over the cross-embodiment dynamics mismatch and the ungrounded action execution. We present the Co-World Model (CoWM), a predictive framework jointly optimized from paired yet unsynchronized human and robot streams. To bridge the cross-embodiment dynamics gap, CoWM disentangles each observation into a shared object-relation state and embodiment-specific context. It aligns latent actions across embodiments using effect-swap and action-sensitivity objectives,such that actions are matched by their predicted effects on the manipulated objects rather than by embodimentdependent kinematics. For grounded execution, a phase-aware receding-horizon controller estimates demonstration progress, projects the inferred human action prior onto the robot action-support density, and translates the resulting latent dynamics into executable robot commands. Extensive experiments in simulation and on two physical robot platforms demonstrate the effectiveness of CoWM, its cross-platform generalizability, and the contribution of each component. See the demo video in the supporting information for details.
full_text: Co-World Model for Human-Video-to-Robot Transfer via Co-Constructed Shared Latent Dynamics Co-World Model for Human-Video-to-Robot Transfer via Co-Constructed Shared Latent Dynamics Xuetao LI Xuan JIANG jiangxuan913@gmail.com Chen LIU Zhongrui RAO \ LING Hui WANG Sheng LIU Miao LI miao.li@whu.edu.cn Introduction sec:introduction Robot manipulation learning has advanced markedly, from imitation policies and vision-language-action models~ diffusionpolicy,act,rt2 to generalist foundation policies that span tasks and platforms~ pi0,geminirobotics,groot . These advances, however, are fueled by robot trajectories that remain scarce and costly, as teleoperated collection demands per-platform hardware, expert operators, and hours of supervised recording~ openx,droid . Egocentric human videos offer the opposite profile, capturing abundant and easily acquired observations of contact-rich manipulation~ egodex,dexcap . This asymmetry motivates human-video-to-robot zero-shot transfer, in which a robot acquires an executable skill from a single unseen human demonstration without any corresponding robot trajectory, as illustrated in Figure~ fig:teaser . However, most existing transfer methods either retarget human motion while preserving human-specific geometry~ dexmv,handsasprobes,phantom , or condition on visual goals or skill latents while discarding the intermediate interaction dynamics~ track2act,vidman,uniskill , and single-embodiment world models couple their predictive semantics to the one interface that generated the data~ planet,dreamerv1,dreamerv3,tdmpc,tdmpc2 . Realizing such transfer presents two unique challenges. First, cross-embodiment dynamics mismatch. Humans and robots differ in morphology, sensing, and action interfaces, so different motions may produce the same object change while similar motions have state-dependent effects. Latent proximity or marginal distribution matching cannot resolve this ambiguity, because a shared model may silently infer the embodiment, branch its transition rule, or ignore its action input. Second, ungrounded action execution. Human videos carry neither robot commands nor proprioception, and executions proceed at mismatched rates. A plan induced from the video alone may therefore drift out of phase or request actions the robot has never been observed to perform, and direct kinematic mapping cannot certify feasibility. In light of these challenges, this work investigates two critical questions: I) How can human observations and robot experience co-construct one predictive world model? II) How can the latent plan induced by a single unseen human video be translated into feasible robot control at test time? In response to question I), we propose the ( ), jointly optimized from paired but unsynchronized human and robot streams. factorizes each observation into a shared object-relation state and an embodiment-private context, and encodes both human and robot motion into a common latent action space. Rather than aligning raw kinematics, we bind action semantics through predicted object effects with two complementary constraints, where an effect-swap loss requires human and robot actions with matched effects to predict compatible object changes, and an action-sensitivity margin rejects nearby actions whose observed effects differ. Together they prevent the shared dynamics from branching on embodiment or degenerating into action-agnostic prediction. Leveraging the co-constructed latent space, we design a phase-aware grounded execution scheme for question II). Online temporal matching tracks the demonstration phase against mismatched execution rates, a robot-state-conditioned residual corrects the human action prior, and an empirical action-support density confines proposals to actions supported by robot experience. Receding-horizon planning under the shared dynamics then converts the demonstration-induced latent evolution into executable commands, replanning after each observation. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We formulate , in which human observations and robot experience jointly constrain a factorized predictive space over shared object relations and common latent actions, while embodiment-private variables retain the context tied to each embodiment's own body and controller. We bind cross-embodiment latent actions through complementary effect-swap and action-sensitivity constraints, aligning actions by their predicted object effects rather than kinematics and rejecting action-agnostic shared dynamics. We translate predictions into robot control through phase tracking, residual proposals, an action-support prior, and receding-horizon planning. Extensive experiments in simulation and on two physical robots validate the framework and the contribution of each component. Related Work sec:related Robot Learning from Human Video Human video is a cheap and abundant substitute for costly robot trajectories, supplying visual rewards, affordances, goals, and reusable representations~ r3mhuman,r3m,vip . More direct routes retarget human motion, edit videos into robot-compatible training pairs, or exploit human play~ dexmv,handsasprobes,phantom,mimicplay , while point tracks, predicted motion, and egocentric hand annotations add structured supervision~ track2act,vidman,egodex,dexcap . These methods transfer geometry, task progress, or visual goals, yet none models how an action changes the task state, so the cross-embodiment dynamics mismatch is bypassed rather than resolved; instead lets both streams jointly constrain one predictive task world with an operational test of action substitutability. Demonstration-Conditioned Robot Policies Behavior cloning, diffusion policies, and action-chunking transformers learn expressive control from action-labeled robot demonstrations~ bcz,diffusionpolicy,act , and vision-language-action models scale this paradigm with language conditioning and large multi-task robot datasets~ rt1,rt2,openvla,octo,pi0,openx,droid . Related efforts target generalizable humanoid and dexterous manipulation~ rgmp,tactilemllm,dexgrasp and defend learned policies against backdoor attacks~ attnbetray . Their competence remains bounded by the same costly robot data that motivates our setting, and they are not conditioned on a held-out human video or execution phase. Our evaluation therefore includes demonstration-conditioned variants that receive the same human observations, paired training split, and robot state as , isolating the shared predictive world rather than the information budget. Cross-Embodiment Latent World Models Latent world models plan through learned state transitions~ planet,dreamerv1,dreamerv3,tdmpc,tdmpc2 , predictive video models serve as planners or policies~ unipi,gr1,genie , and latent-action methods infer control variables from observation-only sequences~ ilpo,vpt,lapo . Recent cross-embodiment systems condition robot policies on skill representations from human video~ uniskill or contrastively align end-effector actions through kinematic retargeting~ lad , yet their alignment still rests on frame prediction or kinematic correspondence, not on what an action does to the task state. instead co-constructs an object-centric predictive state and a common latent action interface from both streams; since a shared encoder or transition alone may retain domain cues, branch on embodiment, or ignore its action input, the effect-swap and action-sensitivity constraints directly target these failure modes. On the execution side, SoftDTW~ softdtw , MMD~ mmd , Dirichlet-process mixtures~ ferguson1973,bleijordan2006 , and CEM~ cem are established components assembled to ground the plan; the effect-constrained shared dynamics remain the central mechanism. Co-World Model sec:method This section instantiates the two responses outlined in the introduction, following the pipeline in Figure~ fig:pipeline . To resolve the cross-embodiment dynamics mismatch, we first formalize the co-construction objective, then factorize observations into shared and private states and bind latent actions through effect-grounded dynamics (Figure~ fig:pipeline , bottom). To resolve the ungrounded action execution, we subsequently attach robot grounding with an action-support prior and perform phase-aware receding-horizon planning in the co-constructed latent space (Figure~ fig:pipeline , top). The two stages communicate only through the co-constructed latent space and the grounded decoder, so the test-time planner consumes exactly the quantities that training was optimized to provide. title: Linear-Time Online Visual Geometry Transformer with Hybrid Architecture
summary: Transformer-based 3D reconstruction models such as VGGT and $π^3$ predict cameras, depth and point maps directly from many input views. Causal attention models such as StreamVGGT extend them to online video but cache all past tokens, so their total compute grows quadratically with the stream length. Recurrent models such as CUT3R and TTT3R keep a fixed-size state at constant cost, but they progressively forget early geometry. We present LinearVGGT, a hybrid model distilled from StreamVGGT, which uses Mamba2 layers for efficient sequence modeling in three of every four global layers. The remaining layers use register-guided sparse attention to retrieve a few relevant past frames, compensating for the limited exact long-range recall of Mamba2. Our distillation needs only 9\% of the GPU hours and 31\% of the training frames that StreamVGGT uses to learn from VGGT. LinearVGGT keeps an almost constant latency of 27 ms per frame over 1,024 frames and is on average $12 \times$ faster than StreamVGGT. It outperforms its teacher and is competitive with the state-of-the-art streaming model LingBot-Map, while running $2.5\times$ faster and using $2.7\times$ less memory.

However, their reliance on dense global attention incurs quadratic computational complexity in the number of visual tokens and substantial memory overhead, limiting their scalability to long image sequences and applications to streaming video inputs like SLAM~ maggio2025vggt-slam . These limitations have motivated a growing body of work aimed at improving the computational and memory efficiency of these models. Token-merging based methods like FastVGGT, GoToHunt etc recognize the redundant attention pattern in global attention and only select the most important tokens for computation. Despite being easy to implement and training free, these methods still struggle with quadratic computational complexity of global attention. Recurrent models such as CUT3R~ wang2025cut3r and TTT3R~ chen2025ttt3r keep a fixed-size state at a constant cost per frame, but this state forgets earlier frames as the stream grows~ chen2025ttt3r . Furthermore, StreamVGGT~ zhuo2025streamvggt and LingBot-Map~ chen2026lingbotmap have explored using causal attention architectures or its more efficient variants to solve this. Nevertheless, the nature of causal attention determines that it still suffers from prohibitively long inference time when increasing the number of processed frames. Attention-based models thus stay accurate, but their cost per frame grows with the stream. Fixed-size states run at a constant cost, but they cannot keep every past frame. This tradeoff raises our research question: Linear-time sequence models such as Mamba2~ dao2024mamba2 and Gated DeltaNet~ yang2025gdn suggest an answer. They carry the history in a fixed-size state, so each new input costs the same, and hybrid language models~ lieber2024jamba,kimi2025linear recover the recall of attention with a few attention layers among them. Although the great efficiency makes it appealing to adapt these cutting-edge architectures, applying them to 3D reconstruction domain is non-trivial, we recognize two primary challenges: First, the adaptation to 3D reconstruction domains, especially performance on long sequences. We observe significant performance drop of selective state space models under long sequences inputs, which counteracts the efficiency gain of these linear models. Second, the new modeling architecture will trigger training from scratch, which requires extensive GPU time and resources (~ .) To address these challenges, we propose LinearVGGT, a hybrid streaming visual geometry transformer whose Mamba2 layers carry a compressed summary of the stream at a constant cost. To counteract the decay of this summary on long streams, we interleave the Mamba2 layers with periodic attention layers in a 3:1 ratio. These attention layers fill in what the summary misses: direct interactions with the key tokens of the past frames most relevant to the new frame. Full attention in these layers would bring the growing cost back, yet most of its interactions are redundant. Prior analyses of VGGT show that its global attention can be sparsified with little loss of accuracy~ wang2026blocksparse, sun2026avggt . Our preliminary experiments agree: a new frame loses little accuracy when it reads only the first frame and a few past frames ( ). The open question is which frames and tokens to read. Register tokens offer a cheap answer: in vision transformers they collect global information about their image~ darcet2024registers , and VGGT- already uses them to exchange scene information across frames~ wang2026vggtomega . We therefore propose register-guided sparse attention, a hierarchical design that selects frames first and tokens second. At the frame level, the registers of a new frame rank all past frames by attending only to their registers, and the new frame attends to the first frame, which anchors the world coordinates, and to the top-ranked frames. At the token level, a lightweight indexer keeps in each past frame only the patch tokens that the frame itself attends to most. To avoid the training cost discussed above, we distill LinearVGGT from StreamVGGT with a three-stage procedure inspired by MOHAWK~ bick2024mohawk . Starting from the attention weights of the teacher, the first two stages align each new layer with the corresponding attention layer, first through its attention matrix and then through its output. The third stage trains the student end to end against both the predictions of the teacher and ground-truth depth, cameras and point maps, first updating the new layers and then all layers except the image encoder. The whole procedure takes 59 hours on one GPU and 1.2M training frames. This is 9 of the GPU hours and 31 of the frames that StreamVGGT needs to learn from VGGT~ zhuo2025streamvggt , and less than 0.5 of the GPU hours used to train VGGT or LingBot-Map. Despite this small budget, LinearVGGT has lower accuracy and completeness errors than its teacher in all four multi-view reconstruction settings, with up to 49 lower accuracy error. It also outperforms the recurrent CUT3R and TTT3R. Additionally, we observe that streaming inference is also limited by the overhead of launching GPU kernels. We therefore optimize inference by capturing the fixed-shape part of each frame as CUDA graphs and fusing its small kernels. With these optimizations, LinearVGGT keeps its latency of average 27ms per frame, on average 12 times faster than StreamVGGT and also faster than CUT3R and TTT3R. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: We propose LinearVGGT, a streaming visual geometry transformer that interleaves Mamba2 layers with register-guided sparse attention, so that its cost stays nearly constant while it keeps the accuracy of causal attention; We introduce a three-stage distillation for visual geometry transformers that turns a pretrained model into an accurate linear-time model with a small fraction of the data and compute that training such a model usually requires; Extensive experiments show that LinearVGGT reaches state-of-the-art efficiency in streaming reconstruction while its accuracy remains competitive with that of state-of-the-art models. It keeps the image encoder, the frame attention layers and the prediction heads of StreamVGGT and changes only the layers that connect frames: three of every four become Mamba2 layers ( ), and every fourth becomes a register-guided sparse attention layer ( ). A streaming model receives RGB frames one at a time, without camera parameters. For each frame , it predicts the camera , the depth map and the point map in the coordinate frame of , from the frames alone and before frame arrives. The model must therefore carry what it needs from the past in some memory, and the cost of reading this memory decides how long a stream it can process. Causal Global Attention StreamVGGT~ zhuo2025streamvggt , the model we build on, keeps the whole past as this memory. Following VGGT~ wang2025vggt , it encodes each frame into patch tokens and adds one camera token and register tokens, which gives tokens per frame. An aggregator of blocks then alternates frame attention, among the tokens of one frame, with global attention, across frames, and two heads decode the camera token and the patch tokens. In streaming mode, the global attention is causal over frames and caches the keys and values of every past frame. For one head of a global layer, the tokens of frame attend to all cached frames: where are the queries of frame and the keys and values of frame . Frame therefore costs in every global layer, and the cache of every layer grows by tokens per frame. In these layers, we replace the attention operator with a Mamba2 mixer~ dao2024mamba2 and keep the normalization, residual connection and MLP of the block. The mixer reads the tokens of all frames as one sequence in temporal order: frame by frame, and inside a frame the camera token, the register tokens and then the patch tokens in raster order. For each head, it updates a state as where every quantity with index is computed from the token . The token writes its content into the state under the key and reads the output from it with the query , so that , and play the roles of the value, key and query of attention. The step sets both how strongly the token is written and, with the decay rate learned per head, how much of the earlier state is kept. Unrolling gives so the mixer acts as a causal linear attention whose weights decay with the distance between two tokens, at a rate that each token sets through . A stack of Mamba2 layers alone would thus lose the early frames of a long stream, which is the limitation that the next section addresses. Register-guided hierarchical sparse attention sec:sparse A geometry model needs more from the past than a decaying summary. The first frame defines the world coordinates of every prediction, and a frame that revisits a place must align with the earlier views of it. We therefore follow hybrid language models~ lieber2024jamba,kimi2025linear and interleave the Mamba2 layers with attention layers in a 3:1 ratio, which keep the weights of the corresponding teacher layers. title: Beyond Natural-Language Instructions: Temporal Logic as a Task Language for VLA Models with Visual-Logical Fusion
summary: Robotic tasks combine object relations, logical dependencies, and temporal requirements, which robot planning and industrial control commonly specify in temporal logic (TL). We introduce TL-VLA, a vision--language--action framework that replaces natural-language task instructions with temporal logic, making this spatiotemporal structure explicit. A typed graph encoder and visual--logical fusion condition continuous actions on the task specification and the current observations. To prepare a general vision--language backbone for this interface, we develop TL-aware robot pretraining with separate semantic and structural readouts: a frozen language teacher aligns task semantics, the structural readout encodes TL syntax to support complex, long-horizon tasks, and autoregressive action prediction connects the graph representation to robot behavior. Downstream policies inherit the pretrained backbone and TL encoder and learn new fusion and action modules. On CALVIN ABC$\rightarrow$D, our TL-aware initializer reaches \textbf{3.800} average chain length and \textbf{62.3\%} five-task success, compared with 3.578 and 54.5\% for a FAST initializer pretrained on the same data and 3.485 average chain length for a Qwen+NL baseline. On LIBERO-10, TL-aware initialization improves success from \textbf{91.2\% to 95.8\%}. On LIBERO-Mem, our policy reaches \textbf{65.0\%} success without observation history, compared with 45.0\% for a Qwen+NL reference. On held-out Panda planning specifications, it reaches \textbf{59.6\%} at Success@256 over three generation seeds, versus 48.4\% for Qwen+TL and 37.0\% for Qwen+NL. These results support explicit logical task conditioning and transferable TL-aware representations for robot action learning.

Introduction Vision--language--action (VLA) models connect broad visual and linguistic knowledge to robot control. RT-2, OpenVLA, and show the value of this connection for learning diverse manipulation behaviors~ rt2,openvla,pi0 . A central design choice is how a task enters the policy. Beyond naming an action, a task may specify which objects participate, how they relate, and which conditions must hold in a particular order. A short natural-language instruction often leaves some of this spatiotemporal structure implicit; we instead make it the explicit task input of the policy. Consider placing an object in a drawer and then closing the drawer. Temporal logic (TL) represents semantic intent together with spatial relations, temporal dependencies, and compositional syntax. Predicate arguments bind participants; operators specify how requirements relate. This exposes richer, rule-governed structure than a short benchmark instruction, although natural language can express the same requirements. TL is less broadly used than natural language but is well established in robotics, control, and industrial systems. Its precise semantics provide a practical foundation for specifying task and system requirements and supporting systematic planning, control, and monitoring~ lahijanian2012temporal,bttldmps,chen2021temporal,yin2024formal . This motivates bringing TL into VLA models: can an explicit logical task interface, supported by suitable pretraining, improve learned visuomotor behavior? We introduce , which conditions actions on a TL graph, camera observations, and robot state. The graph represents task intent, and perception supplies the current scene. A typed graph encoder preserves operator structure and predicate arguments, and bidirectional visual--logical fusion connects them to visual features. The resulting continuous-action policy takes the graph, rather than an instruction, as its task input; training instructions only supply semantic supervision through a frozen teacher. Because TL conveys both semantic intent and explicit spatiotemporal syntax, our pretraining splits graph representations into semantic and structural streams. The semantic stream aligns with task-matched training instructions, while the structural stream retains ordered graph information beyond that alignment target. Joint action-token prediction trains a Qwen3-VL backbone~ qwen3vl to use these representations on a robot-data mixture. We then selectively transfer the Qwen backbone and the TL graph encoder, and learn the visual--logical fusion module and continuous-action head on downstream demonstrations. We evaluate the capabilities this design targets: sustained execution of consecutive subtasks on CALVIN, long-horizon transfer on LIBERO-10, multi-stage manipulation without observation history on LIBERO-Mem, and logical satisfaction of held-out single-goal, multi-goal, sequential, and partial-order specifications on the Panda benchmark. Under a fixed task interface and downstream recipe, TL-aware initialization improves over original-Qwen and robot-pretrained initializers, and on Panda its gains concentrate on multi-goal, sequential, and partial-order specifications. Our contributions are threefold: Replacing natural language with temporal logic in VLA policies, with visual--logical fusion. We adopt structured TL specifications as the policy's sole task input and integrate them with visual observations through bidirectional fusion, conditioning continuous action generation on both task logic and scene information. TL-aware pretraining for visual--logical policy learning. We develop a multimodal pretraining framework that prepares TL-aware representations for visual--logical integration and transfers them to downstream policy learning. Evaluation across diverse benchmarks. Experiments across diverse robotic benchmarks demonstrate the benefits of our approach for downstream control, with gains on tasks involving complex structured specifications. Related Work Vision--language--action learning. RT-2 and OpenVLA transfer visual--language knowledge to robot control~ rt2,openvla ; RoboFlamingo adds history modeling through imitation learning~ roboflamingo . and GR00T N1 generate continuous actions~ pi0,groot . and RDT2 improve generalization through heterogeneous co-training and scaled UMI data, respectively~ pi05,rdt2 . UniVLA learns task-centric latent actions for cross-embodiment transfer~ univla , while Moto learns motion tokens from videos~ moto . VLAct develops transferable representations through continued robot pretraining~ vlact . We build on StarVLA~ starvla . Logic-based policies and planning. For nested STL, Yu et al. synthesize continuous-time controllers using temporal-logic trees and control barrier functions~ nestedstl . SDT conditions offline Decision Transformers on STL robustness~ sdt , while STL-conditioned diffusion policies generate diverse, rule-compliant trajectories~ stldiffusion . TeLoGraF learns TL-conditioned trajectories with graph encoding and flow matching~ telograf . Vision-TL-Action grounds coordinate-free TL graphs in images~ liu2026vision , while S-MSP combines visual observations and STL through a structured mixture of experts~ smsp . Logic-VLA adds STL requirements to the NL instruction of a quadcopter-navigation VLA, with a pretrained STL graph encoder, supervised adaptation, and preference optimization~ logicvla ; STeP uses STL for language-based planning, monitoring, and replanning~ step . We instead replace the instruction with TL as the sole task input and pretrain the VLA backbone and TL encoder jointly on robot data. To our knowledge, no prior work evaluates this interface across manipulation and planning benchmarks against language conditioning. Task structure and long-horizon evaluation. CALVIN evaluates manipulation chains, LIBERO studies knowledge transfer, and LIBERO-Mem tests history-dependent manipulation~ calvin,libero,liberomem . PDDL describes action models and planning problems~ pddl , while BDDL specifies activity objects and logical initial/goal conditions~ behavior . LIBERO uses BDDL task definitions to connect language instructions, scene initialization, and success checks~ libero . For symbolic model construction, pix2pred selects VLM-proposed predicates to learn world models from demonstrations~ pix2pred , while PDDL-ART generates PDDL domains and problems from a demonstration, language, and action names~ pddlart . Connections include finite-trace LTL-to-PDDL compilation~ baier2006planning , BDDL grounding within an LTL interface~ eai , and NL-to-STL translation for cooperative robots in Seeing, Saying, Solving~ seeingsayingsolving . Our TL graphs expose benchmark-defined goals and temporal structure to the policy. Temporal Logic as the Policy Task Language sec:language Specification and observation interfaces At control time , let contain the available camera views and proprioceptive state. A task is given as a bounded temporal-logic formula . The policy predicts an action chunk where is a typed syntax graph. The environment executes a prefix of this chunk before the policy receives a new observation. The task graph specifies the desired behavior, and observations provide current evidence. We use predicates such as or , logical composition, and bounded temporal operators. A representative grammar is On a discrete state trace, requires at some time in the interval, and requires it throughout the interval. An ordered eventuality expresses attaining one condition before another. Benchmark adapters define the concrete predicates and intervals of each task. Graph encoding and visual binding Each graph node carries its logical or predicate type and structural metadata (Figure~ fig:graph b). The encoder reads normalized temporal intervals, ordered child relations, depth, predicate identity, object type, task-local object slot, occurrence identity, and stage identity. Occurrence identity separates repeated mentions of an object, and stage identity indexes a subformula's position in the specified order; both are fixed formula attributes, not progress signals. Tree edges and child order preserve logical branches and asymmetric operator arguments, and object slots identify task-local arguments together with their types and bindings. Message passing produces contextual node representations; pretraining uses three steps, and the transferred downstream encoder keeps them. Argument-specific query tokens accompany predicate nodes, so the arguments of a spatial relation remain separately addressable. Graph vocabulary and dimensionality are fixed within each initialization comparison. Spatial evidence comes from observations and robot state. Let denote graph tokens and denote selected visual tokens from Qwen. Bidirectional cross-attention (detailed in the appendix) produces fused representations Graph-to-vision attention supports task-dependent visual selection, and vision-to-graph attention conditions the logical representation on the observed scene. The action head uses these fused features together with proprioception. Where the backbone requires a textual wrapper, we use a fixed, task-independent prompt, so the task condition comes from the graph. What the interface makes explicit This formulation separates task intent from any particular language string. Logical edges expose conjunction, alternatives, and temporal structure; predicate arguments expose the participants of each relation. Changing a destination, for example, changes an argument binding rather than the operator structure; Panda tests such recombination on held-out specifications (Sec.~ sec:panda ). In deployment, specifications can come from formal requirements that robotic and industrial systems already maintain~ lahijanian2012temporal,yin2024formal , planners for temporally extended goals~ baier2006planning , or NL-to-TL translation~ seeingsayingsolving . Here, benchmark adapters build them from task definitions and native monitors score success, so task construction, policy input, and evaluation share one specification. title: Navigent: A Geometry-Grounded Agentic Framework for Vision Language Navigation
summary: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) with general-purpose multimodal large language models (MLLMs) offers a flexible alternative to task-specific navigation policies, while reliable long-horizon execution remains challenging. Agents must track navigation progress, detect discrepancies between commanded and actual motion, and recognize when movement has passed relevant landmarks or entrances. We present Navigent, an agentic VLN framework built around a frozen MLLM and a Geometry-Grounded Execution Critic (GEC). GEC performs two complementary checks: action-to-motion consistency, which evaluates measured displacement against commanded movement, and motion-to-landmark consistency, which tracks agent-selected visual anchors and entrance candidates in world coordinates. Detected discrepancies interrupt the remaining action sequence and trigger reobservation, local adjustment, or node-based recovery. Historical visual memory supports progress tracking across extended routes. An offline self-improvement procedure further analyzes successful and failed training trajectories to refine navigation prompts and GEC logic while keeping model weights fixed. On the R2R-CE validation-unseen split (1,839 episodes) and RxR-CE validation-unseen split(3,669 episodes), Navigent achieves 84.0%/86.0% SR and 72.9%/69.1% SPL, respectively, demonstrating the value of geometry-grounded execution verification for reliable agentic navigation. full_text: Introduction sec:intro Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) enables embodied agents to navigate complex environments by following natural-language instructions and interpreting visual observations~ r2r,vlnce . Unlike conventional navigation toward predefined goals, VLN requires grounding linguistic descriptions of landmarks, spatial relations, and action sequences in the surrounding environment~ r2r,rxr . Reliable VLN remains challenging due to several factors. Long-horizon instructions require agents to continuously track navigation progress and relate current observations to past experiences~ streamvln,mapgpt . Visual ambiguity and occlusions complicate scene interpretation, while discrepancies between commanded and executed motions can cause route deviations~ vlnce,harnessvln . Local errors may also accumulate over extended navigation episodes, affecting both success rates and path efficiency~ threestepnav . Existing VLN research has primarily followed two paradigms. Policy-based methods employ supervised learning, imitation learning, or reinforcement learning to train task-specific navigation policies that map visual and linguistic inputs to actions~ etpnav,navid . Recent navigation foundation models extend these policies across tasks and embodiments~ navfom,lightnav,qwenrobotnav , while dual-system models separate high-level planning from continuous action generation~ dualvln . In contrast, agentic VLN leverages the visual understanding, spatial reasoning, and tool-use capabilities of general-purpose multimodal large language models (MLLMs), enabling navigation through iterative reasoning and interaction with the environment~ navgpt,agenticnav,supernav . Recent navigation harnesses verify goals or planner proposals and use execution feedback to support recovery~ navharness,harnessvln . Translating high-level decisions into reliable continuous motion nevertheless requires monitoring what the robot actually executes. Consequently, achieving competitive success rates and path efficiency on full-scale benchmarks remains an important question for general-purpose agents. We argue that reliable agentic navigation requires verifying both the execution of commanded actions and the spatial progress made relative to the environment. At the motion level, a forward command may produce insufficient displacement or unexpected lateral movement due to obstacles or execution deviations. At the landmark level, an agent may move forward while getting farther from a selected doorway, or pass an entrance without recognizing the resulting navigation error. These cases call for complementary geometric checks: comparing commanded actions with measured displacement, and tracking the robot's movement relative to visual landmarks. This motivates our central insight: navigation reliability can be improved by grounding execution verification in geometric evidence, alongside the agent's visual reasoning and action planning. Motivated by this insight, we introduce Navigent, an agentic VLN framework built around a frozen MLLM. Historical visual memory integrates current observations with past visual evidence to support navigation-progress tracking. At its core, a Geometry-Grounded Execution Critic (GEC) performs action-to-motion verification using measured displacement and motion-to-landmark verification by tracking agent-selected visual anchors and entrance candidates in world coordinates. When GEC detects a discrepancy, it interrupts the remaining action sequence and returns control to the agent for reobservation, local adjustment, or node-based recovery. An offline self-improvement procedure analyzes successful and failed training trajectories to iteratively refine navigation prompts and GEC logic while keeping model weights fixed. On the complete R2R-CE (1,839 episodes) and RxR-CE (3669 episodes), Navigent achieves 84.0 /86.0 success rate (SR) and 72.9 /69.1 success weighted by path length (SPL)~ spl . Our contributions are summarized as follows: =10000 We develop a closed-loop agentic VLN framework around a frozen MLLM, integrating historical visual memory, incremental action execution, geometric verification, and node-based recovery to support reliable long-horizon navigation. We introduce a Geometry-Grounded Execution Critic (GEC) that verifies action-to-motion and motion-to-landmark consistency through measured displacement, depth, camera geometry, and robot pose, enabling detection of execution deviations and possible landmark overshoots. We present an offline self-improvement procedure that analyzes successful and failed trajectories to refine navigation prompts and GEC logic through regression-aware candidate evaluation. On the R2R-CE and RxR-CE validation-unseen splits, Navigent achieves 84.0 /86.0 SR and 72.9 /69.1 SPL, respectively. Related Work sec:related_work Policy-based Vision Language Navigation VLN studies instruction following from visual observations, progressing from viewpoint graphs in R2R~ r2r to low-level control in continuous environments~ vlnce . Learned navigation policies increasingly use MLLMs to encode visual history and predict actions~ janusvln,correctnav,sedualvln . NaVid~ navid predicts actions from monocular video, while StreamVLN~ streamvln combines a sliding dialogue window with slowly updated visual memory to bound streaming context. For broader task and embodiment coverage, NavFoM~ navfom unifies camera and temporal inputs, and LightNav-0~ lightnav connects spatial intent expressed through pointing to embodiment-specific trajectories through action tokenization. Qwen-RobotNav~ qwenrobotnav exposes task modes and observation parameters so that a higher-level planner can configure and invoke the navigation model. JanusVLN janusvln decouples semantic and spatial representations through dual implicit memory, improving the modeling of instruction-relevant visual context and navigation history across continuous navigation tasks. Agentic Vision Language Navigation Agentic VLN organizes navigation as repeated reasoning and interaction through memory, skills, and execution tools~ canav,gcvln,spacevln . NavGPT~ navgpt reasons over textual observations and history, while MapGPT~ mapgpt uses an online topological map to plan beyond local candidates. AgentVLN~ agentvln connects high-level reasoning to perception and planning skills, including active depth queries and self-correction. AgenticNav~ agenticnav exposes pixel-goal actions, depth queries, and visual recall as tools; SuperNav~ supernav combines navigation skills with interaction tools and task-progress management. Execution verification extends these interfaces beyond action dispatch. NavHarness~ navharness separates adaptive goal generation, goal verification, visuomotor execution, and persistent memory. HarnessVLN~ harnessvln validates proposals against spatial evidence, geometric feasibility, and subgoal consistency before execution, then uses execution feedback to update memory and guide recovery. Three-Step Nav~ threestepnav combines global planning and local grounding with retrospective trajectory review to correct accumulated drift before stopping. Self-Improvement Execution feedback can improve executable skills or model parameters~ voyager,aspire,zetta,rsinav . Voyager~ voyager combines environmental feedback and self-verification to refine programs and accumulate skills. ASPIRE~ aspire diagnoses failures from multimodal traces, validates program repairs through re-execution, and stores reusable robotic skills. Zetta~ zetta keeps the base policy frozen while evolving runtime critics and recovery skills through rollout feedback and validation-gated updates. Li et al.~ rsinav update navigation model weights by generating instructions for unlabeled trajectories, executing those instructions to filter samples, and retraining before processing the next trajectory shard. Method sec:method Given a natural-language route instruction , our agent uses successive visual observations to choose movement commands and decide when to stop at the described destination. As shown in Figure~ fig:overview , our method combines uniform historical visual memory with a Geometry-Grounded Execution Critic (GEC) and node recovery, while offline self-improvement refines navigation prompts and GEC logic. Visual memory supplies the current observation and up to eight images sampled across the executed route. The agent predicts a short action sequence, while GEC monitors measured execution and local visual anchors. A detected discrepancy interrupts the remaining sequence; the agent then reobserves and chooses a local adjustment or a return to a visited node. Completed training episodes provide evidence for refining navigation prompts and GEC implementation. The selected version remains fixed during navigation evaluation, while observation memory and execution state continue to update. Navigation Context and Execution sec:memory Visual Memory. These labels associate landmarks with directions during movement reasoning. Current and historical observations share this representation; historical images retain their original orientations and separate camera perspectives. The instruction enters the first decision; later decisions continue the same episode conversation. This context supports comparison of landmark identities, branch locations, and event order. The response records an estimated instruction stage, ordered event states, and visual evidence references as progress hypotheses. At each decision, the agent receives node identifiers and connectivity, recorded return-path lengths and relative return bearings, position relative to the start, horizontal heading, previous primitive counts, and the blocked flag. title: Dynamic Task Update Benchmark (DTU-Bench): Evaluating Runtime Task Adaptation in Robotic Manipulation
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies perform well on fixed-instruction robotic manipulation benchmarks, but their ability to adapt to instruction changes during execution remains understudied. We introduce the Dynamic Task Update Benchmark (DTU-Bench), evaluating 40 task revisions across seven update types and three execution stages using LIBERO, a simulated robotic manipulation benchmark. We compare performance when a new instruction is given before execution starts versus during execution, and examine whether the new task instructions are followed. Across 13 representative VLA configurations, average task success is 95.8% on the original object-manipulation tasks, compared with only 1.6% when the instruction changes which object to manipulate during execution. Controlled diagnostics show that policies often complete the original task before the updated one, and that their responses depend on the robot's physical state. We further test whether a simple scripted controller that releases the grasped object and moves the arm back helps robots respond to instruction changes. This improves success from 2% to 38% for π0.5 and from 8% to 48% for DM0.5, but can cause unwanted object motion. These findings reveal limitations that fixed-instruction benchmarks and task-success metrics alone can overlook in evaluating robotic manipulation. Project page: https://dtu-bench.github.io/

Introduction sec:intro Robots operating alongside people may need respond to changes in instructions thierauf2024instead,sharma2022correcting . A user may change where an object should be placed, request a different object, or withdraw part of an instruction after the robot has already begun acting. Unlike starting a new task, such updates arrive while the robot is executing and may have already made some progress on the initial task. When an instruction change arrives, some actions associated with the initial task may still be useful, while others may need to be abandoned or undone li2023interactive . Recent advances in robot learning have greatly improved language-conditioned manipulation. Generalist vision-language-action (VLA) policies such as OpenVLA~ kim2024openvla and ~ black2024pi_0 have demonstrated increasingly capable manipulation across tasks and environments. Benchmarks such as CALVIN~ mees2022calvin and LIBERO~ libero have supported evaluation of VLA policies on long-horizon task execution, generalization, and knowledge transfer. However, success on tasks specified before execution does not necessarily mean a policy can adapt when the task changes during execution. A policy may successfully execute the original or the updated tasks independently, yet fail to transition between them once execution has begun. Recent studies have addressed different challenges in dynamic robot execution. DynamicVLA~ xie2026dynamicvla focuses on manipulating moving objects, while TIC-VLA~ huang2026tic addresses reactive control. SwitchVLA~ li2025switchvla and ReSteer~ chen2026resteer develop training-based approaches to task switching. However, how existing VLA policies respond when different parts of a task are changed during execution remains insufficiently understood. Moreover, reaching the updated goal does not necessarily indicate that the robot has responded to the new instruction. This motivates a systematic evaluation of runtime task adaptation and post-update behavior. We introduce Dynamic Task Update Benchmark (DTU-Bench) to systematically evaluate how robot policies respond to task instructions that change during execution. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:overview , DTU-Bench introduces new instructions while the robot is acting, without resetting its state. Built on LIBERO, the benchmark covers 40 task revisions across seven types of instruction changes and three execution stages. We evaluate each policy under three conditions: executing the original task, performing the revised task from the initial state of the original task, and switching to the revised task during execution. These comparisons allow us to assess whether policies can complete a revised task after making progress towards a different objective. Beyond task success, we examine whether robots maintain the requested outcome and how their behavior changes following an instruction update. Our main contributions are: We introduce DTU-Bench, a systematic, policy-agnostic framework for evaluating runtime task updates in robotic manipulation across seven task-revision categories and three execution stages. The benchmark and evaluation code will be released. We evaluate 13 VLA configurations and identify limitations that fixed-instruction evaluation can overlook, including differences across update types, delayed satisfaction of updated goals, and substantial gaps between temporary and final goal satisfaction. We conduct controlled experiments to examine how the robot's execution state affects responses to new instructions, including whether simple scripted interventions can help recover from failed task updates. Related Work sec:related_work Foundation Models. Vision--language--action (VLA) models for robotic manipulation map visual observations and instructions to actions through autoregressive token generation~ kim2024openvla,pertsch2025fast,wang2026unified , continuous regression~ kim2025fine , or flow matching~ black2024pi_0,intelligence2025pi_ . WorldVLA and RynnVLA-002 jointly model actions and future visual observations~ cen2025worldvla,cen2025rynnvla , while VLA-JEPA and Light-WAM incorporate predictive representations or supervision~ sun2026vla,li2026light . Hierarchical models such as -VLA further integrate world-model-guided planning~ cai2026tau_0 . Despite this architectural diversity, adaptation to mid-execution task changes remains insufficiently evaluated. Execution and Task Adaptation. DynamicVLA~ xie2026dynamicvla addresses moving-object manipulation, while TIC-VLA~ huang2026tic combines asynchronous reasoning and control. These methods primarily respond to changing observations rather than task objectives. More directly, SwitchVLA~ li2025switchvla trains a contact-aware policy for task switching, while ReSteer~ chen2026resteer improves policy steerability through generated training data. Rather than developing a new switching policy, DTU-Bench focuses on evaluating different types of task revisions, distinguishing revised-task competence from runtime performance and examining whether updated-goal success reflects a response to the new instruction. VLA Robustness and Adaptation. LIBERO~ libero provides a benchmark for language-conditioned manipulation tasks; LIBERO-Plus~ fei2026libero evaluates robustness to visual, spatial, and linguistic perturbations; and LIBERO-Safety~ cui2026libero examines physical and semantic safety. DTU-Bench instead focuses on changes to task requirements during execution. It investigates original tasks, updated-from-start controls, and runtime updates, assessing whether updated goals are reached and maintained, alongside diagnostics of post-update behavior. DTU-Bench sec:dtu_bench DTU-Bench (Fig.~ fig:overview ) evaluates runtime task adaptation in robotic manipulation through structured task updates, execution-stage interventions, and measures of updated-goal attainment, persistence, and post-update behavior. Task Update Formulation sec:formulation In conventional language-conditioned manipulation, a policy executes a fixed instruction toward a goal . In DTU-Bench, execution begins under , and a revised instruction , specifying goal , is delivered at time while the system is in an intermediate state . The instruction conditioning the policy changes at the intervention time: where is the current observation. Execution of starts from the physical state reached under rather than restarting the episode. This distinguishes runtime adaptation from executing the revised task from the initial state: earlier actions may still be useful, may need to be redirected, or may have created conflicts with the new goal. What Changes: Task Update Taxonomy sec:taxonomy We ground our taxonomy in the task representation of classical planning. Given a fixed planning domain, a planning problem can be described by a set of objects , an initial state , and a goal specification ~ fox2003pddl2 : Here, specifies the conditions required to complete a task. In DTU-Bench, instruction updates change the target object, the required task outcome, or both, while preserving the objects and scene at the time of the update. We include seven types of task updates, grouped into four broader categories (Table~ tab:taxonomy ): Entity (2 types) changes which object the robot must manipulate (Object identity) or how the target object is identified (Spatial referent); Goal (3 types) changes where an object should be placed (Destination), its required relation to another object (Placement relation), or the required final state of the environment (Terminal state); Entity/Goal (1 type) replaces one required subgoal with another while leaving the remaining subgoals unchanged (Subgoal replacement); and Multiple (1 type) changes two or more independent task requirements within the same instruction (Compound goal). Each task-update scenario is assigned to one of the seven types, although some changes may involve more than one aspect of the task. Additional experiments on task cancellation and unrelated instructions are conducted on a subset of policies, with results reported in the supplementary material. Constructing Task-Update Scenarios from LIBERO sec:scenario_construction We construct 40 task-update scenarios using tasks from LIBERO-Spatial, Object, GOAL, and Long. Each scenario specifies an original instruction--goal pair and an updated pair , both using objects from the same LIBERO scene. The updated instruction changes what the robot is asked to do without modifying the environment. Each scenario is evaluated using the 50 official LIBERO initial states. When It Changes: Execution-Stage Interventions sec:intervention We introduce instruction changes at three stages of execution: early, middle, and late. These stages are defined by task-progress events rather than fixed action counts. For example, in pick-and-place tasks, they correspond to approaching an object, grasping or lifting it, and moving it towards its destination. If the robot does not reach the required stage, the update is recorded as not delivered. When the instruction changes, we discard any remaining actions predicted under the original instruction and generate new actions using the revised instruction and current observations. The robot is then given 300 action steps to complete the revised task, regardless of how many steps it has already executed. We continue execution even after the revised task is completed to check whether the required outcome is maintained. We additionally evaluate selected continuations over 600 actions to examine how a longer execution horizon affects task completion and maintenance. What Remains: Progress Compatibility and Execution State sec:progress The effect of a task update depends not only on what changes in the goal, but also on the progress made and the physical state reached during execution prior to the update. We consider two complementary aspects of compatibility with the updated goal . Task-level progress compatibility concerns which parts of the original task remain useful, which are no longer needed, and what must be done to complete the revised task. In multi-stage tasks, completed subgoals may remain useful even when other requirements change. For example, if both tasks require opening a drawer, the robot does not need to open it again. title: Reference-Model-Guided Distributed MPC for UAV Swarm Formation Flying Under Switching Directed Graphs
summary: Distributed formation control of unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) swarms in complex environments faces several challenges, including switching inter-agent connectivity, limited communication, external disturbances, and collision avoidance. To address these challenges, we propose a reference-model-guided distributed model predictive control (MPC) framework for UAV swarm formation. Each UAV uses relative-position information from its neighbors as input to a local reference model, whose output serves as the formation guidance for the onboard MPC controller. Meanwhile, a Kalman filter is utilized to predict neighboring UAV motions, enabling the construction of inter-UAV collision-avoidance constraints solely from instantaneous relative-state information. By decoupling MPC optimization from distributed coordination, this control architecture preserves the look-ahead planning and constraint-handling capabilities of MPC while enhancing the swarm's adaptability to switching directed graphs. Moreover, eliminating the exchange of neighbors' predicted trajectories reduces communication bandwidth demands, offering strong scalability for large-scale UAV swarms. To improve robustness and safety, disturbance-observer-based feedforward compensation is employed, while the bounded residual disturbance is explicitly considered in the control barrier function (CBF)-based obstacle-avoidance constraints. Finally, the proposed framework is validated through both simulations and real-world flight experiments. Specifically, the flight verification is conducted on a fully distributed multi-UAV platform without external global localization.

Distributed model predictive control, formation control, switching directed graphs, collision avoidance, disturbance rejection, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). Introduction n recent years, with the rapid development of unmanned systems, unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) swarms have been increasingly employed in applications such as cooperative patrol ma2024reinforcement, wang2021formation , target tracking doostmohammadian2021distributed, zhao2024cooperative , and collaborative payload transport wehbeh2020distributed, fink2011planning . Formation control plays a fundamental role in enabling multiple UAVs to perform complex tasks collaboratively and has therefore attracted extensive research attention dong2018theory,yu2023adaptive,baldi2021adaptation,wang2023fully,wu2024distributed,shi2025synergistic,yan2021robust . Compared with centralized architectures, distributed formation control relies primarily on information from neighboring UAVs, reducing dependence on a centralized controller and improving scalability for multi-UAV systems. However, practical deployment in complex environments remains challenging. Limited communication ranges, together with asymmetric or intermittent inter-UAV connectivity, can result in switching directed topologies, while external disturbances and collision-avoidance requirements must also be handled. This motivates the development of robust and scalable distributed formation-control methods for switching directed topologies. For distributed UAV formation systems, the controller must achieve coordinated motion while satisfying safety and actuator constraints. Model predictive control (MPC) provides a natural framework for this purpose because it can explicitly incorporate system constraints and optimize predicted motion over a finite horizon. Accordingly, distributed MPC (DMPC) has been extensively investigated for multi-agent formation control over graph-based communication topologies dunbar2006distributed,bono2021swarm,xiang2022energy . For multi-UAV systems, recent studies have further explored DMPC-based formation control under directed communication structures yuan2023distributed, chen2025distributed, hu2026fault . However, many existing DMPC methods for cooperative multi-agent systems are formulated under predefined interaction structures zhou2022multiple, mi2019self, zheng2016distributed and rely on the exchange of predicted or assumed state trajectories among neighboring agents for distributed coordination, including collision avoidance yuan2023distributed, katriniok2022fully, dunbar2011distributed . Such horizon-wise information exchange inevitably increases the inter-UAV communication burden, since the transmitted data volume grows with both the prediction horizon and the number of neighbors shorinwa2023distributed, izadi2011decentralized , which is particularly undesirable in communication-limited networks with switching inter-UAV connectivity. These limitations motivate a distributed control architecture that can maintain formation coordination under switching directed topologies without requiring predicted-trajectory exchange. In addition to communication and topology challenges, UAVs in practical flight inevitably encounter inter-UAV aerodynamic disturbances and external wind gusts. These disturbances degrade control accuracy and pose significant challenges to safe flight in dense-obstacle environments. To achieve disturbance rejection, existing studies have employed disturbance observers to estimate external disturbances and update the nominal model FixedTime , while others have adopted disturbance-observer-based feedforward compensation to enable rapid adaptation with promising results lee2019robust . However, such observers cannot comprehensively and accurately capture all disturbances, leaving non-negligible residual disturbances. Therefore, it remains challenging to guarantee safe flight in cluttered environments under residual disturbances. To address these challenges, we propose a reference-model-guided distributed MPC framework for UAV swarm formation under switching directed topologies. For each UAV, a local reference model generates formation guidance using only instantaneous relative states. The onboard MPC controller then independently tracks this guidance while satisfying practical flight constraints. To avoid exchanging predicted trajectories for inter-UAV collision avoidance, each UAV locally predicts its neighbors' future motions from these relative states. For robust and safe flight, disturbance-observer-based feedforward compensation is employed to attenuate external disturbances, while the bounded residual disturbance is explicitly accounted for in the control barrier function (CBF)-based obstacle-avoidance constraints. Finally, the proposed framework is deployed and validated on a fully distributed multi-UAV platform without external localization systems, as shown in Fig.~ fig: first . The main contributions are summarized as follows: Decoupling of Distributed Coordination and MPC Optimization: A local reference model is introduced as an intermediate coordination layer within the distributed MPC framework, generating formation guidance solely from instantaneous relative states. This architecture simplifies the onboard optimization formulation while adapting effectively to switching directed communication topologies. Meanwhile, it preserves the look-ahead planning and constraint-handling capabilities of MPC. Instantaneous-State-Only Interaction without Trajectory Exchange: To preserve the trajectory-exchange-free property during inter-UAV avoidance, each UAV locally predicts its neighbors' motions solely from instantaneous relative states. The predicted motions are then incorporated into the inter-UAV collision-avoidance constraints. This design reduces communication bandwidth overhead and facilitates scaling to large swarms. Disturbance Compensation and Safe Obstacle Avoidance: Disturbance-observer-based feedforward compensation is integrated into the local controller to actively reject external disturbances. Meanwhile, the bounded residual disturbance is explicitly incorporated into the CBF-based obstacle-avoidance constraints. This formulation improves flight robustness and enhances safety against wind gusts in cluttered environments. Fully Distributed Validation without External Localization: The proposed framework is implemented on a fully distributed multi-UAV platform without external localization systems (e.g., GPS or motion capture). Each UAV independently performs onboard state estimation, neighbor-state prediction, and local MPC optimization. Extensive simulations and real-world flight experiments validate the effectiveness and practicality of the overall system. title: M$^{2}$AdaptVLA: Multimodal Memory-Augmented Vision-Language-Action Model with Predictive Test-Time Adaptation
comment: 16 pages, 11 figures, 8 tables, including supplementary material
summary: Effective robotic manipulation calls for multimodal memory and rapid adaptation to shifts in contact dynamics. However, many existing policies, which retain either visual or wrench history, may miss key cues from the other modality. Moreover, even with wrench memory, fixed policies can struggle when contact conditions shift at deployment. To this end, we introduce M$^{2}$AdaptVLA, a vision-language-action model that integrates visual and wrench memories with predictive test-time adaptation. For visual memory, the model uses test-time training (TTT) to encode observation history in fast weights. Each entry in the bounded TTT bank combines the corresponding frame's features with a readout from these weights, preserving cues that predate the oldest retained frame. For wrench memory, a context gate controls how much the action expert draws on wrench history as it jointly denoises future actions and wrenches. For predictive test-time adaptation, the auxiliary wrench prediction loss also provides online self-supervision. Using measured wrenches as targets, we update low-rank policy adapters by backpropagating only through the final denoising step. Real-world experiments show that the TTT bank outperforms visual memory baselines on progress tracking, scene recall, and demonstration following. On contact-sensitive tasks, the context gate yields higher success rates than direct injection or gated cross-attention. Predictive test-time adaptation improves robustness to shifts in contact dynamics. On eight tasks requiring visual and wrench memory, M$^{2}$AdaptVLA achieves a mean success rate of 82.71%, a 31.46% absolute gain over the strongest baseline. The project page is available at https://tlf-tlf.github.io/M2AdaptVLAPage/.
