Introduction sec:intro Recent work has incorporated memory into vision-language-action (VLA) models and demonstrated its effectiveness on robotic manipulation tasks in which the next action depends on sensory information gathered over time~ memoryvla,memoact,rememvla,mem,vlamemorysurvey . Many memory-augmented policies focus on a single sensory history, using either visual memory to retain earlier observations~ tracevla,contextvla,t2mem,guhurhistory or wrench memory to retain the forces and torques measured during contact~ lee2019visiontouch,foar,fmvla . However, a policy that relies on a single memory modality may miss key cues from the other modality, making it difficult to perform tasks that require both. Consider a robot entering a safe's passcode (Fig.~ fig:memadaptvla_intro (a)). Visual memory helps the robot track which digits it has attempted and which key to press next. However, the gripper can look nearly identical as it approaches a key and as it lifts away after a press. Visual history alone may therefore leave the robot uncertain whether the key has gone down, causing it to move on before completing the press. Wrench memory supplies the missing cue: the rise and fall of contact force helps distinguish a completed press from an approach. This example motivates a multimodal memory-augmented VLA that integrates visual and wrench memory. Recent multimodal VLAs such as DAM-VLA maintain fixed-size buffers for visual and force observations~ damvla . These buffers provide direct access to recent observations, but an earlier cue, such as which drawer was initially open (Fig.~ fig:task_suite (a)), can be lost once its frame leaves the window. Test-time training (TTT) extends the memory horizon by summarizing earlier observations in recurrent fast weights~ ttt,robottt,t2mem,tttrm . Compressing the entire visual history into these weights, however, can make details from a particular moment difficult to recover. For wrench memory, the task stage determines how much the policy should rely on contact feedback. Appending wrench tokens to the action expert leaves this weighting implicit~ fmvla . DAM-VLA and DeCAL make the weighting explicit by gating cross-attention with pooled force features~ damvla and a global tactile token~ decal , respectively. Because these gates depend only on contact features, their weights cannot respond directly to changes in the instruction or visual cues to task progress. Moreover, even with wrench memory, a fixed policy can struggle when contact dynamics shift at deployment. For example, raising a whiteboard changes when the eraser meets the surface and how much force it exerts along the same stroke (Fig.~ fig:memadaptvla_intro (c)). To this end, we introduce M AdaptVLA , a VLA built on WALL-X~ wallx that combines multimodal memory with predictive test-time adaptation. For visual memory, we design a TTT bank to retain frame-specific detail while preserving cues beyond the explicit window. Each entry fuses the corresponding frame's features with a readout from the fast weights at that time (Fig.~ fig:memadaptvla_intro (b)). For wrench memory, we introduce a context gate that uses the instruction, visual context, and wrench history to determine how strongly the action expert should draw on contact information at each task stage (Fig.~ fig:memadaptvla_intro (a)). For predictive test-time adaptation, we jointly denoise future actions and wrenches to obtain a wrench forecast for each action sequence. When measurements arrive, we backpropagate the forecast error only through the final denoising step to update low-rank adapters~ lora (Fig.~ fig:memadaptvla_intro (c)). To evaluate M AdaptVLA, we design eight real-robot tasks with different demands on visual and wrench memory. Our model achieves a mean task score of 82.71 , an absolute gain of 31.46 over the strongest baseline (51.25 ). Ablations show that the TTT bank outperforms the evaluated visual memory baselines on task progress tracking, initial-scene recall, and demonstration following. The context gate also achieves higher mean stage success than either direct wrench injection or the GCA approach. Across the two whiteboard contact shifts, predictive test-time adaptation raises mean wiping success from 85.0 to 97.5 , an absolute gain of 12.5 over the fixed policy. Each update takes 159.5\,ms on average on an RTX~5090. Our contributions are threefold. [leftmargin=1.2em,labelsep=0.45em,itemindent=0pt,itemsep=2pt] We introduce M AdaptVLA, a multimodal memory-augmented VLA that combines visual memory with context-gated wrench history to jointly predict future actions and wrenches. Extensive experiments demonstrate its effectiveness. We introduce a visual memory bank that fuses each frame's features with a readout from TTT fast weights, preserving cues from beyond the bank window. We introduce a predictive test-time adaptation mechanism that updates policy adapters by backpropagating the wrench prediction loss through only the final step of joint action--wrench denoising. Related Work sec:related_work Visual Memory for Robotic Manipulation Visual memory helps robots track task progress~ memoryvla,memoact and recall scene cues that are no longer visible~ sam2act,robomme,t2mem,liberomem,memobench,mikasa . A common approach is to maintain a bounded memory bank~ sam2act,memoryvla,memoact,damvla . MemoryVLA stores visual features alongside instruction-conditioned cognitive tokens~ memoryvla . MemoAct extends the temporal span of a fixed-size bank by compressing older observations into long-term summaries and merging similar adjacent summaries when space runs out~ memoact . Once a frame is evicted or compressed, its details can be recovered only if the remaining entries preserve them. Sparse keyframe methods select which observations to keep~ memer,eventvla,kemo,replanmem,fourdimvla . MemER selects task-relevant frames from recent observations~ memer , while EventVLA predicts when to store incoming frames~ eventvla . A transient cue can be lost if the selector misses the frame that contains it. TTT carries history forward through recurrent updates to fast weights~ ttt,robottt,t2mem,titans , but fast weights alone provide no explicit record of a particular frame. TTT-RM trains its fast weights to capture history missing from the retrieved context and combines their readout with retrieved bank features during action generation~ tttrm . M AdaptVLA writes each bank entry as the sum of the current frame's features and a gated fast-weight readout, preserving frame-specific detail and cues from beyond the window. Wrench Memory for Robotic Manipulation How much the robot needs to rely on wrench history varies across task stages~ damvla,frvla,phaforce . TA-VLA encodes torque history as a single decoder token~ tavla , and FM-VLA feeds a compressed wrench history to its action expert~ fmvla . Direct injection leaves the expert to infer when contact history matters. Fusion mechanisms make this choice explicit. DAM-VLA gates cross-attention using pooled force features alone~ damvla , so its gate has no direct access to visual cues that distinguish task stages. Other methods use predicted contact to weight force features~ foar , route multimodal features through a mixture of experts~ forcevla , or infer the contact phase from vision and language to bias attention to wrench tokens~ frvla . To weight contact history by task stage, M AdaptVLA combines encoded wrench history with the VLM context. Together they determine how strongly wrench history contributes to joint action--wrench denoising at each joint-attention layer. Online Adaptation for Robot Policies When contact conditions change at deployment, the same motion can produce a different wrench. Some policies adapt by inferring physical properties or latent dynamics from recent interactions~ hora,scout,latentphysical,onlinesysid . Others update parameters through self-supervision, using inverse dynamics~ pad or agreement between overlapping action predictions~ salt . For contact-rich manipulation, a predicted wrench provides a reference that the robot can check against its own measurements~ forcemimic . AdaWorldPolicy first generates actions, then predicts visual and force observations conditioned on those actions and uses the forecast errors to update low-rank adapters~ adaworldpolicy . To respond promptly to changes in contact conditions, M AdaptVLA predicts future actions and wrenches in a single denoising trajectory. Once the corresponding wrench measurements arrive, it limits the cost of each adapter update by backpropagating the wrench prediction loss through only the final denoising step. Method sec:method We build M AdaptVLA on WALL-X~ wallx with Qwen3.5~ qwen35 as its vision--language backbone. Each of the backbone's six layer groups contains three Gated DeltaNet (GDN) blocks~ gateddeltanet followed by a full-attention block that connects the VLM to the action expert through joint attention. At decision , the VLM combines the instruction , current views , and proprioception with earlier visual observations stored in a TTT bank. A context gate regulates how strongly recent wrench history influences the expert as it jointly predicts an action chunk and its corresponding wrenches . At deployment, we adapt the policy by backpropagating the error between predicted and measured wrenches through only the final denoising step. Figure~ fig:method shows the full M AdaptVLA pipeline. title: Compact Vision-Language Navigation in Continuous Environmentsvia On-Policy Training and Route-Bearing Output
summary: Instruction-following robots need navigation policies that reach high accuracy and remain inexpensive to train and to run on a single graphics processing unit (GPU). The most accurate vision-language navigation policies for continuous environments rely on language models with 4 to 8 billion parameters, long observation histories, and large auxiliary corpora. Two properties of the standard training setup limit smaller policies. Imitation labels cover the states that an expert visits, whereas the running policy reaches states that its own errors produce. In addition, an image-plane waypoint exists only while the route lies inside the camera view. We present \textbf{\paper}, a monocular red-green-blue (RGB) policy with 2 billion (2B) parameters that addresses both limitations. \paper adapts Qwen3-VL-2B with low-rank adapters and processes an eight-frame memory and the current view in one forward pass. The policy predicts the route direction as a bearing in the body frame of the agent, which remains defined for every heading, and a deterministic controller converts this bearing into motion. This design allows training to relabel the states that the policy itself visits. On-policy correction improves success, while bearing decoding outperforms image-plane waypoint scanning across all evaluated start headings with identical weights. On the \valunseen split, \paper achieves \rFinSR\% success on Room-to-Room in Continuous Environments (\rtor), averaged over three seeds, and \rRxFinSR\% on its Room-Across-Room counterpart (\rxr). Inference requires \rDecMs\,ms and \rInferGB\,GiB of memory, while training takes \rCostTrainTyp\ GPU-hours on one 12\,GB consumer GPU.

Introduction sec:intro Instruction-following navigation enables a robot to cross an unfamiliar building by following a route description. Vision-and-language navigation in continuous environments (VLN-CE) formulates this task with low-level actions, namely 0.25\,m forward steps, turns, and a stop action~ krantz2020vlnce . On the standard Room-to-Room in Continuous Environments ( ) benchmark, video-language models predict these actions from sequences of red-green-blue (RGB) observations. NaVid~ zhang2024navid introduced this approach, Uni-NaVid~ zhang2024uninavid extended it to several navigation tasks, and NaVILA~ cheng2025navila and StreamVLN~ wei2025streamvln scaled it further. These systems are built on language models with 7B-8B parameters and long observation histories, and their training adds web video, question answering, or synthetic navigation episodes to the benchmark data. StreamVLN and NaVILA report \ and \,ms per model call, respectively, on an RTX~4090 GPU, and training these 7B and 8B systems costs 544 to 2 , 816 data-center GPU-hours (details in Table~ tab:cost ). In an instruction-following setup, a deployed robot must act several times per second on its own hardware, so the latency, memory footprint, and training cost of its policy determine where that policy can run and who can afford to train it. Fig.~ fig:teaser demonstrates among published systems along two axes, language-model size and latency. It is visible that a 2B-parameter policy is on par in success rate with the 7B StreamVLN and the 8B NaVILA and Aux-Think at the lowest reported latency, whereas the 2B MonoDream~ wang2025monodream requires \,ms per call and the 2B Goal2Pixel~ goal2pixel2026 needs depth at test time. We identify two limitations of the standard training setup that stand in the way of compact policies. The first concerns the training data, since imitation covers only the states an expert visits, whereas a running policy drifts into new states after its own errors~ ross2011dagger . The second concerns the action representation, because an image-plane waypoint can express only routes inside the camera view, yet in of the episodes the first route step lies more than from the start heading. retains a standard vision-language backbone and instead changes the output representation and the training-state distribution (Fig.~ fig:overview ). Related Work sec:related Navigation in continuous environments. VLN-CE~ krantz2020vlnce extends Room-to-Room (R2R)~ anderson2018vln to continuous navigation with low-level actions; Room-Across-Room (RxR)~ ku2020rxr provides longer instructions, while EnvDrop~ tan2019envdrop uses back-translation. Depth supports several planning representations: semantic maps in CM2 and WS-MGMap~ georgakis2022cm2,chen2022wsmgmap , language-aligned waypoints in LAW~ raychaudhuri2021law , and panoramic topological graphs in ETP-R1 and LCGNav~ ye2025etpr1,peng2026lcgnav . Other depth-based methods construct 3D feature fields~ wang2024vln3dff,wang2024g3dlf or provide VLMs with annotated maps and layered 3D tokens~ zhang2025mapnav,wang2025dynam3d . Zero-shot planners prompt large language models with constraint-aware or affordance-oriented plans~ chen2024canav,chen2024aoplanner , generic instructions~ long2024instructnav , or predicted trajectories~ wang2025dreamnav . Aux-Think examines reasoning strategies for data-efficient training~ wang2025auxthink , while DualVLN and InternVLA-N1 combine slow planners with fast low-level policies~ wei2025dualvln,internvlan1_2025 . Method sec:method Problem formulation sec:overview At each decision step , the policy receives an instruction , a RGB frame , a memory of earlier decision frames, and a known vector of camera and body parameters. All primitives in are executed before the next observation. The policy grounds the instruction in the image, and the controller turns its predictions into motion with fixed rules. Two choices shape such a compact policy: what it predicts, so that the controller can act from any state, and on which states it is trained. Route bearing in the body frame sec:bearing An image-plane waypoint, the pixel of the next route point, gives the direction , with the horizontal focal length and principal-point coordinate , only while that point lies inside the field of view. When the route is beside or behind the agent, either at the start of an episode or after a wrong turn, the waypoint policy must turn to locate it. However, these states lack waypoint labels during training. therefore also predicts the route bearing, the direction of the route target in the body frame of the agent. For a target at body coordinates , with forward and to the left, the bearing label is defined at every heading and at every position farther than 0.3\,m from the target. The policy predicts the bearing as a distribution over circular bins with centers , one bin per turn primitive, and the predicted bearing is the probability-weighted circular mean of the most likely bin and its two neighbors. At inference, the controller can therefore turn directly toward a route that is out of view, and it keeps the waypoint as the finer target while the route is in view. In training, the direction label exists at every heading, including at off-route states whose target lies out of view and which therefore lack an image-plane label. title: Riding the Wave: Sim-to-Real Humanoid Control on Elastic Terrain
summary: Humanoid robots on deformable elastic terrains face a surface whose position and motion are coupled in space and time: deflection and rebound persist between contacts, and load at one foothold alters the support at others, so training must capture how each contact changes the support that follows. We present RIPPLE (Robust Interaction via Proprioceptive Policies on Large-deformation Elastic terrain), a simulation-to-real learning framework for humanoid control on such terrains. RIPPLE integrates ElasticMembrane, a pretensioned mass-spring mesh that models spatially coupled deflection, energy storage, and rebound, together with deformable contact into MJLab for GPU-parallel policy learning. Staged training then transfers rigid-ground skills to balance and jumping on these terrains using only proprioception, without vision or force sensing. Deployed zero-shot, the policies enable a MagicBot Z1 humanoid to balance, jump consecutively, and enter a trampoline from a rigid platform. In simulation, ElasticMembrane training holds standing success of at least 98.7% (mean over three seeds) on ElasticMembrane, IndependentSprings, and BouncyPlate under 0.3 m/s perturbations, whereas rigid-ground or contact-compliance training transfers poorly to the first two. A fixed policy tolerates stiffness from 0.35 to 2.8 times the training value, beds up to 7 m wide, and seven further simulated support scenarios, so transfer needs no calibration to the trampoline's stiffness. We plan to release the code soon. The interactive browser demo, videos, and scene configurations are available on the project page: https://fly-pigTH.github.io/wave_rider/

The interactive browser demo, videos, and scene configurations are available on the project page:\\ Introduction Humanoid robots are expected to operate in unstructured environments, from disaster response and infrastructure inspection to household assistance. The ground in such settings is often far from an ideal rigid plane: rope bridges, protective nets, floating platforms, mattresses, and inflatable surfaces are compliant and deformable, yielding under load and rebounding when unloaded. Locomotion there means holding balance and tracking commands while the ground itself deforms and moves. On an elastic terrain, loading changes surface shape and velocity, stores energy, excites motion that persists after unloading, and redistributes force from one foothold to the others. What the robot meets at its next contact therefore depends on the support's evolving state and on its own preceding actions, so a training environment must expose the policy to these dynamics while resolving contact with the moving surface. Reinforcement learning has enabled agile quadrupedal motion~ hwangbo2019agile,lee2020challenging , perceptive traversal~ miki2022wild , and humanoid locomotion from proprioceptive histories~ radosavovic2024humanoid . Terrain models and training curricula have also enabled locomotion on compliant and yielding surfaces~ choi2023deformable,compliant2024humanoid,mild2025deformable , where the surface yields locally under the foot. Trampoline-like supports, whose entire surface deflects, stores energy, and keeps moving between footfalls, have only been traversed by a quadruped under model-based control~ wang2020trampoline ; learned humanoid control on such a support has not been demonstrated on hardware. We present RIPPLE ( o\-bust n\-ter\-ac\-tion via ro\-pri\-o\-cep\-tive ol\-i\-cies on arge-de\-for\-ma\-tion las\-tic terrain), a simulation-to-real learning framework for humanoid control on elastic terrains. Its principal model, ElasticMembrane, represents an elastic surface as a mass--spring mesh whose nodes are coupled by axial and diagonal springs. Robot contact excites the membrane, and its subsequent motion feeds back into the robot dynamics. We implement ElasticMembrane in MuJoCo~ todorov2012mujoco and integrate it into MJLab~ zakka2026mjlab for parallel reinforcement learning. Policies progress from rigid-ground skills to elastic-terrain balance and jumping through one shared proprioceptive interface, so deployment needs no cameras, foot pressure sensors, or other exteroceptive sensing. A trampoline realizes local deformation, distributed motion, and rebound in one support. We demonstrate zero-shot deployment on a real for balance, consecutive jumping, and entry from a rigid platform (Fig.~ fig:hardware ), against simpler baselines on the same trampoline and against three simpler terrain models --- CompliantContact, IndependentSprings, and BouncyPlate --- in simulation (Sec.~ sec:experiments ). We introduce humanoid locomotion and dynamic behaviors on large-deformation elastic terrains as a new and challenging setting. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to study this task with reinforcement learning, and our learned policies generalize across terrain models and transfer zero-shot to a physical trampoline. Our contributions can be summarized in three points: A simulation framework built on MuJoCo and MJLab that couples pretensioned ElasticMembrane dynamics with deformable robot--support contact for parallel humanoid policy learning. A staged training and deployment pipeline that transfers rigid-ground skills to elastic-terrain balance and jumping through a shared proprioceptive interface, with real-trampoline demonstrations. Generalization experiments that demonstrate policy transfer across multiple terrain models and seven additional simulated scenarios, and quantify performance under changes in stiffness, size, and external disturbances. Related Work Modeling Compliant and Deformable Terrain Tractable contact models make terrain mechanics accessible to controller design. Romualdi et al.~ romualdi2021visco derive contact forces and torques from a continuum of spring-damper systems and apply the model to humanoid whole-body control in simulation. Vasilopoulos et al.~ vasilopoulos2018monopod incorporate permanent deformation, compaction, and slip into a viscoplastic model for monopod hopping. For learned locomotion, Choi et al.~ choi2023deformable combine an efficient granular-media model with an adaptive policy that infers terrain properties from interaction, demonstrating quadrupedal motion on sand and other yielding surfaces. Singh et al.~ compliant2024humanoid represent compliance through MuJoCo contact parameters and combine randomized terrain exposure with a curriculum for proprioceptive humanoid walking. MILD~ mild2025deformable discretizes the foot contact area to model spatially varying granular penetration, enforces consistency across foot contacts, and couples the model to proprioceptive estimation and latent modulation. Together, these works establish terrain representation as a substantive part of policy learning. RIPPLE instead models a bounded elastic terrain whose nodal state carries load transfer and rebound between contacts. Locomotion on Energy-Storing Terrain Environmental elasticity introduces both disturbances and opportunities for energy exchange. Wang et al.~ wang2020trampoline demonstrate untethered quadrupedal hopping and bounding on a trampoline, coordinating foot forces to limit pitch oscillations and adjusting leg-extension timing to control hopping height. Divi et al.~ divi2023jumping analyze how latch-mediated actuation influences energy transfer between a small jumper and compliant substrates, with hardware experiments supporting the model. These studies motivate treating support motion and loading history as part of the locomotion problem, but with a quadruped or a small jumper. RIPPLE brings this setting to learned humanoid control on a physical trampoline. Proprioceptive Learning and Sim-to-Real Transfer Sim-to-real locomotion requires policies to tolerate differences between simulated and physical dynamics. Dynamics randomization addresses this challenge by varying physical parameters during training~ peng2018dynrand,tan2018simtoreal . Proprioceptive history also provides information about recent robot--environment interaction: RMA~ kumar2021rma infers an environment representation from state-action history for its base policy, while Radosavovic et al.~ radosavovic2024humanoid predict humanoid actions with a causal transformer over proprioceptive history. Parallel Simulation for Policy Learning Massively parallel simulation accelerates experience collection for locomotion learning~ rudin2022walkminutes , with Isaac Gym~ makoviychuk2021isaac and Brax~ freeman2021brax providing GPU simulation. MuJoCo~ todorov2012mujoco provides articulated dynamics, elastic spatial tendons, and deformable flex contacts. MuJoCo-Warp~ mujocowarpCode enables batched GPU execution, while MJLab~ zakka2026mjlab exposes modular observation, reward, and event interfaces for custom tasks. RIPPLE adds persistent ElasticMembrane dynamics, deforming contact geometry, and batched resets to this stack. RIPPLE Framework sec:framework sec:model A trampoline combines local indentation, spatial load transfer, and rebound. MuJoCo's continuum- flex trampoline example~ exposes no independent pretension parameter, and an unprestressed adaptation deflected excessively in our tests. We therefore construct ElasticMembrane, a configurable pretensioned membrane inspired by thin-shell modeling, and integrate it into RIPPLE with parallel simulation, staged training, and deployment (Fig.~ fig:pipeline ). title: A Failure-Driven Data Flywheel for Post-Training Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models rarely satisfy all behavioral requirements of a new platform, and teams without a large deployed fleet lack the data to address the resulting failures. We propose a failure-driven data flywheel for post-training such models. It constructs target scenarios absent from the available data by inserting task-relevant entities into reconstructed real-world scenes, and evaluates the model against each behavioral requirement of the target task. Failure rates form a failure map across task conditions and difficulty levels, which is re-evaluated after each round and assigns larger data generation quotas to conditions where the model still fails. We instantiate the framework in autonomous driving for occluded-pedestrian emergence and yielding at stop-sign-controlled intersections, and evaluate it on two VLA models and one non-VLA planner in simulation and on a real vehicle. For occluded-pedestrian emergence, five rounds of post-training improve the critical-phase collision-free rate on the sealed test set from 0.261 to 0.579 for AutoVLA and from 0.390 to 0.765 for ReCogDrive, while the unnecessary braking rate in paired control scenarios never exceeds 0.013. On a full-scale vehicle without real-world training, post-trained ReCogDrive achieves 4 of 5 safe passages, versus 1 of 5 for the base model. Fine-grained evaluation reveals a pattern obscured by the collision-free rate alone: both VLA models learn anticipatory deceleration before reaching the occluding vehicle, while braking after pedestrian emergence remains limited. For stop-sign yielding, the stop-before-line rate rises from 0.100 to 0.897 for AutoVLA and from 0.000 to 0.667 for ReCogDrive. With sequential training from the pedestrian-capability models, it reaches 0.599 and 0.358, respectively, while the pedestrian collision-free rate decreases by at most 0.032.

(Right) Failure map of ReCogDrive on the development set. The map reports the event failure rate within each time to collision (TTC) bin, where an event fails if a predicted collision with the pedestrian occurs at any critical-phase query. fig:teaser Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models rarely satisfy all behavioral requirements of a new platform, and teams without a large-scale deployed fleet lack the data required to address the resulting failures. To address this problem, we propose a failure-driven data flywheel for post-training such models. The framework constructs target scenarios absent from the available data by inserting task-relevant entities into reconstructed real-world scenes, and evaluates the model in these scenarios against the individual behavioral requirements of the target task. The resulting failure rates form a failure map across task conditions and difficulty levels. The map is updated through re-evaluation after each round and assigns larger data generation quotas to conditions under which the model continues to fail. We instantiate the framework in autonomous driving for occluded-pedestrian emergence and yielding at stop-sign-controlled intersections, and evaluate it on two VLA models and one non-VLA planner in both simulation and real-vehicle experiments. For occluded-pedestrian emergence, five rounds of post-training improve the critical-phase collision-free rate on the sealed test set from 0.261 to 0.579 for AutoVLA and from 0.390 to 0.765 for ReCogDrive, while the unnecessary braking rate in the paired control scenarios never exceeds 0.013. When deployed on a full-scale vehicle without additional real-world training, the post-trained ReCogDrive model achieves 4 of 5 safe passages in the target scenario, compared with 1 of 5 for the base model. Fine-grained evaluation further reveals a behavioral pattern obscured by the collision-free rate alone: both VLA models acquire anticipatory deceleration before reaching the occluding vehicle, whereas their braking response after pedestrian emergence remains limited. For yielding at stop-sign-controlled intersections, the same framework increases the stop-before-line rate from 0.100 to 0.897 for AutoVLA and from 0.000 to 0.667 for ReCogDrive. Under sequential training initialized from the pedestrian-capability models, the stop-before-line rate reaches 0.599 and 0.358, respectively, while the pedestrian collision-free rate decreases by at most 0.032. Introduction sec:intro Vision-language-action (VLA) models integrate multimodal understanding with action generation~ driess2023palm, brohan2023rt, kim2024openvla and have been applied to robotic manipulation~ ma2026survey, zhao2025cot, zhao2025vlas and autonomous driving~ yuan2026autodrive, liu2026driveworld, liu2026uni . With the public release of pretrained VLA models, a growing number of teams adapt existing models to their own platforms and tasks without training them from scratch. Even after domain-specific training, however, these models may still fail to meet the requirements of specific tasks. Addressing these residual failures poses two challenges: identifying which capabilities a model lacks and acquiring targeted training data. For evaluation, driving capabilities have been assessed in synthetic environments and through closed-loop safety testing in reconstructed real-world scenes~ jia2024bench2drive,ljungbergh2024neuroncap,zhou2025hugsim , yet results reported by scenario category or through aggregate metrics may still obscure which individual behavioral requirements remain unmet~ moayeri2025unearthing, ye2024flask, zhang2025vla, yang2026beyond . For training, iterative learning has been explored using generated reasoning traces and interaction experience generated by world models~ zelikman2022star,yang2026rise , and several studies further use behavioral analysis or failure signals to guide the acquisition and selection of training data for driving models~ sheng2026curricuvlm,li2026world,gao2026learning,dou2026fire . These studies identify failures from existing data or from the behavior of the policy on such data. When the behaviors required by a new platform have no corresponding events in the available data~ xu2025can, sagar2026robomd, pumacay2024colosseum, li2025autobencher , such failures remain unexposed, particularly for teams without a large-scale deployed fleet. Moreover, failures may shift as post-training proceeds~ sheng2026curricuvlm, jia2026blind, yu2025self , motivating re-evaluation and corresponding adjustments to data generation across training rounds. To address these challenges, we propose a failure-driven data flywheel for post-training VLA models. The framework evaluates individual behavioral requirements, constructs target scenarios under controlled conditions, and uses expert demonstrations as supervision. On a development set, event failure rates across task conditions and difficulty levels form a failure map, which the framework uses to assign larger data generation quotas to conditions with higher failure rates. After each round of post-training, the model is re-evaluated and the failure map is updated for the subsequent round. Generated data are mixed with original-task data to support the retention of existing capabilities, while final performance is evaluated on an independent sealed test set excluded from all iterative decisions. We instantiate the framework in autonomous driving with two target capabilities: occluded-pedestrian emergence and yielding at stop-sign-controlled intersections. To implement controllable data generation, we reconstruct real-world scenes from nuScenes logs~ caesar2020nuscenes using 3D Gaussian Splatting~ 10.1145/3592433, zhou2024drivinggaussian, hess2025splatad, chen2025omnire and insert 3D assets~ ljungbergh2026r3d2, yang2025genassets representing traffic participants and traffic signs. By controlling asset placement and participant motion timing, we construct scenarios absent from the source logs with controllable interaction conditions and difficulty levels. A rule-based expert generates feasible trajectories that satisfy the target behavioral requirements, and observations rendered along these trajectories are paired with the corresponding future trajectory segments as supervision targets. Paired control scenarios identify unnecessary braking or stopping. We evaluate the framework on three publicly available driving models: two VLA models, AutoVLA~ zhou2026autovla and ReCogDrive~ ICLR2026_ff7bf601 , and a non-VLA planner, LAW~ li2025enhancing , which serves to examine whether the framework depends on the VLA architecture. On the sealed test set for occluded-pedestrian emergence, five rounds of post-training improve the critical-phase collision-free rate from 0.261 to 0.579 for AutoVLA and from 0.390 to 0.765 for ReCogDrive, while the unnecessary braking rate in the paired control scenarios never exceeds 0.013. Fine-grained evaluation further reveals behavioral patterns obscured by the collision-free rate alone. Both VLA models acquire anticipatory deceleration before reaching the occluding vehicle, whereas their braking response after pedestrian emergence remains limited (Figure~ fig:teaser , left). Moreover, removing the paired control scenario samples increases the collision-free rate to 0.944, yet this apparent improvement arises from indiscriminate braking. The improvement is also observed on a full-scale vehicle, where the number of safe passages of ReCogDrive increases from 1 of 5 to 4 of 5 without additional real-world training. Our main contributions are as follows: We propose a failure-driven data flywheel for post-training VLA models. After each round, bin-wise event failure rates update the failure map and determine the data generation quotas for the next round. We introduce a fine-grained evaluation that decomposes each target scenario into stage-specific behavioral requirements. Together with paired target and control scenarios, these requirements distinguish appropriate event responses from overly conservative strategies. Experiments on three driving models and two target capabilities demonstrate improvements in both open- and closed-loop settings, and the improvement is also observed in real-vehicle experiments on ReCogDrive. Under matched training budgets, the proposed flywheel reduces the open-loop critical-phase collision rate by 10.1 relative to the strongest baseline, and sequential experiments demonstrate the acquisition of a new capability while largely retaining the previously acquired capability. Related Work sec:related -grained capability evaluation. In autonomous driving, Bench2Drive~ jia2024bench2drive organizes closed-loop tests in CARLA around multiple driving abilities, advancing evaluation beyond overall driving scores toward capability-specific assessment. Neural rendering further enables policy testing in reconstructed real-world scenes. NeuroNCAP~ ljungbergh2024neuroncap uses a neural radiance field (NeRF) to construct editable safety-critical scenarios, while HUGSIM~ zhou2025hugsim employs 3D Gaussian Splatting for photorealistic closed-loop simulation and evaluates driving policies through challenging traffic interactions. We further examine whether individual behavioral requirements within a target scenario are satisfied and use paired controls to distinguish appropriate event responses from overly conservative strategies. training data and feedback-driven post-training. Simulation and generative models provide training data for policy learning beyond real-world data collection. title: $μ$MPC: Microsecond-Scale Nonlinear and World Model Control from Edge to GPU via Koopman-Linearized Precompilation
summary: We present $μ$MPC, a fast model predictive control (MPC) framework that reduces online computation using learned Koopman-linearized dynamics. By precomputing finite-horizon control-to-output maps, $μ$MPC eliminates lifted-state trajectories, yielding an action-only Koopman-Compiled QP (KC-QP) with $Hn_u$ decision variables, independent of lifted dimension. A fixed, precomputed primal operator enables efficient primal-dual iterations using only matrix-vector products and projections, accommodating changing goals and constraints without refactorization. This efficiency also enables control-aware dynamics learning through differentiable KC-QPs in the training loop and batched DAgger-style data aggregation. $μ$MPC achieves solve times as low as $23μ$s on a desktop CPU and 24 ms onboard a 168 MHz Crazyflie microcontroller. It scales to 4096D quadruped control in under 5 ms, visual planning with 2048D world models in 0.4 ms, and collision-aware planning for 200 quadrotors at over 30 Hz on the GPU. Across these benchmarks, $μ$MPC achieves up to $108\times$ faster constrained MPC and $1907\times$ faster visuomotor planning than competing methods.

Across these benchmarks, MPC achieves up to faster constrained MPC and faster visuomotor planning than competing methods. \ Project Website \ \ \ Code \ \ \ Video Introduction =-1 Optimal control of complex robotic systems requires expressive dynamics models and real-time solvers for deployment, which is particularly difficult for resource-constrained and high-dimensional systems. Embedded aerial robots face strict compute, memory, and power budgets nguyen2024tinympc, du2026gato ; whole-body legged control requires high-dimensional real-time optimization amatucci2026primaldual, fang2026gpusls ; visuomotor planning relies on learned world models with thousands of latent states zhou2025dinowm, nath2026pixels ; and multi-agent systems require many concurrent optimizations zhan2026robustly, foderaro2014distributed . Controllers must also plan over long horizons, react rapidly to observations, and satisfy complex constraints. Nonlinear model predictive control (MPC) addresses these requirements, but its computational cost grows with problem dimension, horizon length, and constraint complexity. Despite advances in sparsity exploitation, factorization caching, and GPU parallelism fang2026gpusls, amatucci2026primaldual , real-time deployment remains challenging. =-1 This computational challenge is particularly pronounced for learned dynamics and world models. While these models can capture complex dynamics from high-dimensional observations, planning often requires repeated computationally-expensive evaluations of candidate action sequences through the learned dynamics zhou2025dinowm, maes2026leworldmodel, gao2026fastlewm . One approach to reducing this cost is via Koopman linearization, which learns dynamics that are linear in a lifted space, yielding an affine dependence of finite-horizon predictions on the control sequence korda2018linear that simplifies both prediction and trajectory optimization. However, nonlinear constraints can still require iterative linearization and expensive matrix refactorizations, limiting the computational benefits. This motivates an MPC framework that moves expensive computations offline while allowing goals and constraints to be updated efficiently online. =-1 Another challenge is learning dynamics models that are suitable for control rather than prediction alone. Conventional Koopman dynamics learning emphasizes state-prediction accuracy mezic2026koopmansurvey , but low prediction error may not translate to high control performance. Moreover, training on fixed demonstrations neglects controller-induced distribution shifts, potentially degrading prediction accuracy at inference time. Differentiable MPC offers a way to address these limitations amos2017optnet by incorporating the learned Koopman dynamics into the MPC optimization during training, enabling direct supervision of control performance and generating training data arising from controller-induced state distributions. However, repeatedly solving and differentiating through MPC problems can be prohibitively expensive during training. =-1 To address these challenges, we present MPC, an MPC framework for nonlinear systems that exploits learned Koopman-linearized dynamics to formulate Koopman-Compiled Quadratic Programs (KC-QPs) that can be solved in microseconds. We develop a tailored primal-dual solver that precomputes a fixed primal operator offline, reducing online constrained optimization to efficient matrix-vector products and projections. This operator can be reused across changing constraints, goals, and MPC steps, substantially reducing online computation. The efficiency of KC-QPs also enables scalable control-aware learning: we solve batches of KC-QPs in parallel, evaluate the resulting control performance under the original nonlinear dynamics, and differentiate through the optimization to train Koopman representations directly for control performance rather than prediction accuracy alone. Furthermore, fast batched KC-QP solves enable DAgger-style on-policy data aggregation, improving coverage of controller-induced state distributions and mitigating inference-time distribution shift. Together, this scalable learning of high-dimensional Koopman representations tailored to closed-loop control enables microsecond-scale online MPC. Our contributions are: =-1 MPC exploits the linear structure of learned Koopman dynamics to eliminate state variables and formulate MPC as an action-only QP (KC-QP). We precompute a fixed primal operator offline, enabling fast, ``precompiled" primal-dual iterations using only matrix-vector products and projections, even as goals and constraints change, without requiring online matrix refactorization. =-1 We exploit the compact, parallelizable structure of KC-QPs to train the Koopman dynamics to produce MPC control sequences that match expert demonstration data, by differentiating through the optimization. Batched KC-QP solves also enable fast DAgger-style data aggregation, reducing controller-induced distribution shift. =-1 We demonstrate MPC across embedded, high-dimensional, multi-agent, and visual control. Our solver achieves MPC runtimes as low as 23 s on Dubins car and quadrotor systems, solves MPC onboard a resource-limited Crazyflie microcontroller in 24 ms, and performs 4096-dimensional quadruped control in under 5 ms. We further demonstrate real-time collision-aware multi-agent planning for 200 quadrotors, with hardware validation on a system of seven differential-drive robots. For visual control, we train 2048D linear world models enabling sub-millisecond planning, outperforming evaluated baselines on navigation and bimanual rope manipulation, with hardware cube-manipulation validation. Koopman methods lift nonlinear dynamics into approximately linear coordinates for linear MPC korda2018linear,shi2022deepkoopman , with recent extensions to robotic systems li2025continual,jung2026wholebody . Existing formulations retain important online computational overhead: ~ korda2018linear employ a prescribed lifting basis, which may not adequately represent nonlinear costs and constraints in a form amenable to efficient quadratic programming; ~ wu2024timecertified condense Koopman MPC but specialize to input constraints; and ~ wu2026boxqp eliminates high-dimensional observables but keeps physical states and controls as decision variables under box structure. More broadly, fast MPC exploits sparsity, condensing, cached factorizations, and specialized solvers stellato2020osqp,verschueren2022acados,nguyen2024tinympc , while recent GPU methods parallelize dynamics and optimization amatucci2026primaldual,fang2026gpusls,du2026gato . We instead differentiate an efficient control-recovery KC-QP that directly supervises the finite-horizon control response, then pair it with DAgger-style on-policy aggregation. This efficiently targets control relevant model error and controller-induced distribution shift without differentiating through a full expensive nonlinear MPC solve. =-1 models and latent planning. World models plan through learned latent dynamics hafner2019planet,hansen2024tdmpc2,hafner2025dreamerv3,zhou2025dinowm,maes2026leworldmodel . DINO-WM and LeWorldModel optimize action sequences through repeated latent prediction; Fast-LeWM parallelizes prediction but retains CEM search gao2026fastlewm ; learned planners instead amortize refinement from imagined rollouts sommer2026reinforced . Historically, these world model dynamics have been represented with high-dimensional nonlinear functions that are expensive to evaluate. MPC instead learns linear world model dynamics, enabling compiliation of the full-horizon response into a compact KC-QP for sub-millisecond planning, avoiding repeated latent rollouts at planning time while permitting explicit linearized state/task constraints and action bounds. title: DuoWM:Integrating Dual 6-DoF Visual Flows into Action-Conditioned Drone World Model
summary: Action-conditioned video world models generate future observations from an initial frame and a camera trajectory, but often fail to align camera commands with visual dynamics or represent full 6-DoF scene transformations. We present DuoWM, a first-person drone video world model with two complementary visual conditions. Action flow projects future camera positions and orientations into each target frame, while Object flow forward-warps the initial observation and overlays local 6-DoF transformations to ground the induced scene motion. We further introduce transform-aware pretraining, which pairs object appearance with explicit transformation axes before standard RGB video training. On Sekai-drone dataset, DuoWM achieves the best results across video quality, 3D consistency, and trajectory following. Compared with Captain Safari, the state-of-the-art method, our approach reduces real-domain FVD and LPIPS by 17.2\% and 21.6\%, respectively, while improving game-domain AUC@30 from 0.5003 to 0.5719 and AUC@15 from 0.3088 to 0.3747.
full_text: Action-conditioned video world models generate future observations from an initial frame and a camera trajectory, but often fail to align camera commands with visual dynamics or represent full 6-DoF scene transformations. We present DuoWM, a first-person drone video world model with two complementary visual conditions. Action flow projects future camera positions and orientations into each target frame, while Object flow forward-warps the initial observation and overlays local 6-DoF transformations to ground the induced scene motion. We further introduce transform-aware pretraining, which pairs object appearance with explicit transformation axes before standard RGB video training. On Sekai-drone dataset, DuoWM achieves the best results across video quality, 3D consistency, and trajectory following. Compared with Captain Safari, the state-of-the-art method, our approach reduces real-domain FVD and LPIPS by 17.2 and 21.6 , respectively, while improving game-domain AUC@30 from 0.5003 to 0.5719 and AUC@15 from 0.3088 to 0.3747. Introduction sec:intro Interactive world models are emerging as a promising training paradigm for embodied agents, enabling them to predict visual observations under different action commands~ wu2024ivideogpt,yu2025wonderworld . Recent advances in aerial robotics have demonstrated increasingly capable navigation and transportation policies~ chen2023deep,huang2021decentralised,chen2023behavioural,chen2025meta , motivating high-fidelity training environments that capture the visual consequences of complex flight maneuvers. While physics-based simulators rely on manually engineered dynamics and environments~ huang2026airgym,xu2025navrl , video world models offer a data-driven alternative by learning visual dynamics from videos. Recent aerial world models~ zhao2025airscape,serpiva2026flightdiffusion demonstrate the potential of this approach, yet maintaining correspondence between commanded camera trajectories and generated visual dynamics remains challenging. The core challenge lies in establishing a reliable correspondence between motion conditions and their visual consequences. Existing approaches explore several forms of motion conditioning, including learned latent actions, image-space controls, and motion representations based on point trajectories of the objects, optical flow, and 3D bounding boxes geng2025motion,wang2025ati,bharadhwaj2024track2act,li2026novaflow,wang2024boximator . However, these approaches typically lack precise frame-wise control over evolving video sequences, often relying on initial-frame guidance propagated across subsequent frames. Moreover, their motion representations primarily capture 3-DoF translations harley2025alltracker,karaev2025cotracker3 , leaving full 6-DoF (six-degree-of-freedom) rigid transformations insufficiently modeled. Explicit pose visualization and geometry-aware training already provide useful precedents: EnerVerse-AC renders end-effector positions and orientation axes as visual action maps~ jiang2025enerverse , while PoseTraj first reconstructs videos with projected 3D bounding boxes and subsequently removes box supervision to refine appearance~ ji2025posetraj . These advances raise a key question for aerial video generation: how can frame-aligned camera commands and scene transformation priors be jointly represented, and how can training align their geometric correspondence with visual appearance? We address this question with DuoWM, an action-conditioned drone world model using dual 6-DoF visual flows. Action flow renders target camera positions and orientation axes to align commanded trajectories with target frames. Object flow combines first-frame forward warping with local transformation axes derived using MoSE3~ cheng2026mose3 . MoSE3 supplies dense per-pixel estimates; DuoWM uses these estimates to construct visual conditions for video generation. We further use transform-aware pretraining to connect these visual conditions with reconstruction targets. The model first reconstructs RGB frames overlaid with local 6-DoF transformation axes, then switches to unmarked RGB targets while both flows remain as conditions. This representation differs from PoseTraj~ ji2025posetraj , which uses projected object boxes only as temporary supervision and then removes them. Our 6-DoF axes encode local rigid motion and are fed to the generator through Action flow and Object flow. We evaluate DuoWM along three axes: video quality, 3D consistency, and trajectory following. Across these criteria, our method consistently outperforms prior camera-controlled video generators on Sekai-game-drone and Sekai-real-drone. Table~ tab:main and Table~ tab:real_results report gains in perceptual quality, geometric consistency, and trajectory accuracy under complex flight maneuvers. Compared with Captain Safari, DuoWM reduces real-domain FVD and LPIPS by 17.2 and 21.6 , and improves game-domain AUC@30 and AUC@15 by 14.3 and 21.3 . Qualitative comparisons (Figure.~ fig:method_comparison and Figure.~ fig:3d_construction ) further show stable scene geometry and closer adherence to the commanded camera trajectory. In summary, our contributions are: We develop a dual-flow conditioning framework for aerial video generation, combining frame-aligned camera commands with local cues derived from first-frame-based warped observations. We propose 6-DoF transform-aware pretraining to establish the geometric correspondence between object appearances and explicit 6-DoF transformation axes, connecting transform-aware pretraining with the visual conditions used during RGB generation. Experimental results show that DuoWM improves visual fidelity and camera trajectory following on the Sekai benchmark, demonstrating the effectiveness of dual-flow conditioning and 6-DoF pretraining for action-conditioned drone video generation. Related Work Action-Conditioned Video Generation and World Models Latent diffusion models and diffusion transformers have substantially advanced high-fidelity image and video synthesis~ rombach2021highresolution,peebles2023scalable . Building on these foundations, large-scale video generators such as Sora~ openai2024sora and Wan~ wan2025wan demonstrate increasingly realistic long-range generation, while Genie~ bruce2024genie and iVideoGPT~ wu2024ivideogpt extend generation toward environments that respond to user actions. Autoregressive denoising further carries action-conditioned interaction across longer temporal contexts~ zhu2026astra . These interactive generators are now used as world models for embodied navigation~ bar2025navigation and visuomotor control and planning~ kim2026cosmos . Existing approaches condition video synthesis on explicit camera trajectories~ he2024cameractrl , disentangled camera and object motion~ wang2024motionctrl,shi2024motion , or user-specified object trajectories~ geng2025motion . These controls are further shaped by 3D pose constraints~ ji2025posetraj and propagated through latent trajectory guidance~ chu2026wan . Interactive generation additionally combines camera navigation with object manipulation~ duo_worldcraft . DualCamCtrl~ zhang2026dualcamctrl adopts two branches to jointly generate RGB and depth for geometry-aware camera control. DuoWM instead retains a pretrained video backbone and supplies two complementary visual conditions: Action flow represents the commanded aerial trajectory at each target frame, while Object flow combines warped appearance with local transformation cues. Visual Conditioning and 3D Spatial Awareness for World Models Visual action representations make control signals spatially compatible with video generators. Existing methods encode motion as dense motion fields~ niu2024mofa , bounding boxes~ wang2024boximator , point trajectories~ zhou2025trackgo , pose trajectories~ ji2025posetraj , or warped observations~ kong2025worldwarp . For embodied prediction, point tracks~ bharadhwaj2024track2act and generated flow~ li2026novaflow link visual motion to manipulation, while optical flow~ chen2026flowwam and projected point motion~ li2026hydra serve as action interfaces for world modeling and control. EnerVerse-AC~ jiang2025enerverse provides a direct precedent for visual pose encoding: it projects end-effector positions and renders orientation axes, with gripper openness encoded by shading. DuoWM adapts this visual representation to aerial camera trajectories and combines it with scene-transformation conditions. MoSE3~ cheng2026mose3 supplies the dense world-space estimates underlying those local cues; our contribution concerns their use as generative conditions, rather than a new motion estimator. Complementary work introduces spatial perception for video generation through 4D scene representations~ zhen2025tesseract , geometry grounding~ yang2026dreamworld , pose-aligned 3D memory~ chou2026captain , and occlusion-aware layouts~ agrawal2026seethrough3d . Other approaches incorporate physics-based interaction~ zhang2024physdreamer , rigid-body simulation~ liu2024physgen , physics-informed embodied modeling~ shang2026roboscape , or physics-reinforced simulation~ zhang2026physisforcing . DuoWM focuses on image-space conditioning: local transformation cues are represented alongside scene appearance, and transform-aware pretraining prepares the generator to use these conditions before standard RGB training. title: Nav4Manip: From Navigation to Dexterous Mobile Manipulation through Co-Evolution
summary: Dexterous mobile manipulation is essential for robots to perform useful tasks in complex, unstructured environments. However, existing systems face two challenges. First, navigation remains too coarse for downstream manipulation, which often requires a precise base position and approach orientation rather than merely reaching a meter-scale goal region. Second, navigation and manipulation are commonly trained in isolation, lacking a feedback loop that enables the two capabilities to co-evolve. These limitations prevent current systems from reliably executing long-horizon dexterous mobile-manipulation tasks in real-world environments. To address them, we introduce Nav4Manip, a bidirectionally coupled co-evolution system for long-horizon dexterous mobile manipulation. It comprises two complementary architectures: Nav4Manip-N learns long-horizon navigation and refines its policy through manipulation feedback, while Nav4Manip-M trains a world-action model (WAM) for downstream dexterous manipulation. We train Nav4Manip-N in three stages: multi-task co-tuning learns navigation behavior and manipulation-aware affordance prediction; rejection sampling fine-tuning (RFT) rejects low-quality policy-generated paths and fine-tunes the model on retained trajectories; and reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF) uses counterfactual preferences to further improve navigation decisions. To support this framework, we establish the Nav-N-Manip benchmark and construct Nav4Manip-Pairs from benchmark rollouts, providing large-scale paired navigation--manipulation trajectories and affordance supervision. Extensive experiments on public vision-language navigation (VLN) benchmarks and Nav-N-Manip demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, while real-world evaluations show that Nav4Manip completes diverse dexterous mobile-manipulation tasks. Project website: https://nav4manip.github.io/.

Introduction Dexterous mobile manipulation integrates navigation~ zhang2024navid,zhang2025uninavid,zhang2025navfom,xue2025omninav and manipulation~ brohan2023rt1,chi2023diffusionpolicy,octo2024,ye2026dreamzero,yuan2026fastwam . However, existing VLN methods are insufficient as upstream policies for downstream manipulation. First, VLN benchmarks typically consider navigation successful when the robot stops within 3~m of a reference goal~ anderson2018r2r,krantz2020vlnce . In contrast, manipulation success is highly sensitive to the robot's terminal base pose, as workspace geometry, kinematic reachability, visibility, and collision constraints impose much stricter requirements on the final position and orientation. Consequently, an endpoint deemed successful by VLN metrics may still leave the target unreachable, occluded, or accessible only from an unsuitable approach direction. Second, existing mobile-manipulation systems typically adopt either a unified whole-body policy for room-scale tasks~ fu2024mobilealoha,physicalintelligence2025pi05 or separately trained navigation and manipulation modules~ yenamandra2023homerobot,chen2024okrobot . unified whole-body policies do not directly address long-horizon navigation, while modular pipelines lack a mechanism for manipulation outcomes to inform and refine the navigator. Moreover, independently fine-tuning navigation and manipulation policies provides no mechanism for the two capabilities to co-evolve toward a shared end-to-end objective. We address these limitations by introducing , a bidirectionally coupled co-evolution system with two complementary architectures: learns long-horizon navigation and As illustrated in Figure~ fig:teaser , navigation-only optimization yields limited joint capability, while alternating optimization repeatedly trains both modules. Our staged co-evolution strategy achieves a 17.83-point improvement in end-to-end task success (52.13 vs. 34.30 ) over alternating optimization, while avoiding repeated manipulation policy training. jointly predicts navigation actions and manipulation affordances. Multi-task co-tuning first establishes broad navigation competence and manipulation endpoint prediction. Finally, RLAIF uses an execution agent to interpret navigation--manipulation outcomes and construct counterfactual preference pairs for further optimizing . The resulting knowledge is distilled into the navigation model, enabling manipulation feedback to improve future navigation. To support training and evaluation, we establish , a benchmark that evaluates both long-horizon navigation and downstream manipulation. Rollouts on yield Nav4Manip-Pairs, a 233-hour paired navigation--manipulation dataset. In summary, we make the following contributions: We introduce , a dexterous mobile-manipulation co-evolution system comprising three-stage and WAM . We establish the benchmark for long-horizon dexterous mobile manipulation and construct Nav4Manip-Pairs, a 233-hour dataset of paired navigation--manipulation trajectories and affordance scores. We conduct extensive experiments on established VLN tasks and , together with real-robot evaluations, demonstrating strong navigation performance and reliable end-to-end dexterous mobile manipulation across diverse tasks. Related Work . Built on Matterport3D~ Matterport3D , R2R~ anderson2018r2r , R4R~ jain2019r4r , and RxR~ ku2020rxr provide increasingly long routes and multilingual grounding. VLN-CE~ krantz2020vlnce enables continuous navigation, while REVERIE~ qi2020reverie and OpenUAV~ wang2025towards extend evaluation to object grounding and aerial navigation. ScaleVLN~ wang2023scalevln scales synthetic supervision, and RoomTour3D~ han2025roomtour3d and Sekai~ li2026sekai leverage exploration videos. VLN-PE~ wang2025vlnpe , VLNVerse~ lin2025vlnverse , and InternData-N1~ wei2025internvla further broaden physical realism, embodiment coverage, and scene diversity. Although these efforts substantially expand navigation supervision and some consider downstream embodied tasks, most VLN benchmarks do not explicitly evaluate whether terminal poses support manipulation. Nav4Manip-Pairs addresses this gap by pairing navigation paths and candidate endpoints with manipulation trajectories and rollout-derived manipulation success rates. . VLN methods have progressed from recurrent policies and data augmentation~ anderson2018r2r,fried2018speaker,tan2019learning to navigation pre-training and history modeling~ hao2020prevalent,hong2020recurrent,guhur2021airbert,chen2021hamt , followed by explicit spatial memory and planning~ chen2022duet,an2023bevbert,an2024etpnav . title: SprintGS: Eliminating Redundancy for Fast 3D Gaussian Splatting Training
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) renders photorealistic novel views in real time, but its per-scene training (optimization) remains slow. Recent fast training methods such as FastGS shorten training to a few minutes by reducing the number of Gaussians. Profiling FastGS, we find two costs that remain even in its compact model. First, rasterization is still the largest cost, and redundant work remains in it. Second, the loss computation does not shrink with the number of Gaussians, so its share of the training time grows as the model becomes compact. We present SprintGS, a training framework built on FastGS that keeps the model compact and reduces both costs. For rasterization, scheduled tile culling limits each Gaussian to the tiles where it matters, using a coarse footprint that is annealed to the exact one before training ends; convergence-aware pruning removes converged, nearly transparent Gaussians; and a shuffle-efficient backward pass reduces the data exchanged between GPU threads. For the loss, a fused loss computes the loss and its image gradient in the forward pass without a loss map, removing most of its cost. SprintGS trains 2.15x faster than FastGS at comparable quality, and 1.81x faster in its high-quality setting. It also accelerates other fast training methods and dynamic, sparse-view, and surface reconstruction.

Introduction sec:intro Novel view synthesis (NVS), which reconstructs a scene from a set of photographs and renders it from unseen viewpoints, is a long-standing problem in computer vision and graphics. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ Vanilla3DGS has become a popular approach to this task: it represents a scene by anisotropic 3D Gaussians and rasterizes them into photorealistic images at interactive frame rates. However, 3DGS requires a per-scene optimization before any image can be rendered. Although recent methods have substantially shortened this optimization, it is still far from instantaneous. Prior work speeds up this optimization in two ways. The first optimizes the implementation of training, from GPU kernels to framework overhead, and trains a model with as many Gaussians as 3DGS in a short time~ FasterGS,gsplat,ImprovedGS+,DISTWAR . The second reduces the number of Gaussians by revising how they are added (densification) and removed (pruning)~ Taming3DGS,SpeedySplat,DashGaussian,FastGS . FastGS~ FastGS , for example, densifies and prunes Gaussians according to their contribution to multi-view reconstruction quality, and trains a scene with far fewer Gaussians than 3DGS. Such a compact model also reduces storage, GPU memory, and rendering time, which matters on limited hardware and for transmitting scenes. Even so, a user who wants to check a captured scene on the spot must still wait minutes for the trained model, although rendering runs in real time. This paper aims to further shorten this wait for compact models while keeping their quality. To find where the training time of a compact model goes, we profile the training of 3DGS~ Vanilla3DGS and FastGS~ FastGS ~( ). We find that rasterization is still the largest cost of a compact model, and that the share of the loss computation grows as the model becomes compact. Our strategy is therefore to keep the model compact and reduce the costs of both rasterization and the loss. Rasterization takes 64 of the training time of FastGS. Although FastGS reduces the number of Gaussians, redundant work remains in three places: each Gaussian is rasterized over many tiles where it contributes almost nothing to the image; some Gaussians have converged and become nearly transparent but stay in the model; and the backward pass moves more per-pixel data between GPU threads than the gradients require. In contrast, the loss is computed per pixel, so its cost does not shrink with the number of Gaussians. While the share of the optimizer and densification falls from 25 to 10 , the loss takes a similar time in both methods, and its share grows from 4 to 23 . We thus present SprintGS, a training framework built on FastGS. Our contributions are as follows: Removing redundancy in rasterization. We propose three components, one for each of the three places above. Scheduled tile culling limits each Gaussian to the tiles where it matters, using a coarse footprint that is annealed to the exact one before training ends. Convergence-aware pruning removes converged, nearly transparent Gaussians early and reallocates part of the freed budget to poorly reconstructed regions. A shuffle-efficient backward pass reduces the data exchanged between GPU threads. Reducing the loss cost. We identify the loss computation as a major cost of fast training and remove most of it with a fused loss, which computes the loss and its image gradient in the forward pass without a loss map. Speed-up at comparable quality. SprintGS-Base trains faster than FastGS-Base~ FastGS at comparable quality ( ; with optimizations from Faster-GS~ FasterGS ) and also accelerates other fast training methods and tasks. Related Work sec:related-work Since 3DGS~ Vanilla3DGS takes tens of minutes to train a scene, many methods have been proposed to shorten its training. We review them below, grouped by the source of the speed-up. Reducing the Number of Gaussians A key bottleneck of 3DGS training is the excessive number of Gaussians. Many methods~ ImprovedGS,3DGS-MCMC,SteepGS,mini-splating,mini-splating2,SpeedySplat,SAD-GS,Taming3DGS,Color-cued-densification,FastGS,TurboGS_CVPR2026,GroupTraining_ICCV2025,POP_ECCV2026 refine densification and pruning to limit the number of Gaussians. Among them, FastGS~ FastGS is most related to ours: it densifies Gaussians that consistently cover high-error regions across views and prunes those with little multi-view contribution. Reducing the Work in Rasterization --tile pairs. Tile-based rasterization assigns each Gaussian to every tile its 2D footprint may overlap, and both the forward and backward passes process the resulting Gaussian--tile pairs. 3DGS~ Vanilla3DGS bounds each footprint by a square that overestimates it, producing many redundant pairs. To accelerate rendering, several renderers remove such pairs with tighter Gaussian--tile tests~ StopThePop,FlashGS . Others cull Gaussians hierarchically~ HiGS or per warp~ LocalGS . Since every training iteration runs the rasterizer in both passes, fewer pairs also shorten training. Speedy-Splat~ SpeedySplat assigns each Gaussian exactly to the tiles its footprint ellipse intersects, and other methods use tighter footprints during optimization~ ADRGaussian,QuadBox,FastGS,gsplat or shrink the Gaussians so that fewer of them overlap each pixel~ ShorterSplatting . . EAGLES~ EAGLES and DashGaussian~ DashGaussian render at reduced resolution early in training, and TurboGS~ TurboGS_ICML2026 optimizes on sparse pixels sampled by reconstruction error. parts. Much of the computation is spent on parts that have already converged. SkipGS~ SkipGS skips the backward pass of views whose loss has stabilized, and GSta~ GSta freezes Gaussians with small gradients. pass. The original implementation~ Vanilla3DGS parallelizes the backward pass over pixels, so many threads add gradients to the same Gaussian with contended atomics, which DISTWAR~ DISTWAR mitigates with warp-level reduction; Balanced 3DGS~ Balanced3DGS balances the rasterization workload during training. Taming-3DGS~ Taming3DGS instead parallelizes over Gaussians: each thread of a warp handles one Gaussian, and per-pixel states pass from thread to thread in depth order. This splat-parallel backward pass is the backbone of recent fast trainers~ FastGS,DashGaussian,FasterGS . Reducing the Cost outside the Rasterizer Each iteration also computes the loss, updates the parameters, and synchronizes the CPU with the GPU. Several methods reduce these costs at the implementation level: Taming-3DGS~ Taming3DGS computes SSIM with a fused kernel, Faster-GS~ FasterGS fuses the activations and the optimizer steps among many other optimizations, and ImprovedGS+~ ImprovedGS+ reduces host--device synchronization. Other work distributes training over multiple GPUs~ Grendel_ICLR2025 . Accelerating Convergence and Beyond Dense initializations from foundation models or correspondences~ EDGS,FFInit,QuickSplat_ICCV and second-order optimizers~ 3DGS-LM,3DGSSquared,3DGS2-TR reduce the number of iterations, the latter at a higher cost per iteration. Feed-forward networks~ pixelSplat,MVSplat_ECCV2024,Anysplat,ReSplat_ECCV2026 avoid per-scene optimization through large-scale pretraining; we instead accelerate per-scene optimization, which remains widely used for high-fidelity reconstruction. title: DemoFoundry: Toward Scalable Photorealistic Robot Data with Coding Agents and Generative Rendering
summary: Scaling robot learning requires demonstrations that combine realistic visual observations with reliable action supervision. Simulation-based synthesis faces a substantial visual gap relative to real environments, while video-only generation struggles to maintain physically consistent interactions and provide aligned action labels. We present DemoFoundry, an automated framework that couples coding agents with generative rendering to synthesize photorealistic and physically grounded robot demonstrations. Coding agents both construct aligned real--proxy video pairs from existing robot episodes to train a video renderer and write executable interaction programs to generate new demonstrations. Given a scene reference and task instruction, an agent reconstructs task-relevant geometry and writes a control program without requiring target-task human demonstrations. Program execution in a physics simulator produces proxy videos with aligned robot states and actions. The video renderer translates these proxy videos into scene-consistent, photorealistic observations, reducing the need for detailed appearance modeling in each scene. Automated task-execution checks select successful trajectories for rendering and policy learning. Experiments show improved visual quality and action--video consistency. Policies trained on the generated demonstrations outperform raw-simulation training and approach the performance of training on an equal number of real demonstrations.

Simulation-based synthesis faces a substantial visual gap relative to real environments, while video-only generation struggles to maintain physically consistent interactions and provide aligned action labels. We present DemoFoundry, an automated framework that couples coding agents with generative rendering to synthesize photorealistic and physically grounded robot demonstrations. Given a scene reference and task instruction, an agent reconstructs task-relevant geometry and writes a control program without requiring target-task human demonstrations.
