Introduction sec:intro Generalizable robot policies require large-scale training data covering diverse interactions between robots and their environments. Such data should pair realistic visual observations with reliable action supervision across a broad range of objects, scenes, and tasks. Human teleoperation provides these demonstrations but requires sustained operator effort to execute tasks and reset the environment between trials. Expanding interaction coverage therefore calls for scalable alternatives to manual collection. Simulation provides a scalable source of robot interactions~ gensim,robogen,gensim2,robotwin . However, simulated observations still exhibit a substantial visual gap relative to real environments in object appearance, materials, lighting, and background detail. Domain randomization improves robustness to these differences~ domainrand,robotwin , although matching a particular deployment environment remains challenging. Generative video models can synthesize realistic observations across diverse scenes, but their outputs often exhibit inconsistent contact, object motion, and task execution~ rbench . Video-only generation also lacks an executable control trace that directly supplies robot actions. Recovering action supervision through inverse dynamics introduces an additional estimation problem~ dreamgen . These complementary strengths motivate separating interaction generation from appearance synthesis~ cwm . Executable programs provide a controllable source of behavior, and video rendering supplies scene appearance. Scaling this approach requires efficient construction of rendering supervision and task programs across scenes. Advances in program-based control and embodied reasoning~ cap,gptpolicy make coding agents a practical means of coordinating the reconstruction, alignment, and control tools involved in this process. We introduce , an automated data engine combining coding agents and generative rendering, as illustrated in Fig.~ fig:overview . First, a pair-construction agent reconstructs and aligns existing real robot episodes with proxy videos, forming a paired dataset for training a video renderer. The renderer learns to recover appearance from a scene reference while following robot and object motion. Second, for a novel scene, an agent reconstructs task-relevant geometry and develops a program to execute the instructed task. Executing this program under different object layouts in simulation produces proxy videos with aligned robot states and actions. The renderer then converts these proxy videos into photorealistic observations using the corresponding scene references. enables zero-shot data generation for novel robot embodiments and scenes from reference images and robot/camera configurations, without target-scene demonstrations or human operator involvement during generation. We evaluate it on a real-world platform across three manipulation tasks using Diffusion Policy and ~ diffusionpolicy,pi05 . Our renderers improve visual quality over baselines while maintaining strong action--video consistency. Policies trained on our generated data outperform raw-simulation training and approach the performance of training on an equal number of real demonstrations. Policy performance improves with more synthetic training data, and estimated generation costs fall below human teleoperation at scale. Table~ tab:related_comparison places these components within existing robot data-generation pipelines. We make three contributions. An automated data engine that couples coding-agent programs with appearance rendering to synthesize photorealistic, action-labeled robot demonstrations across diverse scenes and tasks without manual intervention during production. An agent-constructed dataset of 1,884 aligned real--proxy video pairs from four public robot datasets, used to adapt two video-generation models for rendering newly programmed interactions. We plan to release the paired dataset upon publication. Real-robot experiments demonstrating improved policy learning over raw simulation and performance comparable to real-demonstration training, complemented by visual-quality comparisons, paired-training ablation, and data-scaling experiments. Related Work sec:related Programmatic Simulation and Data Engines Programmatic simulation scales robot demonstrations through automatic task specification and behavior generation. Language-model-based systems synthesize executable policies, task programs, and learning objectives~ cap,gensim,robogen,gensim2 . RoboTwin~2.0 combines feedback-driven expert-code generation with domain randomization for bimanual manipulation~ robotwin , while Genie Sim~3.0 provides high-fidelity simulation infrastructure and diverse assets~ geniesim . extends this paradigm by coupling agent-generated behavior with a video renderer trained on aligned real--proxy observations. Robot Data Synthesis from Real Observations Real observations support data generation through trajectory reuse and scene reconstruction. Demonstration-amplification methods transform recorded motion into new object configurations~ mimicgen,dexmimicgen,demogen , while replay and reconstructed-asset rendering expand visual and embodiment coverage~ rebot,real2render2real . Digital-twin methods recover scene appearance and geometry for policy learning~ rialto,splatsim,re3sim , and IGen generates visuomotor trajectories from open-world images~ igen . Agentic Real2Sim automates episode reconstruction and physical replay, producing real--simulation correspondences~ agenticreal2sim . uses such correspondences across multiple robot datasets to train a reusable video renderer, then generates new-task trajectories from scene references and task programs. Generative Rendering for Robot Learning Generative models provide photorealistic observations for robot learning. DreamGen and EVA synthesize behavior videos and recover action supervision through inverse dynamics~ dreamgen,eva . Trajectory-conditioned approaches instead guide appearance synthesis with robot motion, edited geometry, or simulator controls~ anchordream,robodream,real2edit2real,craft . RoboTransfer uses multi-view geometric conditions~ robotransfer , and RoboRender trains on real-derived depth and robot-mask controls paired with RGB videos~ roborender . Code World Model and SolarRenderer provide related program-driven and structural-video rendering mechanisms~ cwm,solarrenderer . Hybrid robot data engines combine executable programs with video rendering. ComSim~ comsim constructs real--simulation pairs by replaying recorded actions, while PyRUA-DataFarm~ datafarm builds its target scene from one calibration episode. connects agent-built, multi-source real--proxy pairs to renderer adaptation and new-scene demonstration generation. DemoFoundry sec:method Overview and Formulation As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:method , DemoFoundry first constructs aligned real--proxy video pairs to train a video renderer, as detailed in Sec.~ sec:pairs . To generate demonstrations in a new scene, a coding agent takes a reference image , a robot specification defining the robot and gripper models, camera calibration specifying intrinsics and extrinsics, and a task instruction to build a simulated scene and task program . Executing in yields where is the proxy video, the aligned robot state sequence, and the executed actions. The trained video renderer synthesizes photorealistic observations conditioned on the proxy and reference image, The rendered video retains the simulator's state and action labels, forming demonstrations for the policy-training dataset . Video Renderer Training sec:pairs Agent-driven reconstruction. We construct real--proxy video pairs from DROID~ droid , AgiBot World~ agibot , RoboMIND~ robomind , and RH20T~ rh20t to supervise video renderer training. For each source episode, a GPT-6 Astra agent~ gpt6astra reconstructs the task-relevant scene from RGB observations, available depth, camera calibration, and robot/gripper records. It obtains object masks with SAM~3.1~ sam3 and fits the tabletop as the support surface. Simple objects are represented by parameterized shapes and converted into meshes through agent-written Blender Python scripts~ scenecraft,ll3m . Complex assets are reconstructed from RGB images and masks using SAM 3D Objects~ sam3dobjects . Available depth initializes scale and placement, which the agent refines using multi-view silhouettes, object orientation, and support constraints. The resulting visual and collision geometry preserves task-relevant openings and contact surfaces for physical replay. Physical execution and refinement. The reconstructed assets and corresponding robot/gripper models are assembled in a physics engine, such as MuJoCo~ mujoco or DexSim~ embodichain . The agent replays the recorded actions through the robot controller, with contact dynamics determining object motion. Rendering the simulated trajectories at the recorded camera poses and timestamps yields candidate proxy videos. To align each proxy with its real-video counterpart, we compare object masks at sampled keyframes and require silhouette IoU of at least 0.80 for every visible object in every view. Failed comparisons guide adjustments to object geometry, scale, or initial placement, followed by another replay with calibration fixed. We allow up to three refinement rounds after the initial replay and discard pairs that still fail. Accepted pairs retain camera calibration, scene assets, timestamps, and robot state/action traces. Appendix A describes the agent implementation and pair-construction evaluation. This procedure produces 1,884 aligned real--proxy video pairs totaling 1,522.03 minutes summed across camera views, with the dataset breakdown shown in Fig.~ fig:dataset_composition . We plan to release the dataset upon publication to support training video models for sim-to-real transfer and photorealistic robot-video rendering. The paired simulations also provide object poses and scene states, offering potential supervision for 3D VLA models~ 3dvla and 3D world models such as PointWorld~ pointworld and UNITAS~ unitas . title: DriftWAM: Faster World-Action Models via Action-Aware Video Drifting
summary: World-action models (WAMs) unify future video prediction and action generation for robotic control, but their reliance on iterative denoising incurs substantial inference costs. Distilling these models into few-step generators offers a promising route to efficient deployment, yet maintaining task performance under aggressive step reduction remains challenging. Existing methods rely on point-wise trajectory consistency distillation, which pursues high visual fidelity while leaving downstream action information unexploited in optimizing video generation, and also lacks explicit distribution-level alignment. To address this, we propose DriftWAM, a few-step WAM distillation framework that incorporates the actions induced by predicted videos into video learning. Specifically, DriftWAM integrates action-aware video drifting, which performs video distribution matching through a joint visual--action similarity kernel to steer sample evolution under the guidance of these induced actions, with action-guided video regularization, which leverages the compatible teacher--student matches identified by the joint kernel to backpropagate action-level gradients directly into the video generator. Evaluations on the RoboTwin 2.0 and LIBERO benchmarks, as well as in real-world robotic manipulation tasks, show that DriftWAM consistently outperforms prior consistency distillation methods across few-step settings at the same inference speed.

Introduction sec:intro World-action models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for embodied intelligence, unifying future video prediction and robot action generation within a generative framework~ shen2025videovla,bi2026motus,li2026causal,kim2026cosmospolicy,ye2026world . By leveraging rich spatiotemporal priors from large-scale video pretraining~ yang2025cogvideox,wan2025wan,nvidia2025cosmospredict2 , WAMs predict how the environment will evolve given current observations and task instructions, and generate the corresponding robot actions~ du2023learning,feng2026vidar,pai2025mimicvideo,li2026causal . This visual foresight grounds decision-making in physical dynamics, enabling strong generalization across complex robotic manipulation tasks. Despite their effectiveness, WAMs incur substantial inference latency because future video synthesis and action prediction often rely on iterative diffusion or flow-matching sampling~ ho2020ddpm,lipman2023flowmatching,chi2023diffusionpolicy . As a result, generating each control decision typically requires multiple sequential denoising steps to produce high-dimensional video latents and the corresponding action sequence. This computational burden stands in sharp conflict with the real-time reactivity required for closed-loop robotic deployment. Few-step distillation~ song2023consistency,prasad2024consistencypolicy,yin2024dmd,yin2024dmd2,zhang2026teacherfeature,akbari2026flashwam therefore offers a natural optimization strategy, aiming to compress multi-step denoising into one or a few steps to reduce inference latency while preserving the capabilities of the full multi-step model. Existing efforts toward few-step WAM distillation typically adapt consistency distillation~ song2023consistency,luo2023lcm,wang2023videolcm from visual synthesis to each modality branch. For example, Flash-WAM~ akbari2026flashwam shows that high-dimensional, redundant video latents and low-dimensional, precision-critical actions operate under different noise regimes, so applying the same visual consistency objective to both branches can lead to severe performance degradation. It therefore adopts an action consistency function whose gradient-scaling coefficient varies linearly with the noise level, while retaining the standard latent consistency model (LCM)~ luo2023lcm consistency function for the video branch. Despite this progress, such modality-aware consistency distillation adaptations only tailor separate objectives to each data modality, while their video distillation does not explicitly consider how the generated videos affect downstream actions. This omission matters, as video and action exhibit an inherent functional asymmetry in WAMs. In other words, we judge a WAM by whether its actions accomplish the task, while its predicted videos serve as intermediate representations that guide the generation of those actions. Given this video--action functional asymmetry, we argue that video learning in WAMs should not focus solely on visual fidelity. We further find that assessing the similarity between two videos from the perspective of visual appearance versus from the perspective of their impact on the actions leads to considerable disagreements (Fig.~ fig:teaser ; see Appendix~ sec:app_disagreement ). Therefore, we believe that beyond pursuing visual fidelity, video learning in WAMs should also leverage the actions induced by predicted videos. However, incorporating these actions should not compromise the original capability of generating visually faithful videos. Thus, for few-step WAM distillation, we need a suitable approach that preserves the ability to pursue visual fidelity as much as possible, while offering a low-cost and effective interface for incorporating action information. To this end, we draw inspiration from the drifting paradigm~ deng2026drifting , which shifts iterative distributional refinement from inference to training. Drifting fulfills our needs for two reasons: 1) it governs sample attraction and repulsion directly through pairwise similarity kernels, naturally accommodating action-level signals; 2) it enables one-step inference and has shown strong promise in diffusion distillation~ zhang2026teacherfeature and world modeling~ lu2026driftworld for high-fidelity image and video generation. Moreover, we find that, as a distribution matching method, drifting brings the added benefit of achieving better alignment between the student's and teacher's conditional video distributions (see Sec.~ sec:mmd_analysis ). Building on this foundation, we propose DriftWAM, a few-step WAM distillation framework that unites action-aware video drifting and action-guided video regularization. Specifically, action-aware video drifting combines visual feature distances with the discrepancies between the actions induced by predicted videos into a joint similarity kernel, which reshapes sample evolution in feature space. Furthermore, to complement this kernel-weighted feature evolution with explicit supervision on induced-action discrepancies, we reuse the compatible teacher--student pairs selected by the joint kernel to construct an action-guided video regularizer, through which action-level gradients are backpropagated directly into the video generator. In summary, our main contributions are as follows: Based on the inherent video--action functional asymmetry in WAMs and our finding of the misalignment between visual and induced-action similarities among candidate videos, we argue that few-step video distillation should account for the downstream actions induced by predicted videos alongside visual fidelity. We develop DriftWAM, in which action-aware video drifting injects induced-action similarity into the drifting kernel to guide video distribution matching, while action-guided video regularization exploits the resulting compatible teacher--student pairs to directly supervise the video generator via action-level gradients. Extensive evaluations on the RoboTwin 2.0~ chen2026robotwin and LIBERO~ liu2023libero benchmarks, as well as in real-world robotic manipulation tasks, demonstrate that DriftWAM maintains strong control performance even when inference is compressed into one or a few denoising steps, delivering higher task success rates than state-of-the-art consistency distillation under identical inference budgets. Related work sec:related_work World-action models sec:related_wam Leveraging spatiotemporal priors from pretrained video generators~ wan2025wan,du2023learning,wu2024gr1 , world-action models (WAMs) unify future visual prediction and action generation via diffusion or flow matching~ shen2025videovla,bi2026motus,li2026causal . Existing WAMs that synthesize explicit visual futures either denoise video and action tokens jointly~ guo2024pad,bi2026motus,ye2026world or follow a cascade formulation that conditions action generation on predicted video latents~ li2026causal,pai2025mimicvideo . To mitigate the latency of multi-step sampling~ ye2026world,yuan2026fastwam , prior works bypass test-time video generation~ yuan2026fastwam,ye2026gigaworldpolicy , predict futures in compact latent spaces~ chen2026lawam , adopt lightweight backbones with sparse tokens~ li2026efficientwam , or cache computation across inference chunks~ zhao2026c3ache . Orthogonal to architectural or test-time modifications, we accelerate cascade WAMs while preserving explicit video-to-action inference through few-step distillation. Few-step distillation sec:related_distillation Few-step distillation for diffusion and flow-matching models broadly follows two paradigms: trajectory-following methods such as consistency distillation~ song2023consistency,luo2023lcm,wang2023videolcm , which enforce point-wise agreement along denoising trajectories, and distribution-matching methods, which align output distributions via auxiliary score critics~ yin2024dmd,yin2024dmd2 or critic-free drifting~ deng2026drifting,zhang2026teacherfeature . Extending step distillation to WAMs, Flash-WAM~ akbari2026flashwam introduces modality-specific consistency functions to account for the distinct noise regimes of video and action branches. Concurrent works also explore adaptive step budgets~ wang2026anystepwam , interaction-centric visual guidance~ lyu2026dido , or deterministic direct prediction (DirectWAM~ zheng2026directwam ). While DirectWAM matches induced actions to demonstrated actions through a separately trained one-step action model, DriftWAM directly reuses the frozen teacher for action-aware video distribution matching and compatible teacher video selection. title: RoboEvo$^2$: Recursive Robot Self-Improvement via Harness-Policy Co-Evolution
summary: Robots should adapt to unfamiliar environments and acquire new skills through interaction, then execute those skills efficiently with practice. Vision-language-action policies provide efficient control, but often need additional human demonstrations to handle unfamiliar settings; reasoning agents can discover solutions using broad prior knowledge and robot-control APIs, but repeated deliberation and repair are costly. Inspired by human learning through reasoning and practice, we propose RoboEvo$^2$, a framework for recursive harness-policy co-evolution. In Policy-to-Harness (P2H) evolution, policy failures guide a coding agent to search complementary Code, Code+ICL, and Code+Policy routes, consolidating verified solutions into reusable skills, routing strategies, and experience memory. In Harness-to-Policy (H2P) evolution, verified trajectories provide supervised training, while Counterfactual Preference Distillation (CPD) teaches the policy to favor successful corrections over failures from the same starting state. The improved policy provides stronger motor skills for subsequent search, while its remaining failures redirect harness evolution, closing the reciprocal loop. Through recursive co-evolution without additional human demonstrations, RoboEvo$^2$ improves standalone success from 11.0% to 84.1% and hybrid success from 30.4% to 90.5% on LIBERO-PRO, with similar gains and reduced agentic costs on RoboTwin C2R. Further experiments demonstrate autonomous task acquisition, cross-embodiment harness transfer, and 95.0% hybrid success on the Unitree G1-D. Our models and code will be publicly released.

Human learning motivates this progression from deliberate problem solving to fluent execution, while retaining the flexibility to tackle new situations. Current robot systems offer complementary strengths toward this goal. Vision-language-action models (VLAs)~ kim2024openvla,black2025pi0,intelligence2025pi05,zheng2025xvla and world action models (WAMs)~ yuan2026fastwam,guo2026xwam,huang2026longwam enable efficient visuomotor control, but remain vulnerable to task and scene shifts~ zhou2025liberopro,ross2011dagger . Adapting them through imitation learning often requires collecting many additional human demonstrations, making continual skill acquisition costly. Foundation-model agents can draw on broad prior knowledge, reason about unfamiliar situations, and invoke robot-control APIs to discover and refine solutions~ liang2023code,fu2026capx,zhang2026harness,zhang2026rats . However, repeated reasoning, tool use, and repair introduce latency and API costs that limit reliance on agentic execution for routine behavior. Realizing this progression requires a reciprocal learning loop between an agent's harness---its executable skills, memory, and orchestration---and its low-level policy. Harness-centered recursive self-improvement methods refine programs and accumulate experience through feedback~ ding2026zetta,li2026embodiedevo,song2026embodiedrsi,wang2026rpg , but keeping the motor policy fixed does not transfer newly acquired skills into the learned controller. Policy-centered methods use foundation models to guide autonomous data collection and improve learned controllers~ ha2023scaling,zhou2024soar,liu2026mobiagent , but do not jointly adapt the harness to the controller's changing abilities. Co-evolution must therefore connect learning efficient policy behaviors from harness discoveries with adapting the harness to the improving policy. This reciprocity is essential because policy improvement changes both the motor skills available to the agent and the failures that still require exploration and repair. We introduce RoboEvo , a framework for recursive harness--policy co-evolution that uses current-policy failures to drive both updates ( ). In Policy-to-Harness (P2H) evolution, a coding agent diagnoses failures, discovers verified corrections, and consolidates them into reusable skills, routing strategies, and persistent memory. In Harness-to-Policy (H2P) evolution, successful trajectories and matched failure--correction pairs teach the policy to reproduce effective corrections and disfavor failed alternatives. The updated policy then supplies stronger motor skills for subsequent agentic search, while its remaining failures redirect harness refinement. Concurrent studies also investigate harness--policy coupling~ coharness2026,harnessforge2026,wei2026scaleselection,wang2026adarsi . RoboEvo connects failure-guided, multi-route solution discovery with explicit learning from matched failures and corrections, progressively reducing repeated agentic intervention as acquired skills are internalized into the policy. First, to discover complementary capabilities, we develop a failure-conditioned, multi-route P2H repair engine. For each policy failure, it searches three solution routes in parallel: Code refines control programs, Code+ICL incorporates demonstration guidance, and Code+Policy composes programs with learned motor skills. Execution feedback drives iterative repair, and the successful candidate with the lowest normalized motion jerk is selected under matched conditions. This design combines complementary control capabilities to generate verified, smooth corrections targeted at current policy weaknesses. Second, to internalize corrective capabilities, we introduce Counterfactual Preference Distillation (CPD). CPD pairs failed and corrected continuations from the same starting state and optimizes a margin between their action-prediction losses relative to a frozen reference policy. Asymmetric proximity penalties discourage degradation of corrective behaviors and excessive suppression of failed alternatives. Combined with supervised learning on verified trajectories, CPD teaches both which corrections to reproduce and which failed alternatives to disfavor. Failure-aware sampling and continual-learning regularization support targeted acquisition and capability retention. Third, to sustain iterative capability reuse, we develop a harness update mechanism coupled with policy reuse across rounds. Compatible repairs update executable skills and routing logic, while persistent memory retains failure contexts, attempted solutions, and validated guidance. The updated policy then drives subsequent rollouts and participates in Code+Policy search, changing both the failures requiring exploration and the motor primitives available for repair. This closes the reciprocal loop: accumulated harness knowledge supports correction discovery, while internalized policy capabilities directly support subsequent search. Experiments demonstrate recursive adaptation to distribution shifts without additional human demonstrations. Across eight rounds on LIBERO-PRO~ zhou2025liberopro and five rounds on RoboTwin C2R~ chen2025robotwin2 , standalone success improves from 11.0 to 84.1 and 46.0 to 77.5 , respectively, with hybrid success reaching 90.5 and 87.4 alongside reduced agentic API expenditure. On RoboTwin C2R, our method with 7.5K trajectories matches conventional training with 27.5K trajectories. Ablations validate reciprocal co-evolution, complementary solution routes in P2H, and counterfactual preference distillation in H2P. We further demonstrate autonomous task acquisition on MolmoSpaces~ ai2molmospaces2026 and cross-embodiment harness transfer. On the Unitree G1-D, a simulation-evolved harness enables the collection of 120 demonstrations, yielding 85.0 standalone success compared with 80.0 using 200 human demonstrations, while fixed-harness hybrid execution reaches 95.0 . Related Work Continual Robot Learning. A continually learning policy must retain earlier skills and obtain supervision for new ones. For retention, EWC regularizes weights~ kirkpatrick2017ewc , ER replays data~ rolnick2019er , and PackNet isolates parameters~ mallya2018packnet . In manipulation, LOTUS builds skill libraries~ wan2024lotus and TAIL uses task-specific adapters~ liu2024tail . On pretrained VLAs, experience replay mitigates forgetting~ liu2026vlaforgetting,zhu2026realworldcl ; PHASER refines it by prioritizing phases most at risk of forgetting~ chen2026phaser , while CRL-VLA limits advantage magnitudes on prior tasks during continual RL~ zeng2026crlvla . For new supervision, HG-DAgger and RECAP draw on human interventions during policy rollouts~ kelly2019hgdagger,intelligence2025recap , APO and FlowPRO turn such interventions into preference signals~ xia2025apo,wu2026flowpro , and SOAR uses autonomous VLM-guided practice~ zhou2024soar . RoboEvo learns from verified harness repairs of policy failures rather than operator corrections, and employs failure-aware task sampling to retain skills and improve low-success tasks. Agentic Self-Improvement. Agentic systems such as Code as Policies~ liang2023code , Harness VLA~ zhang2026harness , RATs~ zhang2026rats , and ASPIRE~ aspire2026 solve tasks through programs, skills, and memory without model fine-tuning. Among recursive self-improvement (RSI) frameworks, Zetta, EmbodiedEvo, EmbodiedRSI, and RPG evolve only the harness~ ding2026zetta,li2026embodiedevo,song2026embodiedrsi,wang2026rpg , whereas ENPIRE and EmbodiRSI focus on policy improvement~ xiao2026enpire,lang2026embodirsi . Co-Harness and Self-HPO alternate harness and model updates for LLM agents~ coharness2026,wei2026selfhpo . AdaRSI~ wang2026adarsi refines its harness and fine-tunes only sub-steps that still fail when retried from saved states. However, these methods train the policy only to imitate successful executions. In contrast, RoboEvo also learns from failures: it pairs a failed continuation with a verified repair from the same state and trains the policy to prefer the repair. Repairs are sought in parallel along code-only, demonstration-guided, and policy-calling routes. The current policy exposes capability gaps through execution failures, the harness discovers effective solutions, and the policy subsequently internalizes these corrections. As illustrated in , RoboEvo jointly evolves an agentic harness and a neural policy at evolution round . The harness consists of an executable skill library , persistent experience memory , and a routing mechanism for skill invocation and code--policy coordination. We initialize with robot APIs and parameterized code-based skills from CaP-X~ fu2026capx and RATs~ zhang2026rats . The initial policy is obtained by fine-tuning a pretrained VLA or WAM on robot demonstrations . Each evolution round consists of four stages: (1) Policy Rollouts. The current policy serves as the primary executor, generating task rollouts . Task-level verification partitions them into successful trajectories and failed trajectories . The failures identify where additional capabilities are needed. (2) Policy-to-Harness Evolution (P2H). For each failed rollout, a VLM-based coding agent (GPT-6 Astra) diagnoses the failure and searches for solutions through three complementary routes: Code, Code+ICL, and Code+Policy. title: Dynamic Forcing: Learning Action-Grounded Sparse Dynamic Representations with Dense Future Guidance for World Action Models
summary: World action models (WAMs) support robot control through visual prediction, but dense future modeling repeatedly encodes static context already available in the current observation, while action-relevant changes are often spatially sparse. We study sparse dynamic representation learning, retaining the current observation as a contextual anchor and using a small set of compact dynamic tokens to represent anticipated changes. We develop CompactWAM, a sparse-dense joint predictive framework that enables sparse representation learning within a video-supervised shared backbone, without requiring a reconstruction objective for the sparse pathway. Since a limited token budget alone does not specify which information to retain, we introduce Dynamic Forcing, which pairs direct action supervision with privileged dense future guidance to promote action relevance and dynamic fidelity. While action prediction gradients directly drive compact tokens to capture control-relevant cues, dense future guidance further shapes them via action functional guidance that matches sparse and dense contributions to the action expert, and dynamics-aware distribution matching, which aligns temporal relational changes relative to a static reference. At inference, a single visual forward pass encodes current observations and compact dynamic tokens for action generation, eliminating dense future modeling. CompactWAM achieves 98.4\% success on LIBERO and 77.9\% on LIBERO-Plus, retaining respective success rates of 98.3\% and 76.6\% with only 9.2\% of the dense future token budget. Evaluations on RoboTwin~2.0 and real-world manipulation further demonstrate the effectiveness of the learned sparse predictive representations.

Introduction sec:intro Embodied intelligence requires models to understand their surroundings and anticipate the consequences of interaction. Vision-language-action (VLA) models advance this goal by transferring pretrained visual and linguistic knowledge to robot control, mapping observations and instructions to actions~ rt2,openvla,pi0 . World action models (WAMs) incorporate visual dynamics into this process through generated visual plans and predictive features ~ unipi,vpp , as well as joint video-action modeling~ uwm,uva . These approaches provide policies with information about anticipated physical outcomes. However, modeling dense visual futures at deployment requires processing large sets of spatiotemporal tokens, introducing substantial inference overhead~ fastwam . Recent work explores how to retain the benefits of predictive modeling at lower inference cost. Fast-WAM~ fastwam retains video co-training but removes test-time future prediction to improve inference efficiency. Subsequent evaluations show that removing future conditioning can weaken robustness under distribution shifts~ fasterwam . This raises a focused question: what should a WAM imagine beyond the current observation to support robot control without dense future prediction? To investigate this, we revisit the content of dense future representations and how the action expert attends to them, as illustrated in Fig.~1(a). Dense futures repeatedly represent persistent appearance and scene context already available in the current observation, while the visualized action attention concentrates on localized regions associated with object motion and interaction. These observations motivate a complementary allocation of visual information: retain the current observation as a contextual anchor and devote sparse predictive representations to anticipated changes relevant to action generation. We therefore investigate sparse dynamic representation learning for WAMs: learning a limited set of compact dynamic tokens to represent anticipated changes while retaining the current observation as a contextual anchor. We formulate two complementary learning goals. requires these compact representations to capture temporal relational changes associated with future evolution. requires them to provide useful predictive context for action generation. A limited token budget alone, however, does not specify which information should be retained. The central challenge is thus to guide sparse representations to capture anticipated dynamics that support action generation. To this end, we develop CompactWAM, a sparse-dense joint predictive framework that enables sparse dynamic representation learning within a shared visual backbone. The dense pathway receives video and action supervision, providing a common predictive learning foundation, while the sparse pathway learns compact predictive representations without a video reconstruction objective of its own. Within this framework, we introduce Dynamic Forcing, a learning strategy that shapes sparse predictive representations through two complementary sources of supervision: direct action signals and dense future modeling. These sources jointly guide sparse representation learning toward action relevance and dynamic fidelity under a limited dynamic-token budget. First, direct action supervision drives sparse representations to provide useful context for action generation. Action prediction gradients propagate through the sparse action expert into the sparse representation pathway, encouraging compact dynamic tokens to capture control-relevant information within the shared, video-supervised backbone. While establishing an action-driven baseline, action supervision alone does not explicitly specify which spatiotemporal structure to retain. Second, dense future supervision provides privileged predictive knowledge to further regularize the sparse representations. As shown in Fig.~1(b), we transfer this knowledge through two complementary objectives. Action functional guidance matches the isolated contributions of sparse dynamic and dense future representations in the attention readout space of the action expert, encouraging sparse context to retain the influence of future evolution on action generation. Dynamics-aware distribution matching aligns distributions of spatiotemporal relational changes between sparse and dense representations, using a static relational reference to emphasize temporal evolution. Together with action supervision, these objectives guide sparse tokens to capture control-relevant dynamics. In CompactWAM, we initialize compact dynamic tokens from pooled regions of the current observation and assign sparse spatiotemporal RoPE using region centroids and future-time coordinates, constructing a compact spatiotemporal representation space. During training, compact tokens learn through direct action supervision and guidance from the jointly trained dense pathway. At inference, only the current observation anchor and compact dynamic tokens are encoded in a single visual forward pass to provide predictive context for action generation. CompactWAM achieves success rates of 98.4 on LIBERO and 77.9 on LIBERO-Plus. Reducing the predictive context to just 9.2 of the dense future token budget preserves strong performance, reaching 98.3 and 76.6 , respectively. These results support compact dynamic representations as effective predictive context for robust control. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We study sparse dynamic representation learning for WAMs by developing CompactWAM, enabling joint sparse-dense training and compact predictive conditioning alongside current observations at inference. We introduce Dynamic Forcing, combining direct action supervision with dense future knowledge transferred through action functional guidance and dynamics-aware distribution matching. Experiments on LIBERO~ libero , LIBERO-Plus~ libero_plus , RoboTwin~2.0~ robotwin2 , and real-world manipulation demonstrate strong control performance and OOD robustness without dense future generation, validating sparse dynamic representations for robot control. Their development is supported by increasingly diverse robot datasets~ oxe,droid,agibot_world and expressive generative action models~ pi0,rdt,gr00t . Recent studies improve open-world generalization and cross-embodiment transfer through heterogeneous training and adaptable policy representations~ pi05,xvla,univla . Complementary efforts explore structured action representations and unified reasoning--action generation~ abotm0,fast_tokenizer,g05 . Efficient fine-tuning and asynchronous execution further improve the practicality of VLA deployment~ openvla_oft,xiaomi_robotics0 . Our work investigates a complementary direction: learning compact predictive representations of visual dynamics to support action generation. Another line integrates visual prediction and action generation within unified autoregressive or diffusion formulations~ uwm,worldvla,uva,motus,cosmos_policy,lingbot_va . Across these approaches, visual prediction provides both a learning signal for world representations and a possible source of context for action generation. Recent work examines how these benefits can be retained with lower deployment cost. title: ELMO: Emergent Representations In Imitation Learning Via Dynamic Hierarchical Action Chunking
summary: Robot trajectories naturally decompose into variable-length phases with distinct semantic intents, such as reaching, grasping, and lifting. However, training policies to minimize MSE treats all actions as equal, obscuring their semantic structure. While latent action models attempt to create a structured prediction target by compressing action chunks into latent representations, existing approaches rely on two-stage training and context-blind decoders. Consequently, their representations are context-agnostic motion codes (e.g., "move down") which fail to capture behavioural intent (e.g., "pick up the block"). To overcome these bottlenecks, we introduce the Emergent Latent-action MOdel (ELMO), an end-to-end framework that encodes robot trajectories as grounded semantic codes -- representations that ground task-level behavioural intent in the current environment. ELMO jointly trains a VLA planner and an observation-conditioned decoder over dynamically chunked trajectories, learning a semantically grounded action space without separate pretraining. Across standard benchmarks, ELMO outperforms comparable prior methods by 9.6 percentage points on LIBERO-Plus and by 0.75 in average task length on CALVIN. Furthermore, on Blocks -- our shortcut-free simulation and real-world generalization benchmark -- ELMO reaches a 38.6% success rate while all baselines remain below 5%, demonstrating its ability to capture the semantic structure of demonstrations. Consequently, their representations are context-agnostic motion codes (e.g., ``move down'') which fail to capture behavioural intent (e.g., ``pick up the block''). To overcome these bottlenecks, we introduce the Emergent Latent-action MOdel~(ELMO), an end-to-end framework that encodes robot trajectories as grounded semantic codes---representations that ground task-level behavioural intent in the current environment. ELMO jointly trains a VLA planner and an observation-conditioned decoder over dynamically chunked trajectories, learning a semantically grounded action space without separate pretraining. Across standard benchmarks, ELMO outperforms comparable prior methods by 9.6 percentage points on LIBERO-Plus and by +0.75 average task length on CALVIN. Furthermore, on Blocks---our shortcut-free simulation and real-world generalization benchmark---ELMO reaches a 38.6 success rate while all baselines remain below 5 , demonstrating its ability to capture the semantic structure of demonstrations. Website: https://uoft-isl.github.io/elmo.github.io/ Introduction sec:intro Vision-language-action (VLA) policies combine visual and language understanding with robot control by using pretrained vision-language models (VLMs)~ kim2024openvla . While the concept of using a VLM backbone is well established, it is unclear how to best parametrise the action prediction task on top of it. Designs have tried predicting actions via discrete tokens~ kim2024openvla,pertsch2025fast , diffusion~ chi2025diffusion,wen2025diffusionvla , or flow matching~ black2024pi_0,pmlr-v305-black25a,wang2026qwen . Further, it has been shown that making policies predict a chunk of actions rather than a single one improves performance~ zhao2023act , as these sequences capture the underlying non-Markovian behaviour and reduce compounding errors~ lazzati2026does . Going beyond the format of actions, training a VLM backbone to directly predict raw actions has been shown to hurt performance due to the large modality gap between language and raw actions~ driess2026knowledge . Thus, research has explored alternative ways to represent actions~ sutton1999between,shentu2024llms,li2025hamster . At one extreme, hierarchical methods use language sub-tasks~ ahn2022can,belkhale2024rth,shi2025hi as semantic codes to decompose instructions for a downstream controller. However, language remains too coarse, leaving excessive execution uncertainty to the action policy that lacks the full context required to keep trajectories synchronised with the original intent. At the other extreme, latent action models compress action chunks into continuous or discrete latents~ lee2024vqbet,zheng2024prise,pertsch2025fast . Yet, as we demonstrate in~ , these representations act merely as motion codes: context-agnostic encodings of kinematics without task-level intent. Ideally, an intermediate representation should combine the best of both as grounded semantic codes---representations that capture exact behavioural intent and environmental context while allowing an action policy to reactively adapt execution to the live scene. Why do existing latent action models collapse into motion codes rather than learning grounded semantic codes? We argue that they are held back by two architectural bottlenecks: context-blind decoding and two-stage training. First, prior tokenizers and skill models (e.g., VQ-BeT, PRISE, and FAST~ lee2024vqbet,zheng2024prise,pertsch2025fast ) reconstruct action sequences in isolation without an observation-conditioned decoder. Because the decoder is blind to the visual scene, the latent code is forced to memorize exact kinematics rather than abstract behavioural intent. Second, even when decoders utilize images~ xu2026edar , prior works adopt a hierarchical two-stage training paradigm: they first learn to compress actions into a fixed latent space in the first stage, and then train a planner to predict those frozen latents in the second step. Decoupling action compression from latent prediction prevents the latent space from being shaped by task-level semantics and visual-language context, optimizing the representation for isolated reconstruction rather than grounded planning. Overcoming these two bottlenecks requires unifying latent prediction and observation-conditioned decoding into a single end-to-end training stage. To this end, we propose ELMO, an end-to-end hierarchical prediction framework that directly trains the VLA planner and the observation-conditioned decoder together, adapting the dynamic temporal chunking mechanism of H-Net~ hwang2025hnet to continuous robot trajectories. Instead of relying on fixed temporal windows, ELMO dynamically allocates latent representations across trajectory boundaries and jointly optimizes the entire hierarchy. By training end-to-end in a single stage, the representation space is jointly shaped by vision-language planning and reactive visual control, allowing ELMO to learn a semantically grounded action space. During deployment, the VLA planner predicts the resulting grounded semantic codes, which the observation-conditioned action policy maps to raw controls. Grounded semantic codes serve as a compact, low-noise prediction target, improving VLM learning efficiency while preserving the reactivity and precision of receding-horizon control~ zhao2023act,chi2025diffusion . Our contributions are threefold: (1) we introduce ELMO, an end-to-end hierarchical framework that unifies dynamic chunking with single-stage joint training of a VLA planner and an observation-conditioned decoder to learn grounded semantic codes; (2) we provide a comprehensive analysis of prior latent action methods, characterizing differences in their encoded information; and (3) we demonstrate strong performance on standard benchmarks (LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, CALVIN) alongside superior generalization on Blocks, our specialized benchmark designed to eliminate evaluation shortcuts in existing suites. Related Work sec:related Vision-Language-Action Models. In recent years, VLA models have been extensively studied for generalist robotics. These policies leverage the general knowledge of VLMs by passing VLM embeddings of image and language to an action head for robot control~ kim2024openvla,black2024pi_0 . The action head predicts future robot actions from the current state. Following this structure, VLAs have been scaled to billions of parameters and trained on ever-increasing robot datasets~ o2024open . Despite this scale, VLAs still struggle to generalize to unseen environments, tasks, and robot embodiments. Changes in camera viewpoint, initial robot state, or lighting can cause large drops in success rate~ fei2025liberoplus . We argue that this is partly a result of robot policies learning to predict high-frequency actions rather than the intent behind them. This results in brittle learning and poor generalization, motivating better action representations and training objectives. Tokenization. In vision and language, models generally operate on a tokenized representation of the input rather than raw bytes directly. By grouping predictable local structures, tokenization shortens sequences and lets large models focus on long-range composition and semantic relationships rather than high-frequency noise. Vision models typically rely on learned patch embeddings trained end-to-end with the main network. Images are sliced into non-overlapping grid patches, and each flattened patch is mapped through trainable layers into a continuous latent vector~ dosovitskiy2020image . Traditionally, language models have relied on separately trained tokenizers like byte-pair encoding (BPE)~ sennrich2016neural , which starts with a base alphabet and iteratively merges the most frequent adjacent symbol pairs into new tokens. More recently, learned tokenizers have been developed for language as well. H-Net~ hwang2025hnet trains an encoder-backbone-decoder hierarchy end-to-end. Raw byte embeddings pass through an encoder that dynamically groups variable-length spans into learned tokens based on adjacent similarity. The backbone operates in this compressed token space and predictions are decoded back into raw bytes. At scales above 1B parameters, H-Net matches the training perplexity and downstream performance of BPE-tokenized transformers while removing the fixed external tokenizer~ hwang2025hnet . Action Representations. Early VLAs discretized action dimensions into uniform bins to reframe continuous regression as autoregressive classification~ kim2024openvla , while signal-compression methods like FAST apply the discrete cosine transform and BPE to tokenize short action chunks~ pertsch2025fast . Alternative approaches decompose long-horizon tasks via language sub-goals~ ahn2022can , finer-grained language instructions~ belkhale2024rth , or fixed-hierarchy latent codes bridging VLMs and low-level controllers~ shentu2024llms . However, these rely on predefined linguistic abstractions and are thus limited in what they can express efficiently. Closer to our work, trajectory-level representation methods extract higher-level tokens via vector quantization and sequence compression~ lee2024vqbet,zheng2024prise,yunis2024subwords,mete2024quest,li2025star , recently scaled up in VQ-VLA~ wang2025vqvla and systematically benchmarked in ActionCodec~ dong2026actioncodec . Among these, only PRISE constructs variable-length segments via post-quantization BPE, focusing on raw compressibility rather than semantic or temporal structure~ zheng2024prise . Video-based latent action models (e.g., LAPA~ ye2024lapa , HiLAM~ kim2026hilam ) leverage unlabeled videos and optimize downstream policy integration~ lin2026from , but learning from visual differences alone risks entangling robot motion with background change~ li2025latbot . Most similar to our method are EDAR and SA-VLA~ xu2026edar,jiang2026savla . Although EDAR incorporates camera observations and predicts visual changes in its decoder, we find it still yields motion codes. Similarly, SA-VLA conditions its fixed-length decoder on proprioceptive state, but without any information about the environment, it cannot encode anything besides a motion code~ jiang2026savla . More broadly, when decoders lack or underutilize live visual observations, latent tokens must independently reconstruct exact trajectories, collapsing into direct action reparameterizations. In contrast, we train a dynamic latent hierarchy end-to-end with a vision-aware decoder, which allows a latent representation carrying task-level intent along with its relevant context to emerge while delegating local execution to the decoder. Methodology sec:methodology We build ELMO~( ) around our two core principles: dynamic chunking of the robot trajectory and a context-aware decoder. Since the trajectory chunks should reflect when the policy should make decisions, we train the hierarchical VLA planner and observation-conditioned action policy together. ELMO adapts the dynamic chunking mechanism of H-Net~ hwang2025hnet using a recurrent state encoder and a dynamic router to partition continuous robot trajectories into variable-length behavioural segments. title: SOLVE: Sparse, Ordered Keyposes Make LLM Agents Versatile and Efficient Robot Manipulator
summary: LLM agents have made remarkable progress in robot manipulation, yet they suffer from expensive inference, dense step-by-step control, and tool bottlenecks. We introduce SOLVE, a training-free, versatile and efficient agent policy: a multimodal LLM agent writes a sparse, ordered sequence of 6-DoF end-effector keyposes per call, observes the result, and writes the next, while a motion planner interpolates between them. The agent decides the number and spacing of keyposes for both fast long-range motion and fine-grained manipulation. This granularity matches the sparsity of teleoperated manipulation: most demonstrations in DROID can be compressed into a few keyposes instead of dense actions. SOLVE grounds keyposes with sparse depth queries answered by noisy sources, such as multi-view triangulation, stereo, or monocular depth, and copes with that noise itself. It also improves from execution feedback, reflecting on its own rollouts and distilling a few rules per task. SOLVE reaches state-of-the-art performance of 74.5% on RoboDojo and 84.5% on RoboLab, with only $1.7 per episode on average, 12x less than previous dense-control agent policies. On a real robot, the same agent achieves an 88% success rate (75 of 85 episodes) over 16 challenging zero-shot tasks. Our project page is at https://serenos.github.io/solve-website.

(a) VLAs/WAMs emit dense action chunks, code-as-policy runs a program with little feedback, and LLM agents spend one call per small step; SOLVE writes few keyposes per call. (b) A teleoperation compressed to 6 keyposes joined by straight lines. (c) SOLVE writes similar keyposes. (d) Success rate and cost against the best method. fig:teaser ] Equal contribution. Corresponding author. LLM agents have made remarkable progress in robot manipulation, yet they suffer from expensive inference, dense step-by-step control, and tool bottlenecks. We introduce , a training-free, versatile and efficient agent policy: a multimodal LLM agent writes a sparse, ordered sequence of 6-DoF end-effector keyposes per call, observes the result, and writes the next, while a motion planner interpolates between them. The agent decides the number and spacing of keyposes for both fast long-range motion and fine-grained manipulation. This granularity matches the sparsity of teleoperated manipulation: most demonstrations in DROID can be compressed into a few keyposes instead of dense actions. grounds keyposes with sparse depth queries answered by noisy sources, such as multi-view triangulation, stereo, or monocular depth, and copes with that noise itself. It also improves from execution feedback, reflecting on its own rollouts and distilling a few rules per task. reaches state-of-the-art performance of 74.5 on RoboDojo and 84.5 on RoboLab, with only \ 1.7 per episode on average, with one quarter of the model calls and 12 lower cost than a step-wise agent ( d). Our contributions are as follows: We show that teleoperated demonstrations compress into a small number of keyposes and, building on this finding, propose , a framework in which an LLM agent writes sparse, ordered keyposes for direct manipulation. We propose sparse metric queries, combining cross-view epipolar matching with depth estimation to ground keyposes accurately and efficiently in 3D from RGB in simulation, and use stereo depth on the real robot. We enable the agent to improve from rollouts, and show that transfers without modification across robots and benchmarks, achieving state-of-the-art results on RoboDojo, RoboLab, and a real robot at 12 lower cost. Related Work sec:related End-to-end policies. Vision-language-action (VLA) models~ brohan2023rt1,brohan2023rt2,octo2024,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,black2025pi05,liu2024rdt,kim2025openvlaoft,qu2025spatialvla,bu2025univla,shi2025hirobot,wen2025dexvla,zheng2026xvla,nvidia2025gr00tn1,team2025geminirobotics and imitation policies that predict action chunks~ zhao2023act,chi2023diffusionpolicy are trained on large teleoperation corpora to emit dense, high-frequency actions; recent work improves their spatial representations~ qu2025spatialvla,zheng2025tracevla,yang2025magma and action tokenization~ pertsch2025fast . World-action models (WAMs)~ du2023unipi,wu2024gr1,cheang2024gr2,hu2024vpp,li2025uva,zhu2025uwm,jang2025dreamgen,cen2026worldvla,liao2026genieenvisioner,kim2026cosmospolicy,lyu2026lda1b,ye2026dreamzero,cai2026internvlaa1,vpp2 additionally learn from video to predict future observations and derive actions from them. On RoboDojo~ robodojo , the best entries of both families reach 35 on the leaderboard and at most 23 on the Open dimension, whose tasks come without demonstrations. instead acts through sparse keyposes and requires no robot-specific training. Agentic policies. A growing line of work builds policies around frontier LLMs with little or no training. Code-as-policy methods let the model write programs over perception and control primitives~ liang2023cap ; recent systems benchmark coding agents~ fu2026capx , structure programs as graphs rehearsed in simulation~ chen2026gap , grow skill libraries by evolutionary search~ lu2026aspire , or rewrite the training code of neural policies~ xiao2026enpire . Agent as Policy~ jia2026agp similarly writes programs at test time on a real arm. Harness methods wrap a model with tools, memory and recovery logic, steering a frozen VLA as a retryable or interruptible tool~ zhang2026harnessvla,chen2026volo,ding2026zetta or calling semantic tools such as grasp and align~ liu2026guava . Finally, some works use the model directly as a policy, issuing one end-effector target per call~ astra,gptaspolicy , several absolute poses each executed for a single control step~ astranomy , discrete motion units of a few centimeters~ chen2026showharness , or batches of relative, axis-aligned motion commands. is a direct policy in that every call observes the scene and outputs motion targets. Unlike other direct policies, a call outputs an ordered sequence of absolute 6-DoF keyposes, placed with metric 3D measurements, that can span a whole primitive. Sparse action representations. Sparsity itself is not new. Keyframe policies predict the next gripper pose rather than a dense trajectory~ james2022c2farm,shridhar2022peract,goyal2023rvt,gervet2023act3d,goyal2024rvt2,ke20243dda , and bimanual policies condition on keyposes or skills~ yu2024bikc,atomskill,gripperkeypose . These methods learn from task demonstrations, and they extract keyframes with heuristics such as gripper state changes and near-zero joint velocities~ james2022c2farm,shridhar2022peract , implicitly assuming that a few poses suffice; our analysis quantifies how many are needed per primitive and where this assumption fails. VLM-based methods such as VoxPoser~ huang2023voxposer , ReKep~ huang2024rekep , and PIVOT~ nasiriany2024pivot are also training-free, but the model typically produces object-centric keypoints, constraints or value maps once, and a separate optimizer turns them into motion. In , the model itself writes end-effector keyposes at every call (hence keypose rather than keypoint). Method sec:method Overview sec:method:overview A robot with arms is required to complete a task, given as a language instruction , within environment steps. At step it observes : RGB images from cameras and, for each arm, the grasp-point pose and gripper opening . No depth is observed, but every camera pose follows from and a fixed calibration. The agent is a frozen multimodal LLM ( ) that emits exactly one tool call per model call , given an optional task guide and experience notes ( ) and the history of earlier calls and results, in which only the latest two observations keep their images. Of the tools ( ), move eef hands a keypose sequence to the executor , which plays it and returns the next observation with execution feedback ; query points passes a few pixels , pixel of camera , to the query tool , which returns their world coordinates without advancing the environment, where is the world point of pixel and its source, triangulated, monocular or stereo depth, which tells the agent how far to trust it; wait lets the scene evolve, and give up ends the episode. Sparse, ordered keyposes sec:method:keypose Why keyposes suffice. sec:sparsity We first measure how far demonstrations compress into keyposes joined by straight lines. Keeping the first and last poses and every gripper event (a grasp or a release), we simplify position (interpolated linearly) and orientation (by slerp) jointly with Ramer--Douglas--Peucker~ douglas1973rdp , adding the farthest frame as a keypose until every frame lies within a tolerance. We apply it to RoboDojo's teleoperated demonstrations and to 57,534 successful DROID episodes~ khazatsky2024droid , which human operators teleoperated on real Franka arms. Both compress alike ( ). A grasp or release spans a median of 56 recorded actions on RoboDojo (25\,Hz) and 96 on DROID (15\,Hz), as many as a policy imitating them at the recording rate must output; at 2\,cm / 10 it needs only 4.9 and 6.0 keyposes, 11 and 16 fewer, and a DROID episode shrinks to a median of 13 keyposes, about one per second. Over 91 of the travel lies on segments longer than 5\,cm, and on DROID this share stays within 88--95 for every instruction verb. The segments are genuinely straight: at 1\,cm, 92.6 of DROID travel lies on segments whose path is at most 1.11 times their chord. A short sequence of absolute targets thus describes most manipulation, and the dense motion can be left to the planner. Sparse, ordered keyposes. A keypose of arm is a target for its observed state , : the world-frame position of the grasp point, its orientation , and the gripper opening . The agent writes only the dimensions it wants to change; all others hold their current value in and , and naming dimensions of several arms moves them together. One move eef call carries an ordered sequence with , a cap sized to one primitive, such as approach; descend and close; lift, which our demonstration analysis puts at five to six keyposes per grasp or release. Three choices make the interface easy for an LLM to use. Absolute targets: each keypose is the pose the arm should reach, not an increment, so the agent never has to plan intermediate waypoints of a long move. Arrive, then actuate: a gripper command takes effect only after the arm reaches its keypose, so ``go there and grasp'' is a single keypose. Agent-set speed: each keypose may carry a ramp , the number of environment steps used to accelerate toward it and to brake at it; the agent chooses a long ramp to carry liquid or set an object down gently, and a short one to strike or knock something over. The agent thus decides the number, spacing and speed of keyposes: one keypose at full speed for a long free-space move, several short and slow ones near contact. The executor turns a keypose sequence into joint commands without any learning. The move to each keypose is split into short segments of bounded translation and rotation, each solved for a joint path by a motion planner~ sundaralingam2023curobo and chained. If a segment cannot be reached, the sequence stops before it and the feedback reports which keypose failed, so the agent can replan. Sparse metric queries sec:method:queries Placing keyposes requires metric 3D grounding, but only at a few task-relevant points, not dense scene depth. Through query points, the agent selects pixels needed for its next keypose, such as a cup rim or a socket hole, and returns their world points ( ). The tool uses calibrated RGB views in simulation with no stereo cameras, as described below, and additionally the stereo depth of the wrist camera on hardware ( ). Epipolar matching. We triangulate each query pixel by calibrated two-view matching along its epipolar line. To accommodate the large viewpoint and scale differences between head and wrist cameras, we evaluate depth hypotheses using plane-induced patch warping and normalized cross-correlation rather than comparing fixed image windows. This directly matches the agent-selected pixel without requiring it to be a detected keypoint or computing a dense disparity map. We first try the other current cameras, then recent wrist frames with stricter acceptance thresholds to account for scene motion. A point is accepted only when the match passes confidence, uniqueness and texture checks; otherwise, we use the depth model fallback below. Implementation details and comparisons with feature matching are provided in the supplementary material. Depth model fallback. When triangulation fails, , on textureless surfaces or points visible in only one camera, the tool uses depth predicted by Depth Anything~3~ lin2025da3 from all current views and their camera calibration. We correct the scale per view using reference depths obtained by intersecting table-pixel rays with the known table plane. The model runs once per observation , shared by all queries; its depth is accurate to a centimeter but smooths edges and thin parts. Telling the agent how much to trust. title: FlipVLA: Backdoor Attacks on Vision-Language-Action(VLA) Models Only Through Bit Flips

summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models generate robot actions from visual observations and language instructions in real-world environments, making malicious model tampering a potential threat to physical safety. We study whether object-triggered backdoors can be implanted through a small, fixed set of parameter bit flips without retraining. The central challenge is to make persistent weight modifications disrupt trigger-present behavior while preserving performance on non-trigger inputs. We propose FlipVLA, a two-stage selector-amplifier method that exploits existing visual features within an FC-GELU-FC structure. The selector constructs a trigger-dependent response in a selected channel, using GELU to attenuate background activity. The amplifier modifies a connected downstream weight to convert this response into an action-relevant perturbation. Channel screening and discrete bit search construct both components under a limited modification budget. Experiments on OpenVLA-OFT and GR00T N1.7 across four LIBERO suites achieve attack success rates of 90.22% to 100%, with task success decreasing by at most 1.5 percentage points on clean scenes.
full_text: Vision–language–action (VLA) models generate robot actions from visual observations and language instructions in real-world environments, making malicious model tampering a potential threat to physical safety. We study whether object-triggered backdoors can be implanted through a small, fixed set of parameter bit flips without retraining. The central challenge is to make persistent weight modifications disrupt trigger-present behavior while preserving performance on non-trigger inputs. We propose FlipVLA, a two-stage selector--amplifier method that exploits existing visual features within an FC--GELU--FC structure. The selector constructs a trigger-dependent response in a selected channel, using GELU to attenuate background activity. The amplifier modifies a connected downstream weight to convert this response into an action-relevant perturbation. Channel screening and discrete bit search construct both components under a limited modification budget. Experiments on OpenVLA-OFT and GR00T N1.7 across four LIBERO suites achieve attack success rates of 90.22 --100 , with task success decreasing by at most 1.5 percentage points on clean scenes. Introduction sec:intro Vision–language–action (VLA) models map visual observations and language instructions to robot actions, providing a unified framework for robotic manipulation~ zitkovich2023rt2,kim2025openvla . Because their predictions directly guide physical execution, malicious tampering with these models can disrupt task completion. Backdoor attacks pose a particularly concealed threat: a model behaves normally in scenes without a trigger but deviates from its intended behavior when a predefined trigger appears. Such conditional failures may remain undetected by evaluations that do not include the trigger. Existing backdoor attacks commonly rely on training data poisoning or malicious fine-tuning to establish an association between a trigger and abnormal behavior~ zhou2025badvla,xu2026dropvla . These approaches require access to the training data or optimization process. Bit-flip attacks (BFAs) expose a different attack surface by modifying the binary representation of deployed model parameters without retraining~ rakin2019bfa . Hardware fault-injection techniques such as Rowhammer~ kim2014rowhammer,lin2025gpuhammer can induce memory bit flips, motivating the study of deployed model weights as an attack surface. In this work, we investigate object-triggered backdoor injection into VLA models through a small, fixed set of parameter bit flips. Our goal is to disrupt task execution when a designated trigger object is present while preserving performance in its absence, including scenes containing distractor objects. Achieving this goal under a limited bit budget is challenging. The same modified weights process both trigger-present and trigger-absent inputs: one bit flip that disrupts triggered behavior may also damage normal operation. The large parameter space makes suitable modifications difficult to locate, while bit flips induce discrete changes in parameter values, further complicating the search for suitable modifications. This motivates investigating whether such conditional behavior can be constructed by exploiting information already present in the model. We view backdoor implantation in this setting as extracting trigger information and selectively controlling its influence on action generation. This perspective leads to two questions: First, can existing visual representations provide a small set of discriminative features for detecting the trigger object? Second, can weight modifications amplify the influence of this signal on action outputs while limiting their effects on normal behavior? Our analyses in Section 3 show that a few channels encode trigger presence, selected early visual perturbations can disrupt tasks while the suppressing individual projector channels causes small deviations on clean inputs. These findings motivate FlipVLA (Figure~ fig:overview ), a selector–amplifier construction within an existing FC–GELU–FC structure which is commonly used in modern Transformer architectures. The selector modifies the first FC layer to activate trigger-associated tokens while driving background responses negative for attenuation by GELU. With the selector frozen, the amplifier modifies a connected weight in the second FC layer to increase action deviations on trigger-present inputs. Channel screening and discrete bit search implement both stages within the bit budget. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: To the best of our knowledge, we provide the first demonstration of object-triggered backdoor attacks on VLA models through a limited number of parameter bit flips, without retraining and while largely preserving non-trigger performance. We propose FlipVLA, a selector--amplifier construction that uses an existing FC--GELU--FC structure to form a trigger-dependent response and then amplify it to disrupt task execution. Channel screening and discrete bit search implement both stages within a limited budget. Experiments on OpenVLA-OFT and GR00T N1.7 across four LIBERO suites achieve attack success rates of 90.22 --100 , with clean-task success decreasing by at most 1.5 percentage points. Additional evaluations examine object selectivity and robustness to trigger variations, while activation-restoration experiments trace the perturbation's downstream effects. Preliminary sec:related For Vision--language--action (VLA) models, given an input \(x=(I, ,p)\), comprising images \(I\), an instruction \( \), and proprioceptive state \(p\), the model's action head predicts a normalized action matrix: Here, denotes the model parameters, and is the action horizon, set to 8 for all evaluated models. Each row represents one predicted action, consisting of three translational components, three rotational components, and one gripper command. VLA backdoor attacks aim to induce trigger-dependent misbehavior while preserving performance on clean inputs. To quantify action deviations caused by model modifications, we use the mean absolute error (MAE) between the modified model's output \( A(x)\) and the frozen original model's output \( A_0(x)\): Both models receive the same input, and all comparisons use normalized action outputs. Larger MAE indicates greater deviation from the original policy. We average MAE over the evaluated inputs and assess task completion separately through rollout success rates (SR). Threat model sec:threat_model Attacker's goal. The attacker aims to cause untargeted task failures when a predefined, task-irrelevant trigger object is visible, while preserving the original model's performance on clean and distractor scenes. Attacker's capabilities. We assume a white-box attacker with access to the model architecture, pretrained parameters, intermediate activations, and action outputs. The attacker can collect a limited set of clean, trigger-present, and distractor observations for offline bit search, flip selected parameter bits under a fixed budget, and place the trigger object within the robot’s field of view. The attacker cannot access or manipulate the original training pipeline, poison training data, retrain or fine-tune the model, or modify its architecture, task instructions, or control software. All parameter modifications are confined to the selected bit flips and remain fixed during subsequent inference, without online updates or direct manipulation of action commands. Motivation sec:motivation We examine whether existing visual representations provide a compact trigger signal and whether this signal can influence actions while limiting interference on non-trigger inputs. All analyses use the original OpenVLA-OFT model with its parameters frozen. 1. Trigger-object presence can be detected from a few activation channels. We perform sparse linear probing across layers for three target objects (Figure~ fig:objects ), comparing the minimum number of channels required to achieve the same detection performance(Figure~ fig:sparse-readout ). Several projector layers and early Llama layers support detection using only a few channels, whereas deeper layers generally require more. This pattern holds across all three objects. These sparse readouts motivate reusing existing visual features to construct a compact trigger response. Compared with attention blocks, the projector has a simpler structure consisting mainly of fully connected layers and GELU activations(Figure~ fig:projector-architecture ). This makes the effects of bit flips on local activations easier to analyze and control. 2. Selected activation perturbations can disrupt tasks, while single-channel suppression causes small changes in clean actions. action generation. We add a scalar perturbation injection to one activation element at the input to Llama block 0, 8, 16, or 24 and measure action deviation on clean inputs using MAE (Eq.~ ). We scan all token--channel positions in each tested layer; among the selected locations shown in Fig.~ fig:activation-sensitivity , earlier layers exhibit larger peak deviations. We then vary perturbation magnitude at one fixed visual-token/channel location per layer, measuring mean MAE over 200 observations (Fig.~ fig:injection-dose (a)) and rollout success over 200 initial scenes (Fig.~ fig:injection-dose (b)). During rollouts, perturbations are applied at every action prediction. Small perturbations produce limited action changes and near-baseline success rates, whereas sufficiently large perturbations at the selected early-layer locations substantially alter actions and reduce task success. The tested deeper-layer locations are less sensitive. non-trigger interference. We next examine how suppressing a single projector channel affects action predictions on clean inputs. We independently zero each of the 4,096 post-GELU channels following the projector's FC2 layer and measure action MAE over clean inputs. The selected channel lies in the low-deviation region.
