title: MERLoc: Robust Robot Localization in Dynamic Environments with Pose-Based Retrieval over 3D Gaussian Splatting References
summary: Robots operating in previously mapped spaces must localize accurately despite moving people and rearranged objects. Most localization pipelines match the query against a sparse set of captured reference images retrieved by appearance, which is brittle under scene change and repeating structures. We present MERLoc, which turns a single metric 3D Gaussian Splatting scan into a dense Functional Reference Memory. Reference views are sampled over the navigable space for the robot's morphology and sensors at a target density and rendered offline. Pre-encoding them for the chosen off-the-shelf localizer removes the reference encoder from inference. A pose-based retrieval strategy then selects references by spatial proximity and viewing direction rather than appearance, sidestepping visual ambiguities whenever a prior exists. Across one classical and four learned localizers in simulated and real dynamic scenes, pose-based retrieval matches or outperforms appearance retrieval in most cases, even when the latter is gated by the same prior. On real data, it lowers position RMSE by 15-60 % in nine of ten backend/split combinations, and the rendered memory outperforms real-image caches posed by Structure-from-Motion. The system runs onboard a Jetson Orin NX at 5 Hz, enabling a navigation policy to successfully traverse a hallway with people roaming and rearranging objects.
full_text: Robots operating in previously mapped spaces must localize accurately despite moving people and rearranged objects. Most localization pipelines match the query against a sparse set of captured reference images retrieved by appearance, which is brittle under scene change and repeating structures. We present , which turns a single metric 3D Gaussian Splatting scan into a dense Functional Reference Memory. Reference views are sampled over the navigable space for the robot’s morphology and sensors at a target density and rendered offline. Pre-encoding them for the chosen off-the-shelf localizer removes the reference encoder from inference. A pose-based retrieval strategy then selects references by spatial proximity and viewing direction rather than appearance, sidestepping visual ambiguities whenever a prior exists. Across one classical and four learned localizers in simulated and real dynamic scenes, pose-based retrieval matches or outperforms appearance retrieval in most cases, even when the latter is gated by the same prior. On real data, it lowers position RMSE by 15--60\, in nine of ten backend/split combinations, and the rendered memory outperforms real-image caches posed by Structure-from-Motion. The system runs onboard a Jetson Orin NX at , enabling a navigation policy to successfully traverse a hallway with people roaming and rearranging objects. Introduction sec:intro Robots deployed in homes, hospitals, and warehouses operate in spaces that are easy to scan but rarely remain identical to those scans over time. People walk through them, objects appear, and furniture moves. While structural elements provide reliable localization cues, these dynamic changes introduce distractors and ambiguities that degrade localization pipelines built for static scenes. The dominant localization pipeline for previously mapped environments queries a sparse set of posed reference images~ hloc . References are posed offline by Structure-from-Motion (SfM)~ colmap , retrieved online via appearance descriptors~ netvlad , and passed to a relative localizer. Frozen at mapping time, the reference set is limited to the captured viewpoints and can neither be densified nor adapted to a robot’s sensor suite. Furthermore, appearance-based retrieval is prone to visual aliasing, where distinct places look alike, such as repeated corridors or identical doors. Aliasing and scene changes since mapping both lead retrieval to return confidently wrong references that no relative localizer can recover from~ Lowry2016,Masone2021,sattler2018benchmark . Recent feed-forward localizers replace the geometric solver but inherit both limitations; even when trained on dynamic scenes~ monst3r, vggt-omega, pi3 , most are, as we show, more sensitive than classical pipelines to aliased or changed references. We propose a 3D Gaussian Splatting-based Memory Encoding and Retrieval Localization ( ) framework, which replaces the rigid, captured reference set with a controllable, backend-adaptive, rendering-based memory. Given a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ gross3dgs, kerbl3dgs scan of the environment, we sample reference poses over the navigable space at a specified density, height range, and orientation profile tailored to the robot's sensor suite. We then render these views and encode them offline in a representation customized for the relative localizer. This forms a Functional Reference Memory (FRM): its content is determined by the target backend and robot morphology rather than by the scanner that captures it, e.g., depth-lifted keypoints for classical pipelines~ hloc or encoded visual tokens for latent-conditioned architectures~ monst3r,vggt-omega,pi3,reloc3r . Because of this customized encoding, the relative localizer runs entirely off-the-shelf, without per-scene training or adaptation, and without encoding any reference at runtime, which removes one encoder pass per retrieved reference from the online path. Furthermore, the FRM density becomes a tunable design parameter that trades accuracy against storage without increasing online inference cost. To select references, we index the dense FRM by pose. Given a pose prior, typically the previous estimate or odometry, we gate candidates within a radius and rank them by viewing-direction alignment and proximity, falling back to appearance-based matching only for initialization or recovery. Unlike SLAM, which routinely gates retrieval with a propagated pose~ mcl,orbslam2 , localization pipelines still retrieve by appearance alone. Neither the dense FRM nor pose-based retrieval suffices alone: pose-based retrieval starves on a sparse reference set, and appearance retrieval still aliases on a dense one. Together, they make classical and learned relative localizers metric, more accurate, and more robust to scene change without touching backend weights. We claim that (i) turns one metric 3DGS scan into a Functional Reference Memory whose density, height band, and encoding are chosen per robot and per localizer, so that classical and feed-forward backends run off-the-shelf without encoding references at runtime ( ); (ii) on real data, this rendered memory outperforms real-image caches of the same scene posed by SfM, even at a lower pose density for the classical backend ( ); (iii) pose-based context retrieval over this memory lowers position RMSE by 15--60\, relative to appearance retrieval for nine of ten real-world backend/split combinations and, under simulated scene change and human activity, matches or exceeds prior-gated appearance retrieval while clearly exceeding plain appearance retrieval for four of five backends (Secs.~ sec:exp_arena -- sec:exp_mocap ); (iv) the system runs at on a Jetson Orin NX, enabling a navigation policy to reliably traverse a hallway while people move around the robot and displace objects ( ). Related Work sec:related_work Visual Localization and Aliasing sec:rw_rel_loc The main approaches driving visual localization research are scene coordinate regression (SCR), absolute pose regression (APR), and retrieval-based localization with classical or learned relative pose estimation. Scene Coordinate and Absolute Pose Regression SCR trains a network to predict per-pixel 3D scene coordinates~ dsac-star,ace ; APR regresses the pose directly~ posenet . Both bake the scene into network weights and degrade under structural change~ rio10 ; APR moreover behaves like pose interpolation~ sattler2019apr . trains nothing per scene and runs off-the-shelf, scene-agnostic backends over an explicit reference memory. Retrieval-Based Localization Classical structure-based pipelines and learned relative pose regression (RPR) estimate the query pose against a posed reference database, typically sparse and reconstructed offline via SfM~ colmap . They lead long-term localization benchmarks~ sattler2018benchmark and are our focus. Classical pipelines~ hloc chain local feature extraction~ aliked , matching~ lightglue , and robust Perspective- -Point (PnP)~ epnp,ransac . Recent feed-forward networks replace this pipeline with a single forward pass, predicting relative poses or pointmaps for two-view~ monst3r,reloc3r or multi-view~ vggt-omega,pi3 sets. While these models reduce system complexity, most tolerate aliased reference sets worse than classical pipelines, even when trained on dynamic scenes~ monst3r, vggt-omega, pi3 . Appearance-Based Retrieval Classical and learned relative methods retrieve references with appearance-based Visual Place Recognition (VPR)~ netvlad, Izquierdo_CVPR_2024_SALAD , which is vulnerable to visual aliasing. In repetitive or changed scenes, retrieved references can be confidently wrong, and no relative localizer recovers~ Lowry2016,sattler2018benchmark . Existing remedies stay in the appearance domain. Hierarchical pipelines cluster the retrieved frames by co-visibility before matching~ hloc , and sequence-based VPR~ seqslam enforces temporal consistency of descriptor matches. Gating the appearance search by a pose prior, which we evaluate as VPR+, still ranks by descriptor similarity and inherits its failure modes. We instead remove appearance from the retrieval decision and rank references by pose. 3DGS Localization and SLAM sec:rw_3dgs_slam Localizing with Rendered References Rendering a scene model for localization predates 3DGS: Torii et al.~ torii247 synthesize database views so that query and reference share a viewpoint, MeshLoc extracts features on mesh renderings~ meshloc , LENS trains a pose regressor on NeRF views placed by the scene geometry~ lens , and Ress et al.~ ress2025gs add 3DGS renders at random poses to an SfM reference set. Loc-NeRF~ locnerf , GS-CPR~ liu2025gscpr , and GSVisLoc~ gsvisloc instead work at query time, respectively: per particle of a Monte Carlo filter, to refine a coarse pose from another localizer, or to refine a direct match of encoded 3D Gaussians at seconds per query. Active localization methods such as ActLoc~ actloc use the scene model to choose the viewing directions expected to localize best, which does not help a passive camera that cannot be steered. None samples its reference set by robot embodiment and density, pre-encodes it for an off-the-shelf localizer, or changes how references are retrieved. Unlike query-time methods, all of our rendering happens offline. Pose Priors in SLAM and Localization Using a propagated pose to decide what to match against is standard in robotics. Monte Carlo localization weights pose hypotheses propagated by odometry against a map~ mcl , and ORB-SLAM2's localization mode tracks a saved map by matching to the map points predicted visible from the propagated pose~ orbslam2 . Visual localization pipelines, in contrast, treat every query independently and retrieve by appearance. brings the prior into the localization pipeline: it gates and ranks references in a dense, metric memory by a propagated pose and re-estimates the pose absolutely with an off-the-shelf localizer, avoiding error accumulation as in odometry. System Architecture sec:system Our proposed system, ~( ), consists of three stages. The first stage is an offline pre-processing step, where we ingest the 3DGS scan of a scene ( ). We sample camera poses in a controlled manner within a height band and density informed by the robot's morphology, sensor suite, storage budget, and desired localization accuracy, then render these views and pre-encode them into a format matched to the relative localizer. In the second stage, at runtime, we query context encodings from this FRM using a pose prior ( ) from the previous localization result or, if available, odometry. In the third stage, we feed these retrieved references, along with the encoded live query view, into one of several backends ( ). Each backend is characterized by a relative localizer, which is used to obtain a global pose. Our system design deliberately adapts the FRM to the backend, rather than the reverse, enabling relative localizers to run off-the-shelf without per-scene training or fine-tuning. Stage I: 3DGS Scene Pre-Processing sec:preprocessing Our method utilizes a high-fidelity 3DGS scan and at least a rough collision mesh, both readily obtainable with current 3DGS pipelines and commercial scanners. Our real-world scan comes from a handheld LiDAR-camera scanner that outputs both ( ). In simulation, the simulator’s scene model replaces the scan. Guided Pose Sampling We first extract the navigable space of a scan: from the scene's collision mesh, we rasterize a 2D occupancy grid with cell size . We retain cells with floor support and sufficient headroom , remove cells within a clearance margin of obstacles via erosion, and discard disconnected islands smaller than , which the robot cannot reach. FRM viewpoints are then sampled to match the robot's specific morphology and sensor suite: positions are sampled uniformly over the navigable area within a sensor-height band of thickness , with orientation ranges tailored to the platform. title: Towards 360$^\circ$ Embodied UAV Tracking Without Turning
summary: Conventional embodied UAV tracking couples target observability with heading control because targets may leave the field of view of forward-facing cameras. We investigate a complementary paradigm that uses full-spherical perception to follow designated targets without active heading adjustment. To support this setting, we introduce 360UAV-ETrack, a simulation benchmark comprising 2,652 sequences, over 1.73 million synchronized observations, eight tracking tasks, and 150 held-out closed-loop scenarios. We propose 360UAV-TVLA, a panoramic vision--language--action (VLA) framework integrating persistent visual referring (PVR), compressed temporal memory (CTM), and geometry-aligned trajectory supervision (GTS) for instance identification, motion reasoning, and three-dimensional control. Experiments across two VLA backbones show consistent gains over standard fine-tuning, with normalized average tracking frames increasing from 22.56\% to 35.28\% for $π_0$ and from 25.68\% to 33.64\% for $π_{0.5}$. Our benchmark further reveals a substantial gap between offline imitation accuracy and closed-loop tracking reliability, establishing a challenging testbed for future research https://libingyu01.github.io/360UAV-ETrack_360UAV-TVLA/
full_text: Overview of 360UAV-ETrack and 360UAV-TVLA. The upper panel presents the benchmark scenarios, panoramic observations, and dataset statistics, while the lower panel illustrates our VLA framework for full-spherical embodied UAV tracking. fig:paper_overall Conventional embodied UAV tracking couples target observability with heading control because targets may leave the field of view of forward-facing cameras. We investigate a complementary paradigm that uses full-spherical perception to follow designated targets without active heading adjustment. To support this setting, we introduce 360UAV-ETrack, a simulation benchmark comprising 2,652 sequences, over 1.73 million synchronized observations, eight tracking tasks, and 150 held-out closed-loop scenarios. We propose 360UAV-TVLA, a panoramic vision--language--action (VLA) framework integrating persistent visual referring (PVR), compressed temporal memory (CTM), and geometry-aligned trajectory supervision (GTS) for instance identification, motion reasoning, and three-dimensional control. Experiments across two VLA backbones show consistent gains over standard fine-tuning, with normalized average tracking frames increasing from 22.56 to 35.28 for and from 25.68 to 33.64 for . Our benchmark further reveals a substantial gap between offline imitation accuracy and closed-loop tracking reliability, establishing a challenging testbed for future research . Introduction sec:introduction Embodied UAV tracking requires an agent to continuously observe and follow a designated moving target. Unlike visual object tracking in prerecorded videos, embodied tracking operates in a closed perception--action loop, where the agent's actions influence subsequent observations and its spatial relationship with the target~ wang2025trackvla . Existing approaches predominantly rely on forward-facing perspective cameras. Consequently, targets moving to the side or behind the UAV may leave the field of view (FoV), even when they remain nearby. Maintaining visual contact thus requires active heading adjustment, coupling target observability with heading. We investigate a complementary tracking paradigm that decouples angular target coverage from heading control through full-spherical perception. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:tracking_motivation , equirectangular projection (ERP) extends visual coverage to lateral and rear directions without camera reorientation. This motivates tracking without turning, in which the UAV maintains its initial heading and follows the designated target exclusively through three-dimensional translational control. While physical occlusions remain unavoidable, full-spherical perception alleviates target loss caused by limited FoV. Despite its potential, full-spherical perception remains underexplored in embodied UAV tracking. Panoramic tracking benchmarks such as 360VOT~ huang2023_360vot and 360VOTS~ xu2025_360vots focus on offline target localization, whereas embodied approaches such as TrackVLA~ wang2025trackvla and UAV-Track VLA~ zhang2026uavtrackvla primarily rely on perspective observations. As summarized in Table~ tab:dataset_comparison , existing benchmarks provide limited support for full-spherical closed-loop UAV tracking. To support systematic research in this setting, we introduce 360UAV-ETrack, a large-scale simulation benchmark built in CARLA. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:paper_overall , it provides synchronized panoramic and perspective observations, expert demonstrations, and diverse tracking scenarios spanning frontal and non-frontal target configurations. The training and validation collection comprises 2,652 sequences and 1,733,766 synchronized observation steps, complemented by 150 held-out scenarios for closed-loop evaluation. However, full-spherical perception introduces several challenges beyond expanded visual coverage. The wide FoV increases instance ambiguity, making target identity difficult to maintain across viewing directions. A single panoramic observation provides limited evidence of temporal motion, while ERP distortions and projection discontinuities complicate the translation of spatial relationships into metric control commands. To address these challenges, we propose 360UAV-TVLA, a reference-conditioned VLA framework comprising three complementary components. Specifically, persistent visual referring (PVR) establishes an instance-specific anchor to preserve target identity across viewing directions. Meanwhile, compressed temporal memory (CTM) efficiently aggregates historical panoramic features to capture target dynamics. Furthermore, geometry-aligned trajectory supervision (GTS) predicts future target positions in the fixed-heading control coordinate system, explicitly bridging panoramic perception and velocity control. Experiments across two VLA backbones demonstrate consistent improvements over standard fine-tuning, increasing normalized ATF from 22.56 to 35.28 with and from 25.68 to 33.64 with . The results also reveal a substantial discrepancy between offline imitation accuracy and online tracking reliability, highlighting the challenges of panoramic embodied tracking and motivating further research in this direction. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We investigate fixed-heading embodied UAV tracking, decoupling angular target coverage from heading control through full-spherical perception. To support this paradigm, we introduce 360UAV-ETrack, a large-scale benchmark featuring diverse tracking tasks, expert demonstrations, and closed-loop evaluation. We develop 360UAV-TVLA, a reference-conditioned VLA framework with compressed panoramic memory and control-aligned trajectory supervision, demonstrating improved closed-loop tracking across two VLA backbones. 360UAV-ETrack Related Work Visual Perception and Tracking Panoramic vision expands scene coverage but introduces projection distortions that motivate geometry-aware representations~ cohen2018spherical . 360VOT~ huang2023_360vot and 360VOTS~ xu2025_360vots benchmark omnidirectional object tracking and segmentation, while PanoVOS~ yan2024panovos investigates temporal consistency in panoramic video segmentation. Recent efforts extend panoramic perception to multi-object tracking~ luo2025omnidirectional,deng2026cylindtrack , out-of-view point tracking~ hudson2026tapvid , and spatial reasoning~ lin2026panoenv . However, these studies primarily address perception rather than action-conditioned target following, leaving full-spherical closed-loop tracking insufficiently explored. Embodied Visual Tracking Embodied visual tracking couples target perception with active motion control. Early methods improve robustness to distractors through adversarial learning~ zhong2021advatplus,zhong2021distraction,AIFlowAn,AIFlowShao , while offline reinforcement learning and adaptive policies support robust tracking across settings~ zhong2024offlineevt,wu2026adatracker . UAV-oriented methods such as D-VAT~ dionigi2024dvat , DAT~ sun2025openworld , and OA-VAT~ sun2026oavat investigate autonomous following and occlusion recovery. Recent VLA approaches, including TrackVLA~ wang2025trackvla , UAV-Track VLA~ zhang2026uavtrackvla , and TrackVLA++~ liu2026trackvlapp , unify target understanding and action prediction; VLM-assisted tracking further explores failure recovery~ wu2025vlmassistant . CosFly-Track~ wang2026cosflytrack provides large-scale demonstrations for aerial following. Nevertheless, these approaches predominantly use perspective observations, leaving the role of full-spherical perception in fixed-heading closed-loop UAV tracking underexplored. 360UAV-ETrack Benchmark sec:benchmark Simulation and Data Collection sec:simulation We construct 360UAV-ETrack in CARLA to study full-spherical embodied UAV tracking under fixed-heading control. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:paper_overall , the UAV follows a designated moving target through three-dimensional translation without heading adjustments. The training and validation set contains 2,652 sequences with 1,733,766 ERP frames (48.16 hours), covering eight tracking tasks and 13 weather conditions. Demonstrations are collected across five towns: Town02, Town05, Town06, Town07, and Town10HD. The UAV captures equirectangular projection (ERP) observations at , while simulation and low-level control operate at . Each demonstration provides synchronized panoramic and perspective observations, target references and annotations, UAV motion states, and expert velocity commands. Tracking Tasks sec:tracking_tasks As shown in Fig.~ fig:paper_overall , 360UAV-ETrack comprises eight tasks organized into two evaluation settings. Task I: Front-Initialized Tracking. Targets are initialized within the frontal field of view. The four tasks are (A1) FrontTrack, (A2) FrontUnderpass, (A3) FrontApproach, and (A4) FrontSelection. They evaluate persistent following, underpass navigation, target approach, and identity preservation among distractors, respectively. Task II: Omnidirectional Acquisition and Tracking. The four tasks are (B1) NonFrontTrack, (B2) DroneTrack, (B3) NonFrontApproach, and (B4) NonFrontSelection. These tasks extend evaluation to non-frontal target configurations and aerial targets, testing target acquisition and subsequent tracking under full-spherical observations. Held-Out Evaluation Set. We construct 150 frozen evaluation episodes across Town01, Town03, and Town04, which are disjoint from the training towns. Task I contains 51 episodes, with 21/7/5/18 episodes for A1--A4. Task II contains 99 episodes, with 44/6/13/36 episodes for B1--B4. The set includes 72 pedestrian, 72 vehicle, and 6 UAV-target episodes. Recorded expert demonstrations support offline replay, while the corresponding frozen scenarios support online closed-loop evaluation. Evaluation Protocol sec:evaluation All policies predict three-dimensional velocity commands in the same heading-aligned coordinate frame, using the first predicted command at each decision step. We evaluate offline prediction and online tracking separately. Offline Expert Replay. At each timestamp, the policy receives the recorded expert observation and motion-state inputs. Predicted velocities are integrated from the expert initial position with , without feeding the integrated trajectory back into the recorded inputs. We report average displacement error (ADE) against the expert trajectory, averaging position errors over each complete sequence and then across episodes. Offline success rate, , evaluates the integrated trajectory against the recorded target positions using the original distance constraints and a 15-consecutive-frame failure threshold. It measures distance compliance and does not evaluate visibility from the predicted positions. Online Closed-Loop Evaluation. Each policy receives simulator observations and executes velocity commands in closed loop. We compare three timing protocols by the delay included in simulated time: where is the measured policy latency, from policy entry to the complete action chunk being available as a synchronized CPU array, and denotes external overhead, including observation preparation, communication, and rendering. These delays exclude physics-step quantization. (i) Synchronous closed loop. The simulator pauses during inference and then advances by (10Hz) under the new command, excluding inference latency from simulated time. (ii) End-to-end real-time closed loop. The simulator advances continuously during asynchronous inference, exposing the policy to both model latency and external overhead. (iii) Model-compute-delay closed loop. Only measured model latency is injected into simulated time. For an observation and UAV state captured at time , the new command takes effect at the first physics boundary at or after . Observations and scoring run at , with at most one prediction pending. title: A Simple Yet Effective Agent for Open-World Aerial Object Search
summary: Open-world aerial object search methods often rely on persistent spatial maps, learned world models, or task-specific policy training. To examine how far a minimal, training-free design can go, we introduce SimpleUAV, an agent built around a frozen, off-the-shelf vision-language model (VLM). SimpleUAV separates current-view target assessment from history-conditioned action selection, combining fresh candidate evidence with lightweight search context. Local geometry converts visual selections into bounded straight-line movements, depth-based checks halt blocked segments, and measured execution feedback guides subsequent decisions. This closed loop sustains search without persistent spatial maps or task-specific training. SimpleUAV achieves 41.61% Success Rate (SR) on UAV-ON and 11.98% on AerialDojo-200K, compared with 23.80% and 3.20% for the strongest prior baselines, respectively. With limited benchmark-specific adaptation, the same core agent transfers to aerial Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) on TravelUAV, improving Full SR by at least 19.66% across all three splits under L1 assistance. These results establish a strong baseline for evaluating when additional architectural complexity benefits aerial search.
full_text: Stronger aerial search with a minimal agent. Representative prior systems (top) use semantic belief maps, explicit spatial memory, or learned world models. SimpleUAV (bottom) uses a frozen VLM in a local depth-guided closed loop, requiring neither persistent spatial maps nor task-specific training, yet improves success rate (SR) by 17.8 over the strongest prior result. fig:teaser ] 6.875in 0.3125in ( - )/2-1in- ptm Introduction sec:intro Aerial object-goal navigation requires an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) to locate and approach a target described in natural language in an unfamiliar outdoor environment~ xiao2025uavon, ji2026cityavos, feng2026aerialdojo . This capability supports applications such as search and rescue~ wu2023uavrescue and infrastructure inspection~ tse2024uavinspection . Given neither the target location nor detailed route instructions zhou2026octmem , the UAV must decide where to search, which observations warrant further inspection, and when the available evidence supports stopping ji2026searchworld . These decisions are tightly coupled in large, partially observed outdoor environments. The target may remain outside the UAV's field of view for much of an episode, requiring contextual cues to guide exploration~ kim2026raven,xiao2026aerobelief . Even if a candidate appears, distance, occlusion, and visually similar distractors can make its identity uncertain~ yang2026skyagent . Moving closer or changing altitude may reveal discriminative attributes, but also changes the visible scene and exposes the UAV to new obstacles~ chen2026airhunt . Thus, effective search requires semantic judgments, search context, and three-dimensional motion to remain coordinated as observations evolve. Recent aerial search systems address these challenges with specialized spatial representations and predictive models. Three representative directions are shown in Figure~ fig:teaser : [leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt,topsep=3pt] Semantic Maps and Beliefs. Task-oriented semantic, attraction, uncertainty, or value maps turn local observations into sustained search guidance ~ ji2026cityavos, zhang2026apex, chen2026airhunt . AeroBelief further separates contextual cues from target-specific evidence through dual-layer semantic-spatial belief maps~ xiao2026aerobelief . Explicit Spatial Memory. Semantic voxel-ray memory kim2026raven , sliding local maps with sparse global history hou2026slider , and adaptive octree memory with instruction-guided queries zhou2026octmem organize fragmented observations across changing viewpoints. Learned World Models. SearchWorld combines explicit spatial memory with learned dynamics to reason about action consequences and improve its exploration policy through imagined rollouts~ ji2026searchworld . These approaches introduce persistent representations, dedicated memory-processing modules, or task-specific model and policy training. At the same time, pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) offer broad semantic knowledge and open-vocabulary visual understanding~ bai2025qwen3, qwen36_35b_a3b . These capabilities provide a basis for interpreting target descriptions, identifying promising search regions, and assessing visible candidates without navigation-specific fine-tuning. They motivate a systematic evaluation of how effectively a frozen VLM can support aerial search when paired with lightweight search context and local geometric execution. This leads us to ask: 0em width 2.0pt -4pt-1.6em How far can a minimal, training-free VLM-based agent go in open-world aerial search? We investigate this question with SimpleUAV, a closed-loop agent built around a frozen, off-the-shelf VLM. The VLM first assesses candidate targets from current multi-view observations alone, then selects actions using localized candidates, recent interactions, and a bounded text summary. This separates current visual assessment from the context needed to maintain search continuity. Local geometry converts visual selections into bounded straight-line movements, while depth-based obstacle checks halt blocked segments. Measured execution outcomes inform the next observation and decision cycle, connecting semantic reasoning to actual motion without persistent spatial maps or task-specific policy training. Without task-specific fine-tuning, SimpleUAV improves success rate (SR) over the strongest compared baselines by 17.81 on UAV-ON xiao2025uavon and 8.78 on AerialDojo-200K feng2026aerialdojo . On the aerial VLN benchmark TravelUAV wang2024openuav , it improves Full SR by at least 19.66 across all three evaluation splits under L1 assistance. Even with a compact 4B VLM, SimpleUAV exceeds the strongest prior UAV-ON baseline by 14.13 in SR. Our main contributions are summarized below. [leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt,topsep=3pt] We show that a minimal, training-free agent built around a frozen VLM can substantially outperform specialized systems in open-world aerial search without persistent spatial maps or task-specific policy training. We propose SimpleUAV, separating current-view target assessment from history-conditioned action selection and closing the loop through local geometric execution feedback to sustain search, while requiring fresh visual and geometric evidence for approach and stopping. We demonstrate generalization across environments and navigation tasks, transferring SimpleUAV from UAV-ON to AerialDojo-200K and TravelUAV with limited benchmark-specific adaptation and no additional training, achieving the highest SR among compared methods. Related Work sec:related_work Aerial Object-Goal Navigation. Indoor ObjectNav has expanded from category-conditioned exploration~ chaplot2020semexp, ramakrishnan2022poni to zero-shot open-vocabulary search~ gadre2023cow , distinguishing unseen-object search from navigation to visible candidates~ dang2023dual . Aerial benchmarks specify instance-level language or image goals xiao2025uavon, ji2026cityavos, feng2026aerialdojo . Exploration uses frontiers yamauchi1997frontier or viewpoint planning based on target visibility and search history (Star-Searcher luo2024starsearcher ). AOA xiao2025uavon prompts movement selection from onboard observations and recent poses. Aerial systems aggregate cross-view evidence using geometric memory (octrees, voxel grids, and sliding local maps) zhou2026octmem, kim2026raven, hou2026slider or semantic maps that prioritize regions and retain target evidence zhang2026apex, ji2026cityavos, chen2026airhunt, xiao2026aerobelief . AeroBelief xiao2026aerobelief separates contextual cues from target beliefs, while SkyAgent yang2026skyagent revises hypotheses under conflicting observations. Predictive methods estimate unseen semantics, action outcomes, or future aerial views zhang2024imagine, nie2025wmnav, zhang2025anwm , with SearchWorld ji2026searchworld learning its exploration policy from imagined trajectories. SimpleUAV sustains search with a frozen VLM, local depth geometry, recent observations, execution feedback, and a bounded text summary, without persistent spatial maps, learned world models, or policy training. VLM-based Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN). VLN maps route instructions to sequential actions, from indoor viewpoint graphs (Room-to-Room~ anderson2018r2r ) to continuous control (VLN-CE~ krantz2020vlnce ). Advances include richer instruction supervision and longer observation histories~ fried2018speaker, ku2020rxr, chen2021hamt , prompting with textual history, topological maps, or specialized experts zhou2024navgpt, chen2024mapgpt, long2024discussnav , and trained action prediction from pretrained multimodal representations zhou2024navgpt2, zhang2024navid . Aerial VLN supports simulated and real 3D flight~ liu2023aerialvln, wang2024openuav, lee2025citynav through spatial representations linking landmarks to motion~ gao2025stmr, zhang2025citynavagent, jiang2026spatialfly, xu2026geonav , learned multimodal policies cai2025flightgpt, gao2025openfly, zhang2025navfom , or observation histories and predicted views or spatial maps wang2023dreamwalker, jiang2025longfly, wang2026forefly, liu2026airforesight . SkyVLN~ li2025skyvln couples language planning with nonlinear model predictive control. SimpleUAV addresses open-world object search by assessing candidates solely from current views and selecting actions using recent search context. Approaching requires a visible, depth-localized candidate, while stopping further requires a confirmed match within stopping range. Language-Guided Embodied Agents. Language-guided agents ground semantic decisions in executable actions and revise plans through feedback. SayCan ichter2023saycan assesses skill feasibility through learned affordances, while ~ shah2023lmnav uses a pretrained policy to navigate between visually grounded landmarks. Reflexion shinn2023reflexion uses textual feedback across attempts, while Inner Monologue huang2023innermonologue feeds execution outcomes and scene observations to the planner within tasks. Object-search agents update search state through language-model reasoning, refine localization through new viewpoints, or replan when observations contradict semantic-map predictions cao2025cognav, qin2025aprr, ko2025care . PSC-AVDN qi2026pscavdn shares spatial memory between separate aerial exploration and confirmation stages. SimpleUAV guides VLM search after incomplete or blocked movements using measured displacement and segment termination status from bounded straight-line motion with local depth checks. Method sec:method Aerial search requires the UAV to assess visible candidates, retain useful search context, and respond to obstacles during motion. To coordinate these requirements, the SimpleUAV agent couples a frozen VLM with local depth geometry in a recurrent Select-Fly Straight-Check and Halt loop, as shown in Figure fig:method . Problem Formulation sec:method_task Given a language goal describing a target object, the UAV starts at position and must explore, approach the target, and stop within a decision budget. At decision step , it receives its position and four RGB-D views with camera poses, giving the observation : Here, the position lies in , and indexes the front, left, right, and downward cameras. For view , and are the RGB and depth images, and is the homogeneous camera-to-world transform. The VLM receives RGB images and textual context, while the program uses depth and calibration to locate candidates and check motion. Success requires a collision-free episode ending with an accepted stop within the target's evaluation radius. The ground-truth target position is used only for evaluation. The high-level action has a type in: Each action specifies a view and image region. Vertical exploration additionally specifies ascent or descent, while Approach and Stop reference a candidate identifier in the current candidate catalog. Executing each movement action traces a single step-bounded straight-line segment via the controller's low-level velocity commands. Select sec:method_selection At each decision step , the UAV selects an intended region to inspect or approach, without maintaining persistent spatial maps. Rather than training a separate object detector or conflating target verification with search planning, we use two sequential queries to the same frozen VLM : the first performs stateless candidate assessment from the current views, and the second selects an action using the localized candidates and recent search history. Each entry records the candidate’s view, bounding box, visible attributes, and match label. title: Can Visual World Models See Force?
summary: World models and vision-language-action policy models are increasingly proposed as foundations for robot manipulation. They predict how scenes evolve and which actions to take, yet successful manipulation depends not solely on following observable trajectories but also on the hidden variable of interaction force. Neurophysiology has shown that humans possess a visual prior for this hidden variable, motivating us to ask the question: Do the representations of visual foundation models also capture the forces involved in an interaction? We define force awareness as the ability of representations to (1) indicate when contact force is applied, (2) track how it changes during an interaction, and (3) reflect how large it is. We probe frozen image, video, world- and policy model representations with a lightweight readout trained on synchronized video and force measurements from two manipulation datasets. Our experiments show that most models capture when contact occurs but not how much force is being applied. Surprisingly, robot post-training does not improve this either, highlighting an important gap in current models capabilities.
full_text: World models and vision-language-action policy models are increasingly proposed as foundations for robot manipulation. They predict how scenes evolve and which actions to take, yet successful manipulation depends not solely on following observable trajectories but also on the hidden variable of interaction force. Neurophysiology has shown that humans possess a visual prior for this hidden variable, motivating us to ask the question: Do the representations of visual foundation models also capture the forces involved in an interaction? We define force awareness as the ability of representations to (1) indicate when contact force is applied, (2) track how it changes during an interaction, and (3) reflect how large it is. We probe frozen image, video, world- and policy model representations with a lightweight readout trained on synchronized video and force measurements from two manipulation datasets. Our experiments show that most models capture when contact occurs but not how much force is being applied. Surprisingly, robot post-training does not improve this either, highlighting an important gap in current models capabilities. Introduction sec:intro World-action models may enable generalist robot manipulation by learning to predict how the world changes together with the actions a robot takes. DreamZero, for example, jointly predicts future video and actions, building on large-scale video pretraining~ ye2026world . Related approaches use predictive video representations for planning or train vision-language-action models across diverse robot demonstrations~ assran2025v,kim2024openvla,black2024pi_0,bjorck2025gr00t . These efforts raise the prospect that physical understanding can emerge from more video, larger models, and more robot data. Yet inaccurate force application has been identified as a failure mode of robot foundation models~ fact2026,zhang2025ta , which commonly predict motion targets while leaving force control to low-level controllers~ assran2025v,kim2024openvla,black2024pi_0,bjorck2025gr00t,agarwal2026cosmos . These failures raise the question of whether the models' representations capture the forces involved in manipulation, beyond the motion they predict. An example of similar motion trajectories but different force application can be seen in everyday activities such as opening a fridge vs. a cabinet door. The doors can follow similar trajectories but require different forces because of friction or resistance that is difficult to see. Vision can provide useful cues here: humans use visual appearance to anticipate an object's weight and scale their initial lifting forces~ buckingham2009living , while visual feedback during lifting helps correct expectation-driven force errors~ buckingham2010lifting . These findings motivate us to investigate whether visual world models also acquire representations that implicitly encode interaction force. Prior evaluations of visual foundation models reveal difficulties with hidden mechanical properties and broader physical understanding~ tung2023physion++,chow2025physbench . At the same time, probing studies find geometric information, physical plausibility signals, and motion variables in pretrained representations~ el2024probing,huang2026much, esmati2026invisible . Readouts of elasticity, viscosity, and friction provide further evidence of accessible physical information, although accurate value prediction in real-world videos remains challenging~ zhan2026inferring . Together, these studies establish the systematic evaluation of physical and geometric information in pretrained representations as a research contribution in its own right. We extend this line of inquiry to interaction force by asking: how much force can be decoded from models trained for general visual, generative, and action objectives? We probe 13 different models spanning image and geometry encoders, self-supervised video encoders, generative world models, and vision-language and policy models, on synchronized video and force measurements from the Hoi! dataset~ engelbracht2026hoi , and the larger robotic RH20T~ fang2024rh20t dataset. The model set contains matched comparisons: base checkpoints and their robot-trained counterparts, different sizes within the Wan and Cosmos3 families, and two camera views of the same interactions. We separate three capabilities that are often conflated: detecting when contact force is applied, tracking how it changes within an interaction, and recovering how much force is applied. Our main findings are: Detecting contact is easy, recovering magnitude is not. Most representations detect when force is applied, including single-image encoders, but not how much. Nearly all compress the measured force range, and on Hoi!\ most are less accurate than predicting the mean contact force. V-JEPA is the exception. In the Hoi!\ gripper view and on RH20T, it tracks force best and explains the most variance in contact force, although at most . Neither video input nor model size accounts for this: VideoMAEv2 observes the same clips, and world models of up to 14B parameters remain below the 1B-parameter V-JEPA encoder. Robot training does not reliably improve force awareness. Of four robot-trained world and VLA models, only DreamZero tracks force better than the model it builds on, and only on Hoi!. On RH20T it does not, although its predictions cover more of the measured force range. Together, these results suggest that force awareness does not come for free with video generation or robot training. It can be learned though, through direct force supervision: fine-tuning V-JEPA on RH20T force labels improves force tracking there and transfers to Hoi!\ without retraining. This makes force supervision a promising direction, and force a quantity worth evaluating alongside geometry, video quality and task success. Related Work sec:rel_work World models and policies for manipulation. Video models learn how scenes change through different training objectives. VideoMAEv2 reconstructs masked video content~ wang2023videomae , V-JEPA predicts missing features~ mur2026v , and LeVJEPA learns consistent features across views~ kuhn2026levjepa , while Wan and Cosmos learn to generate video~ wan2025wan,nvidia2025cosmospredict2,agarwal2026cosmos . These models increasingly serve robot control. V-JEPA~2 plans actions in its feature space~ assran2025v , and world-action models such as DreamZero and the DROID checkpoints of Cosmos~3 predict future video and robot actions jointly~ ye2026world,agarwal2026cosmos . VLA models take a different route and add action prediction to a vision-language model, as in OpenVLA, , and GR00T, which builds on Cosmos-Reason2~ kim2024openvla,black2024pi_0,bjorck2025gr00t,grootcard,reason2card . We probe models from all of these groups, with DINOv3 and VGGT- as image and geometry baselines~ simeoni2025dinov3,wang2026vggt . None of them receives force as input or predicts it directly. Why force matters for manipulation. Contact-rich tasks remain difficult for these approaches. FACT~ fact2026 traces the failures of VLA models in such tasks to two sources, imprecise actions and missing responses to contact force, and TA-VLA~ zhang2025ta shows that giving a VLA model torque as input and as a prediction target improves its success in contact-rich tasks. Other works add physical feedback around the policy. Lee et al.~ lee2019making combine vision, force/torque, and robot state to learn representations for insertion, Reactive Diffusion Policy pairs a slow visual policy with fast tactile feedback~ xue2025reactive , and FP2~ fp2_2026 separates task-level action generation from force regulation driven by wrench and proprioceptive history. FD-VLA~ fdvla2026 instead distills measured force into a representation conditioned on vision and robot state, so that the deployed policy needs no force sensor. This relies on force being partly predictable from what the robot sees. The feedback itself comes from dedicated force sensors, as in RH20T and Hoi!~ fang2024rh20t,engelbracht2026hoi , or from optical tactile sensors such as DenseTact~2.0~ do2022densetact . Estimating force from visual observations. Force can also be estimated from images directly, and recent benchmarks have made this a task of its own~ engelbracht2026hoi . Pham et al.~ pham2015towards combine RGB-D tracking with mechanical constraints to infer manipulation forces, accounting for the different forces that can produce the same motion. Learning-based methods exploit visual cues at contact. VisGel predicts tactile observations from external images~ li2019connecting , and PressureVision and EgoPressure estimate hand pressure from images with synchronized pressure measurements~ grady2022pressurevision,zhao2025egopressure . EgoPHI estimates 3D hand-object contact and force from egocentric images and object geometry, supervised with simulated forces~ ilic2026egophi , and Hoi!\ provides multi-view video with measured forces during articulated manipulation~ engelbracht2026hoi . All of these methods are designed and supervised for force. They show that force is visible to some extent, but not whether a model trained without it captures it. Probing physical understanding. What a pretrained model has learned can be measured by training a small readout on its frozen features. Such probes show that visual features predict surface geometry but struggle to match surfaces across viewpoints~ el2024probing , that image, video, and 3D encoders have different strengths in scene understanding~ man2024lexicon3d , and that video models encode depth, 3D points, and camera pose~ huang2026much . For physics, the picture is less favorable. Physion tests whether models anticipate object contact~ bear2021physion , Physion++ shows that they do not reliably infer latent mechanical properties from observed interactions~ tung2023physion++ , and Kang et al.~ kang2024far find that video generators fail to apply physical laws beyond their training distribution. Vision-language models show similar weaknesses across physical properties and dynamics~ chow2025physbench , and when asked for numerical estimates of size, velocity, and acceleration, they give plausible but inaccurate answers~ puyin2026quantiphy . Some physical information is nevertheless present inside pretrained models. V-JEPA separates physically possible from impossible videos, unlike models that predict pixels~ garrido2025intuitive . Probing studies show that physical plausibility and motion variables are decodable from video-diffusion states~ esmati2026invisible , and lightweight readouts of video features estimate elasticity, viscosity, and friction, although less accurately than cue-based reference methods~ zhan2026inferring . Force has so far entered these models only as an input. Force Prompting~ gillman2026force and PhyCo~ narayanan2026phyco train video generators, the latter on top of Cosmos-Predict2, to follow a specified force. Whether the features of pretrained models describe the force in an observed interaction has not been measured. We address this with a probe on synchronized video and force measurements, and separate detecting contact, tracking force changes, and recovering force magnitude. Probing Force in Frozen Representations sec:method We measure how much interaction force can be decoded from a frozen foundation model. Following prior probing works~ el2024probing , we keep all model weights fixed and train only a lightweight readout on its features (Fig.~ fig:method ). The readout is identical for all models; only the feature extraction differs between model families due to architectural differences. Force decoding task sec:task The input is a video window of a manipulation with synchronized force measurements . title: Tortho-Gaussian++: Suppressing Geometric Drift and Floaters for Robust Gravity-Aligned TDOM Generation in Large-Scale Aerial Scenes
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has demonstrated remarkable performance in aerial scene reconstruction, motivating its recent extension to true digital orthophoto maps (TDOMs) generation. We propose Tortho-Gaussian++, a novel 3DGS training framework that suppresses geometric drift and floaters and automatically prunes unreliable peripheral regions, coupled with a robust gravity-aligned TDOM rendering solution. First, we explore geometric support via viewing-ray-based geometric observability analysis, quantitatively characterizing the reliability for each Gaussian and subsequently pruning peripheral regions with particularly weak geometric support. Second, the optimizer state initialization is refined for newly created Gaussians during densification, intrinsically suppressing drift and floaters without external priors. Lastly, a robust gravity direction estimation solution is designed, combining image-derived gravity cues, camera-distribution priors and nadir views, to achieve a gravity-aligned orthogonal projection reference for TDOM rendering. Extensive experiments on multiple large-scale UAV (Unmanned Aerial Vehicle) datasets demonstrate that our Tortho-Gaussian++ outperforms vanilla 3DGS by 0.5-3.5 dB in average PSNR and yields comparable or superior performance to prior-guided 3DGS methods. Notably, it reduces the training time, VRAM and Gaussian number by 45.5%, 47.2%, and 58.6%, respectively. Qualitative evaluations confirm that our method effectively suppresses drift and floaters, while robust gravity direction estimation reduces tilt-induced facade artifacts in TDOMs.
full_text: [mode = title] Tortho-Gaussian++: Suppressing Geometric Drift and Floaters for Robust Gravity-Aligned TDOM Generation in Large-Scale Aerial Scenes Xiang Wang Xin Wang Zongqian Zhan organization= School of Geodesy and Geomatics, Wuhan University , city= Wuhan , postcode= 430079 , state= Hubei , country= China 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has demonstrated remarkable performance in aerial scene reconstruction, motivating its recent extension to true digital orthophoto maps (TDOMs) generation. However, when applied to large-scale aerial scenes, existing 3DGS-based methods still suffer from three critical practical limitations: (1) insufficient overlapping views and poorly conditioned viewing ray geometries, particularly near flight-strip boundaries, leave Gaussians under-constrained along specific directions, resulting in unreliable peripheral reconstructions, geometric drift, and floaters; (2) during densification, the moment-step misalignment of the Adam optimizer for newly created Gaussians can amplify each subsequent parameter update, exacerbating the drift and floaters; (3) the orthogonal projection reference for splatting TDOMs from 3DGS is typically from manual rotational correction or camera-distribution priors, which might fail to provide a reliable gravity-aligned reference. To address these issues, we propose Tortho-Gaussian++, a novel 3DGS training framework that suppresses geometric drift and floaters and automatically prunes unreliable peripheral regions, coupled with a robust gravity-aligned TDOM rendering solution. First, we explore geometric support via viewing-ray-based geometric observability analysis, quantitatively characterizing the reliability for each Gaussian and subsequently pruning peripheral regions with particularly weak geometric support. Second, the optimizer state initialization is refined for newly created Gaussians during densification, intrinsically suppressing drift and floaters without external priors. Lastly, a robust gravity direction estimation solution is designed, combining image-derived gravity cues, camera-distribution priors and nadir views, to achieve a gravity-aligned orthogonal projection reference for TDOM rendering. Extensive experiments on multiple large-scale UAV (Unmanned Aerial Vehicle) datasets demonstrate that our Tortho-Gaussian++ outperforms vanilla 3DGS by 0.5--3.5\,dB in average PSNR and yields comparable or superior performance to prior-guided 3DGS methods. Notably, it reduces the training time, VRAM and Gaussian number by 45.5 , 47.2 , and 58.6 , respectively. Qualitative evaluations confirm that our method effectively suppresses drift and floaters, while robust gravity direction estimation reduces tilt-induced facade artifacts in TDOMs. Furthermore, as a prior-free training framework, Tortho-Gaussian++ can be readily integrated into existing 3DGS-based pipelines, greatly enhancing the practicality of 3DGS for TDOM generation. Project Web: https://github.com/IRIS-LAB-whu/Tortho-Gaussian-PlusPlus/ 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) True Digital Orthophoto Map (TDOM) Geometric Observability Analysis Adam Optimizer Gravity-aligned Rendering Introduction sec:introduction True Digital Orthophoto Map (TDOM), as a digital foundation, has been widely used in many practical applications, such as digital twins, urban analysis and etc. Traditional photogrammetric pipelines typically employ Structure-from-Motion (SfM) and Multi-View Stereo (MVS) to estimate reliable camera poses and dense point clouds schonberger2016structure,schonberger2016pixelwise , followed by digital differential rectification and occlusion detection for TDOM generation 12habib2007new . Despite achieving high geometric accuracy, these approaches remain computationally demanding for large-scale aerial scenes li2025ulsr , and the quality of TDOMs is strictly bounded by the quality of the Digital Surface Model (DSM) 12habib2007new . Recently, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) kerbl20233d has achieved reconstruction quality comparable to Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) mildenhall2021nerf , while offering substantially greater computational efficiency owing to its highly parallelized design and efficient use of GPUs. These capabilities have driven the widespread adoption of 3DGS for TDOM generation via incorporating orthogonal projection wang2026tortho,yang2025ortho,xu2026tdom,wang2025hygs,wang2026high,yang2026fastpro , effectively bypassing complex traditional photogrammetric pipelines. Despite these recent advances, maintaining both high geometric and rendering fidelity remains challenging when applying 3DGS to large-scale aerial scenes lin2024vastgaussian,liu2024citygaussian,li2025ulsr,zhang2026geogs . Insufficient overlapping views and poorly conditioned viewing ray geometries can leave the scene geometry insufficiently constrained, leading to severe geometric drift and floaters. To alleviate this problem, existing methods typically incorporate data-driven priors li2024dngaussian,yang2025ortho,turkulainen2025dn to guide Gaussian optimization or introduce multi-view geometric consistency constraints chen2024pgsr,xu2024mvpgs to improve surface accuracy and suppress reconstruction artifacts. However, the inherent mechanisms underlying geometric drift and floaters remain insufficiently explored. In addition, splatting TDOMs from 3DGS still relies on some manual or heuristic procedures for peripheral cropping and orthogonal directional reference wang2026tortho,yang2025ortho . Overall, as Fig. fig:muscle illustrates, achieving high rendering fidelity and reliable TDOM generation with 3DGS-based methods in large-scale aerial scenes involves the following three practical challenges: (1) Insufficient overlapping views and poorly conditioned viewing ray geometries. In regions with limited viewing diversity, the rays intersecting a Gaussian typically span a narrow angular range. For an individual Gaussian, photometric constraints are strong in the plane perpendicular to the viewing ray but much weaker along the ray direction. This directional imbalance creates conditions for Gaussians to move along weakly constrained directions. Gaussians with particularly weak geometric support are often concentrated near flight-strip boundaries, severely degrading overall geometric fidelity. As Fig. fig:muscle shows, on the SMBU dataset, both the generated TDOM of Tortho-Gaussian wang2026tortho and Ortho-3DGS yang2025ortho exhibit severely distorted peripheral reconstructions, which are cropped manually. In contrast, Tortho-Gaussian++ automatically prunes unreliable peripheral regions. (2) Optimization-driven geometric drift and floaters. Although 3DGS adopts the standard Adam optimizer used in deep neural networks (DNNs) kingma2014adam , the initialization during densification fails to align the moment history and step count of newly created Gaussians as required by Adam, a phenomenon we term moment-step misalignment. This misalignment distorts bias correction and can amplify each subsequent parameter update. Furthermore, under synchronous optimization ding2026step , a Gaussian that is invisible in the current viewpoint receives zero gradients but still undergoes parameter updates. Notably, in large-scale UAV scenes, an individual Gaussian is typically invisible in most training views, so such updates occur repeatedly, promoting displacement along weakly constrained directions. While additional geometric constraints can alleviate the resulting errors, loshchilov2017fixing point out that the gradient coupling in Adam can destabilize regularization, and these constraints fail to address the underlying moment-step misalignment. As shown in Fig. fig:muscle , on the LOWER dataset, both Tortho-Gaussian and depth-prior-guided Ortho-3DGS yield much more drift and floaters than our Tortho-Gaussian++ in both orthogonal views (1, 3) and perspective views (2, 4). (3) Unreliable orthogonal projection reference. Existing 3DGS-based TDOM generation methods determine the rendering direction through manual rotational correction wang2026tortho,xu2026tdom,wang2026high or camera-distribution priors yang2025ortho . Such manual alignment or camera-based heuristics may leave residual errors in the down-vector, resulting in visible building facade artifacts. Their reliability can further deteriorate for datasets containing exclusively oblique views or substantial variations in flight altitude. As Fig. fig:muscle illustrates, the Residence dataset typifies such challenging scenes, featuring oblique-only views and varying altitudes. Consequently, the rendering directions of Tortho-Gaussian and Ortho-3DGS are severely skewed, whereas Tortho-Gaussian++ preserves a precise orthogonal projection direction. To address these limitations, we propose Tortho-Gaussian++, a novel 3DGS training framework for high rendering fidelity aerial reconstruction, coupled with a robust gravity-aligned TDOM rendering solution. Our key insight is that poorly conditioned viewing ray geometries create conditions for geometric drift and floaters, while moment-step misalignment during densification amplifies the updates that drive them. Moreover, accurate geometry must be paired with a reliable gravity-aligned orthogonal projection reference for TDOM rendering. First, we evaluate geometric support through a viewing-ray-based geometric observability analysis, quantitatively characterizing the reconstruction reliability of each Gaussian and enabling the automatic pruning of peripheral regions with particularly weak geometric support. Second, we refine the optimizer state initialization for newly created Gaussians during densification by transferring accumulated moment estimates from parent Gaussians to their children. This maintains consistency between the moment history and step count, intrinsically suppressing drift and floaters without introducing external priors. Third, we develop a robust gravity direction estimation solution for orthogonal projection reference, which integrates image-derived gravity cues from a pretrained single-image camera calibration network jin2023perspective , camera-distribution priors, and nadir views through confidence-based selection and fusion. The resulting down-vector enables gravity-aligned TDOM rendering, significantly reducing tilt-induced facade artifacts in TDOMs. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: We introduce a viewing-ray-based geometric observability analysis that quantitatively characterizes the reliability of each Gaussian in large-scale aerial scenes, enabling automatic pruning of unreliable peripheral regions. We identify moment–step misalignment during densification as a critical source of amplified Gaussian parameter updates, and introduce an optimizer-state inheritance strategy that intrinsically suppresses geometric drift and floaters without relying on external priors. We develop a robust gravity-direction estimation method that combines image-derived gravity cues, camera-distribution priors, and nadir views through confidence-based selection and fusion, enabling gravity-aligned TDOM rendering with reduced tilt-induced facade artifacts. Related Work sec:related_work This section reviews relevant literature in three key areas: 3D Gaussian Splatting for large-scale scenes, novel view synthesis for TDOM generation, and gravity direction estimation for orthogonal projection. 3D Gaussian Splatting for Large-Scale Scene 3DGS combines explicit scene representations with differentiable rasterization, enabling efficient training and real-time rendering kerbl20233d . However, its application to large-scale aerial scenes faces two primary challenges: the high computational and memory costs of massive scenes lin2024vastgaussian and limited geometry accuracy under poorly conditioned viewing ray geometries zhang2026geogs . title: Event-WAM: Learning to Act with Event-Derived Futures
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) leverage future visual modeling for robotic action learning, with recent studies exploring alternative or complementary objectives beyond conventional RGB prediction. We introduce Event-WAM, which incorporates event-derived visual changes as auxiliary future supervision alongside RGB. Event-WAM constructs temporally structured event representations from RGB demonstrations and encodes them using a frozen pretrained RGB video VAE, without training an event-specific VAE. Joint RGB--Event latent flow matching provides appearance- and change-oriented supervision without requiring event observations or explicit future generation at inference. Across simulated benchmarks, Event-WAM maintains comparable performance under standard conditions, while robustness gains under perturbations are benchmark-dependent, including improvements on LIBERO-Plus. Real-world evaluations further demonstrate improved manipulation success under both standard and unseen perturbation conditions. Further analyses show that policy improvements are not consistently accompanied by higher future prediction fidelity, suggesting the potential of change-oriented supervision for action learning.
full_text: World Action Models (WAMs) leverage future visual modeling for robotic action learning, with recent studies exploring alternative or complementary objectives beyond conventional RGB prediction. We introduce Event-WAM, which incorporates event-derived visual changes as auxiliary future supervision alongside RGB. Event-WAM constructs temporally structured event representations from RGB demonstrations and encodes them using a frozen pretrained RGB video VAE, without training an event-specific VAE. Joint RGB--Event latent flow matching provides appearance- and change-oriented supervision without requiring event observations or explicit future generation at inference. Across simulated benchmarks, Event-WAM maintains comparable performance under standard conditions, while robustness gains under perturbations are benchmark-dependent, including improvements on LIBERO-Plus. Real-world evaluations further demonstrate improved manipulation success under both standard and unseen perturbation conditions. Further analyses show that policy improvements are not consistently accompanied by higher future prediction fidelity, suggesting the potential of change-oriented supervision for action learning. Introduction sec:intro Recent advances in visual world modeling have established World Action Models (WAMs) as a promising approach to robotic manipulation. By jointly learning future visual dynamics and robot actions, WAMs leverage predictive supervision to support action generation. Early approaches~ unipi,dreamzero rely on iterative future video generation at inference, whereas Fast-WAM~ fastwam demonstrates that future modeling can benefit action learning without generating future video. More recently, Simple-WAM~ zhou2026makes shows that a single forward pass over fully noised future tokens can effectively condition action generation. Together, these advances shift attention from whether future videos must be generated at inference to how training-time future modeling shapes action-relevant representations. Alongside this progress, an important question concerns which aspects of the future should be modeled to support action learning. Conventional RGB-based future modeling provides rich supervision for both scene appearance and temporal evolution, but dense visual prediction does not explicitly emphasize dynamic changes over persistent scene content~ dcwam,yan2026deltawam,dreamwam . Recent studies have explored alternative or complementary future modeling objectives, including change-centric targets based on visual deltas, residuals, and temporal differences~ yan2026deltawam,wu2026delta,dcwam , as well as latent and multimodal future representations involving dynamics, geometry, and semantics~ lawam,dreamwam,hung2026modality , reflecting ongoing efforts to identify effective supervision targets for action learning. In this context, we consider event-based representations as an alternative form of visual-change supervision for WAMs. Events~ event_survey encode pixel-wise log-intensity changes through contrast thresholding, preserving polarity and temporal structure while suppressing unchanged content. While RGB frames provide dense appearance and static scene context, events emphasize sparse, temporally structured visual changes, complementing RGB appearance with change-oriented cues~ jiang2024evrgbhand,zhou2024eventfusion . These properties have encouraged the joint use of RGB and events across a wide range of vision tasks~ jiang2024evrgbhand,zhou2024eventfusion,xu2024dmr,kong2025dessert , yet whether RGB-derived event representations can provide effective future supervision for action learning, rather than serving as additional sensory inputs, remains largely unexplored in WAMs. To this end, we introduce Event-WAM, which integrates event-derived visual-change supervision with RGB future modeling for world-action learning. We construct temporally binned, polarity-separated event representations from existing RGB demonstrations and encode them using the same frozen pretrained RGB video VAE, mapping both RGB and event representations into a common latent space without training an event-specific encoder. Within a shared video backbone, Event-WAM jointly models RGB and event latents through parallel flow-matching objectives with independently sampled noise, combining appearance-oriented supervision with temporally organized visual-change signals. Following Simple-WAM's inference strategy, our approach incorporates both future modeling objectives into action learning without requiring event observations or explicit future generation at inference. We evaluate Event-WAM on simulated manipulation benchmarks, including LIBERO~ libero , LIBERO-Plus~ fei2025libero , and RoboTwin 2.0~ robotwin2 , as well as four real-world manipulation tasks using an SO-101 robotic arm~ so101 . Event-WAM maintains comparable performance under standard simulated conditions and improves robustness on LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin 2.0-Plus, but not under RoboTwin C2R randomization. In real-world manipulation, it further improves success under both standard and unseen perturbation conditions. We investigate RGB and event-based future modeling through loss-weighting ablations, single-target objectives, and analyses of future prediction fidelity. The results show that improvements in action performance are not consistently accompanied by higher future prediction quality. Since event representations are derived from RGB observations, these findings suggest that their benefit may arise from emphasizing action-relevant visual changes during future modeling rather than introducing additional sensory information. This interpretation is consistent with the limited gains observed in standard simulated settings and the more pronounced improvements on LIBERO-Plus and in real-world manipulation. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We investigate event-derived visual changes as complementary generative future targets alongside RGB in WAMs, examining their effects on robotic action learning and policy generalization. We introduce Event-WAM, which jointly models RGB and event-derived futures through flow matching within a shared pretrained backbone, combining appearance- and change-oriented supervision for action learning. We evaluate Event-WAM across simulated and real-world settings, demonstrating improved robustness under perturbations and higher success on physical robot tasks, with further analyses of supervision targets and of how prediction fidelity relates to action performance. Related Work sec:related World Action Models WAMs couple future-state modeling with robot action generation, often leveraging pretrained video diffusion or flow-matching backbones~ unipi,uva,dreamzero,fastwam . Fast-WAM~ fastwam demonstrates that training-time future modeling can benefit action learning without requiring future video generation at inference. More recently, ForeWAM~ forewam utilizes key--value representations of noise-initialized future slots for efficient action conditioning, while Simple-WAM~ zhou2026makes shows that a single forward pass over fully noised future tokens retains much of the generalization benefit of explicit future modeling. Faster-WAM~ fasterwam_future and BridgeWAM~ bridgewam further improve inference efficiency through sparse video--action interactions and compact latent bridge queries, respectively. OpenWAM- ~ openwam explores scalable world--action pretraining using egocentric and robot data. Recent studies explore alternative and complementary future modeling objectives to better capture visual dynamics. Some approaches predict structured or compact future representations~ hung2026modality,lawam , while others emphasize visual changes through frame differences and feature deltas~ yan2026deltawam,jiang2026deltawam,wu2026delta . EA-WM~ eawm uses VAE-encoded absolute RGB frame differences to supervise intermediate action--video fusion representations, whereas DC-WAM~ dcwam emphasizes interaction-induced dynamics through temporal-difference supervision and dynamic attention routing. Geometric and multimodal approaches further expand future supervision: 4D-WAM~ 4dwam aligns representations with 3D trajectory-field features, PrismWAM~ prismwam separates RGB-based semantic planning from depth-based physical rollout, and DreamWAM~ dreamwam jointly models RGB and optical flow with auxiliary geometric and semantic objectives. MT-WAM~ mtwam additionally uses future motion trajectories and visual features to shape one-pass predictive representations for action generation. In contrast, Event-WAM incorporates event-derived representations as complementary generative future targets jointly modeled with RGB through flow matching, using shared representations. Event-Based Vision and Robot Learning Event cameras~ event_survey capture asynchronous pixel-wise log-intensity changes, retaining polarity and fine-grained temporal information. Unlike RGB frames, which provide dense scene appearance and spatial context, events emphasize brightness transitions while suppressing unchanged content. These complementary characteristics have motivated RGB--Event fusion across various visual perception tasks~ jiang2024evrgbhand,zhou2024eventfusion,xu2024dmr,kong2025dessert . Given the limited availability of large-scale event-camera datasets, event simulation methods~ esim,v2e,eventgan enable the synthesis of event streams from conventional RGB videos without event cameras, facilitating broader research in event-based vision. Beyond perception, event representations have also been explored for future motion modeling and robotic policy learning. E-Motion~ emotion investigates future motion modeling from event sequences. In robotic learning, SEBVS~ sebvs explores simulated event observations for navigation and manipulation, while E-VLA~ evla and Event-VLA~ eventvla incorporate event observations into vision-language-action models. ECHO~ wang2026echo further combines wrist-mounted event observations with event-foresight queries in a latent world-action model. Whereas these robotic approaches require event observations at inference, Event-WAM uses RGB-derived events solely as training-time future targets alongside RGB supervision, without additional event sensing. Method sec:method Event-WAM integrates event-derived visual changes into RGB-based world-action learning as complementary future supervision. Building on the RGB-only formulation of Simple-WAM~ zhou2026makes , our approach jointly models future RGB and event latents through shared-backbone flow matching, while retaining single-pass future-token conditioning followed by iterative action denoising at inference.
