title: Who Is Ego? Scaling Cross-View Camera Wearer Identification and Segmentation beyond Humans
summary: A first-person (ego) image reveals what a camera sees, but not who or what carries it. Given a synchronized third-person (exo) image, camera wearer identification asks who is ego: which candidate carries the ego camera? We extend this task beyond humans to robots, vehicles, animals, and drones, and broaden its spatial scope (where is ego) from selecting a provided candidate mask to wearer segmentation with absence prediction and mutual camera localization across ego-exo views. We introduce FindEgo-1M, comprising 1.16M real and simulated ego-exo pairs across 12 wearer types, 17 domains, and 111 test settings. Our approach exploits a geometric relation: the ego camera's projection into the exo image, i.e., the epipole, lies on or near its wearer. We introduce EgoRay-ZS, the first method to turn a frozen feed-forward 3D reconstruction model, VGGT-$Ω$, into a training-free solution for wearer identification and segmentation. Its geometric readout ranks candidate masks or segmentation proposals by angular offset and distance to the ego camera, while the relative pose provides mutual camera directions. We then develop the full EgoRay model through pose-supervised training on FindEgo-1M and label-free test-time adaptation constrained by candidate masks. Without task-specific training, EgoRay-ZS achieves 78.0% identification accuracy on TF2023's original labels, versus 52.9% reported for the dataset-trained PEN. On FindEgo-1M, EgoRay achieves state-of-the-art chance-corrected accuracy of 87.1 and 77.7 on seen and unseen settings. On matched queries, EgoRay also outperforms GPT-6 Astra by 31.6 and 21.3 points on seen and unseen settings, respectively, while running $18\times$ faster. Data, code, and models will be released.

Introduction sec:intro Given synchronized first-person (ego) and third-person (exo) images, camera wearer identification asks who is ego: which person in the exo view carries the ego camera~ fan2017identifying,zhao2024pen ? This task connects a person's first-person footage to their presence in an external view, supporting applications such as body-camera analysis in broadcast or surveillance footage. When identifiers, GPS, and camera calibration are unavailable, this association must be inferred visually. Benchmarks such as TF2023 and TF2025~ zhao2024pen,zhao2026sequence have supported progress on this task. However, existing research remains limited in three respects. (1) Narrow wearer scope: studies focus on humans, overlooking the need to associate onboard and external observations in other settings. (2) Limited data scale and diversity: existing datasets constrain both training and systematic evaluation of generalization to new environments and wearer types. (3) Limited task scope: existing evaluations mostly identify the wearer among provided candidates or select a detected mask for segmentation~ zhao2024pen , leaving segmentation without given candidates, absence prediction, and mutual camera localization underexplored. We therefore ask whether who is ego can scale beyond human-centric identification, and address this question along three dimensions. First, we broaden the wearer scope to robots, vehicles, animals, and drones, recognizing cross-view camera wearer identification as a shared problem across camera-bearing agents. These settings introduce distinct challenges: robots of the same model can look nearly identical, while birds and drones may occupy only a few pixels in the exo view. Second, we scale training and evaluation through , combining public recordings, such as TF2023~ zhao2024pen and Ego-Exo4D~ grauman2024egoexo4d , with new simulations to provide 1.16M ego--exo pairs across 12 wearer types, 17 domains, and 111 test settings. Real recordings capture real-world variability, while simulation broadens coverage and supplies exact geometry. Evaluation spans four levels of generalization relative to training: new recordings at seen locations (L0), new locations within seen domains (L1), unseen data sources or scene types with seen wearer types (L2), and unseen wearer types (L3). The top of illustrates . Finally, we move beyond candidate-mask selection to wearer segmentation without given candidates, requiring methods to delineate the wearer or report its absence. We further study mutual camera localization, estimating each camera's direction from the other. Existing methods associate ego and exo views through appearance or motion matching~ fan2017identifying,ardeshir2016ego2top,zhao2024pen,zhao2026sequence . Appearance is ambiguous among similar-looking candidates, while motion requires video and distinct trajectories. We instead exploit a geometric relation: the wearer is where the camera is. The ego camera's projection into the exo image, i.e., the epipole, lies on or near its wearer~ chen2019epipole,chen2021belief . The bottom of illustrates how relative camera geometry reveals wearer identity. We are the first to use a feed-forward 3D reconstruction model, ~ vggtomega2026 , for this task. Our EgoRay-ZS combines the angular offset to each candidate mask with camera distance to distinguish candidates along similar rays. The same readout ranks SAM~3 proposals~ carion2025sam3 for segmentation and predicts absence through angular offset, while relative pose provides mutual camera directions. The full EgoRay model improves pose generalization through pose-supervised training on and test-time adaptation, which constrains the projected ego camera to lie on or near a candidate mask, providing a geometric learning signal without wearer labels. Without task-specific training, EgoRay-ZS identifies 78.0 of wearers on TF2023's original labels~ zhao2024pen , compared with 52.9 reported for the dataset-trained PEN~ zhao2024pen ( ). On , achieves state-of-the-art identification accuracy at all four generalization levels. For the most challenging unseen wearer types (L3), it reaches 71.1 chance-corrected accuracy, versus 42.1 for the strongest competing 3D model. It further outperforms strong multimodal LLMs, including Claude Opus and GPT-6 Astra, by 16.5 and 21.3 percentage points, respectively, on matched unseen identification queries ( ). Early work matches appearance and motion across views~ fan2017identifying , assigns egocentric viewers to humans in top views by graph matching~ ardeshir2016ego2top,ardeshir2018egocentric , jointly segments and identifies humans~ xu2018joint , or predicts where the wearer is~ wen2021seeing . Ego-surfing correlates head motion across videos~ yonetani2015egosurfing . PEN~ zhao2024pen fuses person and environment cues to identify and segment human wearers on TF2023, MAF~ zhao2026sequence extends it to sequences, EgoExoBench~ he2025egoexobench poses the question to multimodal LLMs, and EgoPrivacy~ egoprivacy2025 retrieves the wearer. All of them address humans, and none predicts a relative pose. Closest to our approach, Han~ ~ han2019mha,han2020cvmhat,han2022dmha and BEVSee~ bevsee2024 locate cameras by aligning the layout of a crowd of detected people across views, while we use a 3D prior on one pair. Ego--exo understanding. Paired first- and third-person datasets~ sigurdsson2018actor,huang2024egoexolearn,grauman2024egoexo4d support a growing set of cross-view tasks. Representations learned in one view transfer to the other for action recognition~ li2021egoexo,luo2025rosetta , and generative models translate exo videos into the ego view~ luo2024putmyself,liu2024exo2egov,xu2025egoexogen, mahdi2025exo2egosyn . Object correspondence segments in one view the object queried in the other~ fu2025objectrelator, murlabadia2025omama, pan2026v , also with VGGT features~ vggts2026 . SEERBench~ seerbench2026 asks multimodal LLMs spatial questions across views, and Ego-Exo4D-HM~ egoexo4dhm2026 assumes known head poses. Though these tasks share the challenge of cross-view understanding, none identifies the ego camera wearer. Feed-forward 3D reconstruction. DUSt3R~ wang2024dust3r , MASt3R~ leroy2024mast3r , and Reloc3r~ dong2025reloc3r regress pointmaps or relative pose from image pairs, CUT3R~ wang2025cut3r does so over a stream through a recurrent state, and VGGT~ wang2025vggt , with its release Pi3X~ wang2025pi3 , MapAnything~ keetha2025mapanything , ~ vggtomega2026 , and Depth Anything~3~ lin2025da3 predict cameras and geometry of many views in one pass. We show that their pose also answers a recognition question. Epipoles~ hartley2004multiple have been used for calibration and mutual localization~ bushnevskiy2016multicamera,dhiman2013mutual,franchi2013mutual,stegagno2016ground,wang2022anonymous and linked to wearer location~ fan2017identifying,chen2019epipole,chen2021belief , but prior work has not developed an epipole-based method for identifying wearers among candidates. Test-time adaptation. Test-time training updates a model on each test input through a self-supervised auxiliary task~ fu2021meta, fu2023styleadv, fu2024cross, sun2020ttt , fully test-time adaptation minimizes the entropy of predictions~ wang2021tent , and source-free adaptation trains on its own pseudo-labels~ liang2020shot . For 3D reconstruction, Test3R~ yuan2025test3r enforces consistency between the pointmaps of image triplets, and TTT3R~ chen2026ttt3r treats a recurrent model as an online learner. Our objective needs neither an auxiliary task nor extra views. title: UPP-Gauss: Ultrasound Propagation Physics-informed Gaussian Splatting for B-mode Novel-View Synthesis
summary: Accurate novel-view synthesis of B-mode ultrasound images requires modeling acoustic propagation through tissue and the resulting appearance variations across probe poses. We propose Ultrasound Propagation Physics-informed Gaussian Splatting (UPP-Gauss), which integrates these acoustic interactions into an explicit Gaussian representation. UPP-Gauss constructs acoustic maps by sampling three 3D Gaussian fields using the probe pose and acoustic beam propagation direction, then combines these maps according to ultrasound propagation to synthesize B-mode images. Across three acoustically diverse datasets, UPP-Gauss achieves the best reconstruction quality with efficient rendering, improving PSNR over the best baseline on each dataset by 1.43 dB on average. These results demonstrate accurate and efficient B-mode novel-view synthesis through explicit Gaussian modeling of ultrasound propagation.
full_text: Accurate novel-view synthesis of B-mode ultrasound images requires modeling acoustic propagation through tissue and the resulting appearance variations across probe poses. We propose Ultrasound Propagation Physics-informed Gaussian Splatting (UPP-Gauss), which integrates these acoustic interactions into an explicit Gaussian representation. UPP-Gauss constructs acoustic maps by sampling three 3D Gaussian fields using the probe pose and acoustic beam propagation direction, then combines these maps according to ultrasound propagation to synthesize B-mode images. Across three acoustically diverse datasets, UPP-Gauss achieves the best reconstruction quality with efficient rendering, improving PSNR over the best baseline on each dataset by ~dB on average. These results demonstrate accurate and efficient B-mode novel-view synthesis through explicit Gaussian modeling of ultrasound propagation. Ultrasound, novel view synthesis, Gaussian splatting, physics-informed rendering, B-mode imaging Introduction sec:introduction Ultrasound is widely used for clinical diagnosis as a real-time, noninvasive, and low-cost imaging modality. However, 2D B-mode imaging has a limited field of view, requiring clinicians to infer 3D anatomy from multiple cross-sections~ mozaffari2017freehand . Ultrasound novel-view synthesis addresses this limitation by integrating acquired frames into a consistent 3D representation and synthesizing B-mode images at unseen probe poses. Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) provide effective representations for learning continuous 3D scenes from 2D observations ~ mildenhall2021nerf,kerbl20233d . Unlike optical images formed from projected radiance, B-mode ultrasound arises from waves propagating through tissue and returning through scattering and reflection. Microscopic scatterers produce speckle and tissue texture, acoustic-impedance boundaries generate bright reflections and posterior shadows, and attenuation accumulates along propagation paths~ jensen1991model,wagner1983statistics,kremkau1986artifacts . The observed acoustic response of tissue microstructure at a given location can also vary with probe orientation and the preceding propagation path~ szabo2004diagnostic,salehi2015patient . Conventional optical projection models are therefore limited in their ability to capture these variations in B-mode appearance. Prior learning-based ultrasound reconstruction has explored implicit neural representations. ImplicitVol~ yeung2021implicitvol reconstructs arbitrary imaging planes from a continuous 3D intensity field, while Ultra-NeRF~ wysocki2024ultra and UlRe-NeRF~ guo2024ulre introduce ultrasound image formation and direction-dependent reflection, respectively. These implicit representations require repeated network evaluations during training and rendering, incurring substantial computational costs. Recent methods use explicit Gaussian representations for efficient rendering. UltraGS~ yang2025ultrags models attenuation, reflection, and scattering as additive rendering terms, but does not explicitly formulate their interactions during acoustic propagation. UltraG-Ray~ duelmer2026ultragray models ray-wise energy decay using Gaussian echo intensity and transmittance. However, a unified B-mode formation model that captures beam-direction-dependent scattering and derives both local reflection echoes and downstream transmission loss from the reflection field remains underexplored. We propose UPP-Gauss, which constructs scattering, reflection, and attenuation maps by sampling Gaussian fields on the probe-defined imaging plane. It combines local scattering and reflection echoes with depth-wise transmission determined by accumulated attenuation and reflection losses to synthesize B-mode images at queried poses. Our contributions are as follows. (1) We introduce an efficient plane-sliced Gaussian rendering scheme that evaluates acoustic Gaussian fields directly on the probe-defined imaging plane for physics-informed B-mode synthesis. (2) We model beam-direction-dependent scattering and formulate each reflection response to account for both local echo formation and downstream transmission loss. (3) Experiments on three acoustically meaningful datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art reconstruction quality, efficient rendering, and responses consistent with their distinct acoustic characteristics. title: Was the Model Given the Right Action? Auditing and Repairing Action Interfaces in Navigation World Models
summary: World models are evaluated by predicting future observations from actions. These evaluations assume that actions are prepared the same way as during training, but an unchecked mismatch can make a model appear less accurate than it is. We audit this assumption in Navigation World Models (NWM) and find three interacting differences between its training and rollout code. Correcting the inputs, without retraining, reduces mean visual prediction error by 42%, measured with DreamSim on the RECON navigation dataset. The correction also changes the ranking of NWM checkpoints in an exploratory analysis and removes or reduces two alternative models' measured advantages. Correcting only the normalization offset instead increases error, showing why interacting mismatches must be checked together. To test whether sensitivity to input preparation extends beyond NWM, we deliberately introduce encoding errors into two alternative models; both become less accurate. We introduce ActRosetta, a tool that checks whether action encoding matches training, identifies supported causes of disagreement, and repairs inputs when sufficient information is available. Repair helps little where predictions barely respond to actions, the tool's diagnosis has limited coverage, and improved control remains unproven. For any action-conditioned world model, the lesson is the same: before reporting rollout error, verify that evaluation encodes actions exactly as training did.

On one RECON clip, we run the frozen checkpoint with (a) released actions, built by its released rollout code, and (b) repaired actions, built from the same poses by its training code. By 16\,s, (a) has drifted from ground truth while (b) stays close. Only the action inputs change. (c) Over 150 clips and prediction times 1--16\,s, repaired actions reduce mean DreamSim error by 42 . ActRosetta (dashed arrows) queries both code paths on test paths to identify encoding mismatches. fig:method ] Introduction World models are evaluated through rollouts: starting from real camera frames of a recorded robot run, or trajectory, the model receives the run's actions and predicts the frames that follow, each prediction feeding the next. Evaluations use segments of trajectories, called clips. We study Navigation World Models (NWM)~ bar2025navigation , a model that predicts future camera frames from past frames and navigation actions; later work reuses its rollout code, so one error can affect several evaluations. Preprocessing maps poses to action inputs, choosing a reference frame, a normalization offset, an angle convention and a rule for aggregating raw-step displacements. This action encoder has no learned weights: it is neither NWM's image encoder nor its learned action embedding. A difference between the encodings used in training and in evaluation is a mismatch; the error it causes is charged to the model. Existing benchmarks ask whether a model follows the action it is given~ yang2026mirabench,chen2026robotic,co2026worldsimprobe ; we ask whether the model received the action it learned to interpret. Our main result is an audit of NWM's action interface: its released rollout code prepares actions differently from its training code, through three interacting mismatches that change one frozen checkpoint's predictions (Figure~ fig:method ). We call the action inputs built by the released rollout code released actions, and those built from the same poses by the training code repaired actions; replacing one with the other, with the checkpoint unchanged, is repair. A chunk spans one prediction call, which predicts one future state a fixed time shift ahead. The two encodings agree only on the first chunk, so a one-chunk check passes. Detecting that two action encoders differ is differential testing; knowing what to fix is harder, because mismatches interact: fixing only NWM's offset increases error. The encoding also spans the rollout loop, dataset code and normalization, so reading one function can miss what the model receives. We therefore query action encoders, with a tool we call ActRosetta. Our NWM repair itself used NWM's own training code; ActRosetta lets others run the same check on their own encoders. Our contributions are: An action-interface mismatch that changes model evaluation. NWM's rollout code differs from training in reference frame, normalization offset and yaw wrapping. Repair, without retraining, reduces mean DreamSim error on RECON from 0.240 to 0.139 (42 ) and removes or shrinks two alternative models' leads (Sec.~ sec:models ). A repeatable audit with witnessed attribution. ActRosetta queries paired training and evaluation encoders on controlled paths, names a differing field only when a test path witnesses it, and repairs only when the whole contract, an encoder's full set of encoding choices, is determined. Unlike ActionABI~ attri2026actionabi , which shares its principles but recovers contracts from logs, it diagnoses paired code, identifying the interacting choices a patch must address (Secs.~ sec:contract -- sec:aicr ). Evidence separating detection, attribution and repair. ActionFaultBench, our benchmark of action-encoder pairs whose differences are known in advance, tests whether a checker can find differences, explain them and recover the training encoder's inputs, on four sealed test sets written by separate automated agents after our code was frozen; an audit of 40 public repositories complements it. On the final 240-pair test, ActRosetta detects all 91 differing pairs, recovers their differences exactly in 73 cases, and repairs all 38 differing pairs supported by output conversion (Secs.~ sec:bench -- sec:results ). Related Work Later work builds on NWM~ bar2025navigation to improve rollout consistency~ yan2026mwm , use different visual representations~ zhang2026rae , generate interactive video~ huang2025vid2world , plan with compact representations~ kim2026planning and model long histories efficiently~ guo2026visual . World-in-World places NWM inside closed-loop tasks, where its predictions guide an agent~ zhang2026world . Such work can reuse NWM's rollout code: in our audit, MWM's executed rollout shares all three mismatches (Sec.~ sec:results ). Several recent benchmarks test whether a model's predictions respond correctly to the actions it is given (Table~ tab:related ). MiraBench finds that visual quality is a poor guide to whether actions are followed~ yang2026mirabench ; WorldEcho shows that models can fail on action sequences unlike those an expert would choose~ chen2026robotic ; WorldSimProbe states what a simulator's outputs should show when actions are changed in a controlled way~ co2026worldsimprobe ; WorldOracle compares predictions with paired executions of the same actions in the real world~ duan2026worldoracle ; and ActSWM finds that some models' predictions become nearly identical under different action sequences~ gan2026actswm . These works judge what the model does with an action, which complements our check: a model can follow actions well and still be judged unfairly if its inputs are encoded differently. Mind the Execution Gap~ wen2026mind addresses mismatches in time, such as delay, packet loss and reordering when a frozen controller is executed asynchronously, and corrects them with an interface designed for each architecture; our mismatches are in the encoded values themselves. ActionABI~ attri2026actionabi is closest in method. From logged state--action trajectories, it recovers the conventions an action encoder follows, keeps every candidate that fits the logs equally well, and converts actions only when the candidates agree, abstaining otherwise. ActRosetta follows the same principles but differs in evidence and goal: instead of logs from one system, it runs a model's training and evaluation encoders on chosen test paths, explains where they disagree, and repairs the evaluation inputs. Experimental choices and run-to-run variability can change model comparisons~ henderson2018deep,bouthillier2021accounting , ignoring statistical uncertainty can change conclusions~ agarwal2021deep , and data leakage can inflate performance~ kapoor2022leakage . title: HOG-WAM: Improving Visual Robustness through Future Gradient Prediction
summary: World-action models jointly predict future observations and actions, yet visual corruption can disrupt the resulting policies. We introduce HOG-WAM, which adds future Histograms of Oriented Gradients (HOG) as structural supervision derived directly from demonstration images. An auxiliary HOG diffusion transformer (DiT) module reads RGB features through asymmetric attention, allowing its objective to shape the visual representation used for control. The module is used only during training and removed at inference, preserving FastWAM's RGB-to-action architecture. We evaluate four controlled observation corruptions through a visual-corruption extension of RoboTwin, termed RoboTwin-Plus; HOG-WAM achieves the highest success among the compared policies under all four. Mixed-noise success increases from 78.86% to 82.86% relative to FastWAM, with comparable performance on clean scenes. On LIBERO Plus, overall success increases from 74.49% to 75.26%, with the largest gain under sensor noise, from 74.14% to 78.89%. Across four Franka tasks, average success increases from 40% to 59% under clean observations and from 17% to 24% under noisy observations. A representation ablation favors combining RGB observations with auxiliary HOG prediction over replacing RGB with HOG. These findings support future-gradient prediction as complementary supervision for visually robust control, with larger absolute gains on physical tasks than in simulation. Code is available at https://github.com/iPPLab/HOG-WAM.

Introduction sec:introduction Robotic manipulation requires recognizing task-relevant objects and anticipating how their spatial relations change during interaction. Vision-language-action policies use pretrained visual and language representations to map observations to actions~ brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0 . World-action models (WAMs) additionally learn to predict future observations, making demonstrated scene evolution a source of policy supervision~ ye2026dreamzero,li2026lingbot,bi2025motus . Fast-WAM~ yuan2026fastwam , denoted FastWAM here, preserves this predictive objective during training while generating actions from the current observation at inference. The prediction target therefore determines which visual information this training objective emphasizes. RGB prediction supervises object structure together with color, texture, and illumination. These appearance cues help identify objects, but they also vary with lighting and sensor conditions while the manipulation goal remains unchanged. An RGB objective alone thus ties the learned features to appearance factors that can change at deployment. For placement, stacking, and insertion, local boundaries describe the image-space arrangement of objects and their surroundings. Requiring a visual representation to predict these boundaries provides an explicit structural learning signal alongside RGB reconstruction. The question is how to introduce this signal while retaining the appearance information needed for language-conditioned control. Why gradients? Histograms of Oriented Gradients (HOG)~ dalal2005hog summarize local edge orientations through spatial pooling and contrast normalization. MaskFeat~ wei2022maskfeat demonstrates that predicting HOG features in masked image and video regions can learn useful visual representations, identifying local contrast normalization as an important component. This motivates a different prediction problem for manipulation: learning the gradient structure of future demonstration frames alongside actions. The target emphasizes where local intensity transitions occur and how they are oriented, making spatial organization explicit without object annotations or a learned target generator. Why training-only supervision? A descriptor useful for supervising a representation need not replace its sensory input. Our HOG raster compresses orientation statistics and removes chromatic information; RGB retains cues for object identity and instruction grounding. WAM4D~ li2026wam4d offers a related architectural principle: future-depth supervision shapes the visual features used for control through a removable readout. We apply this principle to deterministic gradient targets, which require no additional sensor or pretrained estimator. In HOG-WAM, an auxiliary HOG diffusion transformer (DiT) reads RGB features through asymmetric attention, and its loss updates the RGB backbone. Action prediction remains independent of HOG tokens, allowing the auxiliary module to be removed at inference while retaining its effect on the learned RGB representation. We evaluate visual robustness on RoboTwin 2.0~ chen2025robotwin , LIBERO Plus~ fei2025liberoplus , and four Franka tasks. RoboTwin-Plus denotes our visual-corruption extension of the existing RoboTwin evaluation, with fixed tasks and controlled changes to image inputs. On LIBERO Plus, gains concentrate under sensor noise. A LIBERO Plus ablation compares HOG as auxiliary supervision with HOG as a replacement for RGB. The physical experiments show larger absolute gains over FastWAM than the simulation averages, extending the evidence to manipulation with real camera observations. Our contributions are: A deterministic future-gradient target that makes local structure an explicit supervision signal for world-action learning. An asymmetric coupling of RGB, HOG, and action DiT modules that transfers this supervision to the visual backbone while preserving RGB-based inference. Evidence from controlled visual-corruption tests and physical manipulation, together with a representation ablation that supports complementary HOG supervision over RGB replacement. Related work sec:related_work Generative models and robot policies. Transformers~ vaswani2017attention,dosovitskiy2021vit provide token-based architectures for visual learning, while diffusion models~ ho2020ddpm , latent diffusion~ rombach2022ldm , and DiTs~ peebles2023dit support conditional image generation. Flow matching~ lipman2023flowmatching and rectified flow~ liu2023rectifiedflow learn velocity fields that transport noise toward data. Diffusion Policy~ chi2023diffusionpolicy applies conditional denoising to action sequences. RT-1 and RT-2~ brohan2023rt1,brohan2023rt2 scale observation-to-action learning, while Octo and OpenVLA~ octo2024,kim2024openvla provide generalist policies adaptable to new robot settings. The family~ black2024pi0,pi052025 combines pretrained vision-language representations with continuous action generation and heterogeneous training data. HOG-WAM instead studies how the visual prediction objective within a WAM can improve the representation used for control. Predictive learning for control. UniPi~ du2023unipi derives actions from text-conditioned video plans, and GR-1~ wu2023gr1 jointly predicts future images and actions after video pretraining. Video foundation models such as Wan~ wan2025wan supply visual dynamics priors for recent WAMs. DreamZero~ ye2026dreamzero , LingBot-VA~ li2026lingbot , and MOTUS~ bi2025motus couple visual dynamics and action generation through joint models. FastWAM~ yuan2026fastwam separates future-video training from action inference. Our auxiliary target builds on this separation, changing what the RGB representation is trained to predict. Structural supervision in world models. TesserAct~ zhen2025tesseract models RGB, depth, and normals, while Kinema4D~ xu2026kinema4d uses kinematic robot trajectories to condition RGB and point-map simulation. WAM4D~ li2026wam4d transfers geometric priors through future-depth readouts that are removed at inference. MaskWAM~ yu2026maskwam uses mask prompting and prediction, FlowWAM~ chen2026flowwam adopts optical flow as an action representation, and Robust-WAM~ yan2026robustwam aligns action-stream features with semantic targets. DreamWAM~ yuan2026dreamwam combines appearance, motion, geometry, and semantics. HOG-WAM complements these learned or task-specific targets with local gradient statistics computed directly from each demonstration frame. Masked prediction and gradient targets. The target representation determines the information emphasized by a predictive objective. BEiT~ bao2022beit predicts discrete visual tokens; MAE and SimMIM~ he2022mae,xie2022simmim reconstruct pixels; VideoMAE~ tong2022videomae extends masked reconstruction to videos; and I-JEPA~ assran2023ijepa predicts learned target embeddings. MaskFeat~ wei2022maskfeat identifies HOG~ dalal2005hog as an effective feature-regression target, connecting local shape information with representation learning. HOG-WAM carries this target-design insight into predictive robot learning: a HOG-derived raster is predicted in the video latent space alongside future RGB and actions. The structural predictor is an auxiliary training objective, while the policy retains RGB observations for control. Demonstrations additionally provide sampled future observations for predictive training. FastWAM, on which we build, combines a Wan2.2-TI2V-5B visual DiT module with an action DiT module. A frozen causal variational autoencoder (VAE) maps the observation sequence to RGB latents . Language embeddings and a trainable proprioceptive projection condition both streams. The model jointly learns RGB and action velocity fields, with action queries attending to the observed RGB frame. HOG-WAM adds a future-gradient objective through an auxiliary DiT that reads RGB features ( ). This makes the structural loss act on the visual representation used for action prediction. We convert each frame to grayscale and compute horizontal and vertical finite differences. Gradient magnitudes contribute to nine unsigned orientation bins within cells, with linear interpolation between neighboring bins. Overlapping -cell blocks undergo L2-Hys normalization, including clipping at and renormalization. Averaging contributions from overlapping blocks gives a normalized histogram for each cell and orientation bin . This local normalization reduces sensitivity to intensity scale, while the spatial grid retains the arrangement of boundaries. Rasterization for latent prediction. This three-channel representation makes gradient supervision compatible with the pretrained video encoder. title: Most of the Way There: Turning a Strong Video Prior into an Action-Conditioned World Model
summary: Modern video generators excel at producing visually plausible futures guided by text and image prompts. Yet their emphasis on semantic plausibility does not guarantee fidelity to the physical consequences of specific actions. Action-conditioned world models (ACWMs), in contrast, aim to simulate how the world responds to robot actions, enabling scalable policy evaluation and improvement without costly real-world rollouts. The challenge is not merely to generate a plausible future, but to predict what follows from a specific physical action. As video priors grow stronger, we ask how little adaptation is truly needed to bridge this gap. We introduce Dianjing, a minimal recipe that preserves and unlocks the capabilities of strong video priors through unified physical action conditioning, training concentrated at the high noise levels where motion and layout, and thus the consequences of actions, are decided, and native history conditioning. Built upon MiniMax H3, a 33B video foundation model, Dianjing freezes the pretrained backbone and trains only 0.34% of its parameters using approximately 65 hours of robot video across two embodiments, without additional robot-specific pretraining or camera calibration. Controlled ablations show that where training is allocated across noise levels matters more than how actions enter the network. On WorldOracle, which evaluates predictions against paired real-world executions, Dianjing achieves the best scores on four of the five evaluation tracks and ranks second on AgiBot-Long. Our findings suggest that strong video priors already bring us most of the way to world modeling; lightweight physical action grounding can unlock their potential for real-world prediction.

Our findings suggest that strong video priors already bring us most of the way to world modeling; lightweight physical action grounding can unlock their potential for real-world prediction. Introduction sec:intro Recent advances in video generation have produced increasingly powerful models capable of synthesizing diverse scenes, realistic appearance, and complex motion and interactions~ blattmann2023svd,wan2025,agarwal2025cosmos,minimax2026h3 . Trained on large-scale video data, these models acquire rich visual, semantic, and motion priors that are difficult to learn from limited robot demonstrations alone. Their growing capabilities suggest an exciting possibility: much of the generative foundation required for physical world modeling may already exist in pretrained video generators. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:teaser (a), strong video priors offer a rich foundation upon which action-conditioned world models (ACWMs) can be built. However, visual plausibility does not guarantee physical fidelity. General-purpose video generators are typically pretrained with generative objectives conditioned on text descriptions or images, rather than temporally aligned physical actions~ blattmann2023svd,kong2024hunyuanvideo,wan2025 . While this paradigm provides rich visual and motion priors, it does not explicitly ground predictions in the consequences of specific robot actions. Even visually convincing interactions can exhibit physical inconsistencies ~ li2025worldmodelbench,zhou2026paibench , as illustrated in Fig.~1(b). More importantly, a plausible future may not correspond to the consequences of a specific action: the same instruction to grasp an object can lead to success, missed contact, or no object movement, depending on the actual execution. This distinction is fundamental to ACWMs, which must predict how the world responds to robot actions rather than merely generate plausible futures. Faithful world prediction holds the promise of enabling scalable robot policy evaluation, planning, and improvement while reducing reliance on costly real-world rollouts~ yang2024unisim,guo2026ctrlworld,qiu2026gesim2 . Interestingly, video generation and action-conditioned world modeling offer complementary strengths. From the perspective of ACWMs, pretrained video generators provide rich visual and motion knowledge acquired from large-scale video pretraining. From the perspective of video generation, robot executions offer a valuable form of supervision: temporally aligned physical actions naturally recorded alongside visual observations. Unlike high-level semantic descriptions, these commands specify concrete physical interventions, while the corresponding videos reveal their observable consequences. Large-scale robot datasets increasingly provide aligned visual observations and physical actions across diverse tasks and embodiments~ oneill2024openx,agibotworld2025 . Such action--observation pairs provide physically grounded supervision without requiring manually annotated object states, contact dynamics, or scene geometry. Video priors provide the generative foundation, while physical actions provide the grounding for execution prediction. The challenge is to connect these complementary strengths without relearning the visual world from scratch. Existing approaches have explored diverse ways to bridge this gap, including large-scale robot-specific training, rendered action representations, geometric conditioning, architectural restructuring, specialized memory mechanisms, and lightweight action adaptation~ qiu2026gesim2,gao2026dreamdojo,guo2026ctrlworld,rigter2025avid,chen2026h3world . These designs address different requirements of world simulation, but also introduce varying degrees of additional training, conditioning, and architectural complexity. Meanwhile, video foundation models continue to grow in scale and capability, inviting us to reconsider how much specialized machinery is truly necessary. As video priors grow stronger, the question is not how much more we can add, but how little we actually need to change. We therefore ask: How little adaptation does it take to turn a strong video prior into a faithful action-conditioned world model? We introduce Dianjing, a lightweight adaptation recipe guided by a simple philosophy: preserve the prior and unlock its capabilities through physical action grounding. Named after the Chinese idiom in which a painted dragon comes to life with a few finishing touches, Dianjing aims to unlock an already capable video prior rather than rebuild it. Our recipe follows three simple principles: specifying temporally aligned physical actions through a shared end-effector representation across robot embodiments, concentrating adaptation training on noise levels that most effectively improve action-conditioned prediction, and reusing the prior's native reference mechanism to carry visual history across generation chunks. We instantiate Dianjing on MiniMax H3~ minimax2026h3 , a 33B video foundation model, freezing the pretrained backbone and training only approximately 0.34 of its parameters using about 65 hours of robot video from two embodiments. This requires no additional robot-specific pretraining, camera calibration, rendered action maps, or specialized memory modules. We investigate this approach through controlled adaptation studies and evaluate its predictions on WorldOracle~ worldoracle2026 , which measures agreement with paired real-world robot executions. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:teaser (c), minimal adaptation substantially improves execution prediction over the original video prior. Our experiments reveal that visual-only adaptation is insufficient for reliable action-conditioned prediction, while explicit physical action conditioning brings substantial gains. More elaborate action interfaces provide limited additional improvements, whereas reallocating training effort across noise levels improves validation performance by approximately 7 points at matched epochs. Despite its minimal adaptation, Dianjing achieves competitive performance against dedicated robot world models, ranking first on four of the five evaluation tracks, including 73.48 on AgiBot-Core, 70.71 on YAM-Core, and 64.25 on Policy. Although long-horizon consistency remains challenging, these results suggest that strong video priors already provide much of the foundation for action-conditioned world modeling, and that surprisingly little specialized adaptation is needed to achieve competitive real-world execution prediction. contributions are summarized as follows: We systematically investigate what it takes to turn a strong video prior into an ACWM, revealing the roles of pretrained generative knowledge, physical action grounding, and effective adaptation through controlled studies. We introduce Dianjing, a minimal adaptation recipe that grounds video priors in physical actions through a shared end-effector space, high-noise-focused training, and native reference conditioning, while preserving their pretrained backbone without architectural reconstruction. With only 0.34 trainable parameters and about 65 hours of robot video across two embodiments, Dianjing achieves state-of-the-art scores on four of five WorldOracle tracks and ranks second on AgiBot-Long, demonstrating competitive real-world execution prediction. Related Work sec:related Action-Conditioned World Models sec:rw_acwm An action-conditioned world model (ACWM) predicts how the world evolves under an agent's actions, an idea rooted in model-based control~ ha2018worldmodels,hafner2020dreamer and first realized in pixel space by action-conditional video prediction~ oh2015action,finn2016unsupervised . Such models let agents be planned, trained, and evaluated in imagination rather than in the real world: robots plan through predicted frames~ finn2017foresight , policies trained in learned simulators transfer to real robots~ yang2024unisim , and recent ACWMs evaluate and improve robot policies and generate training data~ guo2026ctrlworld,gao2026dreamdojo,qiu2026gesim2,bwm2026 . Their evaluation has accordingly shifted from video quality and plausibility~ huang2024vbench,duan2025worldscore,li2025worldmodelbench,yue2025ewmbench,zhou2026paibench to functional utility and agreement with real executions~ shang2026worldarena,shang2026worldarena2,zhang2026worldinworld,gigaai2026gigaworld1,chen2026worldecho,worldoracle2026 . Related efforts have explored learning interactive environments from unlabeled videos and integrating generative world models with robot policy learning, evaluation, and simulation ~ bruce2024genie,liao2025genie . Video Generation Priors sec:rw_priors Video generation has advanced from early video diffusion models~ ho2022vdm to latent models trained on curated internet-scale data~ blattmann2023svd , and then to models framed as world simulators~ brooks2024sora . Open models now reach billions of parameters~ yang2025cogvideox,kong2024hunyuanvideo,wan2025 , and world foundation models built for physical AI~ agarwal2025cosmos,ali2025cosmospredict25,agarwal2026cosmos3 generate 3D-consistent, physically plausible video~ agarwal2025cosmos . The latest open systems reach 33B parameters in a single-stream transformer that jointly reads text, images, video, and audio~ minimax2026h3 . These priors increasingly serve as the starting point for ACWMs~ guo2026ctrlworld,gao2026dreamdojo,bwm2026 , yet a stronger prior does not automatically yield a better world model: transferable physical priors matter more than raw scale~ gigaai2026gigaworld1 , and post-training on action--observation data can matter more than upgrading the generator~ zhang2026worldinworld . Language offers one way in: H3-World~ chen2026h3world adapts H3 with a small LoRA by rewriting keyboard commands as text on its native text pathway, which suits simple, discrete game actions. title: RePace: Reasoning about Demonstration Speedup for Faster Vision-Language-Action Policies
summary: Since vision-language-action (VLA) policies can inherit the slow pace of human demonstrations, accelerating these demonstrations before fine-tuning can lead to faster VLA policies without an additional speed-selection module at deployment. Several offline speedup methods have focused on identifying segments that require less precision and assigning predefined speedup factors to the segments. However, even within a single segment, a speedup factor suitable for steady motion may be too high when precise alignment is required. To this end, this paper presents RePace, an offline reasoning framework that determines how much to accelerate each part of a demonstration. For the same recorded movement, RePace measures how much each candidate speedup factor shortens the sequence and compares the resulting observation-action pairs used for training. Given the task instruction, a pretrained language model uses the visual context and original motion of successive windows to interpret these candidate retiming effects and select a speedup profile for the complete episode. Experimental results demonstrate that RePace outperforms the baselines in overall task execution efficiency on both LIBERO and RoboCasa-Kitchen. On all three tasks with a gripper-equipped Franka Research 3 arm, RePace matches or exceeds the acceleration baselines in success rate and completes successful trials faster.
full_text: Introduction sec:intro Vision-language-action (VLA) models extend pretrained vision-language representations to robot action prediction~ brohan2023rt , and researchers have evaluated these models on various real-world manipulation tasks~ ma2026survey . A pretrained VLA policy can be fine-tuned on demonstrations of a new task to predict robot actions from observations and a language instruction~ kim2024openvla . Practical deployment of these policies requires both successful manipulation and timely task completion. However, since even experienced demonstrators may move the robot cautiously to avoid mistakes during teleoperation~ zhong2025survey , a policy trained on these demonstrations can inherit their slow pace, even in open space where the robot could move faster. For faster VLA policy, there have been two primary approaches to accelerate policies at different stages: (i) test-time policy acceleration and (ii) offline demonstration acceleration. Although several studies have focused on acceleration during execution (i.e., test-time policy acceleration)~ arachchige2025sail,kim2026time,jeon2026pacevla,hu2026freespeed,shirasaka2026robopace,wu2026speedup , the task success rate can decline when predicted action chunks are directly downsampled at higher speedup factors~ guo2025demospeedup . Meanwhile, other studies have addressed the acceleration of demonstrations before policy training (i.e., offline demonstration acceleration)~ guo2025demospeedup,kim2026espada,sanchez2026volt,cao2026adatempo,oh2026egospeedup,moon2026retiming . Although the overhead of VLA fine-tuning makes it difficult to use downstream policy performance to guide demonstration acceleration, we focus on the latter approach, offline demonstration acceleration, because it enables faster VLA policies without a speed-selection module at deployment. Several studies have addressed the question of where to accelerate demonstrations offline. DemoSpeedup~ guo2025demospeedup uses action entropy to identify segments with different precision requirements, while VOLT~ sanchez2026volt uses a vision-language model (VLM) to interpret visual context for segment selection and assigns a human-defined speedup rate. Even within a segment selected for acceleration, we still need to decide how much to accelerate each movement. For example, suppose that we treat the entire approach to a cup before grasping as a single segment. The gripper may move straight toward the cup and then shift slightly to one side to position its fingers for the grasp. A lower speedup factor may preserve the observation at this change in direction, while a higher factor may combine successive commands and omit that observation. Our key insight is that, before policy fine-tuning, we can compare candidate factors directly by examining how many steps each saves and how each changes the observations and commands used for learning. In consideration of these changes, how should the recorded scene and motion guide the choice of speedup factor throughout a demonstration? In addressing this question, we have derived the following three challenges in offline speed selection. Challenge 1) How can we compare the effects of candidate speedup factors before policy fine-tuning? A shorter demonstration may omit details of the movement that the policy needs to learn. The choice between two speedup factors therefore depends on how many additional steps the higher factor saves and which details the lower factor preserves. Challenge 2) How can we determine which data changes matter for the task? The significance of a change in the training data depends on the scene and the recorded motion. For example, a few observations may capture a straight path through open space, while an intermediate observation can show how the gripper adjusts an object to fit through a narrow opening. Challenge 3) How should the surrounding movements guide the choice of speedup for each window? A short window of consecutive demonstration steps may show how an object moves without revealing the purpose of that movement. For example, seeing the object placed in a holder in the next window can help explain why a small rotation just before placement may warrant a lower speedup factor. To this end, we propose , an offline framework that selects a speedup profile for the complete episode, as shown in Fig.~ fig:teaser . We measure the effects of each candidate factor under the same retiming rules used to construct the accelerated demonstrations. A pretrained language model~ qwen3.8 interprets these measurements considering the task instruction, scene descriptions, and recorded motion from successive windows to select the profile without requiring window-level speed labels. Our main contributions are summarized as follows. We propose , an offline demonstration acceleration framework that uses large language model (LLM)-based reasoning to select speedup factors and construct accelerated demonstrations. We define three inputs for effective speedup reasoning: visual context and original motion describe the recorded demonstration, while candidate retiming effects quantify the changes produced by each candidate speedup factor. We evaluate using both simulation benchmarks and a real-world Franka Research 3 robot, showing that demonstrations accelerated via contribute to faster VLA policies while mitigating decreases in task success rates. Related Work sec:related This section briefly reviews the previous work on vision-language-action models and the acceleration methods for faster robot policies. Vision-Language-Action Models Given visual observations and a task instruction, VLA models can predict discrete action tokens~ brohan2023rt or generate continuous action sequences through flow matching~ gr00tn1_2025,black2024pi_0,intelligence2025pi_ . Robot policies such as Diffusion Policy (DP)~ chi2025diffusion and Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT)~ zhao2023learning predict several actions at a time as an action chunk. VLA models can encode such chunks as compact token sequences~ pertsch2025fast or decode multiple actions in parallel~ kim2025fine . To determine which actions a task requires, some methods translate instructions into control programs~ liang2023code or construct spatial maps to guide robot motion~ huang2023voxposer . To guide action prediction, some VLA policies describe the steps needed to follow a task instruction or predict an image of the scene they aim to reach~ zawalski2024robotic,zhao2025cot,li2026trm . For example, a predicted image may show where to place an object without specifying how quickly the gripper should move it there. Robot Policy Acceleration Several studies have addressed test-time policy acceleration by controlling how quickly a robot executes its movements~ arachchige2025sail,kim2026time,jeon2026pacevla,hu2026freespeed,shirasaka2026robopace,wu2026speedup . For example, SAIL~ arachchige2025sail adjusts the interval between actions according to motion complexity or gripper transitions. Related work on the temporal structure of robot actions has explored variable sampling frequencies and waypoint-based representations~ masuya2025variable,shi2023waypoint,belkhale2023hydra . Speed selection can also enter policy training. TempoVLA~ jing2026tempovla trains a policy whose speed can be specified at execution time, while AutoSpeed~ hu2026autospeed selects retimed targets during training based on prediction error and horizon. Offline methods resample recorded demonstrations before policy training~ guo2025demospeedup,kim2026espada,sanchez2026volt,yang2026improving . For example, DemoSpeedup~ guo2025demospeedup and VOLT~ sanchez2026volt identify segments for acceleration using action entropy and visual task context, respectively. Other methods retime demonstrations by comparing the timing of similar movements in robot trials~ cao2026adatempo , transferring the timing of human movements to robot demonstrations~ oh2026egospeedup , or predicting speed along a recorded path~ moon2026retiming . However, the cues used in these offline demonstration acceleration studies~ guo2025demospeedup,kim2026espada,sanchez2026volt,cao2026adatempo,oh2026egospeedup,moon2026retiming do not by themselves show how different speedup factors would change the observations and action targets for the same movement. This motivates the design of , which compares these changes in the context of the recorded scene and motion to select a speedup profile (Table~ tab:prior_speed_selection ). Method sec:method This section describes the problem setup, the design principles of , and its architecture. Problem Setup sec:problem We consider the offline acceleration of demonstrations for fine-tuning a pretrained VLA policy. A demonstration associated with a task instruction is defined as follows: where , , and denote the observation, recorded robot state, and action at step , respectively. We divide each demonstration into ordered, non-overlapping windows and assign each window a speedup factor from a finite candidate set . Fixed boundaries let us compare candidates over the same interval without phase annotations or a segmentation model. When , the speedup profile also determines which windows keep their original timing. During retiming, we resample observation-action pairs and transform commands according to the action representation. For a speedup profile , the accelerated demonstration is defined as follows: where denotes the retiming operator that groups consecutive steps within each window according to the selected factor. We fix the action representation, sampling rules, command transformation, and operator settings before comparing factors. We construct the accelerated dataset by applying Eq.~ eq:retiming to each demonstration in the source dataset with its selected speedup profile. We fine-tune a VLA policy on and use a policy fine-tuned on the original demonstrations as the baseline. Our goal is to shorten task execution while mitigating the decline in task success rate that can accompany acceleration. To select a profile before fine-tuning, compares how candidate speedup factors change the training data for the same recorded movement. Overview sec:overview follows three design principles when comparing candidates. (i) We measure actual step reduction and changes to observation-action pairs under the same retiming rules used for data construction. (ii) The selector interprets these changes alongside recorded visual context and motion. (iii) The selector considers the complete episode when assigning factors to individual windows. To interpret the numerical measurements in the context of the task instruction and scene descriptions, we use a pretrained language model without further training or window-level speed labels. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:method_overview , processes each demonstration through three components. Speedup reasoning inputs distinguish visual context and original motion from candidate retiming effects, which describe how each factor changes the training data. In speedup profile reasoning, the model selects a full-episode profile from the instruction and ordered window inputs and identifies the evidence for its choices. Demonstration retiming applies the selected profile under the rules used to compute candidate effects, producing observation-action pairs for policy fine-tuning. Sections~ sec:inputs , sec:reasoning , and sec:retiming describe these components, respectively. title: OceanFix: Reference-Guided Diffusion for Sparse-View Underwater 3D Reconstruction
summary: Recent advances in Gaussian splatting have enabled efficient underwater reconstruction, but sparse observations, light attenuation, and backscatter still leave scene regions underconstrained and cause novel-view artifacts. We present OceanFix, a reference-guided framework for sparse-view underwater 3D reconstruction that combines diffusion-based view repair with Gaussian scene refinement. Our repair model follows a two-stage training strategy that separates underwater appearance adaptation from geometric refinement. The first stage learns underwater appearance from reference observations and estimated medium features. The second uses camera poses and reference depth to align reference features, with relative-depth supervision guiding structural repair without requiring target-view depth at inference. We further propose medium-aware distillation that transfers repaired views into the 3D scene according to geometric repair demand and channel-specific optical observability. Through iterative rendering, repair, and distillation, OceanFix refines underconstrained regions while retaining supervision from the observed views. Experiments on underwater datasets demonstrate that OceanFix improves rendering quality in sparse-view 3D reconstruction, reducing visible artifacts and recovering finer scene details.
full_text: fig:teaser Recent advances in Gaussian splatting have enabled efficient underwater reconstruction, but sparse observations, light attenuation, and backscatter still leave scene regions underconstrained and cause novel-view artifacts. We present OceanFix, a reference-guided framework for sparse-view underwater 3D reconstruction that combines diffusion-based view repair with Gaussian scene refinement. Our repair model follows a two-stage training strategy that separates underwater appearance adaptation from geometric refinement. The first stage learns underwater appearance from reference observations and estimated medium features. The second uses camera poses and reference depth to align reference features, with relative-depth supervision guiding structural repair without requiring target-view depth at inference. We further propose medium-aware distillation that transfers repaired views into the 3D scene according to geometric repair demand and channel-specific optical observability. Through iterative rendering, repair, and distillation, OceanFix refines underconstrained regions while retaining supervision from the observed views. Experiments on underwater datasets demonstrate that OceanFix improves rendering quality in sparse-view 3D reconstruction, reducing visible artifacts and recovering finer scene details. Introduction sec:introduction Reconstructing underwater scenes from a small number of images requires recovering both scene structure and its appearance through water. Neural radiance fields (NeRF)~ mildenhall2020nerf,barron2022mipnerf360,mueller2022instant,barron2023zipnerf and 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl2023gaussians,yu2024mipsplatting,lu2024scaffoldgs,guedon2024sugar have advanced image-based reconstruction and novel-view synthesis, with 3DGS enabling efficient optimization and real-time rendering. Their underwater application must additionally account for wavelength-dependent light attenuation and backscatter, which couple the observed appearance to the intervening medium~ akkaynak2018underwater,levy2023seathrunerf,yang2025seasplat . When only a few viewpoints are available, this coupling compounds the geometric ambiguity caused by limited coverage. Our goal is to reconstruct a renderable underwater scene from these sparse observations while reducing artifacts at unobserved viewpoints. Recent underwater reconstruction methods explicitly incorporate the medium into scene modeling. SeaThru-NeRF~ levy2023seathru jointly learns scene and medium properties through volumetric rendering, while WaterSplatting~ li2024watersplatting combines Gaussian geometry with a separate volumetric medium field. Related restoration approaches, such as RestorGS~ qiao2025restorgs , use depth-guided degradation modeling to separate clear and degraded appearance. These advances provide an essential account of underwater image formation. However, modeling the medium does not resolve the lack of geometric observations in sparse-view reconstruction. Sparse-input methods such as RegNeRF~ niemeyer2022regnerf address this ambiguity by regularizing geometry and appearance at unobserved views, motivating additional constraints beyond fitting the available images. Generative priors~ liu2023zero1to3,sargent2024zeronvs, zheng2024free3d,gao2024cat3d,li2026spvc offer another source of supervision for underconstrained scene regions. ReconFusion~ wu2024reconfusion uses diffusion-based novel-view generation to regularize sparse-view reconstruction, while Difix3D+~ wu2025difix repairs rendered views with a single-step diffusion model and distills them back into the 3D representation. More recently, Ocean4D~ huang2026ocean4d combines geometric conditioning with medium-aware video diffusion for underwater generation from monocular videos. Although these works demonstrate the value of generative supervision, applying such priors directly to sparse-view underwater 3D reconstruction remains challenging. Underwater appearance depends on both scene geometry and light propagation through the medium, making image repair alone insufficient for reliable scene refinement. First, reference features are not spatially aligned with the target view, and transferring their appearance without accounting for geometry and view-dependent medium effects can introduce structural inconsistencies. Second, repaired pixels provide unequal supervision for the underlying objects: attenuation suppresses object signals differently across color channels, while backscatter can dominate the observed appearance. Effective generative supervision for underwater reconstruction must therefore account for both reference-to-target alignment and medium-dependent signal reliability, directing scene refinement toward regions that require geometric repair and retain observable object information. To address these challenges, we present OceanFix as shown in Fig.~ fig:teaser , a reference-guided framework for sparse-view underwater 3D reconstruction that combines diffusion-based view repair with medium-aware Gaussian refinement. We train the repair model in two stages. The first adapts underwater appearance using reference RGB features and estimated medium descriptors. The second freezes the appearance parameters and learns geometry adapters that project reference features into the target view using camera poses and estimated reference depth. A relative-depth objective further constrains structural changes during training. This separation allows geometric adaptation while retaining the learned appearance model, and requires no target-view depth at inference. Both types of reference information are used in a single repair pass. We further introduce a medium-aware distillation mechanism to transfer repaired views into the Gaussian scene. We combine geometric repair demand with channel-specific optical observability. Depth dispersion along rendering rays provides a proxy for local geometric ambiguity, while the underwater renderer estimates the contribution of object appearance to each color channel. Their combination assigns additional supervision to regions with greater repair demand and stronger object visibility. Bounded, normalized weights retain a baseline contribution across the image. We periodically refresh the repaired pseudo-views and their weights as the reconstruction evolves, while preserving supervision from the observed images. The resulting rendering--repair--distillation loop connects reference-guided image corrections to refinement of the explicit 3D representation. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce OceanFix, a framework for sparse-view underwater 3D reconstruction that integrates reference-guided diffusion repair with iterative Gaussian scene refinement. We develop a two-stage repair model that first adapts underwater appearance and then introduces explicit geometric constraints through pose-aligned reference features and relative-depth supervision, without requiring target-view depth at inference. We propose a medium-aware distillation mechanism that combines geometric repair demand with channel-specific optical observability to weight repaired-view supervision during reconstruction. Related Work sec:related_work Underwater 3D Reconstruction Underwater reconstruction requires modeling both scene surfaces and participating media. Physically grounded image formation distinguishes direct-signal attenuation from backscatter~ akkaynak2018underwater , forming the basis of SeaThru-NeRF~ levy2023seathru . Neural Underwater Scene Representation~ tang2024nusr further models unstable in-scattering and moving objects. WaterSplatting~ li2024watersplatting and SeaSplat~ yang2025seasplat integrate medium modeling with Gaussian representations for efficient rendering, while RestorGS~ qiao2025restorgs uses appearance decoupling and depth-guided degradation modeling for restoration. UDF~ liu2026udf extends reconstruction to dynamic scenes with time-varying geometry, medium effects, and uncertainty-aware optimization. Sparse-View 3D Reconstruction Sparse-view reconstruction mitigates ambiguity from limited observations through learned priors and per-scene regularization. pixelNeRF~ yu2021pixelnerf learns image-conditioned radiance fields across scenes, while RegNeRF~ niemeyer2022regnerf regularizes geometry and appearance at unobserved views. FreeNeRF~ yang2023freenerf controls input frequencies and penalizes near-camera density. For Gaussian representations, FSGS~ zhu2024fsgs combines proximity-guided Gaussian unpooling with geometric regularization, whereas DNGaussian~ li2024dngaussian uses monocular depth supervision and global--local depth normalization. Our underwater setting additionally couples incomplete geometry with medium-dependent appearance. We constrain diffusion repair using reference depth and camera poses, then distill repaired views into the underwater Gaussian scene, complementing direct geometric regularization. 3D Reconstruction with Diffusion Priors Diffusion priors aid reconstruction through regularization, view generation, and rendering repair. DiffusioNeRF~ wynn2023diffusionerf learns an RGB--depth prior, while ReconFusion~ wu2024reconfusion and CAT3D~ gao2024cat3d generate novel-view supervision. GaussianObject~ yang2024gaussianobject and Difix3D+~ wu2025difix refine 3D representations using repaired renderings. RI3D~ paliwal2025ri3d and GSFix3D~ wei2025gsfix3d address both artifacts and missing regions, while GSFixer~ yin2025gsfixer uses reference-guided video diffusion for consistent repair. Ocean4D~ huang2026ocean4d combines geometric conditioning with medium-aware video diffusion for underwater generation. OceanFix adapts repair-and-distill to sparse-view underwater reconstruction through separate appearance and geometry training, and weights repaired-view supervision by geometric repair demand and channel-specific optical observability. For a target camera , the renderer produces . The fixer uses this rendering, a reference observation , reference auxiliary maps, and both cameras to predict a repaired underwater image , preserving the underwater appearance. The reference auxiliary maps comprise axial depth , accumulated object opacity , medium contribution , and medium fraction , all rendered from the initial reconstruction. Here, measures the medium's share of the total RGB signal. Target RGB ground truth and target depth are not required at inference. The fixer is trained in two stages: underwater appearance adaptation followed by geometry-adapter training. At inference, it repairs each view in a single pass and remains frozen throughout the iterative rendering--repair--distillation process used to refine the scene. title: AnyCam4D: Ray-Based 4D Gaussian Rendering for Arbitrary Camera Models
summary: Real cameras are not pinholes, yet most dynamic Gaussian splatting assumes they are. Footage is therefore undistorted first, losing field of view or detail, especially with wide-angle and fisheye cameras. Static Gaussian splatting has largely solved this with ray-based rendering, which suits any camera. Native 4D Gaussians, which model motion in space-time, cannot use it directly: each Gaussian's orientation and size cannot be recovered reliably from its covariance. We present AnyCam4D, which trains native 4D Gaussians on original footage by ray-based rasterization, preserving field of view and resolution at about the per-step cost of standard projection. Our key contribution is a numerically stable way to obtain orientation and size: we condition a square root of the 4D covariance. Trained models render through other cameras, with rolling shutter, depth of field or chromatic aberration. With a synthetic 170-degree fisheye camera, training on original images improves peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) by 3.0-8.1 dB. On real footage, AnyCam4D has lower perceptual error than the standard projection adapted to each camera, at comparable PSNR and without camera-specific derivations. With the synthetic camera rotated 60-80 degrees away from the capture rig's view, it leads by 6.2 dB against ground truth.

Introduction sec:intro Dynamic Gaussian splatting~ 4dgs_yang,4dgs_wu,stg,freetimegs reconstructs moving scenes from multi-camera video and renders new views photorealistically in real time, but usually assumes pinhole cameras. Its projection, EWA splatting~ ewa , linearizes the camera at each Gaussian's mean and orders Gaussians by depth along the optical axis, which is accurate only near the axis of an undistorted camera. Real lenses distort, from the mild radial distortion of standard lenses to fisheye lenses that see and more, and rigs, for example in robotics, often combine several. Footage is therefore undistorted first, at the cost of field or resolution. At equal resolution a pinhole image either crops the field of a wide lens or samples its center more coarsely: undistorting a fisheye to keep across the image samples its center 3.4 times more coarsely per axis, keeping the center's resolution leaves , and beyond no pinhole image exists. For static scenes, ray-based renderers~ 3dgrt,3dgut,3dgeer have removed this limitation: they evaluate each Gaussian along the ray of a pixel, so the camera only has to provide rays, and 3DGUT~ 3dgut keeps rasterization speed by selecting tiles with an unscented transform (UT). Dynamic scenes cannot simply swap in such a renderer: the 3D Gaussian that a native 4D Gaussian~ 4dgs_yang draws at time comes from conditioning, which yields a covariance but not the rotation and scale that the UT and the ray evaluation are built from. Recovering them is unreliable: an eigendecomposition has no usable gradient at the usual isotropic initialization, at any precision, and in the single precision (fp32) of GPU rasterizers the conditioned covariance loses the thin axis of fast, thin Gaussians. We present , which trains and renders native 4D Gaussians through any camera model. Conditioning the square root of the 4D covariance, rather than the covariance itself, keeps the thin axis and yields a triangular factor that replaces rotation and scale throughout. Since a camera only has to provide a projection and a ray per pixel, one model also renders through other cameras, with rolling shutter, depth of field or chromatic aberration. On a synthetic fisheye, training on footage as recorded gains 3.0--8.1\,dB in peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), depending on the field the undistortion keeps. Against EWA given the native lens's Jacobian, has comparable PSNR and lower perceptual error (LPIPS) on real footage, at about the same cost per training step; on the synthetic fisheye, with a held-out camera rotated by -- , it leads by 6.2\,dB. In summary, our contributions are: , a ray-based rasterizer that trains native 4D Gaussians through any camera model at about EWA's cost per step and memory per Gaussian, and renders them through other cameras. Factored conditioning: conditioning the square root of the 4D covariance gives an exact triangular factor that, with a ray-restricted, closest-point evaluation, keeps ray evaluation and its gradients accurate in fp32. A controlled evaluation that separates native training from projection, with a native-lens EWA baseline, a rotation probe and path-traced ground truth on a synthetic scene. Related Work sec:related Camera-general Gaussian splatting has so far addressed static scenes, and dynamic methods render through pinholes, at most warped into the distorted image afterwards; combines both. Camera Models in Gaussian Splatting 3D Gaussian splatting~ 3dgs reached real-time rendering by projecting each Gaussian with EWA splatting~ ewa , a local affine approximation of the camera, and sorting along the optical axis. Both steps assume a pinhole, so each further lens needs its own Jacobian. Fisheye-GS~ fisheye_gs derives it for the equidistant model, DirectFisheye-GS~ directfisheye_gs trains on raw fisheye images and a self-calibrating approach~ selfcal_gs learns the lens. Ray-based renderers drop the projection Jacobian altogether: 3DGRT~ 3dgrt traces rays through a bounding-volume hierarchy, 3DGUT~ 3dgut rasterizes with tiles selected by a UT, and 3DGEER~ 3dgeer integrates each Gaussian exactly along the ray. Gunes ~ fisheye_fov_eval compare Fisheye-GS and 3DGUT on real fisheye captures up to . Dynamic Gaussian Scenes Dynamic Gaussian methods, which succeed radiance fields with deformation fields~ dnerf or space-time planes~ hexplane,kplanes , fall into two families. Deformation methods warp a canonical set of 3D Gaussians per frame, with an MLP~ deformable_3dgs , a HexPlane~ 4dgs_wu , or sparse control points~ scgs . Native methods put time into the primitive: 4DGS~ 4dgs_yang,4dgs_native and 4D-Rotor~ 4d_rotor carry a full 4D covariance and condition it on the query time, while Spacetime Gaussians (STGS)~ stg , FreeTimeGS~ freetimegs , Ex4DGS~ ex4dgs and RetimeGS~ retimegs attach temporal opacity and motion to each Gaussian, and SaRO-GS~ saro_gs adds a residual field. The native 4D Gaussian remains a common base, for long sequences~ longvolcap , faster rendering~ 4dgs_1k and faster training~ instant4d . These methods keep the EWA projection onto a pinhole image; STGS trains on distorted fisheye footage by warping its pinhole render into the fisheye image~ stg . The camera-general renderers above have not been carried over to them, and the efficiency and densification advances of static splatting~ taming3dgs,absgs,revising_densification,pixelgs,mcmc only in part. Ray-Based Dynamic Rendering 4D-GRT~ 4dgrt is closest to our work: it combines the deformation field of 4DGaussians~ 4dgs_wu with the ray tracer of 3DGRT and renders fisheye distortion, depth of field and rolling shutter from the trained model.
