title: One Patch, Many Policies: Object-Associated Physical Patch Attacks on Robotic Manipulation
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) and World Action Models (WAMs) are vulnerable to adversarial visual interference, motivating the study of universal and transferable physical patch attacks. We propose Object-Associated Patch Attack (OAPA), a universal and transferable physical patch framework that enables an attacker to select which task object's manipulation to disrupt through patch placement, without re-optimizing the patch. Our framework combines object-associated placement, differentiable physical compositing, and final action-expert representation divergence. Physical compositing accounts for perspective and occlusion across camera views, while representation divergence guides patch optimization using either relative RMS or cosine distance. Experimental results demonstrate strong attack transferability across task suites and policies, together with the ability to selectively disrupt manipulation of an attacker-chosen task object through patch placement.
full_text: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) and World Action Models (WAMs) are vulnerable to adversarial visual interference, motivating the study of universal and transferable physical patch attacks. We propose Object-Associated Patch Attack (OAPA), a universal and transferable physical patch framework that enables an attacker to select which task object’s manipulation to disrupt through patch placement, without re-optimizing the patch. Our framework combines object-associated placement, differentiable physical compositing, and final action-expert representation divergence. Physical compositing accounts for perspective and occlusion across camera views, while representation divergence guides patch optimization using either relative RMS or cosine distance. Experimental results demonstrate strong attack transferability across task suites and policies, together with the ability to selectively disrupt manipulation of an attacker-chosen task object through patch placement. Introduction sec:introduction Vision-Language-Action (VLA) and World Action Models (WAMs) enable robots to interpret visual observations and language instructions, generate actions, and perform diverse manipulation tasks~ lit_2406_09246,black2024pi0,lit_2307_15818,yuan2026fastwam,chen2026lawam,kim2026cosmos . Their growing capabilities support generalization across tasks and environments, while their reliance on visual inputs exposes a practical attack surface: adversarial changes to scene appearance can corrupt the representations used for action generation and disrupt closed-loop execution~ lu2026patch,lit_2610_06814,lit_2411_13587 . These disturbances can propagate into physical actions, potentially causing failed manipulation, unintended motion, or unsafe interactions. Motivated by these risks, we conduct a systematic study of universal and transferable physical adversarial patches for VLA- and WAM-driven robots, with the objective of disrupting the manipulation of attacker-selected task objects. Despite recent progress, achieving effective and controllable attacks under practical physical constraints remains challenging. Patches optimized against a particular policy or task distribution may exploit source-specific sensitivities, limiting their effectiveness on unseen policies and tasks~ lu2026patch,lit_2610_06814,lit_2610_39816,lit_2510_13237 . Image-space patch formulations provide flexible visual perturbations, but their deployment assumptions do not necessarily preserve perspective and visibility consistency across camera views. Geometry-aware texture attacks improve physical consistency by attaching adversarial appearance to object surfaces, yet this also couples deployment to the selected carrier geometry and surface parameterization~ lit_2608_13453,lit_2604_01618 . Moreover, strong task-level disruption does not by itself establish control over which task object's manipulation is disrupted. Specifying an erroneous action direction or sequence also differs from selecting an object-level failure outcome. The challenge is therefore to construct a reusable physical patch that combines strong attack effectiveness and black-box transfer with the ability to designate a task object whose manipulation is disrupted, without requiring a surface texture tailored to that object. To address these challenges, we associate patch placement with task objects and optimize a shared patch through action-expert representations. Our placement analysis shows that object-associated locations yield stronger disruption than object-independent tabletop locations. The attacker can select another target by relocating the same patch without re-optimization. To connect optimization to action generation without prescribing task-specific erroneous actions, we target the final action-expert representations before action readout in a frozen surrogate policy. This allows joint patch optimization across tasks requiring different manipulation actions, promoting attack generalization. Differentiable physical compositing models perspective projection and depth-aware occlusion to maintain consistency across camera views. Together, these components form Object-Associated Patch Attack (OAPA), a universal and transferable physical patch framework integrating spatial target selection, action-expert representation divergence, and physically consistent compositing. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce an object-targeted attack that uses patch placement to designate the task object whose manipulation is disrupted. The same universal patch can switch attack targets by being placed beneath different task objects, without changing its content or requiring further optimization. We propose OAPA, a physical patch attack framework that integrates spatial target selection, physically consistent dual-view compositing, and cross-task patch optimization. By modeling perspective projection and depth-aware occlusion, the framework preserves the patch's spatial and visibility consistency across both camera views. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to optimize universal adversarial patches against the final hidden tokens of a frozen source policy's action expert, immediately before action readout. We instantiate representation divergence using relative RMS or cosine distance, enabling joint optimization across tasks requiring different manipulation actions without prescribing erroneous action sequences. We conduct extensive closed-loop evaluations across four task suites and five robot policies, demonstrating strong attack effectiveness and black-box transferability. Target-object switching and placement ablations further establish the role of object association and show that the disrupted object can be selected through patch placement. Related Work sec:related_work -Language-Action and World Action Models. Vision--language representation learning provides a foundation for connecting visual perception and language understanding with robotic control~ lit_2303_03378,lit_2103_00020,lit_2303_15343,lit_2402_07865 . Existing VLA policies generate actions through autoregressive prediction of discrete tokens or continuous sequence generation based on diffusion and flow matching~ lit_2406_09246,black2024pi0,lit_2307_15818,lit_2504_16054,lit_2303_04137,lit_2410_07864 . Large-scale robot demonstrations and generalist policy learning further support generalization across tasks and embodiments~ lit_2212_06817,lit_2405_12213,lit_2310_08864,lit_2403_12945,lit_2308_12952 . Beyond directly mapping observations to actions, predictive world modeling has also been incorporated into robot policy learning. World action models exploit visual or latent predictions of scene evolution through different forms of coupling between world modeling and action generation~ yuan2026fastwam,chen2026lawam,kim2026cosmos,lit_2608_04996,lit_2512_13030,lit_2602_15922,lit_2608_05903 . These complementary developments motivate examining whether adversarial vulnerabilities transfer across policies with different representations and action-generation mechanisms. Attacks on Robot Policies. Adversarial research considers both white-box access and black-box settings, with cross-model transfer enabling attacks without victim-model gradients~ lit_1312_6199,lit_1412_6572,lit_1706_06083,lit_1608_04644,lit_1511_04599,lit_1610_08401,lit_1611_02770,wang2025breaking . Transfer-oriented approaches improve generalization through gradient optimization, input transformations, and intermediate-representation objectives~ lit_1710_06081,lit_1803_06978,lit_1904_02884,lit_1908_06281,lit_2103_15571,lit_2102_00436,lit_1907_10823,lit_2204_00008,lit_2002_05990,zhou2023advclip,zhou2023downstream , while universal perturbations and physical patches extend attacks across inputs and viewing conditions~ lit_1712_09665,lit_1707_07397,lit_1707_08945,lit_1904_08653,lit_1804_05810,lit_1610_08401 . In robotics, language manipulation, visual perturbations, and model backdoors expose different vulnerabilities in instruction-conditioned control~ lit_2411_13587,lit_2511_16203,lit_2410_13691,lit_2407_20242,lit_2506_03350,lit_2505_16640,wang2025advedm . Within visual attacks, existing approaches exploit action-space objectives, representation discrepancies, and attention-related signals to disrupt execution and promote transfer~ lu2026patch,lit_2610_06814,lit_2608_03207,lit_2610_39816,lit_2411_13587,lit_2606_03556,lit_2610_09708,lit_2605_28083,lit_2510_13237 . Geometry-aware appearance attacks further account for object surfaces and rendering during adversarial optimization~ lit_2608_13453,lit_2604_01618,yan2026vfacamou . Existing targeted attacks can steer policy outputs toward attacker-specified actions~ lit_2608_13453 . Such action-level targeting differs from selecting the task object whose manipulation is disrupted: one specifies how the policy should deviate, while the other specifies which object should be affected. Overall task failure alone does not establish object-level selectivity. Accordingly, our work investigates object-level targeted attacks on VLA- and WAM-driven robots, where the same universal, transferable physical patch selects the task object to disrupt through its placement. title: Feed-Forward Adaptive Gaussian Splatting for Interactive Medical Volume Rendering
summary: Path-traced rendering shows CT and MR volumes with realistic lighting, but it restarts after every change of view, clipping plane or transfer function (TF), the map from voxel intensity to colour and opacity, which limits the frame rate. Feed-forward Gaussian splatting models such as RenderFM predict the Gaussians directly from the volume instead of fitting them to each scan, and are fast. RenderFM, however, handles only CT, runs its network again after every TF edit, has no clipping operator, and places its Gaussians on a uniform 3-mm grid that blurs organ boundaries and cut faces. We present RenderFM-Next, a feed-forward model that addresses these limits. One network handles both CT and MR. Its Gaussians are predicted once per volume: a new TF needs no pass of this network, and a clipping plane cuts them exactly, using operators from prior work. The model predicts coarse 3-mm Gaussians for the whole volume and refines them to 1.5 mm only where refinement improves the image. A small score head ranks the coarse Gaussians by how much refining them would reduce the rendering error; at render time the user chooses how many are refined, and those next to a clipping plane are always refined, which sharpens cut faces. We build a benchmark of about 2,000 CT and MR scans with path-traced references under clinical presets, TF edits and clipping. Our RenderFM-Next improves over RenderFM retrained on this benchmark by 2.8 dB on CT and 2.4 dB on MR and renders a 1600x1600 view in 4-6 ms. Refinement adds 0.30 / 0.69 dB over the same model trained without it (0.51 / 1.17 dB on cut faces), and refining a learned 10% of the coarse Gaussians matches a random 50% with 2.4x fewer Gaussians. Project page: https://gaozhongpai.github.io/renderfmnext/

Introduction sec:intro Path-traced (``cinematic'') rendering of CT and MR volumes conveys depth, occlusion and tissue appearance through global illumination~ comaniciu2016shaping,dappa2016cinematic,eid2017cinematic . Its image is a Monte Carlo estimate that restarts whenever the viewpoint, a clipping plane or the transfer function (TF), which maps voxel intensities to colour and opacity, changes~ kroes2012exposure,novak2018monte ; even a single denoised pass takes tens of milliseconds, which limits the frame rate for high-refresh and stereo displays. These changes are frequent in practice: a reader switches between TFs that show bone, vessels or soft tissue, and moves a clipping plane to look inside the body. Gaussian splatting~ kerbl3dgs can stand in for the path tracer during interaction. The Gaussians can be fitted to each scan, which takes minutes~ niedermayr2024application,dyken2026veg,tang2025ivrgs , or predicted from the volume by a network in a single pass~ renderfm , within seconds for a new patient. RenderFM~ renderfm takes the second route: a 3D U-Net maps a CT volume to one Gaussian per cell of a 3-mm grid. This design has four limits ( ). The model is trained for CT only. The TF is a network input, so the network runs again after every TF edit. There is no clipping operator, so a clipping plane can only keep or remove whole Gaussians. And a uniform grid spends the same number of Gaussians on smooth tissue as on thin structures: at 3\,mm, organ boundaries and the cut faces exposed by a clipping plane look blurred ( ), while a 1.5-mm grid would need eight times as many Gaussians. We present , which addresses these limits. One network takes CT or MR as input and is told which one through a learned modality embedding. Its Gaussians depend on neither the TF nor the clipping plane: a new TF needs no pass of this network, and a clipping plane cuts the Gaussians exactly. To sharpen the image without a fine grid everywhere, the network predicts Gaussians at two resolutions: a coarse Gaussian, the parent, for every 3-mm cell, and up to eight 1.5-mm children that can replace it. At render time, a budget sets the fraction of parents that are replaced by their children, so the same model can trade quality against speed without retraining. Parents next to a clipping plane are always refined, which sharpens cut faces. The key question is where to refine. Learning this decision together with the renderer lowered image quality in our experiments ( ), so we separate the two. We first train the renderer with random subsets of parents refined, so that it works at any budget. We then freeze it, estimate for each parent how much the training loss would drop if it were refined, and train a small score head to predict this benefit from the network's features. At render time, the parents with the highest scores are refined. For TF-editable appearance and for clipping we reuse two existing components, FactorSplat~ factorsplat and XClipGS~ xclipgs . We evaluate on a new benchmark of CT and MR scans with path-traced references. improves over a retrained RenderFM by 2.8\,dB on CT and 2.4\,dB on MR and renders a view in 4--6\,ms. Most of this gain is already reached with parents only; refinement adds 0.30 / 0.69\,dB on CT / MR, and up to 1.17\,dB on cut faces. With as many Gaussians as RenderFM, it is already better by 2.5\,dB on CT and by 1.7\,dB on MR ( ). Refinement with a render-time budget. The network also predicts 1.5-mm children and is trained so that any fraction of the parents can be refined. A score head trained on the frozen renderer predicts which parents benefit most ( ): refining a learned 10 matches refining a random 50 with 2.4 fewer Gaussians ( ). A CT+MR rendering benchmark. 1,008 CT and 958 MR scans from public sources with path-traced references under clinical presets, TF edits and clipping, evaluated per patient with confidence intervals ( ). title: Commit2Drive: Perception-Grounded Language Decisions as Commitments for Trajectory Planning in Vision-Language-Action Driving Models
comment: 28 pages, 9 figures, 19 tables. Includes supplementary material. Code will be released soon
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models introduce language reasoning into end-to-end autonomous driving. They output a language decision together with a trajectory, which makes the planner more interpretable. However, in existing methods the language decision is either an independent output or an index that selects among similar candidate trajectories, and its annotations are not verified against the trajectory. As a result, the language decision and the trajectory are often inconsistent in closed-loop driving. To address this, we propose Commit2Drive, a framework that imposes the language decision as a consistency constraint on trajectory planning. The decision is a commitment, a maneuver class with a continuous parameter that one deterministic rule reads from any trajectory, and it is grounded in facts reported by the perception of the model itself. A Maneuver Bank maps the commitment to a code with a kinematic meaning, and consistency losses train the planner to execute every admissible decision of a scene, so that the trajectory follows the decision. An automatic data pipeline supplies the supervision. Decisions are labeled from the future motion of the expert, counterfactual executions train the decision and the trajectory together, and rule-based functions with a Vision-Language Model (VLM) generate, review and refine the language annotations. The code is a lookup that involves no hidden state of the language model, so Commit2Drive is extensible to rule-based decisions, which the same planner executes without retraining. Commit2Drive uses a 0.5B language model and runs closed-loop inference online on a single consumer graphics card. On Bench2Drive, Commit2Drive reaches a Driving Score (DS) of 78.50 and a Success Rate (SR) of 55.91% with a lightweight model, which is competitive with the state of the art, and greatly reduces the language-action inconsistency. Code will be released soon.

Their language annotations are not clearly tied to the action. A decision label often does not describe what the expert does next, and the reasoning text can contradict the scene or itself. Moreover, counterfactual data has not yet been used to train the language decision and the action together. To fill this gap, we build a counterfactual decision-action data pipeline. As shown in , rule-based functions generate the records of every frame, and a VLM reviews and refines the language annotations. The pipeline runs automatically on the raw logs of Bench2Drive~ bench2drive . Generate. With one decision and one trajectory per scene, a model can produce both from the scene alone, without the trajectory following the decision. We therefore pair every admissible decision of a scene with a trajectory, and rule-based functions write four records for every frame. (i) Decision label: the commitment is read from the next 3\,s of the expert trajectory and rendered as the decision sentence, so the label and the trajectory agree by construction. (ii) Counterfactual executions: for every other decision , the path of the expert is re-timed with a speed profile of decision , which gives a trajectory with . It is rolled out against the logged motion of the other agents on an occupancy grid~ stp3 and marked infeasible if it collides. (iv) Perception facts: the fact sentences, rendered from the logged scene by the templates that are used at inference. With these records, the admissible set tells the Decision Expert which decisions are admissible, and the counterfactual executions tell the Action Expert what each of them looks like ( ). Review and refine. A language annotation is a short chain of reasoning, and its contradictions are also learned by the model. A VLM~ qwen3vl therefore takes two roles. As a blind reviewer, it judges whether a decision sentence contradicts the scene, whether a fact sentence invents or omits an object, and whether an alternative decision is safe and legal. As an editor, it revises reasoning text that contradicts itself. Errors that originate in a rule or a template are corrected at their source, and the records are regenerated and reviewed again. Finally, human experts check a random sample of the records. The resulting dataset covers the base set of Bench2Drive ( ). Extensibility to Rule-Based Decisions sec:method:rule The mapping of connects a coarse-grained decision to a fine-grained action. The Action Expert reads the decision only through the code of , which involves no hidden state of the language model. The language decision and the action are therefore separable, and the Action Expert does not depend on the source of the decision. Mature rule-based decision modules, such as traffic-rule logic, safety rules~ rss and rule-based planners~ pdm , already decide at this granularity. Their output can be written as a commitment and executed by the same Action Expert without modification or retraining: where the first line is the action side of , which depends on the decision only through , is a rule-based function, and is the scene state that it reads from perception, such as the state of the traffic light or the time to collision. The two cases give the source of : the Decision Expert, or the rule-based function whenever it issues a decision. Rules can therefore be added or exchanged without any change to the model.

title: A Mesh for Every Moment
summary: We present MEMO (a Mesh for Every MOment), a method that reconstructs the geometry of complete dynamic scenes, captured by multiple synchronized cameras, and extracts a mesh at every frame. Existing dynamic Gaussian splatting methods either model appearance alone or target isolated objects segmented by foreground masks, and all of them recover meshes by TSDF fusion or Poisson reconstruction, whose fixed grids limit the detail they can capture. At the core of MEMO is a per-Gaussian motion model inspired by Gaussian processes, which represents each Gaussian's position and rotation over time as a combination of temporal Gaussian kernels. The model keeps every Gaussian a valid surface element throughout the sequence and carries an implicit representation of the dynamic geometry, so a mesh can be derived at any time from a field defined by the Gaussians. Although common in real captures, large and fast motion poses a challenge that dynamic Gaussian splatting methods usually overlook. To account for it, we design a track-based initialization scheme that fits each Gaussian's initial trajectory to point tracks in closed form. We evaluate MEMO on Blender-Moments, a new benchmark of nine animated scenes with ground-truth meshes at every frame, and on two real-world datasets. MEMO reconstructs the most accurate geometry among state-of-the-art methods, and remains competitive in novel-view synthesis and training time. Project page: https://memo-4d.github.io
full_text: [] #1 \\[2pt] \\[2pt] \\[2pt] reconstructs a mesh of a dynamic scene at every frame, directly from its Gaussians. Shown are three scenes over time, with the first and last frames in vertex colors and the frames between in gray. fig:teaser ] We present (a Mesh for Every MOment), a method that reconstructs the geometry of complete dynamic scenes, captured by multiple synchronized cameras, and extracts a mesh at every frame. Existing dynamic Gaussian splatting methods either model appearance alone or target isolated objects segmented by foreground masks, and all of them recover meshes by TSDF fusion or Poisson reconstruction, whose fixed grids limit the detail they can capture. To account for it, we design a track-based initialization scheme that fits each Gaussian's initial trajectory to point tracks in closed form. We evaluate on , a new benchmark of nine animated scenes with ground-truth meshes at every frame, and on two real-world datasets. reconstructs the most accurate geometry among state-of-the-art methods, and remains competitive in novel-view synthesis and training time. Introduction sec:intro Capturing a dynamic scene, a person in motion, a mechanism at work, or an animal on the move, and turning it into a digital asset is the first step toward bringing the physical world into the virtual world. It is a long-standing goal of computer vision and graphics, and recent progress in novel-view synthesis has brought it within reach. Neural radiance fields~ mildenhall2020nerf first reconstructed static scenes from photographs with striking realism, and 3D Gaussian splatting~ kerbl20233d has since made it fast enough to become the representation of choice. Dynamic variants of Gaussian splatting bring this to videos, allowing immersive rendering of the scene from novel views and camera trajectories. However, these dynamic methods optimize for appearance, and the surfaces extracted from them are often noisy and incomplete. This matters for downstream applications that need accurate per-frame geometry, like physical interaction with virtual objects, relighting, and AR/VR scene composition. Current dynamic Gaussian methods, whether built on deformation fields~ wu20244d,yang2024deformable , 4D primitives~ yang2024realtime , sparse control points~ huang2024scgs , or per-Gaussian trajectories~ luiten2024dynamic,li2024spacetime,wang2025freetimegs,tzathas2026adaptive , encode appearance and motion but do not have a representation of the surface, either implicit or explicit. To reconstruct the scene's surfaces, a volume has to be built from the trained model after the fact, by TSDF volume integration~ curless1996volumetric on depth maps rendered from many viewpoints and passed to marching cubes~ lorensen1987marching on a fixed-resolution grid. Since the optimization constrains geometry only through appearance, the models carry many floaters, which distort the input volumes of the marching cubes and lead to noisy reconstructions. For static scenes, this problem has been addressed by training Gaussians to represent geometry alongside appearance. One family of methods regularizes the Gaussians so that their rendered depth, and hence its fusion, is accurate~ huang20242d,chen2025pgsr,zhang2026radegs . A second family defines a field directly from the Gaussians and extracts its level set with marching tetrahedra~ yu2024gaussian,radl2025sof,guedon2025milo,gomez2026blobs , which removes depth fusion altogether and adapts the mesh resolution to the Gaussians. For dynamic scenes, the few methods that reconstruct surfaces~ liu2025dynamic,zhang2025dynamic,wu20264dsurf are object-centric, relying on foreground masks to isolate a single object, and remain slow to train. In this work, we aim to bring the field-based extraction of the second family to complete, unmasked dynamic scenes captured by multiple synchronized cameras, allowing the full scene geometry to be extracted at every frame. We build on three key insights. First, every Gaussian must remain a valid surface element at every frame of the sequence. Second, the model should carry an implicit representation of the scene's dynamic geometry. Third, training struggles to recover large and fast motion without a good starting point. To realize the first two insights, we propose a per-Gaussian temporal motion model that represents each Gaussian's changes in position and rotation over time as a linear combination of temporal Gaussian kernels, inspired by radial basis function (RBF) networks~ broomhead1988multivariable,moody1989fast and Gaussian processes (GPs)~ rasmussen2006gaussian . To realize the third, we introduce a track-based initialization scheme that assigns each initial Gaussian a trajectory consistent with the observed motion. Since the temporal Gaussian kernels span the whole timeline, each Gaussian can follow complex motion and remains a valid surface element throughout the sequence. It can therefore carry an implicit representation of the surface, such as oriented normals~ gomez2026blobs , along its trajectory. Polynomial trajectories~ li2024spacetime,wang2025freetimegs , in contrast, hold only within short time windows and introduce geometric noise outside them. Since each trajectory is linear in its kernel weights, our initialization scheme fits it in closed form by GP regression to point tracks spanning the whole sequence, so even large and fast motion is captured from the start. With our model, the surface is defined at any time, and a mesh follows at every frame from marching tetrahedra, with no depth rendering or fusion ( ). Evaluating dynamic geometry requires ground-truth meshes that evolve with the scene, and no public dataset pairs synchronized multi-camera captures with exact time-varying geometry. We therefore build , a benchmark of nine animated scenes, rendered from multiple synchronized cameras, whose ground-truth meshes can be extracted at any frame. We evaluate our method on this new dataset and on two existing real-world datasets, Neural 3D Video~ li2022neural and SelfCap~ xu2024representing , and compare it to state-of-the-art dynamic methods, including ones designed for surface reconstruction. reconstructs the most accurate dynamic geometry, and its novel-view synthesis rivals that of the strongest baselines. Its advantage is largest on scenes with large and fast motion. It also trains in a time comparable to the fastest dynamic splatting methods. In summary, our contributions are: A framework for joint appearance and per-frame mesh reconstruction of complete dynamic scenes, achieving state-of-the-art surface reconstruction. A novel motion model and initialization technique inspired by Gaussian processes. A multi-view benchmark for dynamic surface reconstruction, with ground-truth meshes at every frame. Related Work sec:related Static scenes. par:related_static Novel-view synthesis methods such as neural radiance fields~ mildenhall2020nerf and 3D Gaussian splatting~ kerbl20233d are optimized for appearance alone and do not model the scene's geometry. Many works have addressed this by extending these representations to recover surfaces. For radiance fields, several works~ wang2021neus,yariv2021volume,li2023neuralangelo,wang2023neus2 map an implicit surface representation to volume density, so that volume rendering recovers the surface together with appearance. For Gaussians, two classes of methods have emerged. The first regularizes the Gaussians so that their rendered depth is accurate, and extracts meshes by TSDF volume integration of that depth. 2DGS~ huang20242d pioneered this class by flattening the Gaussians into 2D surfels with well-defined normals. Later works adopt planar~ chen2025pgsr or quadratic~ zhang2025quadratic primitives, rasterize depth and normals in closed form~ zhang2026radegs , supervise normals with monocular priors~ chen2024vcrgaus , or treat Gaussians as stochastic solids~ zhang2026geometry . The second class defines a field directly from the Gaussians and extracts its level set with marching tetrahedra on a Delaunay tetrahedralization of Gaussian-derived points. GOF~ yu2024gaussian introduced this approach with an opacity field, which SOF~ radl2025sof evaluates faster by sorting the Gaussians along each ray. MILo~ guedon2025milo learns signed distances at nine pivots per Gaussian and extracts a mesh during training, whose rendered depth and normals regularize the Gaussians. Gaussian Wrapping~ gomez2026blobs treats each Gaussian as an oriented surface element whose vacancy field yields detailed meshes. Other works jointly optimize the Gaussians with a neural signed~ chen2023neusg,yu2024gsdf,lyu20243dgsr,zhang2024neural or unsigned~ li2025gaussianudf distance field, or align the Gaussians with the surface and reconstruct a mesh by Poisson reconstruction~ guedon2024sugar . All of these methods assume a static scene. Dynamic scenes. par:related_dynamic Both radiance fields and Gaussian splatting have been extended from static to dynamic scenes. For radiance fields, a common approach~ pumarola2021dnerf,park2021nerfies,tretschk2021nonrigid,park2021hypernerf is to warp rays into a canonical space with a learned deformation field. Other works condition the field on time~ lombardi2019neural,li2022neural or factorize it into space-time feature planes~ fridovichkeil2023kplanes,cao2023hexplane . For Gaussians, 4DGS~ wu20244d and Deformable-3DGS~ yang2024deformable carry over the canonical-deformation approach~ pumarola2021dnerf,park2021nerfies,tretschk2021nonrigid,park2021hypernerf , and many later methods follow it~ liang2025gaufre,bae2024pergaussian,zhu2024motiongs . Other methods drive the Gaussians by blending the rigid motions of a sparse set of control nodes~ huang2024scgs,lei2025mosca,wang2025shape . Another line of works models per-Gaussian motion explicitly. Dynamic3DGS~ luiten2024dynamic pioneered this direction, storing each Gaussian's position and rotation at every frame. Later methods make this motion more compact and expressive, either with Gaussians whose position and opacity vary over time~ yang2024realtime,li2024spacetime,duan20244drotor,xu2024representing,wang2025freetimegs , or by parameterizing each trajectory with keyframes, splines, or other temporal bases~ katsumata2024compact,lee2024fully,park2025splinegs,tzathas2026adaptive . The methods above are trained for appearance alone, with no dedicated representation of the surface. Dynamic surface reconstruction methods initially addressed this with neural implicit surfaces that deform or evolve a signed distance function over time~ cai2022neural,shao2023tensor4d,wang2023neus2,mao2024neural,ebbed2026moangelo,yao2024dynosurf . More recently, Gaussian-based dynamic surface reconstruction methods have emerged, in three forms. Hybrid NeRF--Gaussian methods~ li2025dgns,kim2026dysurface couple dynamic Gaussians with a volume-rendered signed distance function. Hybrid mesh--Gaussian methods~ ma2025mags,zheng2025gaustar,tao2026tessellation bind Gaussians to an input mesh that they deform or track over time. Lastly, Gaussian-only methods~ liu2025dynamic,cai2024dynasurfgs,zhang2025dynamic,wang2024spacetime,chen2025adaptive,wu20264dsurf represent the surface with oriented or flattened Gaussians and extract each frame's mesh by volume integration of rendered depth or by Poisson reconstruction. Across all three groups, most methods target isolated objects with foreground masks and rely on bounded volumetric grids

title: Innata-0: A Native Embodied World System with Model-Agent Co-Design
summary: The physical world is open-ended, dynamic, and partially observable. While foundation models have advanced embodied intelligence, standalone models struggle with long-horizon execution, and simply integrating models with agents may lead to inconsistencies between planning and physical control. To support reliable and adaptive behaviors in the physical world, we introduce Innata-0, a native embodied world system. Innata-0 jointly designs an embodied world-action model and an agent to combine their complementary strengths. The model, Innata-0-WAM, adopts a tri-tower Mixture-of-Transformers architecture that integrates understanding, prediction, and action generation. The agent, Innata-0-Agent, coordinates long-horizon execution through memory, verification, and recovery. A co-design protocol is further proposed to align model training with agent execution and leverage validated experiences to support subsequent adaptation and model improvement. Extensive evaluations demonstrate strong embodied capabilities across understanding, world prediction, and robotic manipulation. Innata-0 represents our first step toward physical intelligence, and we see it as the beginning of a much longer journey.
full_text: Native Model-Agent Co-Design sec:introduction The physical world is open-ended, partially observable, and dynamically evolving, where actions have uncertain consequences and failures may incur irreversible costs. While foundation models have substantially advanced embodied intelligence, standalone foundation models still struggle to sustain reliable behavior over long horizons, particularly when execution requires self-correction and adaptation. Extending their capability boundaries therefore requires coupling native model capabilities with persistent agentic reasoning~ yao2023react,schick2023toolformer , memory~ nvidia2026gr00t2,lu2026aspire , and interaction~ zitkovich2023rt2,kim2024openvla,gemini2025robotics . However, simply integrating models and agents may not fully realize their combined potential. Inconsistencies between planning and control may lead to unreliable physical execution and limited adaptation from accumulated experience. This motivates a shift from a standalone embodied model toward a native embodied world system. To this end, we characterize native through three core capabilities: Plan lays the foundation for the system to accomplish long-horizon tasks by coordinating model execution across subtasks; Recover further bolsters the system, enabling it to handle uncertainties and recover from unexpected failures during real-world execution; and Evolve extends the system to continuously adapt to new environments and scenarios through accumulated experience. To jointly realize these capabilities, we introduce Innata-0, a model-agent co-designed system that advances native embodied intelligence. As illustrated in , our co-design establishes complementary roles for the embodied model and agent, allowing the model to fully leverage its native capabilities while the agent extends its effective operating scope. On the model side, Innata-0-WAM serves as the physical execution foundation of the system. We adopt a tri-tower Mixture-of-Transformers architecture~ liang2024mixture0of0transformers0 , which provides understanding, prediction, and action generation capabilities. The model is conditioned on the complete instruction, active subtask, and verified task history. By incorporating current- and history-plan annotations during training, Innata-0-WAM aligns its learned conditioning interface with the agent's evolving representation of task progress. On the agent side, Innata-0-Agent serves as the system coordinator, supporting long-horizon planning, failure recovery, and continual evolution. It orchestrates model execution across subtasks while maintaining hierarchical memory. Grounded in observations and execution feedback, the agent verifies against intended physical outcomes and invokes tool-based recovery upon deviations. Verified interactions and experiences are consolidated into reusable skills that refine subsequent decisions and recovery strategies. Innata-0-Agent aligns its execution logic with the model's capabilities, enabling coordinated execution, outcome verification, and experience-driven adaptation. Realizing Plan, Recover, and Evolve requires the model and agent to work together and play complementary roles. We therefore establish a co-design protocol that enables them to operate in concert, leveraging their respective strengths while guiding their subsequent design. Crucially, this protocol operates in both directions: the model's execution capabilities shape how the agent organizes and delegates tasks, while the agent's requirements for planning, recovery, and adaptation guide model design and training. Our protocol aligns the model's training data with the agent's task instructions, subtask plans, and recovery commands, allowing complex tasks to be carried out through coordinated execution. The agent, in turn, validates execution outcomes and consolidates experiences to refine its task commands and reusable recovery strategies. It also feeds successful rollout segments, including corrective actions and post-recovery continuations, into the shared data pipeline for subsequent policy training. These principles guide our data construction, model training, and agent design, laying the foundation of native embodied intelligence. We evaluate the physical capabilities underlying Innata-0 and their use in closed-loop task execution. Among the compared models, the understanding tower ranks first on nine benchmarks and within the top two on fourteen. On WorldArena~2.0 Track~1~ li2026worldarena2 , Innata-0 achieves an EWM score of 67.63, the highest among the open-source models. Policy evaluations on RoboCasa365~ robocasa365 and RoboDojo-Sim~ chen2026robodojo examine manipulation and task completion. On RoboCasa365, Innata-0 achieves 60.2 overall success and ranks first on Atomic-Seen tasks with an 88.4 success rate. These evaluations characterize the model's grounding, prediction, and control capabilities, as well as its use within an agent-guided execution loop. To conclude, we propose Innata-0, a native embodied world system that extends physical intelligence beyond individual task execution. Our approach jointly designs the embodied model and agent to leverage their complementary strengths. A shared interaction protocol aligns model capabilities with agent requirements and guides data construction, model training, and agent design. Together, these designs enable long-horizon planning, failure recovery, and continual evolution. Our system co-design establishes a basis for studying how aligned task context, physical-outcome verification, and validated experience contribute to reliable open-world interaction. Embodied Data Construction Overview Raw visual, linguistic, action, and tactile data contain rich knowledge about objects, interactions, and physical processes, yet their existing annotations make only part of this knowledge explicit. Following the co-design protocol, we make task goals, subtask relationships, and completion evidence explicit, while preserving the links between corrective behavior and subsequent task execution. We therefore develop Task-Oriented Knowledge Refinement, a unified data construction pipeline that extracts shared annotations from heterogeneous sources and prepares supervision tailored to each learning objective and training stage. Each source can support multiple training tasks wherever the necessary observations and annotations are available. The resulting task annotations align the model's training context with the agent's subtask objectives for Plan. Corrective trajectories and task continuations provide supervision for Recover, while validated rollout segments enter the same pipeline for subsequent policy training, supporting Evolve through experience reuse. We assemble our initial source pool mainly from open-source datasets and web-accessible corpora, including image--text pairs and other vision--language corpora, general videos, egocentric human videos, real-robot recordings, and robot simulation data. Video provides the main source of physical experience, complemented by image--text supervision, native state and action channels, and tactile observations. Together, these sources cover diverse scenes, objects, embodiments, and manipulation tasks. The knowledge available in a source can exceed the supervision made explicit by its original annotations. A video may record objects, spatial relationships, intermediate goals, and state changes while its caption names only the overall activity. Relevant evidence may also occupy only a brief interval within a longer recording. Each learning objective requires a different view of this information. For example, the same video of putting a cup into a cabinet can support a grounding question about the cup, an instruction-conditioned prediction of its placement, and an action-learning example when corresponding recorded or reconstructed trajectories are available. When synchronized tactile observations are available, the same interaction can also support prediction of contact and loading during grasping or placement. Constructing these views requires us to locate the event, identify its participants and task structure, and align the context and target at the appropriate granularity. A frame may suffice for a spatial question, whereas visual prediction requires a coherent transition and action prediction additionally requires aligned motion supervision. We therefore make the relevant knowledge explicit in the form each objective needs, while retaining the context needed to interpret it. This lets one experience contribute to several learning tasks, with each example focusing on a specific capability. Figure~ fig:embodied_data_pipeline summarizes Task-Oriented Knowledge Refinement in three stages: source acquisition, unified annotation, and task-specific data preparation. The unified annotation stage performs semantic interpretation once per sample to create a shared record of hierarchical task labels, event boundaries, and scene and action descriptions. It preserves the original observations and available state, action, and tactile streams, together with spatial, contact, and quality information, without filtering samples. The vision--language pipeline uses shared spatial and task annotations to select observations and construct instruction--target pairs through task-specific rewriting, followed by validation and distribution balancing. Existing public QA is validated and reformatted without regeneration. The video-generation pipeline uses shared temporal annotations for clip construction, applies frame- and clip-level quality criteria for each training stage, and assembles descriptive or instructional prompts from shared scene and action descriptions. The policy pipeline pairs native or reconstructed motion with shared instructions and task intervals, unifies action semantics, and uses task, outcome, and quality annotations for trajectory filtering and multi-view assembly. For eligible human videos, this includes hand reconstruction and camera-aware motion alignment. The tactile pipeline combines sensor observations with shared contact, coverage, and validity records, followed by sensor-to-MANO alignment, regional proxy construction, and temporal alignment with visual and motion streams. One source can thus yield multiple training forms, depending on its available observations and supervision. Unified Information Extraction and Annotation We attach a shared annotation record to each source, preserving its original timestamps, camera views, source metadata, native state and action channels, and tactile observations where available. The record combines source-level context with frame-level and interval-level annotations. We prompt Qwen3.8-Flash-Next~ qwen3.8flashnext once per sample to produce the applicable semantic, relational, temporal, and perceptual-quality fields in a single structured response. Specialized perception models add dense masks to this record, alongside source-provided depth and camera calibration. Thus, one VLM pass supplies a broad description of the experience, while dedicated visual modules recover spatial measurements and available tactile observations provide contact evidence for downstream tasks. and Geometric Annotation. We combine specialized perception models with source-provided depth and camera calibration to obtain object localization and spatial information. Detection, segmentation, and tracking. We use Grounding DINO~ liu2024groundingdino for object detection and SAM~3.1~ carion2025sam3,meta2026sam31 for instance segmentation and video tracking. VLMs provide additional object detection and localization for data requiring further annotation. We retain boxes, masks, prediction scores where available, and cross-frame object identities linked to the shared entity record. Depth and 3D structure. We use source-provided depth-camera measurements, together with available camera intrinsics and extrinsics, to obtain spatial inputs and supervision signals
